News.title: Labour Brexit civil war deepens as Cabinet ministers refuse to back Burnham’s dream of rejoining EU
News.content:
Next

LABOUR’S Brexit row deepened tonight as two Cabinet ministers distanced themselves from Andy Burnham’s aim to rejoin the EU.

Chancellor John Healey and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds both failed to back the PM’s wish to return to Brussels within his lifetime.



Mr Reynolds suggested he would be uncomfortable returning to a Europe swept by right-wing populism.

Asked if he shared the PM’s dream, he told The Sun: “I genuinely can’t answer that, because I don’t know what the future of the EU is — because some of the very strong political currents in member states.



“For me, it’s an approach to issues. What is their approach to how they regulate technology, AI? How dynamic will the economy be?”

Many European countries are odds-on to be governed by parties well to the right including the AfD in Germany, Vox in Spain, and the National Rally in France.



Mr Reynolds also swerved questions about free movement of people, which would give 450million EU nationals the right to live and work here.

Mr Burnham hinted it could be brought back in a new relationship with Brussels.

But Mr Reynolds said: “No decisions have been made. The British public will decide.”

Meanwhile, the Chancellor seemed just as reluctant. On the UK joining the EU in his lifetime, he told Channel 4: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.”



He also appeared to disagree with the PM on Brexit “weakening” the UK economy.

Mr Burnham has told ministers to avoid publicly backing specific options for the future UK-EU relationship following confusion — although he has denied silencing his Cabinet.

The PM is hoping for EU deals on food and drink, plus youth mobility, but says there will be no “fundamental change” to the relationship with Europe this Parliament.

News.title: Chancellor now admits he WON’T slash spiralling £400bn welfare bill before next election after 24 hours of Budget chaos
News.content:
Next

AFTER a day of Budget chaos, back-tracking John ­Healey tonight admitted he would not cut welfare before the next election.

The Chancellor started the day by insisting handouts would be whittled down this parliamentary term — and ended it by conceding this was not possible.



In between, his initial pledge was rubbished by his own aides and even disowned by Downing Street.

The fallout to Mr Healey’s first Budget came as economists said he was staring at a £28billion funding gap between hitting defence spending targets and avoiding having to make cuts to Whitehall departments.



Britain’s annual welfare bill is on course to hit £431billion by 2031 — but on Wednesday Mr Healey just told voters to wait for a system overhaul at a later date.

In a breakfast interview with the BBC yesterday he was asked if he would ensure total welfare spending was falling before the election, due in 2029.

He responded: “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill. We’ll do that in a Labour way”.

But following his appearance, Treasury sources soon sought to downplay his commitment and suggested he had not made a firm pledge.

And at lunchtime No10 said the Government will not be setting an “arbitrary target or timetable” on reducing the welfare bill.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham then said he wanted to make welfare cuts “as soon as possible” — but refused to put a date on the promise.



Last night Mr Healey completed the U-turn by telling Channel 4: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this Parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.”

Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick told The Sun: “Benefits Burnham can’t say when he’ll make savings to the spiralling bill, so taxes will have to go up to pay for his cowardice.

“The Chancellor has been utterly humiliated by his handlers in the Labour Party.



“You can change the Chancellor but you will never change the Labour Party’s addiction to ­benefits spending.”

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said the climbdown was “unbelievable”. He added: “This morning, the Chancellor said the welfare bill would be cut before an election. Now he’s being slapped down by Number 10.”

But an ally of the Chancellor — who yesterday joined the PM on a visit to the Rolls-Royce factory in Derby — told The Sun: “Healey has kept both the markets and the Labour Party on side. If that’s not a Labour budget to be proud of, then I don’t know what is.”

According to polling for More in Common, voters on all sides believe current welfare spending is unsustainable — even including 51 per cent of Labour supporters.

Meanwhile, the Institute for Fiscal Studies warned that hits to public finances could add ­£17billion to the £11billion already needed for existing defence plans.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

IFS boss Helen Miller, said: “We should all hope John Healey has more than hope up his sleeve when the time comes to settle the next spending review.”

After delivering his Budget, Mr Healey went for a traditional pint with Treasury staff at a Westminster pub — downing in one a beer named Chancellor’s Choice.

News.title: Caribbean leaders are playing ‘white guilt’ card to try and grab British cash — it’s time we called out this racket
News.content:
Next

WHAT have the British ever done for us?

That’s the question that many in the Caribbean are asking as King Charles continues his tour of the Bahamas and Guyana before ending in Antigua and Barbuda for next week’s Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.



One thing’s for certain, the answer to that question from Caribbean slavery reparation campaigners is very clear: Britain has done NOTHING for the people of those islands other than enslave their ancestors to enrich ourselves — and for that we must pay.

Which is why those campaigners are demanding that Britain pays compensation to the descendants of slavery, in what they call an act of “restorative justice”.



While the Atlantic slave trade was undoubtedly a moral abomination that should make anyone weep, these demands for reparations are nothing short of laughable.

They are not asking for millions or even billions in blood money but £18TRILLION — that’s six times larger than Britain’s entire annual economy.

The Bahamas National Reparations Committee warned the King in advance of this trip to not “come empty-handed”, while the Guyanese president insisted his people want both “reparative justice” and a “full and unconditional apology”.

The King has this week spoken of the “great suffering” caused by slavery but, in line with official British government policy, he will neither apologise for slavery nor offer any reparations.

Walking that diplomatic tightrope is not an enviable task for anyone, but it is high time Britain stopped trying to be diplomatic about the slavery reparations demands and call them out for what they really are — a GRIFT.

This racket has nothing to do with righting the wrongs of the past and everything to do with incompetent and often corrupt Caribbean governments hoping to grab some cash from Britain as they seek to blame ALL of their islands’ current problems on a slave trade abolished centuries ago.



The official British position is to refuse all demands for reparations — as there is no duty to pay compensation for slavery because it was not illegal at the time — while also pointing out that every empire in history has used slaves.

Britain was the first country to abolish slavery, at great financial cost.

Yet despite every refusal by us to cough up the cash, the calls for reparations grow louder by the day.

The Secretary-General of the Commonwealth has chimed in, and so has the African Union.



Meanwhile, both the Caribbean countries and the African Union are planning reparations cases in the International Court of Justice — no doubt buoyed by Britain’s willingness to bend over backwards to Mauritius’s unwarranted claim on the Chagos Islands.

Why do they keep on pushing at what appears to be a closed door?

Because the reparation campaigners know full well that the British establishment has a fatal weakness that they can — and will — exploit.

Our Achilles heel is our governing classes, who suffer from inexplicable hand-wringing liberal white guilt over our country’s past as a colonial power, combined with an embarrassment about our history and traditions, and even contempt for our national flag.



Yet while they self-flagellate over the terrible deeds of the past, there is no moral case for Brits to pay Caribbean nations a penny.

No one alive today in the Caribbean is a direct victim of slavery, and no one alive today in Britain is responsible for the sins of our great-great-great-great-great grandfathers.

Indeed, for most of us, it wasn’t even our own ancestors who took part in the slave trade. They were busy working in the factories or fields and living in abject poverty.

Even if we were responsible for what happened 300 years ago, surely the African kings who rounded up their fellow men and women to sell them to the Europeans for huge profits are equally at fault.

Yet we don’t hear anything about reparation demands from those modern African nations.



And how far back do reparations claims for the past go? Can we Brits claim reparations from the Italians for the cruelty of the Roman empire?

And what about a class legal action against the Danes for all that raping and pillaging by the Vikings?

The fact is that the trafficking of human beings was a near-universal feature across the world for most of human history — right up until Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807, going on to spend the modern equivalent of billions to bring it to an end.

It’s high time we threw away the sackcloth and ashes and started standing up to the reparations extortionists.

Forget the hand-wringing about bad deeds of the past, it’s time to shout loudly from the rooftops about the huge list of GOOD things this country has given to those Caribbean islands — and to the rest of the world.



In the Monty Python comedy film Life Of Brian, Reg fam-ously asks his fellow rebellious Judeans: “What have the Romans ever done for us?” — a question which is met by a long list of benefits delivered by the Roman empire including sanitation, medicine, education, public order, irrigation, roads, a fresh water system, public health and wine.

Britain has a far longer list of achievements — with the abolition of slavery among our proudest.

We also gave the world the Industrial Revolution, which has delivered the greatest wealth to the largest number of people in human history.

From the steam engine and mechanised production to railways and steamships, to modern banking and capital markets, it all started here in Blighty.

Britain has long been at the very forefront of modern science and medicine, not to mention the earliest innovations in computing and the invention of the world wide web.



We also exported our democratic institutions to much of the world, including parliamentary democracy, the concepts of common law and individual rights, as well as habeas corpus, trial by jury, property rights — and constraints on the arbitrary power of kings.

Add to that our civil service structure, educational system, the English language and many of the most popular sports on the planet, including football, cricket, rugby, tennis and golf, all of which were invented on the playing fields of Britain.

Oh, and then there is the small matter of us being the only European nation which stood firm in the face of the threat from the evils of Nazism.

All in all, we have a track record of which we should be proud, not a history of which we should be ashamed.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

So, when the reparations grifters ask, “What have the British ever done for us?”, we should tell them.



And, instead of demanding apologies and cash from us for the sins of the past, they should be thanking Britain for our unique contribution to making the world a far better place today.

News.title: Social media users may have to show photo ID to prove age under Labour ban on under-16s
News.content:
Next

SOCIAL media users may have to show photo ID to prove their age under the Labour ban on under-16s.

Media watchdog Ofcom said the AI analysis of facial ­features from uploaded videos or photographs is not accurate enough on some apps.



It recommends Facebook, TikTok and others consider using bank checks, photo ID and digital ID services instead.

It comes after under-16s in Australia cheated AI facial age checks by drawing on wrinkles and facial hair to beat a social media ban.



Ofcom boss Dame ­Melanie Dawes said: “We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions.

“But there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk.”

Andy Burrows, of the Molly Rose Foundation, a suicide and online safety charity, said Ofcom admitted last week that it had failed to reduce children’s exposure to harmful content.

If they are to enforce the new ban with the same “insufficient powers”, he said, the same “dismal results” seen in Australia should be expected.

Two in five young people aged 11 to 15 set to be hit by the social media ban will move to apps outside the restrictions, a survey finds.

Forty-four per cent of the youngsters are already discussing the plans with their pals, research from EE shows.



Andy Burnham is expected to push through plans with the age-based social media ban announced by Sir Keir Starmer.

Labour’s ban is set to come in next March.

News.title: Alarm at ‘sex rap’ star’s gag bid as leading lawyers say mental health should not be ‘automatic veto’ to block exposure
News.content:
STAR'S GAG BID Alarm at ‘sex rap’ star’s gag bid as leading lawyers say mental health should not be ‘automatic veto’ to block exposure







Next

LEADING legal voices have told The Sun that mental health should never be used as an “automatic veto” to stop claims about exploitative sexual behaviour being exposed by the Press.

A “well-known” man is currently suing the Guardian and ITN in the High Court, claiming he would take his own life if they published allegations about him.

The individual, who cannot be named, is seeking an injunction to stop the broadcast of the allegations, which he denies.

He will find out if his bid is successful next week. Lawyer Matt Jury, of McCue Jury & Partners, said if the injunction is granted it will stop crime victims being heard.





He said while mental health must be treated seriously, “it cannot become an automatic veto on reporting something clearly in the public interest”.

Mr Jury added: “People who come forward with serious allegations must not be silenced. The Press must be free to investigate and report what they say.

“If you choose a life in the public eye, you accept greater scrutiny. If allegations are false, deny them, challenge them and clear your name.”

Marcus Johnstone, a specialist in criminal defence for those accused of sex crimes, said: “If anybody accused of an offence could say ‘I’m at risk of ­suicide, therefore nobody’s allowed to report on this’, then where do you draw the line?”

Written submissions stated the two media outlets had evidence of misconduct “towards a large number of women over a prolonged period”, including possibly criminal behaviour.

Sara Mansoori KC, representing the man, told the court publication “would have a potentially fatal impact”.

The individual has twice attempted suicide in recent months and is “seriously ill”, it is claimed.

News.title: How Russia’s new jet-powered death drones that killed innocent Ukrainians are secretly being built with BRITISH parts
News.content:
Next

RUSSIA’S new jet-powered drones are secretly being built with British components — to kill innocent civilians in Ukraine.

The revelation came as warmonger President Vladimir Putin last night warned the West to prepare for attack.



He said: “We are ready for war with Europe, but we don’t want it.

“As for them — if anyone desires such a thing, let them prepare.”



Ukrainian intelligence said the drones now hammering the country contain flight control micro-computers made by Cambridge firm Raspberry Pi.

They were found during analysis of downed hardware.

Ukraine sanctions chief Vladyslav Vlasiuk said: “You will find this flight control in most of the drones.

“This is one of the crucial parts. I would really expect Raspberry Pi to do much more of the internal compliance, to scrutinise who they are selling their parts to.”



Other components in the weapons have been traced to the US, Germany, Switzerland and China.

The parts are sold to third party firms and shipped to sanctioned Russian businesses for use in Putin’s war machine.

The Sun was yesterday given access to the Geran-4, Geran-5 and shark-shaped Filin warheads which rely on the components.



The Geran-5 can hit 375mph — outrunning Ukraine’s interceptor drones, the success rate of which has fallen from 90 per cent to 60 since Russia began using the weapon.

Launch bases on the Belarus and Ukraine border put targets deep inside Nato territory in range.

Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelensky urged the US and Europe to impose “new, stronger sanctions” to stop drone hardware from reaching Russia.



The British link to the drones emerged as 14 people were killed and another 14 hurt in an attack on a train station in Dnipro yesterday.

Five more, including two girls of 15, died in Poltava and Chernihiv.

Raspberry Pi said: “The company is disappointed at evidence of its products making their way to Russia and deplores these illegal trades.

“The company applies the strictest of measures to prevent this.”

The Department for Business and Trade said it took Ukraine’s claims “incredibly seriously”.

News.title: Full heartbreaking statement after Patrick Stewart’s death – Star Trek and X-Men icon was 86
News.content:
Next

ICON Patrick Stewart died in the care of his wife of 13 years following a battle with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia, as the world of Hollywood mourns the renowned actor.

Stewart, who was 86 at the time of his death, died on Wednesday in his home in Los Angeles, his representatives said in a statement.



The heartbreaking statement read, “We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all.



“We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

The statement continued, “A son of Mirfield in the West Riding of Yorkshire, he travelled from the Royal Shakespeare Company to an equally acclaimed career spanning six decades on Broadway, the silver screen and television.

“His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre.

“He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise.

His professional accomplishments were humbly matched by his philanthropy and activism on behalf of human rights, survivors of domestic violence, global refugees, veterans’ mental health services, and animal welfare, particularly his cherished foster pitties.

“He was a Knight, Chancellor, motor sport enthusiast, and lifelong Huddersfield Football fan. He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role – in his art and life.



“Like me, Jean-Luc has lived an unusual life that has taken him far beyond the bounds of normal human experience.

“But he is also someone who has remained true to his earthbound roots, for they are what gave him his identity. In the end, he feels the call of home, as do I. — Patrick Stewart, Making It So: A Memoir.”

Stewart, whose illustrious career began in London as a theater actor, rose to prominence as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the hit science fiction television series Star Trek: The Next Generation.

He played Captain Picard for seven seasons from 1987 to 1994, and later reprised the role on the big screen for four blockbuster films, Generation, First Contact, Insurrection, and Nemesis.

After an 18-year hiatus, Stewart reprised the role in the standalone series Star Trek: Picard, on Paramount+ from 2020 to 2023.



Stewart’s list of accolades includes two Laurence Olivier Awards, a Grammy Award, and a Drama Desk Award.

The Mirfield-born actor became globally recognized for his role as Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise on Fox and then Marvel.

He brought a sense of command to the comic book adaptation, leading the X-Men against the Brotherhood of Mutants and their leader, Magneto, who was portrayed by Stewart’s close friend Ian McKellen.



Stewart reunited with McKellen for his final live-action film role before his death, bringing the two acting veterans together as Professor X and Magneto in the upcoming Marvel blockbuster Avengers Doomsday.

Fellow Avengers: Doomsday actor Danny Ramirez, who stars as the Falcon, recently reflected on sharing the set with Stewart and McKellen.

“When Sir Ian McKellen is speaking, you listen because you never know what nugget might change your life,” Ramirez told CinemaBlend in July.

“And in the same way as Sir Patrick Stewart or anybody.”

Asked specifically what he had learned from Stewart, Ramirez summed up the actor’s presence in two words, “Gravitas. Real gravitas.”



Ramirez said he had watched old videos of Stewart and McKellen analyzing Shakespeare and was struck by their command of language.

He said their understanding of the words was so strong that they could take an audience on a journey even with a simple sentence.

Directors Joe and Anthony Russo have also spoken of their excitement at directing Stewart, McKellen, and the returning X-Men cast.

Joe said the brothers had once been fans watching the original movies at midnight screenings.

“And so to be able to work with those actors is like a dream come true for us,” he said.



Marvel Studios praised Stewart as a “generous collaborator, and a true gentleman.”

“All of us at Marvel Studios are deeply saddened by the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart,” the production company said in a statement.

“Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from ‘X-Men’ to ‘Logan’ to ‘Avengers: Doomsday.’

“He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art.”

Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside Stewart as Wolverine in the X-Men franchise, wrote, “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”

Stewart is survived by his wife, Sunny, 47, and their two children, Daniel and Sophie Alexandra.

News.title: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
News.content:
The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".

The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.

Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.

These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.

The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.

Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.

He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."

Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.

"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."

News.title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
News.content:
People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.

Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by Â£1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.

Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.

The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.

In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a Â£100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.

But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.

"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.

"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.

However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.

News.title: Jury shown CCTV of Huntingdon train staff using frying pan in defence
News.content:
CCTV footage of a crew member using a frying pan to fend off a knifeman aboard a train has been shown in court.

Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said Samir Zitouni showed "sheer courage and bravery in seeking to save lives and defend others", during the mass stabbing on the Doncaster to London King's Cross train.

Jurors at Cambridge Crown Court saw footage of Zitouni using the pan against Anthony Williams, before the train made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, denies attempting to murder 10 people aboard the train, three people in Peterborough the day before and a boy at a London railway station.

The trial has been told that whether Williams carried out the attacks was not in question, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals.

News.title: Met refers itself to police watchdog over letter about Meghan's father
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has referred itself to the police complaints watchdog over its handling of a letter with allegations against Thomas Markle, which was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.

The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.

Markle has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".

The force said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) "in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex."

The Met added it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".

The letter that will be considered by the IOPC was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Roslyn Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.

The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".

Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason for not visiting Thomas Markle and not allowing him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.

Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".

Confirming that it had referred itself to the IPOC, the Metropolitan Police said it was aware of media reports that it had try to obtain a copy of the letter.

"While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," it said.

It added that the Met has carried out an initial review in recent days which has led to the voluntary referral to IOPC.

The watchdog will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas, it contained claims of alleged offences.

There are also reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to get a copy from the Sussexes.

Meghan, in a statement last week, said she believed the allegations in the letter "were being investigated".

But the watchdog will have to consider what happened to the warnings.

There are also likely to be questions about what royal officials knew about the letter, which was sent when Meghan was still a working royal, and which was forwarded to the Sussexes' office rather than to her personally.

Jim Gamble, former head of the Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre, previously told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he would have expected the police to have shared any warnings.

"If you get information that comes to you about someone from a foreign jurisdiction who represents a threat to children, there's a well-worn path and generally you'd expect a UK police force to share that information," said Gamble.

"I would have expected the Metropolitan Police to have gone to the FBI to say, 'Look, this isn't proven, it's an allegation, you might want to look at it'.

Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".

"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken, why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies," she said.

"I believe those questions deserve clear, transparent answers."

Reports of the Met's handline of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.

Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.

Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims.

Philippine Police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.

However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.

Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

News.title: Hundreds of GP practices lose online services after collapse of tech firm
News.content:
Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.

Silicon Practice ran digital services, including websites, online booking and consultations, for around 500 practices in England â just under 10% of the total.

Practices across the country, including in London, Gloucestershire and Norfolk, have reported problems. Services in Wales are also affected.

GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking that now takes places.

Patients in areas that are affected are being advised they will have to make appointments via the phone. The NHS app is working.

Since last year, all practices in England have had to offer online appointment booking. Currently, more than 40% of appointments are made that way.

An NHS England spokesperson said while "the majority" of GP practice websites were running as normal, some using Silicon Practice will be affected.

"If your GP practice website is unavailable and you need help, you should contact your practice by phone or in person as usual."

News.title: King Charles arrives in Guyana as Bahamas visit declared 'diplomatic success'
News.content:
King Charles has arrived in Guyana for the second leg of his Caribbean tour, following a visit to the Bahamas which Buckingham Palace described as a "sensitive balancing act" and "diplomatic success".

The main themes of the two-day state visit to Guyana will be the environment and sustainability - alongside the growing commercial ties between the UK and Guyana.

The King is due to have an audience with the country's President, Irfaan Ali, and will attend a state reception celebrating the 60 year bilateral relationship between the two countries.

After visiting Guyana, King Charles will visit Antigua and Bermuda where he will open a major Commonwealth leaders summit in his role as the head of the "family of nations".

Guyana - formerly British Guiana - is the world's fastest growing economy due to the discovery of oil reserves there in 2015.

More than four fifths of Guyana is covered by rainforest and it has one of the lowest rates of deforestation in the world.

Cultural exchanges will also feature with a group of bagpipers from the National Piping Centre in Scotland joining the royal tour.

As the King left the Bahamas on Thursday to fly to Guyana for the second leg of his Caribbean tour, his spokesman said the islands had "a special place in the King's heart."

"The great wall of cheers he received when greeting crowds will echo long in his memory - and be a source of tremendous pride and encouragement as the tour continues to Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda."

The two day trip to the Bahamas saw the King meet young boxers, environmentalists and politicians.

He also joined the dancing in a Junkanoo parade to celebrate island life.

News.title: Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the government is "ready to support" Poundland staff as the retailer teeters on the brink of collapse.

The prime minister called for answers over why an offer to buy the business from its current owners, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.

"This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families," Burnham told the BBC.

The discount chain is teetering on the edge after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).

Burnham said: "We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn't been accepted, then the Business Secretary and I want to know why that is the case.

"We stand ready to support the workforce however we can."

The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.

The move comes after managing director Barry Williams told its 12,000 staff the chain's US owner had cut off a vital supply of funding despite Poundland's strong sales.

It is understood Gordon Brothers wants to break it up, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up its stores.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds earlier said he was "very much concerned" by the uncertainty clouding Poundland's future.

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal Â£1. A little over a year later, it put the business up for sale.

Despite an offer on the table for the business, Poundland's managers and owners have not been able to agree on a buyer, which has left it on the brink of collapse.

It could still be purchased out of administration in a so-called pre-pack deal, but the most likely option is for it to be broken up and for Poundland's stores to be sold off.

Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year.

It has across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades as Dealz.

It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.

News.title: Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove
News.content:
A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.

The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.

Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.

The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".

The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."

Footage, first unearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.

However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in the clip originally posted by the Telegraph, external.

The incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.

Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.

In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.

"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.

"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."

Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there â but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."

Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."

News.title: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
News.content:
Laura Brand said she knew before they met that "he liked women", and found out that while they were dating that he had been having sex with others.

"I wasn't interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people", she said.

"I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."

She said she remained friends with Brand while he was married to singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012, and got back together with him in 2015.

Asked if she was "aware of his promiscuity" during their time apart, she said: "I was very aware of it. I could read about it regularly in the papers, so I was aware of it and he also told me."

Turning to their relationship now, she said: "We have a very honest, frank, and clear relationship and marriage.

"It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest."

The charges against Brand relate to allegations made by six female complainants spanning a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

The entertainer has displayed little emotion during the course of his trial, but was seen smiling broadly during parts of his wife's evidence.

He let out a laugh when she told the court: "We do have many friends and there are colleagues, and we are grateful for those people."

Her evidence came a day after the star appeared in the witness box himself.

He told the jury the allegations had a "devastating" impact on his relationships with friends and colleagues, meaning they would not touch him "with a bargepole".

He also said on Wednesday he had been promiscuous but believes sexual consent is "fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself".

On Thursday, the court also heard statements from two of Russell Brand's ex-girlfriends

Elia Alvarez Diaz said they were in a relationship and lived together for about a year from 1998 to 1999, and described the defendant as "gentle" and "loving".

She described him as being "highly persuasive... a complex character" and "exciting to be with".

"When I said no, however, he accepted it," she said in a statement.

Their relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly, she said.

Amanda Alguero Alejos told the court in a statement that Brand had also repeatedly cheated on her.

"He was undoubtedly promiscuous, never in front of me and never when I was around. That was not what mattered to me at the time," she said.

She recalled women "circling" around Brand "like birds", even when they were out as a couple.

The trial continues, with the jury likely to retire to consider the verdicts on Tuesday.

News.title: Ex-Top Gear host Richard Hammond's 'brave' new Welsh life wild swimming and running
News.content:
Former Top Gear star Richard Hammond says he has swapped vintage cars for food festivals and running as he settles into life in a Welsh market town.

The 56-year-old bought a Â£2m Georgian mansion in Llanwenarth, near Abergavenny in Monmouthshire, in November 2025 following his divorce from wife Mindy after 23 years.

The presenter previously told BBC Wales he had "never been happier" since moving into the 19th Century home, and each week he has discovered a new reason to be "delighted that I live there".

With Bannau Brycheiniog - Brecon Beacons - in his back garden, Hammond told the High Performance Podcast he had taken up open water swimming as he becomes "braver" than he has ever been.

News.title: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment
News.content:
The environmental performance of water companies worsened again last year despite industry investment, according to the first joint report by the regulators.

Eight of the nine companies in England were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement", with only Severn Trent receiving the highest rating.

Companies were praised for reducing service disruptions but serious pollution into the environment remained a "major concern".

The chair of the environmental regulator, Alan Lovell, said the results showed the industry continued to "fall well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public".

"I'm very angry," he told BBC News. "I think it's extremely disappointing to see the level of pollution incidents... and I completely sympathise with the public."

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said she was "demanding answers from the companies that are failing" and would be "shining a spotlight on the worst offences around the country".

Four different regulators currently oversee water companies in England and Wales - the Environment Agency (EA), Natural Resources Wales (NRW), Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate - and this marks the first time they have come together to assess the industry.

It is a nod to the commitment made by Sir Keir Starmer's government to merge the organisations covering England into a single body as part of efforts to streamline regulation.

But it is on environmental performance that the report is most critical.

Serious pollution incidents in 2025 were a "major concern", the Environment Agency said, and remained at similarly high levels to those seen in previous years.

Overall, England's water companies were awarded 16 out of a possible 36 stars for environmental performance - the worst total on record.

The EA said this was due to "declining performance in some areas but also due to our tighter performance standards".

And in Wales, DÅµr Cymru Welsh Water was given a two-star rating, out of four, by NRW.

Industry body Water UK acknowledged that "the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough".

But it also pointed out that more than half of all pollution incidents were as a result of "blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies".

"It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth, and end sewage entering rivers and seas," a spokesperson said.

Today's report did highlight some "strengths to build on", with UK drinking water quality remaining "among the best in the world".

And the regulators also noted that "leakage has reduced over the long term" but said improvement was still needed.

News.title: Chancellor's £30m pledge for train station is insult to the people of Wales, minister says
News.content:
A Â£30m rail funding pledge announced by Chancellor John Healey in the Budget is "an insult to the people of Wales", a Welsh government minister says.

Wales' Transport Minister Mark Hooper said the investment in the proposed Cardiff Parkway station was "a tiny fraction" of the cash needed to improve Welsh rail.

The Plaid Cymru-led Welsh government had called on Healey to bring forward Â£1bn of the Â£14bn the UK Labour government had promised for long-term rail funding in Wales.

UK government finance minister Emma Reynolds said the cash was part of a Â£445m package aimed at tackling years of "chronic under-investment" in rail.

Hooper made the comments after a meeting with the UK government in Whitehall on Thursday.

The proposed Cardiff Parkway in the city's eastern St Mellons area would link passengers on the South Wales Metro network to north Wales, Bristol, Manchester and London.

News.title: 'I died twice', says man saved by off-duty police sergeant
News.content:
A dad who suffered a cardiac arrest and collapsed in a shop said his 12-year-old son could have lost his dad if a "hero" off-duty police officer had not saved him.

James Ashley, 52, from Merthyr Tydfil, had just finished parkrun and was shopping in Cwmbran when he was hit by a "wave of dizziness" and fell to the floor on 4 April.

Sgt Adam Hollings from Gwent Police was nearby and immediately started CPR.

"I clinically died twice but by the time the paramedics got there, I was sitting up talking... the difference with Adam knowing what he was doing is that my son didn't lose his dad as a 12-year-old," he said, and called him an "absolute hero".

Hollings, who has spent 21 years on the force, was awarded a Royal Humane Society Resuscitation Certificate for his role in saving Ashley's life.

"We're very lucky to have the first aid training that we do, and if we can occasionally be in the right place at the right time to help people out, then fantastic," he said.

The 40-year-old from Abergavenny told Radio Wales Breakfast that even though he was off-duty his training and lifesaving skills kicked in and he acted on "autopilot".

He told someone in the shop to call an ambulance, and then used a defibrillator.

A defibrillator is a device that gives a jolt of energy to the heart, external. It helps get the heart beating again when someone is in cardiac arrest and their heart has stopped.

News.title: Watch the moment bridge hit at least 45 times is driven into again
News.content:
Video footage from Victoria Road resident Mark Needs shows a number of lorries and other vehicles getting into difficulty over the years, despite warning signs alerting drivers to its presence.

"The worst one was when a van with a cherry picker got stuck under it, it took four to five hours to get it out," he said.

"Another time a lorry coming down the hill hit the bridge, then a car and a telegraph pole."

Needs said there were sensors on poles set some way back on either side of the bridge. He said they activated flashing signs close by the bridge when vehicles of a certain height drove past.

The flashing sign on the Fairwood Terrace side of the bridge did not appear to flash when the lorry approached on 25 October, but Swansea council said the sensor system was functioning correctly.

Needs said there had been some interesting collisions, including a lorry transporting potatoes that got stuck.

"Everybody had free potatoes that day," he said.

Network Rail said staff carried out precautionary safety inspections following the latest incident but identified no damage.

Network Rail said: "Alongside collision protection beams, which have been in place since 2014 to protect the main railway structure from vehicle impacts and reduce the risk of damage, the bridge is also clearly marked with low-headroom warning signs, with additional advance and illuminated LED signage on the approaches to alert drivers before they reach the structure.

"We continue to work closely with Swansea Council to improve highway signage, and make sure these warning systems remain operational and effective."

Gowerton councillor Susan Jones said: "Obviously that bridge is a problem. When they extended the railway station it was strengthened - if they hadn't, I dread to think."

News.title: Google stock price crashes and wipes $500 billion off company amid panic over AI
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Google’s share price has dramatically plunged amid a panic over AI.

Parent company Alphabet finished Thursday down more than 12 per cent, wiping $500 billion from its value. It represents the biggest ever crash in Google’s history, and second only among US listed companies to a $593 billion plunge in Nvidia’s value last year, after the rise of China’s DeepSeek AI brought concerns that US artificial intelligence companies could lose the race.

It comes after Alphabet’s latest results showed disappointing earnings in its search advertising business and the full scale of its vast spending on artificial intelligence. But shareholders are concerned that those huge bets may not come off, and that the company and the rest of the tech industry may not recover its investment in AI.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai has looked to aggressively embrace AI – even at the cost of its reliable business such as search ( Getty )

The results did show that Google is already earning from the AI boom, with revenues in its cloud business more than doubling. But investors are concerned that in the search business that still represents a large part of its earnings, Google is yet to see its embrace of AI results turning into profit.

Google and its chief executive Sundar Pichai have looked to aggressively embrace AI, after a relatively slow start against other companies such as OpenAI. It has begun to use its Gemini model to answer many search queries, for instance – despite the fact that advertising in search results has been a reliably huge business for parent company Alphabet.

"In a market ⁠worried about AI cannibalising the franchise, investors need to see search accelerating, not decelerating," said Dave Wagner, portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors.

"Cloud is carrying the story, but until search shows AI is additive, the stock's probably going to trade lower."

The Mountain View, California company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, versus analyst expectations that it would come close to breaking even.

Aggressive efforts to boost cloud capacity and fund AI development led Alphabet to burn $5.9 billion last quarter, the first time it went into the negative in 22 years as a ⁠public company.

Total revenue missed Wall Street targets: revenue growth for Google Cloud outpaced expectations but was ​not enough ⁠to offset a $1.4-billion miss in advertising.

Alphabet's second straight quarter of negative cash flow was a sharp turn for a company that was long one of the tech sector's most prolific cash generators.

Moreover, Alphabet still plans to significantly increase its 2027 capital expenditures from this year's spending forecasts of $195 billion ⁠to $205 billion, Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi told analysts on a conference call.

While executives did not put a number on 2027 outlays, investors were nervous about ​a big jump.

"A $300-billion (capex) ⁠number could potentially scare the market because free cash flow now ‌is finally negative," said Jeremy Saltsburg, senior investment officer at Check Capital.

In contrast, rival Microsoft, which also reported results on Wednesday, saw shares rise more than 5%, fueled by positive free cash flow that outstripped analyst estimates.

Ashkenazi added that she expected near-term margin pressure from the use of third-party cloud capacity.

Net income available to ‌common Alphabet shareholders fell 25% to $26.17 billion, and adjusted earnings per share of $2.67 missed Wall Street targets ‌of $3.02.

The results reflect the huge costs of the AI buildout, with investors concerned both by potential overspending and the risk of falling behind rivals by not spending enough.

Total third-quarter revenue of $127.6 billion fell short of analysts' estimate of $128.2 billion, LSEG data showed. Revenue from ads came in at $82 billion, missing expectations of $83.4 billion.

Chief business officer Philipp Schindler attributed a larger-than-expected deceleration in search advertising growth to greater use of AI Mode, a chatbot interface ⁠for the search engine with which the company is still experimenting on ads.

Google would begin rolling out s in AI Mode to international markets, Schindler told a conference call.

Alphabet attempted to offset the disappointing advertising performance by playing up its cloud computing unit, most notably by debuting Thomas Kurian, CEO of GoogleCloud, as a speaker on the earnings call.

Revenue at Google Cloud exceeded estimates and more than doubled to $30.71 billion in the third quarter ended September 30.

Kurian said sales of Google's tensor processing units (TPUs), which compete with Nvidia's GPU chips, had become a meaningful contributor to his business unit.

Alphabet started recognizing revenue from direct sales of what it called its "TPU Systems", spanning not only the chips but also associated hardware and software, last quarter.

But Ashkenazi cautioned that the buildout of TPU inventory would further place pressure on free ‌cash flow.

Google Cloud's backlog had grown to $561 billion and Alphabet expected to recognize more than 55% of it as revenue in the next 24 ​months, she added.

The third-largest cloud services provider globally after Amazon Web Services and Microsoft's Azure, Google Cloud has expanded enterprise commitments, supported by multi-year cloud and ‌AI infrastructure deals across cybersecurity, retail and financial services.

Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, and ⁠Meta are projected to collectively spend well over $700 billion in 2026 to expand AI data center footprint, chips and high-performance networking capacity.

In the face of supply ⁠bottlenecks for advanced silicon and data center power, Alphabet's investments in custom tensor processing units alongside third-party GPUs have helped expand its service delivery capabilities.

Earlier on Wednesday, Google sought to preempt the results and counter a perception ‌of losing out in the AI race ​by unveiling the new Gemini 4 Carbon model.

This meant the company was again "leading at ‌the frontier," CEO Sundar Pichai said on the call.

Afterwards, analysts at Bernstein asked ​in a note, "Did Google rush the deployment of Gemini 4 models as an offset to softer financial metrics? And are the models ready for commercial deployment?"

Sir Patrick Stewart, who was known for his roles in X-Men and Star Trek, has died at the age of 86, his family announced Thursday.

The English actor died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” his longtime spokesperson announced Thursday.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” the statement said. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

The Emmy-winning actor rose to fame for playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the 1987 hit Star Trek: The Next Generation. He later became known for playing Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men movie franchise.

In the years before he became a movie star, Stewart was already a revered theater veteran in Britain, having made his first stage appearance in 1959.

Stewart was 86 years old ( AFP/Getty )

He started working with the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966 and performed with actors including Helen Mirren and Ben Kingsley, according to the New York Times. In 1986, he won the London Fringe Theater best actor award for his performance as George in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? He also won Olivier Awards for his performances in two Shakespeare plays: Antony and Cleopatra in 1979 and Hamlet in 2009.

He is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, and his two children, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.

News.title: Gang jailed over smash-and-grab robberies that caused £1 million worth of damage in London's West End
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Three men have been jailed following a string of high-profile smash-and-grab robberies in London’s West End, police have confirmed.

The gang targeted five luxury fashion stores over a three-month period between November 2025 and January 2026, using stolen cars to crash through storefronts before raiding the premises, according to the Metropolitan Police.

CCTV footage released by the force on Thursday depicts vehicles reversing directly into shop display windows before thieves rush inside to steal as many items as they could carry before escaping.

The group focused on designer boutiques in exclusive shopping areas, including YSL in Bond Street, Bottega Veneta and Lora Piana in Sloane Street, and End in Broadwick Street.

At Inner London Crown Court on Thursday, Max Tyson, 26, and Ryan Brough, 34, were sentenced to three years and four months in prison after pleading guilty to two counts of conspiracy to commit burglary.

open image in gallery A screengrab from CCTV footage of the robbery at Lora Piana ( PA )

Harry Johnson, 25, was jailed for one year and 10 months after pleading guilty to handling stolen goods.

Two other men, Sonny Stringer, 29, and Olivier Ndayizeie, 36, received suspended sentences at the same court after pleading guilty to handling stolen goods and encouraging or assisting an offence, respectively.

Police said the total damage caused to the boutiques, combined with the value of the stolen items, reached £1 million.

During the raid on Lora Piana on 16 December 2025, the gang stole more than 105 items—including handbags, clothing, boots, and a coat worth over £30,000—with the total value of stock taken in that single incident coming to nearly £385,000.

Detectives later discovered that the stolen merchandise was frequently resold at a fraction of its retail value, with messages showing Tyson once received just £1,800 for items worth more than £30,000.

Officers from the Met’s Flying Squad identified the gang through a combination of CCTV, forensic evidence, and Automatic Number Plate Recognition footage, which revealed the group had used several stolen vehicles.

Investigators found that one car used to ram a store was insured to Ndayizeie, of Freegrove Road in Islington, while DNA gathered from the scene was matched to Max Tyson.

The investigation subsequently tracked Tyson, of St Peters Street in Islington, to a shop in Cornwall where he had fled to avoid being caught.

However, police discovered receipts in his name demonstrating that stolen goods had been resold to the shop for thousands of pounds.

open image in gallery A screengrab from CCTV footage of the attempted robbery at YSL ( PA )

Tyson and Brough, of Courtney Road, Islington, were arrested on 23 January 2026, the same day as the final raid at the YSL store on Bond Street.

Stringer, of Essex Road, Islington, was arrested on 26 January, while Johnson, of Tilney Gardens, and Ndayizeie were detained on 10 February.

Detective Constable Will Wigzell, from the Met’s Flying Squad, said: "These robberies have a lasting impact on businesses, their staff and the wider community, affecting livelihoods as well as causing significant emotional and financial harm through the threats, violence and intimidation involved.

"This organised crime group carried out a series of brazen smash-and-grab robberies across some of London’s busiest shopping districts.

"They carefully planned their offences, using stolen vehicles and mopeds in an attempt to evade detection, but thanks to the determination and expertise of Flying Squad detectives, they were identified and brought to justice.

"These sentences mark a significant milestone in what has been a detailed and determined investigation.

"I hope they demonstrate our commitment to tackling smash-and-grab robberies in London by pursuing those involved, wherever they are."

News.title: Sweaty Trump loses it over questions about if he is skipping Kansas rally because of his health
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump unloaded on a reporter who questioned why he canceled a Saturday appearance at a Kansas rally, one of his only scheduled campaign-trail appearances the weekend before Election Day.

Trump, who appeared to be sweating as he briefly addressed reporters following his remarks at a campaign rally in South Carolina, called a reporter with Reuters “way out of shape” and mocked him for asking whether the president was “feeling well.”

“You know what the reason is? I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump told reporters Thursday. “He said, ‘You’re not going to Kansas, sir, are you feeling well?’ You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect.”

He then called the reporter “disgusting.”

“Put yourself in shape,” he said. “You look like hell.”

open image in gallery Donald Trump called a reporter ‘disgusting’ and said they ‘looked like hell’ when asked why he canceled a campaign rally in Kansas days before Election Day with the balance of power in Congress at stake in midterms ( Reuters )

The president will instead participate in a series of virtual rallies. It’s unclear whether he will reschedule the Kansas event, or if his Sunday rally in Iowa is still in the cards.

Trump was scheduled to appear at Salina Regional Airport to support embattled Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, who is polling closely in a race for re-election against Democratic candidate and pastor Adam Hamilton. The last time voters in the state elected a Democratic U.S. senator was in 1939.

Pieter Miller, executive director of the Salina Airport Authority, said “all Salina events are cancelled” due to the president’s schedule.

Protesters repeatedly interrupted the president’s last appearance in the state, which Trump falsely claimed were “paid” to be there. At least 11 people were escorted from the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City that night.

It was at that event where the president invoked the antisemitic slur “shylock” while defending Marshall’s history of suing former patients for failing to pay medical debt when he worked as an OB-GYN.

“And they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a shylock-type guy. And if he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law,” Trump said at the Kansas rally earlier this month. “He would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability. And he didn’t do it. He has a law firm that did it.”

Kansas GOP Chair Danedri Herbert told The Kansas City Star that she heard about the president’s plans to scrap the event through the Republican National Committee.

“That’s all they told me that it was canceled and we’d get more information,” she said. “They are going to do a series of telerallies but I don’t have any information about those.”

Rob Fillion, executive director for the Kansas Republican Party, told Wichita’s CBS affiliate KWCH that “Salina and Kansas are very important to our nation, but there are a lot of other races that are in play.”

Trump being able to speak at “multiple locations at the same time is probably more valuable for his time,” Fillion said.

open image in gallery Recent polling from CNN/SSRS show Democrat Adam Hamilton (left) leading among likely voters in Kansas at 49 percent to Republican Roger Marshall’s 45 percent in the race for Senate. The last time voters in the state elected a Democratic US senator was in 1939. ( AP )

The White House said the president will “continue connecting directly with Americans nationwide through more than 20 telerallies before election day.”

“Telerallies give him the opportunity to highlight his accomplishments and expand his reach across the country,” the White House added.

Kansas is among several states where Democrats appear to be in striking distance to reclaim a Senate majority and tip the balance of power in Congress, according to polling data.

The results of a recent CNN/SSRS poll published Thursday show Hamilton leading among likely voters at 49 percent to Marshall’s 45 percent. Marshall’s favorability rating among likely voters is only 36 percent to Hamilton’s 41 percent.

Sacha Baron Cohen has issued a first-time apology to the people of Kazakhstan over his portrayal of Borat.

News.title: Scottish football could end Saturday 3pm blackout in major broadcasting shake-up
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Scottish Professional Football League has signalled openness to ending the Saturday 3pm television blackout in Scotland from 2029, the Press Association understands.

The SPFL has indicated flexibility to potential bidders for its next broadcast cycle, which is due to start with the 2029-30 season, according to PA.

The Saturday 3pm blackout is a UK-wide broadcasting restriction on football fixtures that has been in place since the 1960s. It was originally brought in to protect live attendances.

The rule has survived opposition thanks to Uefa's Article 48, which contains a clause allowing leagues to impose broadcasting restrictions if 50 per cent or more of professional matches are scheduled for that kick-off time.

Under the SPFL's approach to the next rights sale, broadcasters have been invited to bid for more games than the current cycle contains, PA understands.

open image in gallery Celtic are the reigning champions in Scotland, and the league could be set for a major broadcasting shake-up ( PA )

The league is not, however, trying to sell all of its games in the next cycle.

Should the sale result in fewer than 50 per cent of fixtures kicking off at 3pm on a Saturday, Uefa's Article 48 would not have to be implemented. In that case, the Saturday 3pm blackout in Scotland could be lifted.

Such a move would be a significant moment for live football coverage in the UK.

Other domestic leagues, such as the Premier League and the EFL, could then attempt to implement a similar policy.

The Premier League still has a 3pm blackout on a Saturday, but now shows all games across the rest of the weekend.

Premier League TV slots include 8pm games on Fridays and Mondays, while matches can also be shown at 12.30pm, 5,30pm and 8pm on Saturdays.

Sky Sports now airs all matches starting at 2pm on a Sunday, plus the 4.30pm game, which tends to be reserved for the biggest match of the weekend.

News.title: Prime Minister watches beloved Everton thrash Newcastle to reach quarter-finals
News.content:
David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind to the posh seats, Moyes would have seen Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction this proved to be. Moyes had spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care and want to sell up, and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window.

And then, ahead of Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have opened the door for Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season. But, once again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality and was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without any hinges, and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – will not have done anything to convince those who view German manager Matthias Jaissle with ambivalence to change their minds.

News.title: Trump administration loses grip on bird flu, experts warn
News.content:
The Trump administration has been criticised for losing control of a bird flu outbreak that has spread among mink and cattle farms across the United States.

The H5N1 virus has infected around 1,000 people since it was first detected in the late 1990s, killing roughly half of them. While it currently does not spread among humans, scientists have long worried that it could trigger a pandemic, and that each human infection raises the risk of the virus mutating.

A new variant emerged in 2020 and has since spread to millions of birds and hundreds of animal species across the globe, leading to devastating losses in both wildlife and farmed livestock and poultry.

While some countries have introduced tough measures to curb its spread, including mandatory culls of infected animals, “flockdowns” (where birds are kept indoors) and vaccination of farm workers who handle at-risk livestock, experts say the US is allowing the virus to run rampant.

For more than two months, an outbreak has raged unchecked on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur, news outlet ProPublica reported last week.

Mink in captivity have previously been described as pandemic “time bombs”. The size and density of the farms give invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate.

Mink have very similar respiratory systems to humans, increasing the risk that a virus can spread between the animals and people, and undergo a process known as “reassortment”, when two or more viruses mix together to make a new, more dangerous strain.

News.title: Britain faces unprecedented squeeze on incomes, IFS says
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. John Healey has ruled out making “crude cuts” to welfare after he failed to tackle the rising benefits bill in Wednesday’s Budget.

The Chancellor acknowledged last night that the current benefits system is “unsustainable” but said he will only look to make cuts “in a Labour way”.

Speaking to the BBC in the wake of Wednesday’s Budget, Mr Healey promised that “there will be a reduction in the benefits bill” before the next election.

However, he said this will not include “crude cuts” to payments.

He said: “We will do that in a Labour way, and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain, or progressive, to have a bigger and bigger benefits bills.

“This system is unsustainable. I’ve been clear about that. The Prime Minister’s been clear about that. It’s what you do about it.”

He added: “We have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures.”

His comments on welfare come after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch accused Labour of presiding over a Government that had left Britain “overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system”.

She said: “Next year, under Labour, the tax burden will be the highest in our country’s history and our benefits bill is going up by tens of billions of pounds because this Government has put welfare first.”

The latest figures from the Office for Budget Responsibility released on Wednesday revealed that benefits spending is expected to jump by almost 30pc to £431bn by 2032.

Almost half the total is pensions and disability benefits for pensioners, despite the planned abolition of the triple lock. Here is what you need to know.
