“What I want to stress is we know our bodies best. And if something doesn’t feel right, please go get it checked. It could literally have a massive impact on your treatment plan as well as your future.”

World.title: ‘That increase is more realistic’: South Africans back the proposed SASSA old-age grant amount
World.content:
Not every South African is holding out for a dramatic jump in the SASSA old-age grant. Some say the amount currently on the table is the one most likely to happen.

The comments followed The South African’s report on a push for Parliament to support raising the Older Persons Grant to R3 000 a month.

‘More realistic’

On The South African’s Facebook page, Detlef Weber said the proposed figure strikes the right balance. “That increase is more realistic…” he wrote.



His comment drew a reply and several reactions, with some users agreeing that a smaller, achievable increase is better than a bigger promise that never arrives.

Weber’s view stands apart from many others in the thread, where commenters called for the SASSA old-age grant to rise to R5 000, R6 000, or tomatch the national minimum wage.

Every rand counts in the grant

Tania Steenkamp shared a similar outlook. “R600 is better than nothing. Would be a great addition,” she wrote.



For pensioners who rely on the grant alone, an extra few hundred rand each month can cover a grocery top-up, transport to a clinic or part of a municipal bill.

Supporters of a moderate increase argue that government is more likely to approve an amount that fits within existing budget pressures, rather than a figure that would require major cuts elsewhere.

Weighing ambition against affordability

The debate highlights a tension many grant recipients face. On one side are those who say the grant has never matched the true cost of living. On the other are those who fear pushing for too much could stall any progress at all.



Both groups agree on one thing: the current grant is under strain as food and electricity prices continue to rise.

What happens next

The proposed increase has not been approved. Any change to grant amounts must be announced by the Minister of Finance, usually in the Budget Speech each February, with new amounts taking effect from April.

Until then, grant recipients will continue to receive their monthly payments at current rates and should check official SASSA channels for confirmed updates.

If you receive a SASSA grant and want to share your story, we want to hear from you.

Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: ‘Not everyone is eligible’: Refugee programme sparks backlash
World.content:
The US Embassy has clarified expectations about the refugee resettlement programme. Image via Canva

The US Embassy’s statement that “not everyone is eligible” for the refugee programme, open to racial minorities like white Afrikaner farmers, has been met with backlash from applicants.

This comes amid reports that hundreds of South Africans have been rejected for various reasons.

It also follows news that one refugee – Arno Venter – who resettled in Ohio with his family, was arrested on over 11 charges of child porn distribution.



US EMBASSY: ‘NOT EVERYONE IS ELIGIBLE FOR REFUGEE PROGRAMME’

In a statement shared on their X account, the US Embassy set the record straight regarding expectations for the refugee programme.

It shared: “Not everyone seeking refugee resettlement in the United States is eligible.

“U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has informed some USRAP applicants in South Africa that their cases are ineligible for continued processing, meaning their applications will not move forward.



“USCIS reviews each application on a case-by-case basis to determine whether applicants meet all requirements under U.S. law.

🇺🇸 𝐀𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐔𝐒𝐑𝐀𝐏 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝?



Not everyone seeking refugee resettlement in the United States is eligible.



U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has informed some USRAP applicants in South Africa that their cases are… pic.twitter.com/OQoIe6g2KY — U.S. Mission SA (@USEmbassySA) October 25, 2026

The US Embassy emphasised that all refugees admitted to the United States must meet the necessary eligibility requirements and must pass security and medical screenings.



Applicants to the refugee programme must meet the following requirements:

Must be a South African national, living in South Africa

Belong to a racial minority in South Africa, for example, a white Afrikaner.

Must be able to explain a past experience of persecution or a fear of future persecution.

Must be at least 18, or be referred with a qualifying parent.

WHY ARE APPLICATIONS BEING DENIED?

According to authorities, refugee applications have been rejected, and some individuals have had their status revoked by USCIS based on the following reasons…

Fraud and misrepresentation

Ineligibility as per requirements

Security and terrorism concerns

Criminal history

The UCIS has stated that it is under no obligation to grant an appeal to a rejected refugee applicant.



However, in rare cases, the application may be reviewed if evidence is missing or a factual error is found. This is entirely discretionary.

BACKLASH FROM REJECTED APPLICANTS

The US Embassy’s statement has been met with scores of comments criticising the refugee programme and its growing rejection of applicants.

Here’s what a few had to say on X…

@FredAmerikaner: “The high rate of ineligibility decisions will be the death of the programme. Why risk it if it means you will be stuck here forever?”



@ShadowEchoX: “Hundreds of us were lied to and dragged along for almost a year, believing that today we would get our tickets. But all we got was a letter that crushed all hope and belief that we were saved”

@art03837827: “All bullsh*t. People who met all the criteria were rejected.”

World.title: Big Blow! Orlando Pirates key defender to miss the Kaizer Chiefs match
World.content:
Orlando Pirates could be without Kamogelo Sebelebele for the match against Kaizer Chiefs this weekend.

The Buccaneers play rivals Amakhosi at the FNB Stadium on Saturday afternoon in a Betway Premiership.

Sebelebele was the hero for Pirates in the last Soweto Derby as he scored the equalising goal in the 1-1 draw last season. On Saturday, however, the speedy wingback is set to miss out.



He sustained an injury during the MTN8 final and has been sidelined since, missing subsequent fixtures, including a recent CAF Champions League and Carling Knockout Cup match against Milford FC on Tuesday.

Sebelebele has been one of Pirates best players so far this season.

Who will Pirates field against Chiefs at right back?

Abdeslam Ouaddou will put his trust in Bulelani Sigomoshe to do the job at right-back if Sebelebele is not fit for Saturday’s match.

The 26-year-old has played six matches for the Sea Robbers this season and has hardly put a foot wrong. Although he doesn’t have Sebelebele’s pace, he is solid in defence and rarely goes forward.

This means Abdeslam Ouaddou will rely on either Mohau Nkota or Kabelo Kgositsile to run at the Chiefs left side. Given Sigomoshe can also slot into midfield, it can give the likes of Thalente Mbatha the freedom to go forward during the match.

Pirates will need to be solid at the back to stop Chiefs from hitting them on the counter. The likes of Wandile Duba will feast if the Bucs defence is unsettled.



Which player do you think will make the Soweto Derby?

World.title: Peter Ndlovu makes winning start as a head coach
World.content:
Mamelodi Sundowns legend Peter Ndlovu made an encouraging start to life as Scottland FC’s interim head coach after guiding the Zimbabwean champions to a 1-0 victory over CAPS United on Thursday.

Emmanuel Jalai scored the decisive goal in the sixth minute as Scottland secured maximum points in Harare, giving Ndlovu an immediate boost following his promotion from team manager to head coach.

The result offers a positive beginning for the former Zimbabwe Warriors captain, who has been tasked with guiding the ambitious club through the remainder of the 2026 season.



Peter Ndlovu gets off to a winning start

Ndlovu stepped into the hot seat following Norman Mapeza’s departure after Scottland’s disappointing exit from the CAF Champions League.

The former Mamelodi Sundowns team manager was handed the responsibility of steadying the team and keeping its domestic ambitions alive.

His first assignment against CAPS United was a significant test, with Scottland needing points to maintain pressure on Castle Lager Premier Soccer League leaders Hardrock FC.

Jalai’s early strike proved enough to settle the contest, allowing Ndlovu to begin his tenure with a victory rather than the setback that could have increased the pressure on the club.

Although one result is not enough to establish whether Ndlovu can sustain a title challenge, the win provides a timely confidence boost for the new coach and his players.

Peter Ndlovu takes over after Mapeza’s exit

Scottland parted ways with Mapeza following the club’s elimination from the continental competition, where they surrendered a two-goal first-leg advantage against Angola’s Petro de Luanda before losing 3-2 on aggregate.



The coaching change also brought an overhaul of the technical team, leaving Ndlovu with the responsibility of helping restore stability.

According to The Herald, Ndlovu will be assisted by Danger Fourpence, who was promoted from the club’s academy.

Veteran forward Knowledge Musona has also taken on a player-assistant coach role.

a big task ahead

Despite his limited experience as a senior head coach, Ndlovu holds a CAF A Coaching Licence, providing a foundation for his transition from administration to the technical area.

His stature in Zimbabwean football and previous experience at Mamelodi Sundowns give him valuable experience within the professional game.

However, leading a team from the touchline presents a different challenge from managing its off-field operations.

Scottland, owned by businessman Scott Sakupwanya, have invested heavily in building a competitive squad and will expect results from their new interim coach.

World.title: 'Star Trek', 'X-Men' star Patrick Stewart dead: statement
World.content:
LOS ANGELES - Patrick Stewart, the British Shakespearean actor who became a Hollywood megastar through roles in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises, has died at the age of 86, an official statement said Thursday.

"We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," the statement said.

World.title: Canada buying stake in AI firm Cohere to bolster tech sovereignty
World.content:
TORONTO - Canada is investing CAN$1.6 billion ($1 billion) in the AI firm Cohere, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday, a move aimed at strengthening sovereign alternatives to counter US and Chinese AI dominance.

Cohere was founded in Toronto in 2019 and has tried to distinguish itself from artificial intelligence behemoths like OpenAI and Anthropic by focusing on models built for businesses and governments, with less attention paid to consumer applications.

Announcing the investment ahead of a major Canada-EU summit in Montreal, Carney said "this is the moment that will decide where AI is built, how AI is governed, and who AI serves."

"We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don't know or by those we don't trust," he added.

The concentration of AI systems in the hands of a few companies carries systemic risks, the prime minister said, warning that while those companies may profess to be "global," they "often prove national in the breach."

- Tech you 'can trust' -

Cohere is led by Aidan Gomez, an AI researcher who co-authored a seminal paper that laid the foundations for modern AI systems, underscoring the role of the Canadian AI research ecosystem in the field's development.

The company has already moved to make itself a transatlantic power insulated from US and Chinese control.

In May, Cohere announced a deal to acquire German AI firm Aleph Alpha, creating a combined entity with dual headquarters in Toronto and Berlin, in a deal backed by Ottawa and Berlin.

Gomez told AFP in June that Europe risks "total technological irrelevance" if it fails to develop sovereign capabilities, warning that without home-built technology, everything from defense to productivity will be partly controlled by foreigners.

At Carney's announcement on Thursday, Gomez said the federal investment is part of a funding round targeting CAN$7 billion, which would take the company to a CAN$35.7 billion valuation.

"We are now the largest AI company outside the United States and China," Gomez said.

"Around the world, organizations are looking for technology that they can trust and control, and that reflects their values," he added, pledging that Cohere would be rooted "in Canada always."

In an address to a Montreal research institute before the summit with Carney, EU chief Ursula von der Leyen mentioned the Cohere-Aleph Alpha merger, citing the "strong appetite for teaming up."

Brussels and Ottawa are working on forging unprecedented levels of cooperation, including on AI policy alignment.

By Mathieu Gorse

World.title: The Big Metro Face-Off: DA and MKP battle for eThekwini
World.content:
DURBAN - With local government elections approaching, political parties are making their case to voters.

A debate during eNCA's The Big Metro Face-Off between the DA and MK Party was heated. It followed discussions on coalition numbers and allegations of financial mismanagement.

World.title: MKP plans 10,000 ‘AmaPanyaza’ for Durban as DA sounds alarm
World.content:
DURBAN - The MK Party plans to combat crime in eThekwini by creating its own version of Gauteng's "AmaPanyaza" in the city should it be voted into government after the local government elections on 4 November.

The MK Party’s proposal is similar to Gauteng’s Crime Prevention Wardens, popularly known as "AmaPanyaza".

Launched by Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi, the initiative is aimed at strengthening crime prevention and supporting law enforcement in the province.

The wardens have since been declared peace officers.



In a heated elections debate on eNCA, the DA's Haniff Hoosen and the MK Party's Visvin Reddy clashed over plans to tackle crime in the city.



Visvin Reddy from the MK Party says they plan to employ 10,000 people from the community as Community Safety Officers using the Expanded Public Works Programme (EPWP).



"We are going to use that programme to create volunteers from communities who are currently doing the work, patrolling the streets in the late hours without getting any assistance, without getting any payment from the municipality, so you will get 10,000 community safety officers," Reddy said.



He said they will put these officers in uniform, train them and give them radios to be in constant communication with the police.



Hoosen warned that Durban could be in serious trouble if the MK Party’s plan to deploy 10,000 people to tackle crime went ahead.



He said he would instead channel the money into putting more metro police officers on the streets to make the city safer.



“That will ensure neighbourhoods are safe where people live,” Reddy said.



“We are in trouble, we are serious trouble if the MK Party wants 10,000 of you to fix the crime problem in Durban,” Hoosen said.



“I want to put that R400-million on metro police on the streets,” he said.



Hoosen said the city is already spending R400-million on bodyguards to protect politicians and officials.



“I want us to make sure we have drone technology in eThekwini, so we can close the space for criminals."

According to the eNCA MarkData poll, the MK Party is set to be the largest party in eThekwini as it is polling at 48% while the DA will be the second-biggest party in council at 25.2%.

World.title: ‘Chaos or good governance’: DA and MKP clash over eThekwini
World.content:
DURBAN - Chaos or good governance in eThekwini: that's the grim reality facing residents of the city after the local goverment elections, according to the Democratic Alliance.

The battle for control of eThekwini is intensifying ahead of the local government elections.



According to the eNCA MarkData poll, the MK Party is set to be the largest party in eThekwini as it is polling at 48% while the DA will be the second-biggest party in council at 25.2%.



The DA's mayoral candidate in eThekwini, Haniff Hoosen, says the MK Party will bring nothing but chaos to the eastern coastal city.



"What you see there in the polls is that on the 5th of November, you're going to wake up either to an MK government, that's going to bring chaos to eThekwini, or you can wake up to a DA government, that's going to bring good governance to Durban," Hoosen said.



"That choice is yours, and you can prevent an MK government, an MK chaos in eThekwini, if you get out and vote for the Democratic Alliance.



"Wherever people have given us a chance, we've built better cities, we've built better towns, we're the experts in local government."

However, Visvin Reddy, an MKP Member of Parliament, hit back at Hoosen.



Reddy said a vote for the DA in eThekwini is a vote for the ANC, as the two parties are currently in coalition nationally and provincially in KwaZulu-Natal.



"Now, 25% is what the graph is showing. They're going to get 25%," Reddy said.



"For him to be the mayor, he needs to get 26% more of the vote. MK, in your polls, is polling us at 48%. and I can tell you, as night follows day, on the 5th of November, MK will have a clear majority in Durban and when we take over the city, you are going to see change at another level.



"The one thing we don't do is we don't ignore the poor. We don't ignore the marginalised."

World.title: Number Of The Day | 72.5% | 29 October 2026
World.content:
South Africa's Reform Paradox: Why Better Policies Are Not Delivering a Better Economy

South Africa's economic reforms are gathering momentum, but the country faces a difficult truth: changing the rules is not the same as changing the reality.

South Africa has spent years trying to repair the structural weaknesses holding back its economy. Electricity shortages, inefficient freight networks, failing water infrastructure and weak public institutions have all contributed to an environment in

which businesses struggle to expand and investors question whether the country can deliver on its promises.

Now, there is measurable evidence that some of those reforms are advancing. Business Leadership South Africa's Reform Completion Index reached 72.5 in the third quarter of 2026, up from 71.3 in the preceding quarter and its highest reading since monitoring began in March 2024.

That represents meaningful progress. But it also presents an uncomfortable paradox. South Africa's reform performance is improving while economic growth remains weak, municipalities continue to struggle with basic services and corruption remains a major concern.

The explanation lies partly in the difference between reforming a system and making that system work.

The distance between policy and delivery

Economic reform is rarely a single event. It is a sequence of decisions that may begin with a new law, followed by regulations, institutional restructuring, investment, procurement and finally implementation. Progress at one stage does not guarantee success at the next.

Consider the electricity sector. Opening the market to greater private participation can create the conditions for increased generation capacity and competition. But expanding generation alone does not solve every problem. Power still needs to move through a functioning transmission network, and local distribution systems must be maintained to deliver it reliably to customers.

The same principle applies to freight logistics. Allowing private operators greater access to rail infrastructure is an important change, particularly for an economy that depends on moving minerals, agricultural produce and manufactured goods to ports. Yet the economic benefit depends on whether infrastructure is maintained, operators can obtain practical access and goods actually move more efficiently.

These distinctions are crucial because businesses do not experience reform as a completed policy document. They experience it through the availability, reliability and cost of the services they need.

A manufacturer deciding whether to expand production is less interested in the number of reforms announced than in whether it can depend on electricity, receive raw materials on time and deliver finished products to customers without unpredictable disruptions.

When those conditions improve, reform becomes economically meaningful.

Why water reveals the implementation problem

Water provides one of the clearest examples of the distance between national reform and everyday experience.

BLSA's latest assessment records progress in the water reform programme. Yet that improvement exists alongside severe service delivery problems in many communities. For residents dealing with prolonged interruptions or unreliable supply, the suggestion that water reform is advancing may seem disconnected from reality.

Both observations can be true.

National reforms may improve regulatory arrangements, institutional responsibilities and the framework for holding service providers accountable. But the delivery of water depends heavily on municipal capacity, infrastructure maintenance, sound financial management and appropriately skilled personnel.

A municipality cannot repair a broken system simply because national policy has improved. It needs working equipment, operational budgets, competent management and mechanisms to ensure that failures have consequences.

This is why progress at the national level must eventually be judged against outcomes at the local level. Without that connection, reform risks becoming something government can measure but citizens cannot experience.

Governance is an economic issue

The most troubling finding in the latest review is not the overall index reading. It is the deterioration in governance reform.

BLSA reports that governance declined from 55.0 to 54.6, its first fall since tracking began. Among the factors was the Constitutional Court's invalidation of the Public Procurement Act because Parliament had not met constitutional public participation requirements during the legislative process.

This illustrates how weaknesses in institutional practice can undermine reforms that are otherwise intended to strengthen public administration.

BLSA+1

Governance is sometimes treated as a separate concern from economic performance, associated with audits, political accountability or public sector ethics. In reality, it influences nearly every aspect of the investment environment.

Businesses need predictable rules, credible institutions, enforceable contracts and fair procurement processes. When decisions are inconsistent or corruption creates advantages for politically connected interests, investment becomes more expensive and riskier.

Poor governance can also undermine improvements achieved elsewhere. A new electricity framework cannot deliver its full benefits if procurement is mishandled. Better freight policy will have limited impact if infrastructure management remains ineffective. Water reforms cannot succeed where local institutions are unable to maintain essential systems.

The problem is therefore not merely that governance is lagging behind economic reform. It is that weak governance can reduce the value of economic reform itself.

The financial cost of unresolved corruption

South Africa's recent experience with the Financial Action Task Force offers another illustration.

The country was removed from the FATF grey list in October 2025 after addressing shortcomings identified in its anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing systems. That was an important milestone because increased international monitoring can complicate financial transactions and affect perceptions of risk.

But removal from the list did not mean the underlying work was permanently complete.

BLSA's latest tracker places the corruption reform area at 51.2, unchanged during the quarter. It also warns of vulnerabilities as South Africa undergoes a new FATF mutual evaluation, with concerns about whether improvements in financial oversight are matched by effective action against financial crime.

South African Government+2

A return to increased monitoring could create additional compliance burdens and uncertainty for businesses involved in international payments, trade finance and investment.

More fundamentally, the warning raises a question about the durability of reform. Changing procedures and satisfying an international assessment are important, but institutions must continue demonstrating that they can investigate wrongdoing, enforce rules and respond effectively to emerging risks.

The next phase must be measured in outcomes

South Africa's reform programme deserves recognition where real progress has been made. The latest index suggests that momentum has returned in several areas that are essential to the country's long-term economic prospects.

But the next test is more demanding than raising the score again.

Electricity reform must support dependable supply and investment. Freight reform must improve transport capacity and lower the cost of moving goods. Water reform must strengthen services in communities and industrial areas. Criminal justice reform must help create an environment in which corruption and organised crime face meaningful consequences.

Most importantly, government must demonstrate that deadlines are commitments rather than targets that can be repeatedly moved without consequence.

The real measure of success will not be whether South Africa can announce more reforms or achieve another record index reading. It will be whether those reforms reduce the cost of doing business, improve public services and create conditions in which companies are willing to invest, hire and expand.

A score of 72.5 is evidence of movement. Whether that movement becomes sustained economic growth depends on what happens after the policies are adopted.

World.title: eThekwini voters could deal ANC another massive blow
World.content:
DURBAN - The ANC's gradual decline in eThekwini is expected to be another party's gain next week.

Campaigning politicians have had no shortage of service-delivery issues to leverage for votes.

The eThekwini Municipality was established 26 years ago, intended to signal a new era in Durban.

Residents heard all the right words – more housing, better basic services, improved public infrastructure.

After enjoying an outright majority for 21 years, the ANC had to eat humble pie after the previous local government elections.

Support dropped significantly, and the MK Party emerged as a serious contender for the metro.

Now, polling suggests the party and the ANC’s long-standing opposition in eThekwini, the DA, will go head-to-head next week.

Residents will once again decide who they believe can restore the quality of KwaZulu-Natal’s only metro.

eNCA's Dasen Thathiah reflects on Durban's state in the video above.

World.title: Musonye to lead AFCON 2027 preparations
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Sports Cabinet Secretary Salim Mvurya with Local Organising Committee (LOC) Standing Committee chairperson Nicholas Musonye on October 29, 2026. [Jonah Onyango, Standard]

Sports Cabinet Secretary Salim Mvurya has unveiled the Local Organising Committee (LOC) Standing Committee for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON PAMOJA 2027), with Nicholas Musonye appointed chairman to oversee Kenya’s preparations for the continental football tournament.

Musonye will be deputised by Hussein Mohammed, while Anthony Lung’aho Inzihuli, also known as Antony Emmanuel Inzahuli Lung’aho, will serve as head of the secretariat and chief executive officer.

The committee is tasked with coordinating Kenya’s preparations, including stadium renovations, infrastructure development, operational planning and logistical arrangements ahead of the tournament, which Kenya will co-host with Uganda and Tanzania.

Mvurya said the committee brings together individuals with experience, professional expertise and leadership to help deliver a successful competition that meets the expectations of football fans, participating teams and the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

“I have unveiled the TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) PAMOJA 2027 LOC Standing Committee, entrusting its members with the national responsibility of coordinating and overseeing Kenya’s preparations towards delivering a world-class, memorable and successful continental football tournament,” Mvurya said.

He challenged members to move from planning to implementation, emphasising operational readiness, coordination, strategic partnerships, financial accountability and adherence to delivery timelines.

“With less than eight months to kick-off, I challenged the committee to move decisively from planning to execution,” he said.

Besides Musonye, Mohammed and Lung’aho Inzihuli, the listed committee members include Football Kenya Federation (FKF) Vice-President McDonald Mariga and FKF National Executive Committee representative Robert Macharia.

Other members named in the roster are Timothy Nabea, a former FKF NEC member; Gabriel Mghendi; Peter Kamau; Kerubo Momanyi; Benard Lagat; Collins Kalee; Caleb Amwayi; Ken Rungu; and Dan Shikanda, the former AFC Leopards chairperson.

The list also includes Charles Njagi, Thomas Karugu, Evelyn Cheluget, Miriam Chepkoech, Rodgers Chimega, Diana Injendi Manyengo and Collins Were.

The 38 committee members also comprises representation across functional areas, including finance, technical matters, refereeing, legal affairs and youth development.

The committee is expected to coordinate the different aspects of tournament preparation and ensure that the relevant agencies and stakeholders work towards agreed targets.

Kenya’s preparations also include the development of Talanta Sports City, officially known as the Raila Odinga International Stadium, which is expected to strengthen the country's capacity to host major international football matches.

Mvurya said the planned high-profile encounter between German giants FC Bayern München and Dutch powerhouse AFC Ajax, scheduled for January 5, 2027, would provide an opportunity to assess the country’s readiness.

The event is expected to test security arrangements, transport and logistics, crowd management, operational systems and the overall fan experience.

The CS also disclosed that representatives of the two European clubs had visited Kenya to assess its capacity to host the proposed fixture.

He said the government was adopting a whole-of-government approach, involving relevant agencies responsible for security, immigration, tourism, travel and hospitality.

AFCON 2027 is expected to attract thousands of supporters, officials and international visitors, creating opportunities for hotels, airlines, tour operators, transport businesses and other service providers.

The government is also positioning the tournament as an opportunity to promote tourism, attract investment, develop sporting infrastructure and inspire young footballers.

Mvurya said the committee carries the responsibility of delivering an event that would bring national pride while creating a lasting legacy for the country.

“I reaffirmed their mandate and reminded them that they carry the hopes and aspirations of over 55 million Kenyans to deliver a tournament that brings pride and joy to the country while securing a lasting legacy in sports development, tourism, investment and economic opportunities,” he said.
