World.title: Liberia: As Many as 1,600 Babies Are Born With Sickle Cell Disease Each Year and Up to Half Die Needlessly Before 5. Finally the Government is Doing Something About it
World.content:
Summary:

Sickle cell disease is an inherited blood disease that kills up to half of the 1600 Liberian babies born with it each year before age 5. Until now most of them have died without ever knowing they had it.

Low-cost care can help children with sickle cell live long lives, but Liberia has lacked the testing, medicine and specialists to provide it. Some patients leave the country for treatment. The government is now working on a plan to expand treatment.

Most babies are never tested. Three hospitals in three of Liberia’s 15 counties now test newborns for sickle cell. The government plans to test in every county by 2030. And there are plans for a national count of how many people have the disease.

By Gloria Wleh, senior reporter with New Narratives

72ND COMMUNITY, Montserrado County — Suitcases are being packed here for yet another flight. For 19-year-old Tilnette Woods and her mother, Johnetta Harris-Kamara, plane journeys have become part of their lives.



Tilnette has sickle cell disease, an inherited condition that changes the shape of red blood cells, making them difficult to flow through the body. It causes extreme pain and frequent infections. Untreated, it kills half of the Liberian children born with it by the age of five.

Restricted blood flow to Tilnette’s hip bones has caused them to crumble and die. Now, she has travelled to India for her second hip replacement surgery. She had the first hip replaced in Nigeria in 2023.

Mother and daughter know this is another stopgap measure. Until now, it has been impossible to get the medicine and support she needs to stay alive in Liberia.

“What am I coming back to?” Tilnette asks. “Am I coming back to a country that is going to give up on me? Like it always been giving up on me?”

Through her family’s sacrifice and her suffering Tilnette has beaten the odds. Half of children born with sickle cell disease in Liberia die before their 5th birthday.

The question captures the challenge facing thousands of Liberians diagnosed with sickle cell disease, forced to spend all their money on drugs that keep them alive and seek surgery overseas when that fails.

Sickle cell disease is one of Liberia’s most common inherited illnesses, and one of its least visible. The country has never conducted a nationwide prevalence study and has no national registry for sickle cell disease patients. But a screening study of newborns at a Monrovia hospital found that about one in every 100 babies is born with the disease. Applied to Liberia’s roughly 160,000 births a year, that suggests that 1600 children are affected annually.

Without early diagnosis, most will die before their fifth birthday from infections their bodies cannot fight. But simple, cheap treatments – penicillin, vaccines and malaria prevention – can keep most of them alive.

Now patient advocates are seeing some cause for optimism. The Boakai administration’s health ministry’s has worked with partners to initiate newborn screening in the J.J. Dossen Hospital In Maryland, the John F. Kennedy Hospital in Montserrado and the C.B. Dunbar Hospital in Bong counties, according to Jamesetta Smith, director of the ministry’s Non-Communicable Diseases and Injuries Unit.

Smith says the government plans to expand newborn screening nationwide by the end of 2030 and to include sickle cell in the next national demographic survey to get real data on sufferer numbers.

More than 300 health workers have been trained, Smith says. The building blocks for better treatment are in place.

“Sickle cell can be prevented. Sickle cell can be managed if people are aware early,” Smith says.

A Childhood of Unexplained Pain

As a baby, Tilnette cried whenever she tried to stand. Her family thought she simply did not want to walk. At 11 months, she was taken to Redemption Hospital, where doctors diagnosed an abscess in her leg and performed surgery. Finally, when she was a teenager, after repeated years of tiredness, dizziness, dehydration and anemia, Tilnette was diagnosed with sickle cell disease.

It was a devastating blow for her mother, Johnetta. “I was like, ‘God, how am I going to manage? How am I going to continue to carry on this load?’”

By then, the condition had already begun taking a toll. Tilnette loved dancing and playing with friends. But as the disease progressed, ordinary physical activities became increasingly difficult. During one dance performance, she attempted a split and could not get back up.

“My friends and my dance mates literally had to carry me off,” she recalls. “That was so humiliating.”

The experience forced her to begin researching her condition. She learned that she had to manage the illness every day, not just during crises. She must have plenty of water and avoid extreme heat, cold and physical exertion to prevent dehydration. Sleeping under a treated bed net was essential because malaria can trigger a life-threatening crisis.

Medicines matter – folic acid to help make new blood cells, penicillin to prevent infections, and hydroxyurea, a daily pill, to help stop red blood cells from turning hard and curved. Together they can cut crises by half. Hydroxyurea is now on the World Health Organization’s list of essential medicines, the basic drugs every health system should have. It was added to Liberia’s essential medicines list just last year, but the government is not currently purchasing it. Tilnette has to find it at local pharmacies and pay US$30 a month.

Any fever is an emergency because the disease damages the spleen and leaves the body unable to fight certain infections. Regular clinic visits, up-to-date vaccines and knowing the early signs of a crisis – pain in the chest, a sudden weakness on one side, yellowing eyes – can mean the difference between a hospital stay and a funeral.

By the time Tilnette was diagnosed, the damage to her hip bones was already done. Tilnette was preparing to enter her second semester of college in 2023 when her shattered hip sent her to the hospital. The cost for the replacement in Nigeria was US$10,000. She has started an online funding campaigns at Fundraizer and GoFundMe to raise the money needed for the India trip.

“You can’t be going to school, especially when you’re spending about $500, $600 a semester while you’re saving up for $10,000,” she says. “So I had to drop.”

For Johnetta, 50, her daughter’s illness has meant years of sacrifice. Money that she earns as a civil servant that might have gone toward clothes, shoes or other household needs is instead kept for emergencies. Tilnette’s father, her ex-husband, sometimes helps with money and provides his blood when the need arises.

“I won’t fix my hair. I won’t buy new bag. I won’t buy new shoes,” she says. “I must always have money on me to take care of her.”

The medication can be difficult to obtain. When local pharmacies run out, she has to order it from Ghana at a cost of $50. A month. Without it, the pain can be unbearable.

“Even lying down is painful,” she says. “I turn and toss and turn about 50 times a night before I go to sleep for a couple of hours.”

She has also faced stigma. “Sickle cell patients, when we ask for medicines, like pain medicines, back-to-back, people look at us like, ‘Oh, she’s a drug addict,’” she says.

‘Every Air You Breathe, You Face Severe Pain’

The pain caused by the disease is difficult to explain to people who have never experienced it, according to Wegee Taylor, acting executive director of the Sickle Cell Association of Liberia, a private organization, and a sufferer himself.

“If you look at the level of pain a sickler goes through, when he or she is in crisis, every air you breathe, you face severe pain,” he says.

Misconceptions about sickle cell remain widespread. Some people still attribute the disease to witchcraft or other supernatural causes. The Sickle Cell Association has raised private funds for awareness activities, training of health workers and providing nutritional support to more than 100 sickle cell patients in the association’s database according to Taylor. The Ministry of Health’s Non-Communicable Diseases and Injuries Unit has now focused on awareness-raising to reduce stigma and spread the message that the disease is medical, not a curse.

Just $1000 Allocated for Sickle Cell in Health Ministry’s Budget

The funding gap remains an obstacle. Sickle cell is now included in the Ministry of Health’s five-year non-communicable diseases strategy and 10-year policy. But from the ministry’s total $102 million annual budget, the entire Non-Communicable Diseases and Injuries Unit, which covers cancer, hypertension, diabetes, stroke and disabilities- diseases responsible for two in every five deaths in the country – received just $20,000. Only $1,000 was set aside for sickle cell.

“Generally, the entire department is under-supported,” says Smith.

The main donor-led effort is the American Society of Hematology’s Consortium on Newborn Screening project, run in Liberia since 2025 through the pediatrics department at John F. Kennedy Medical Center in Monrovia. A heel-prick test at birth, costing a few dollars, allows babies to start penicillin and malaria prevention in their first months, get the vaccines that protect a damaged spleen, and have parents who know that a fever is an emergency.

“We’re not waiting for the sickness to start showing itself,” says Dr. Patience Franklin, national coordinator for newborn screening. “We’re running in front of the sickness.”

But the pilot has only reached newborns delivered within JFK’s catchment and the consortium’s five-year period of work ended in September.

Liberia’s neighbors have already shown what is possible. Ghana has screened newborns in Kumasi since 1995, and children found early there survive at rates close to 90 percent. In 2024 the government launched a national sickle cell strategy and now covers hydroxyurea, folic acid and penicillin under its national health insurance, the first African country to offer that standard of care. Nigeria, which has more sickle cell births than any country on earth, has added sickle cell screening to babies’ immunization visits.

Dr. Franklin remains upbeat. The JFK program has trained 175 health workers. The foundation for expanding the program is there.

“What we need to do as a government is to integrate it into our care and make it a priority,” she says. The work on a national strategic plan is a good sign. “That gives me hope that there is some light. I don’t want to be too excited, but I see morelight.”

Knowledge Can Stop the Disease Before it Starts

A simple blood test for would-be parents, costing a few dollars, could be game-changing. Carriers of the gene that causes the disease are healthy and usually have no idea. But when two carriers have a child, there is a one-in-four chance with every pregnancy that the baby will be born with the disease. If people knew their status before they married or had children, couples could plan and seek counseling.

Other African countries have made the test routine. In Nigeria, many churches and mosques now require couples to show their genotype results before a wedding, and several states have passed laws encouraging premarital testing. In Ghana, testing is widely available through public hospitals and church-run pre-marriage counselling, and the government’s 2024–2028 sickle cell strategy makes carrier awareness a national goal.

In Liberia, the test is rarely offered outside a handful of Monrovia hospitals. But the Ministry of Health says it is working toward making genotype testing a compulsory part of premarital counseling once testing capacity improves.

Harris-Kamara wishes she had known more before her daughter was born.

“If I had really known, I would have never had to make her to go through all of this,” she says.

For now, Tilnette is grateful to the public donors who have made this latest hip surgery possible. But she also knows that fundraising cannot replace a health system designed to treat her. Her future and the future of thousands of other children suffering from sickle cell disease now depend on how much of a commitment the health ministry decides to make to helping them.

This story is a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the “Investigating Liberia” project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The funder had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: When The Shepherd Bleeds- Bishop Klayee Breaks the Pulpit’s Silence on Pain
World.content:
Monrovia- Every Sunday, pastors across Liberia climb into pulpits to comfort the grieving, counsel the broken and lift the weary. Few in the pews stop to ask who comforts the preacher.

By: Rodney D. Sieh

That question is the heart of The Bleeding Leader: Leading While Wounded in the Battle of Ministry and Life, the new book by Bishop J. Allan Klayee of Jubilee Ministries International.



Published in 2026 and printed by Denva Books in Accra, the 123-page work makes a case that is simple to state and hard for many churches to accept: leaders bleed, and a ministry culture that forbids them to say so is setting them up to collapse.

The book will be officially launched this Saturday, October 31, at the Monrovia City Hall.

“Followers see the polished sermon, the steady hand guiding a congregation through crisis,” the book’s introduction says. “They see the fruit. They see the confidence. What they rarely see is the bleeding.”

The foreword is written by Bishop Nathaniel N. Zarway, Sr., Diocesan Bishop of the Church of Our Lord Jesus Christ of the Apostolic Faith in Liberia, who calls the author his “son in the gospel” and recommends the book “to every leader who has ever shed tears in private while standing strong in public.”

Although it is written mainly for pastors, the author insists its reach is wider. “The book is not only for the church but speaks to every leader in every sector,” Bishop Klayee said.

Twelve chapters, one wound at a time

Across twelve chapters, Bishop Klayee takes the hidden injuries of leadership one by one. There is the bite from inside the flock (“When Sheep Bite, It Hurts”), the betrayal of trusted friends, the loneliness of being “surrounded by people, known by none,” the weight of carrying other people’s burdens, and the danger of suffering in silence. The final chapters turn toward healing, and toward the idea that a scar can become a source of wisdom rather than shame.

His guides are the great figures of Scripture, chosen, he writes in the preface, “precisely because they were not” invincible. Moses tells God the burden is too heavy and asks to die. Elijah sits under a broom tree days after his triumph on Mount Carmel and prays for death. David writes psalms from caves and flees his own son Absalom. Peter weeps in a courtyard. Paul admits the “daily pressure” of his concern for the churches.

The second chapter, “Protecting the Bleeding General,” turns the lens on congregations. Using the image of Aaron and Hur holding up Moses’ tired arms during the battle with the Amalekites, the author argues that the church has been “far more practiced at expecting protection from its leaders than at providing protection to them.” He calls protecting a pastor “the most self-interested thing a community can do for its own future.”

Where the book is strongest

The book’s greatest service is that it names something many church cultures prefer to keep quiet. It rejects outright the teaching that suffering is proof of weak faith. That kind of “false comfort,” the author writes, adds “a layer of shame and spiritual self-condemnation” to people who are already struggling.

Some of its readings of familiar passages are fresh and memorable. When Moses breaks down in Numbers 11, the author notes, God does not rebuke him. He appoints seventy elders to share the load. When Elijah collapses in the wilderness, the first thing God sends is not a sermon but food and sleep. “The body had to be addressed first,” Bishop Klayee writes, a line that every overworked pastor and every demanding church board should read twice.

The chapter on why

congregations turn on their leaders is wise and generous. The author identifies three causes: misunderstanding, because leaders often cannot explain decisions built on confidences; displaced pain, where a member’s own suffering is aimed at the nearest authority figure; and disappointment when a pastor fails to live up to an idealised image. He urges leaders to ask what may be happening in the life of an attacker, so that an attack becomes “information” rather than only a wound.

The book also offers practical warning signs that a leader is running on empty: emotional flatness, sharpness out of proportion to events, and a quiet withdrawal from prayer and Scripture. And it has lines that stay with the reader, none sharper than this: “The prayer meeting that prays for everyone in the congregation except the person leading it has missed the most obvious application of the very theology it is practicing.”

Importantly, the call to protect leaders is not a call to shield them from scrutiny. Bishop Klayee treats accountability as protection, arguing that “the leader who operates without accountability is not free. They are exposed.” At a time when public trust in institutions, including churches, is fragile, that balance matters.

Where it falls short

The book is not without flaws. The most noticeable is repetition. Elijah under the broom tree appears in at least four chapters. Moses’ plea in Numbers 11 and Paul’s “daily pressure” of concern for the churches are each worked through twice. Galatians 6:9 both opens and closes the argument, and a full passage about the congregation that watches its pastor suffer faithfully appears almost word for word in both the first and last chapters. A firmer edit would have tightened the book considerably.

The prose, while clean and readable, leans heavily on certain words. “Genuine” and “genuinely” appear about 170 times, and “specific” is not far behind. In places, the sentences grow long and abstract, circling an idea rather than landing it. More significant is what is missing.

In the preface, the author says the book grew from years of walking with wounded pastors and from “my own seasons of wounding.” Yet readers hear almost nothing of those stories. Beyond the biblical figures, there are few real cases, no Liberian pastor who burned out and recovered, no congregation that learned to care for its leader.

Those stories would have given the book a local heartbeat and made its lessons easier to apply.

The practical guidance is also thinner than the diagnosis. The book briefly names compassion fatigue and clinical depression but says little about when a pastor should seek professional counselling, how a church might arrange rest or sabbatical time, or how to build the kind of shared leadership Moses received. Readers looking for a step-by-step plan will find encouragement more than instruction.

Verdict

The Bleeding Leader is a sincere, pastoral and timely book. Its central message, that a wounded leader is not a disqualified leader, needs to be heard in Liberian churches and beyond, in boardrooms, ministries and public offices where leaders are expected never to break. Its repetitions and missing personal stories keep it from being the definitive work on the subject. But for the pastor preparing a message of hope on Saturday night while privately feeling hopeless, it offers what its author promises: the assurance that “you are seen. You are not alone.”

It should be read by pastors, and perhaps even more by the deacons, elders and church members who sit in front of them every Sunday.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Signals Plans for Creation of Sovereign Wealth Fund, National Mining Company At Int’l Confab
World.content:
Unification Town, Margibi County – While launching Liberia’s first mining and energy conference within a decade and a half, President Joseph Nyuma hinted at the imminent establishment of two major institutions: the National Mining Company of Liberia and the Liberia Sovereign Wealth Fund.

Speaking at the landmark international conference that brought together a thousand-plus delegates from Liberia and the globe, the Liberian leader pointed out that for long, resource-rich countries, including Liberia, have exported raw materials while importing finished products, technology, and expertise, stressing that Liberia intends to take a different path.

“Our minerals should support domestic processing, industrial development, infrastructure, technology, and decent jobs. Electricity should power industry, agriculture, small businesses, and public services, improve competitiveness, and help reduce poverty,” asserted President Boakai.



Move Towards State Participation

The Liberian Chief Executive announced the government is advancing three important initiatives as it aims to change the narrative in the mining and energy sectors.

In a bid to achieve this, he disclosed that the first step is the establishment of a National Mining Company of Liberia that moves the country toward more active state participation through equity and strategic ownership, rather than relying only on royalty collection.

Secondly, he revealed that within two years, Liberia seeks to establish its first gold processing facility, advancing the African Minerals Strategy Group’s call for value addition before minerals leave the continent.

According to him, Liberia intends to contribute to this continental agenda by retaining more value at home and creating skilled jobs.

“The Government’s stated policy is for gold extracted in Liberia to undergo primary and secondary refining to internationally recognized purity standards at licensed domestic facilities before export,” he furthered.

Third, President Boakai informed the gathering that government has authorized the creation of the Liberia Sovereign Wealth Fund, which is intended to operate as an independent investment vehicle in line with the international Santiago Principles.

“By directing a fixed percentage of mineral revenues into diversified domestic and global investments, the Fund would help convert finite mineral wealth into long-term financial security for future generations as well as reduce exposure to commodity-market cycles.”

“If mining is one engine of Liberia’s economic transformation, energy must power that engine. Unreliable, expensive, and limited electricity constrains businesses, raises production costs, discourages investment, and limits services for hospitals, schools, agricultural processors, manufacturers, small enterprises, and households.”

More Energy Generation

On the energy side, he explained that the government is pursuing renewable generation, stronger transmission and distribution, regional electricity integration, better utility performance, and greater private-sector participation.

“The 20-megawatt solar photovoltaic facility associated with the Mount Coffee energy development program is an important step toward diversifying generation and reducing dependence on more expensive and less sustainable power sources.”

It could be recalled that the government sometimes ago announced additional financing to expand solar generation capacity from 20 to 30 megawatts, install a 12-megawatt battery energy storage system, and make further improvements to the Mount Coffee facility.

The Liberian leader indicated that the government will encourage utility-scale solar, distributed renewable energy, mini-grids, and other technically and commercially viable clean-energy investments.

An Ambitious Energy Plan In Sight

The President asserted that the national ambition is to increase renewables to 75 percent of the electricity generation mix while expanding access and improving reliability, adding that government will pursue this through sound planning, credible procurement, environmental and social safeguards, and partnerships capable of delivering results.

“Liberia’s hydropower resources offer important long-term opportunities. The Government will continue technical, environmental, financial, and procurement preparations for additional capacity, including the proposed Saint Paul River hydropower development.”

“These projects require careful consideration of financing, construction costs, environmental impacts, any necessary resettlement, water-resource management, and long-term operations.”

Accordingly, the Liberian chief executive intoned that the key objective is to strengthen energy security, support industrial growth, and contribute to regional electricity supply where feasible.

“Generation alone cannot solve our electricity challenges. Power must be transmitted efficiently and distributed reliably to businesses, communities, and households. Our I Government will continue working to improve transmission capacity, strengthen distribution networks, reduce technical and commercial losses, and expand connections to underserved communities.”

Mining, A Major Pillar To Economic Growth

The President reminded Liberians and international partners that mining remains a major pillar of Liberia’s economy, contributing to exports, foreign exchange, public revenue, employment, infrastructure, and community economic activity.

Since January 2024, he recalled that mining and energy have been central to our national growth strategy. Mining expanded by 17 percent.

“Liberia achieved overall GDP growth of 5.1 percent, with real GDP growth of 5.5 percent projected. Mining contributed 18.4 percent of real GDP in 2025 and is projected at 19.4 percent in 2026.”

Statistically, President Boakai reported that the sector contributed approximately US$124 million directly to national revenue in 2024 and US$432 million to domestic revenue to date.

“This supports the US$1.1 billion domestic revenue milestone projected for this year, compared with US$699 million in 2024, and helps fund infrastructure, education, and healthcare.”

“Liberia is entering a new investment cycle. Iron ore remains an important foundation, while gold, diamonds, and emerging mineral opportunities offer prospects for diversification. Our priority is to attract investment while strengthening governance, geological information, domestic participation, and national economic returns.”

A Need For Reliable Geological Data

He also informed the conference that the government is advancing geological mapping, analysis of new findings, improved mineral information management, and access to technical data through a coordinated national exploration program over the next five years.

“A US$30 million airborne geophysics data collection is planned under the MCC compact to support systematic exploration and improve knowledge of critical and strategic minerals. Transparent procedures will improve qualified investors’ access to geological information while protecting legitimate commercial interests and the public interest. Our objective is to reduce uncertainty and build a stronger pipeline of viable mining projects.”

“Our Government is strengthening mineral-rights administration, licensing, oversight, and accountability. We will review the Minerals and Mining Law and related regulations to reflect investment practices, environmental standards, technology, and Liberia’s development objectives.”

Seeking Fair Trade

In a clarion call to would-be investors, President Boakai sounded a caveat for fair and responsible investment that lays to bed equity revenue for them and returns for the country.

“We seek clear rules, fair administration, and predictable procedures. Operators must obey the law, pay required fees and taxes, meet environmental obligations, and respect workers and host communities. Mineral resources are finite, and we must ensure they generate lasting returns for Liberians.”

An Aggressive Approach

Also speaking at the occasion, Mines and Energy Minister R. Matenokay Tingban says Liberia is moving aggressively to build a domestic gold refinery and formalize its artisanal mining sector as part of a broader push to retain more value from its mineral wealth.

Min. Tingban reckoned that about 80% of Liberia remains geologically unexplored since early mineral mapping in the 1970s, leaving the country without reliable data to negotiate.”No data, no view,” the Minister stressed. “We must know what we have before negotiating how it is developed.

Gold Refinery and State Miner Confirmed

Prior to President Boakai’s official opening remarks, Tingban, who first took the podium, confirmed the government’s pursuit of a domestic gold refinery, saying the Ministry has opened a transparent process to attract technically capable and financially credible partners who meet recognized standards for responsible sourcing, assaying, refining and certification.

“A domestic refinery could retain more value in Liberia, strengthen oversight of the gold trade, improve traceability and revenue collection, create skilled jobs, and provide small miners, brokers and dealers with credible local markets.”

He indicated that the facility will require reliable electricity, sound environmental management, anti-money laundering controls, and a traceable supply chain that includes artisanal and small-scale miners.

The company, he noted, will serve as a vehicle for responsible state participation and will pursue viable exploration, mining, processing and value addition with qualified Liberian and international investors.

“The company must have high professional management, transparent financial reporting, strong corporate governance and clear accountability,” Tingban noted, adding that its commercial activities must remain separate from the Ministry’s regulatory function to avoid conflict of interest.

Artisanal Miners Organization Drive

Min. Tingban also announced the launch of Liberia’s Artisanal and Small-Scale Mining Organization initiative, aimed at bringing thousands of miners currently operating outside the formal system into the legal economy.

“Many miners remain outside a system that will improve safety, protect rights, and connect production to formal markets. Our approach must be practical and inclusive.”

The initiative, he said, will make licensing and registration more accessible, help miners form cooperatives, provide training in occupational safety and environmental protection, and improve access to equipment, financing and mineral traceability systems.

US Eyes Liberia, But Calls For Reforms

On behalf of the Government of the United States of America (USA), U.S. Chargé d’Affaires, Kristin Gilmore says American businesses are now actively considering Liberia for long-term mining and energy investments, but their decision to stay will depend on Liberia’s ability to deliver transparent and predictable reforms.

The American diplomat Gilmore, stated that her introductory meetings since arriving in Liberia a few weeks ago showed a clear desire by the Liberian government to move up the value chain, create jobs, and attract international investors.

The US envoy Gilmore believes that those goals align directly with Washington’s push to diversify global supply chains and secure reliable access to metals, critical minerals, and derivative products.

She disclosed that the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) last year reaffirmed Liberia’s eligibility for a second compact, which is now under development and will focus on mining and electricity sector reforms, two areas she described as critical to unlocking private investment and long-term economic growth.

The US envoy also announced that the U.S. Trade and Development Agency (USTDA) is finalizing a grant to assess Liberia’s rail infrastructure capacity in support of President Joseph Boakai’s vision for a multi-user rail system.

“Multi-user rail is key to unlocking opportunities in Liberia’s minerals and agricultural sectors,” Gilmore declared, stressing that Washington welcomes government’s commitment and looks forward to timely passage of legislation establishing a transparent, independently regulated rail system.

World.title: Liberia: Discharged AFL Sergeants Demand Reinstatement, Allege Due Process Violations
World.content:
Lawyers for Abu S.B. Sheriff and Robert Menyon say the military summarily dismissed the soldiers over a viral assault video without an investigation or hearing, asking the Defense Ministry to reverse the decision and restore their salaries and benefits.

MONROVIA — Lawyers representing two Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL) sergeants dismissed after a viral video showed one of them allegedly assaulting a young woman are demanding their immediate reinstatement, accusing the military leadership of violating their constitutional rights and bypassing established disciplinary procedures.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

In a letter dated October 27, 2026, and addressed to Acting Minister of National Defense Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh, the law firm Kailondo & Associates argued that the October 21 discharge of Sergeants Abu S.B. Sheriff and Robert Menyon was unlawful because the soldiers were allegedly dismissed without a formal investigation, hearing, or opportunity to respond to the allegations.



The lawyers are asking the Defense Ministry to reverse the decision, reinstate the two former soldiers, and restore their salaries, privileges, and pension contributions. They have also requested a formal, confidential, and impartial investigation into the incident should the authorities wish to pursue disciplinary action.

The demand places the military’s response to the viral video under scrutiny, raising questions about how the AFL balances discipline and accountability with the constitutional and statutory protections afforded to its personnel.

Lawyers Cite Constitutional, Legal Violations

According to the letter, the two sergeants served the Liberian military for more than 18 years and maintained clean service records before their discharge.

The firm argued that their dismissal violated Article 20(a) of Liberia’s 1986 Constitution, which protects individuals against deprivation of their rights and privileges without due process of law.

It also invoked Article 21(h), which guarantees the presumption of innocence until guilt is established beyond a reasonable doubt, arguing that the military’s public action against the soldiers effectively punished them before a formal determination of their alleged misconduct.

The lawyers maintained that the circulation of a video on Facebook could not, by itself, replace an investigation or a disciplinary hearing.

They further cited Sections 7.7 and 7.13 of the National Defense Act of 2008, arguing that although the law provides grounds for discharging military personnel, disciplinary action must comply with applicable AFL regulations and the Uniform Code of Military Justice.

Section 8.4, which provides AFL personnel with legal protections and safeguards comparable to those enjoyed by other Liberian citizens, was also cited in the complaint.

The firm argued that the military could not invoke the need to preserve discipline or the good of the service as justification for bypassing established procedures.

“The military justice system must not be sacrificed on the altar of public opinion,” the lawyers stated in their letter, warning against what they characterized as “social media justice.”

They contended that allowing dismissals based on viral videos without appropriate procedural safeguards could expose other military personnel to arbitrary punishment.

Viral Video Triggers Military Action

The two sergeants were dismissed after a video circulated on social media showing an altercation involving a soldier and a young woman identified as Blessing.

According to Blessing’s account, the incident began when soldiers pursued a group of boys who were playing football in their community. Her younger brother was among the boys and reportedly ran into their home as the soldiers chased them.

Blessing said she intervened and pleaded with the soldiers to leave her brother alone. She alleged that Sergeant Sheriff began beating her while she was holding her baby.

She said Sergeant Menyon attempted to intervene and stop his colleague but was unsuccessful.

The woman also indicated that the soldiers later apologized and that she forgave them. She reportedly wanted them to face some form of punishment but did not want them to lose their military careers.

Her account has added another dimension to the controversy surrounding the dismissals, particularly as the military’s disciplinary response has consequences beyond the two former service members.

AFL Chief of Staff Major General Davidson F. Forleh condemned the soldiers’ alleged conduct, describing them as “bad apples” within the military and likening them to an “Ebola virus.”

Following the dismissals, the two men were publicly presented, and Forleh reportedly instructed the Liberia National Police to handcuff them.

He also directed that their families leave the AFL barracks and that the former soldiers be taken to an area near the Samuel Kanyon Doe Sports Complex to find their way home.

The measures have raised further questions about the treatment of the dismissed personnel and their families, although the lawyers’ October 27 letter primarily challenges the legality of the discharge itself.

Defense Ministry Asked to Intervene

Kailondo & Associates has called on Acting Defense Minister Tweh to intervene and reverse the decision, arguing that the military should investigate the incident through established procedures rather than impose what it considers summary punishment.

The firm requested a response within 10 working days of receipt of the letter.

Copies were sent to President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, who is commander-in-chief of the AFL; Major General Forleh; and Senator Momo T. Cyrus, chairman of the Senate Committee on National Defense, Security and Veteran Affairs.

The letter was signed by Counsellor-at-Law Sylvester G. Lormie II.

The legal challenge does not dispute the need for the military to address allegations of misconduct by its personnel. Instead, it argues that accountability must be pursued within the framework of the law and that the soldiers should have been afforded an opportunity to answer the allegations before the dismissal decision was made.

The Defense Ministry and AFL leadership are yet to respond.

The outcome could test the military’s disciplinary procedures and the extent to which administrative decisions affecting service members must comply with constitutional due-process protections.

World.title: Liberia: RREA Showcases Energy Achievements atLiberia International Mining and Energy Conference
World.content:
FARMINGTON HOTEL, LIBERIA — The Rural and Renewable Energy Agency (RREA) has showcased its ongoing initiatives and achievements in expanding access to reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy across Liberia on the opening day of the Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference and Expo.

The agency, which is a proud sponsor of the conference being held at the Farmington Hotel, used the exhibition to highlight its efforts toward improving electricity access, promoting renewable energy, and delivering sustainable energy solutions to underserved communities across the country.

During the first day of the event, RREA engaged with key government officials and stakeholders, including His Excellency the President of Liberia, the Minister of Mines and Energy, and the Minister of Information. The engagements provided an opportunity to showcase the agency’s work and underscore the importance of collaboration in advancing Liberia’s energy sector.



RREA is calling on development partners, investors, and other stakeholders to join efforts to expand energy access, accelerate renewable energy investments, and support the delivery of sustainable electricity solutions to communities with limited or no access to power.

The agency emphasized that mobilizing resources, fostering innovation, and building strategic partnerships are essential to transforming lives, strengthening communities, and driving national development through improved energy access.

Through its participation in the conference, RREA reaffirmed its commitment to promoting sustainable energy development and ensuring that more Liberians benefit from reliable and affordable electricity.

World.title: Chamber of Mines President Amara Kamara Calls For Liberia’s Mineral Wealth to Create Jobs, Build Infrastructure and Deliver Lasting Benefits to Citizens
World.content:
FARMINGTON, Margibi County-Chamber of Mines President Amara Kamara has called for Liberia’s mining industry to deliver greater benefits to citizens, saying the country’s mineral wealth must translate into jobs, stronger local businesses, improved infrastructure, better living standards and deliver lasting benefits to citizens.

By Jaheim T. Tumu- [email protected]

Addressing Liberia’s Second International Mining and Energy Conference and Exhibition (LIMEC 2026) opening which was held under the theme: “Transforming Liberia’s Economy: Driving Development Through Sustainable Mining and Energy Investments,” Kamara said the success of the sector should go beyond the export of gold, diamonds and iron ore to include tangible improvements in the lives of Liberians.



President Joseph Nyuma Boakai delivered the keynote address, setting out his government’s plans for drawing investment and promoting responsible development of the country’s mineral resources.

Chamber of Mines President Kamara’s remarks came as President Boakai delivered the keynote address, outlining his government’s plans to attract investment and promote the responsible development of Liberia’s mineral resources.

The event brought together international guests, investors, development partners, technical experts and business leaders from across Africa and beyond to explore opportunities in Liberia’s mining and energy sectors.

Their presence underscored growing global interest in the country’s mineral wealth, energy potential and prospects for sustainable economic transformation.

Kamara said the country must judge the value of its mining industry by the opportunities it creates for its people, including employment, business development, infrastructure, skills transfer and long-term economic benefits.

“Our success must not be measured simply by our traditional minerals export, gold, diamonds, and iron ore,” he said.

“It must be measured by the jobs we create, the businesses we develop, the infrastructure we build, the skills we transfer, and the lasting benefits we deliver to the Liberian people.”

He emphasized that Liberia has an opportunity to attract investment as global demand grows for critical minerals, renewable energy and reliable supply chains.

However, he warned that the country’s natural resources alone would not guarantee the investment needed to expand the sector.

“Mineral potential alone does not attract investment,” Kamara said, pointing to the need for reliable geological data, adequate infrastructure, affordable energy, skilled professionals, project financing, transparent regulation and a predictable investment environment.

He argued that Liberia must create the right conditions to move mining projects from exploration to discovery and production while ensuring that the benefits extend beyond mining companies to the wider economy.

Kamara called for sustained investment from international investors, Liberian businesses, development finance institutions and strategic partners, stressing that the country needs capital accompanied by expertise, technology, skills development and a long-term commitment to national growth.

Infrastructure and Energy Key to Mining Growth

Kamara said the expansion of the mining sector would remain difficult without reliable roads, railways, ports, electricity and efficient transportation systems.

He urged Liberia to treat infrastructure development as a national priority rather than an investment intended only to serve individual mining operations.

He identified railway corridors, the Port of Buchanan, the Port of Greenville and standalone river-barging ports as important opportunities to improve transportation and support economic activities across the country.

“These investments in railway corridors, the Port of Buchanan, Port of Greenville, Stand alone river barging port, and other strategic infrastructure must be viewed not merely as mining assets, but as platforms for broader national development,” he stated.

Kamara explained that infrastructure designed to support mining could also benefit other industries, improve the movement of goods and create opportunities for communities beyond mining areas.

He also called for greater investment in affordable and reliable electricity, identifying hydropower, solar energy, mini-grids and hybrid power systems as possible ways to support industrial development and expand access to electricity.

He said mining and energy development must advance together to improve the operating environment for investors while creating wider economic opportunities for Liberian businesses and communities.

Local Businesses Must Benefit

Kamara described local content as a national priority, arguing that Liberian companies should have greater opportunities to supply mining operations, provide technical services and participate in major infrastructure projects.

He said local content should go beyond meeting legal requirements and focus on building the capacity of Liberian businesses to compete and grow within the mining and energy industries.

“As President of The Liberia Chamber of Mines, I consider local content a national priority,” he said.

He also called for greater investment in Liberian geologists, engineers, technicians, environmental professionals and managers, saying the country needs a skilled workforce capable of taking on more responsibilities in the sector.

Kamara urged international investors and contractors to develop local partnerships, transfer technology and strengthen the skills of Liberian workers. He said such efforts would help ensure that more of the economic benefits generated by mining remain within the country.

Responsible Mining Remains Essential

While encouraging increased investment, Kamara said mining activities must be guided by environmental protection, worker safety, community engagement and transparency.

He warned that economic growth would be difficult to sustain without public confidence and meaningful benefits for communities affected by mining operations.

“Responsible mining must remain non-negotiable,” he said, adding that fiscal responsibility and meaningful benefit-sharing were essential to building trust and sustaining investment.

His remarks highlighted the need for mining companies to consider the environmental and social effects of their operations while ensuring that resource development contributes to broader national prosperity.

Kamara maintained that responsible resource development and economic growth should advance together, allowing Liberia to attract investment without losing sight of its obligations to citizens and affected communities.

Liberia Seeks Long-Term Investment

Addressing international investors and development partners, Kamara urged them to look beyond mineral deposits and consider opportunities in exploration, mining services, energy, transportation, logistics, infrastructure and local supply chains.

He said Liberia was open to international capital but needed investors willing to contribute more than money to the country’s development.

“Liberia invites international capital. We need investment accompanied by expertise, technology, skills, infrastructure, and a long-term commitment to our country,” he said.

Kamara said the Liberia Chamber of Mines was ready to work with the government, investors, development institutions, communities and Liberian businesses to address investment challenges and promote sustainable growth.

Looking Toward 2030

As Liberia looks toward 2030, Kamara said the country should aim to advance more exploration projects, develop new mines, unlock critical mineral opportunities, improve infrastructure, expand electricity access and increase the participation of Liberian businesses throughout the mining and energy value chains.

He said the ultimate goal should be to ensure that natural-resource development contributes to employment, economic diversification, government revenue and improved living standards.

Kamara urged participants to make LIMEC 2026 a platform for practical action rather than simply a gathering for speeches and discussions.

“LIMEC 2026 must therefore be more than a conference. It must be a platform for practical action and advancing investment in our enriched sector,” he said.

Kamara said Liberia’s mining and energy future should not be defined only by what the country extracts from the ground, but also by the industries, infrastructure, businesses and skills it builds for future generations.

World.title: UPND’s Adrian Banda wins Mandevu unopposed as all three rivals pull out
World.content:
Banda set to take Mandevu unopposed as three rivals pull out

UPND candidate Adrian Banda is set to become the sole contender in the Mandevu Constituency parliamentary by-election after all three of his rivals withdrew from the race ahead of the November 5 poll.

Forum for Democracy and Development (FDD) candidate Daniel Chisenga, independent candidate Daniel Daka and Leadership Movement candidate Ntazana Muntungwa each formally notified the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) of their withdrawal in separate letters dated October 28, 2026.

Mr Chisenga, a former Lusaka Mayor who was contesting as the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance candidate under the FDD, the alliance’s special purpose vehicle, gave no reasons for his decision. Mr Daka simply asked the commission to exclude him from the election, while Mr Muntungwa cited financial constraints.

Their exit leaves Mr Banda as the only candidate among the four previously approved contenders, although his election unopposed will depend on the applicable electoral procedures and formal confirmation by the ECZ.

The development marks a dramatic turn in a contest that has been troubled from the start. Mandevu voted with the rest of the country on August 13, but no Member of Parliament was ever declared. On 18 August, unknown individuals stormed the Mandevu totalling centre, attacked staff, destroyed result transmission kits and fled with election documents, and ballot papers were later found dumped in drainages and burnt, leaving the returning officer unable to declare a result.

ECZ Chief Electoral Officer Brown Kasaro said the decision to hold a fresh poll followed an official report dated August 18 from the Lusaka District Electoral Officer. The move drew criticism from the Zambian Civil Liberties Union, which argued that the ECZ had no legal basis to conduct a fresh parliamentary election in the constituency and questioned what vacancy had triggered a by-election when a targeted remedy at the affected polling stations might have sufficed.

The commission went on to set November 5 for the Mandevu poll, alongside by-elections for the Mbala mayoral seat, the Lumezi parliamentary seat and eleven wards across five provinces. Nominations were held on October 8, with campaigns running from October 10 until 18:00 hours on November 4.

Mr Banda’s own route to the seat has been a notable turnaround. He contested the August 13 election as an independent and was among the leading contenders, alongside UPND candidate Christopher Shakafuswa and Jean Kapata, before the ruling party adopted him as its by-election candidate.

The opposition picture also shifted along the way. The Tonse Pamodzi Alliance had initially announced Ms Kapata, a former MP for the constituency under the Patriotic Front, as its Mandevu candidate, but Mr Chisenga ultimately carried the alliance’s ticket under the FDD.

News of the withdrawals quickly sparked accusations. A statement circulating on social media from opposition supporters accused the ruling party of corruption, likening the episode to what happened with the Lusaka Mayor’s seat, and turned on the candidates themselves for what it called disloyalty and the acceptance of open and public bribes. These allegations have not been independently verified.

Socialist Party President Fred M’membe described the withdrawals as a tragedy for democracy, insisting they were no accident and blaming what he called a hostile and heavily skewed political environment created by the UPND. He said a win secured by clearing the ballot of alternatives was no victory at all, arguing that it denied more than 100,000 registered voters in Mandevu their constitutional right to choose their representative.

Dr M’membe noted that the Tonse Alliance leadership had earlier raised concerns over security threats facing its candidate. He accused the ruling party of pursuing a rubber-stamp parliament and a two-thirds majority, and urged the ECZ to handle the matter with transparency and to protect voter choice.

On social media, many questioned how a victory without a contest could be celebrated. “How can there be a victory without a fight?” asked Malama Charles, while Lawrence Mwale pointed to the timing: “On the same day, three candidates withdrawing? Chalo ichi.”

Several users warned of a slide towards one-party rule. “One party state loading,” wrote Chikondi Jonathan, as Cephas Nkole said he was worried about Parliament. Max Chulu drew on history, writing that Zambians had “watched this movie before,” and warning that it ended badly, even for those who had been clapping.

Mukombo Owen said the real question was why candidates were withdrawing. “Is it because they want to support UPND or is it they are afraid of something? Truth be told, this is not good for our democracy,” he wrote. Benson Kansumba claimed candidates feared attacks from party cadres, reminding the ruling party that power is temporary, while several readers asked what had become of Ms Kapata’s candidacy.

Not everyone was critical. UPND supporters welcomed the outcome, with Victor Siamate writing, “If you can’t beat them, join them,” and Kelvin Hantete urging the party forward.

Others raised practical concerns about what now happens to the November 5 poll, and to the money set aside for polling staff, with only one candidate left standing.

World.title: Mandevu withdrawals expose UPND’s creeping dictatorship
World.content:
Comrades, fellow citizens, and members of the press,

What we witnessed in Mandevu today, October 29, 2026, is a tragedy for our democracy, but it is not an accident. The sudden, simultaneous withdrawal of all three opposition and independent candidates, Daniel Chisenga (FDD/Tonse Alliance), Ntazana Muntungwa (Leadership Movement), and independent candidate Daniel Daka, is the direct result of a calculated, oppressive, and heavily skewed political environment engineered by the ruling UPND regime.

As I have consistently warned the nation over the last 24 hours, “Our nation is hurtling toward a dangerous precipice. The democratic foundations and economic sovereignty of Zambia are not merely under threat. They are being systematically dismantled before our very eyes.” What happened today in Mandevu is a vivid, painful confirmation of that reality.

It is deeply alarming that an opposition alliance candidate can be forced out of a race through persistent, state-backed intimidation, financial strangulation, and a hostile playing field. Prior to this capitulation, the Tonse Alliance leadership had explicitly raised the alarm over the intense security threats their candidate was facing.

Let us be clear: a victory achieved by clearing the ballot of any alternative choice is no victory at all. It is a manufactured walkover that strips well over 100,000 registered voters in Mandevu of their constitutional right to choose who represents them.

To the UPND and Mr Hakainde Hichilema, we say what we have always said: “By clearing half-baked, politically manufactured charges… you are actively bypassing constitutional rights. This is not prosecution; it is persecution.”

By leaving the ruling UPND candidate, Adrian Banda, as the sole contender ahead of the scheduled November 5 poll, this regime is executing its broader authoritarian agenda. They are hungry for a rubber-stamp parliament and a two-thirds majority, and they care nothing for the democratic principles our nation has fought for decades to maintain.

We, as the Socialist Party, “refuse to sit idly by while the hard-won liberties of the Zambian people are traded away for authoritarian control.” “The time for polite diplomatic silence is over; the crisis facing our republic demands immediate, uncompromising action.” We can not defeat this creeping dictatorship if the opposition is easily intimidated.

We call on the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) to handle this matter with utmost transparency and constitutional adherence. Their primary duty is to protect the integrity of the ballot and voter choice, not facilitate uncontested walkovers for the ruling party.

To the people of Mandevu and all across Zambia: do not be disheartened. We must remain vigilant, organised, and resolute. We will continue to stand together, fight for an equitable nation, and defend our democracy against those who seek to capture it for themselves.

The struggle continues. Aluta Continua!

Fred M’membe

SP President

World.title: Catholic church urged to support Grow Zambia agenda
World.content:
A Catholic clergy in Monze, Father Cletus Mwiila, has urged the church to support the government’s Grow Zambia Agenda by actively contributing to national development.

Father Mwiila also called on Christians to continue praying for President Hakainde Hichilema so that God grants him wisdom and guidance as he governs the nation.

He noted that the church has a critical role to play in complementing the government’s efforts to improve the welfare of citizens and foster national development.

Father Mwiila said this during a thanksgiving Mass to celebrate the 99th birthday of John Michelo of Kayuni settlement in Monze district.

And in his homily, Father Mwiila urged congregants to emulate Mr Michelo’s spirit of generosity, selflessness and dedication to the work of God.

He described Mr Michelo as a committed Christian who has demonstrated his faith through service to the Church for several decades.

Father Mwiila cited Mr Michelo’s contribution towards the establishment of the Catholic Church in Kayuni in 1979, including offering land for the construction of the church in his settlement, supporting priests and maintaining the church surroundings.

He further encouraged Christians to cultivate a spirit of thanksgiving and always appreciate God’s blessings.

Drawing from Luke Chapter 17, verses 11 to 19, which recounts the healing of ten lepers, Father Mwiila reminded congregants that only one of the ten returned to thank Jesus after being healed.

He urged Christians not to take God’s blessings for granted but to remain grateful in all circumstances.

Mr Michelo, who was among 38 people allocated land by government at Kayuni settlement, is one of only four surviving members of the original group.

In 1979, he was entrusted with helping to establish the Catholic Church in the area and has since remained committed to its growth, serving as a catechist then and supporting the clergy.

His dedication to the Church extended to personally clearing weeds around the church premises during the rainy season and travelling long distances on foot to fulfil his Christian responsibilities.

The thanksgiving Mass brought together family members, friends and members of the Catholic community to celebrate Mr Michelo’s 99 years of life, faith and service to the Church.

World.title: REA records 13,286 subsidised electricity connections
World.content:
The Rural Electrification Authority (REA) has registered 13,286 electricity connections in Southern Province under the Accelerating Sustainable and Clean Energy Access Transformation (ASCENT) subsidised programme.

REA Director of Services Suzyo Silavwe says the programme aims to make electricity more affordable for households and businesses, with eligible customers paying 300 kwacha instead of 4,846 kwacha for a standard single-phase connection.

Mr Silavwe said Southern Province had recorded the highest number of connections, with Sinazongwe district accounting for 750.

He was speaking during a visit to Sinazongwe district by a team of REA Board members and staff.

Meanwhile, Sinazongwe Acting District Commissioner Passmore Ntiindu has commended REA for implementing electrification projects worth about 8 million kwacha in the district to enhance electricity access and promote socio-economic development.

Mr Ntiindu said the projects were in line with government’s efforts to improve digital access in marginalised communities and provide learners with opportunities to acquire computer skills.

“We are happy that we are tapping this development of electricity to enhance socio-economic development and provide computer lessons for pupils,” he said.

REA Southern Province Regional Manager Wazingwa Mugala said one of the two projects had been completed, while the second was still underway.

The projects include the Matambo grid extension, which has connected Matambo Health Clinic, a school and the Chief’s palace, currently under construction through the Constituency Development Fund, to electricity.

Meanwhile, Sinazongwe district Director of Health Services Christabel Musonda has commended REA for connecting Matambo Health Clinic to the electricity grid, saying the development would improve healthcare delivery.

Dr Musonda said the facility serves 2,062 people who would benefit from improved health services following the electricity connection.

“We are very excited as a district to have this facility electrified; it is a facility servicing 2,062 people, and all these are going to benefit from quality healthcare services through the Rural Electrification Authority project,” she said.

Chief Mweemba’s representative, Victory Mwiinde, has also thanked REA for the Matambo grid extension, saying the connection of the chief’s palace, school and health facility would support improved service delivery and community development.

World.title: Government calls for concerted efforts in achieving Zambia’s climate objectives
World.content:
ma has called for strengthened institutional coordination, adequate financing and clear implementation strategies to ensure Zambia achieves its climate commitments.

Speaking during the validation meeting held in Lusaka today, Dr Chibamba said the implementation of the country’s third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC3) required measurable targets, clearly defined institutional responsibilities and sufficient technical capacity to translate climate policies into practical action.

Dr Chibamba said this in a speech read for him by the Ministry of Green Economy and Environment Human Resource and Administration Director Ranford Simumbwe.

The Permanent Secretary said achieving Zambia’s climate objectives required coordinated efforts across key sectors such as agriculture, forestry, renewable energy and energy efficiency, transport, tourism, infrastructure, mining, water security and waste management.

He said the Ministry, in collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme Copenhagen Climate Change Centre (UNEP-CCC), with financial support from the NDC Partnership, was validating three instruments aimed at strengthening the implementation of Zambia’s climate commitments.

The instruments are the updated NDC implementation framework, the NDC investment plan and the capacity needs assessment.

He explained that the implementation framework will provide a clear pathway for translating Zambia’s NDC3 commitments into practical actions, while the investment plan will identify financing requirements and investment opportunities.

Dr Chibamba said the capacity needs assessment that will help establish the institutional and technical capacity required to implement the country’s climate commitments effectively.

He urged stakeholders to ensure that the instruments contained measurable targets, appropriate indicators and effective monitoring arrangements that reflected the realities of institutions responsible for implementation.

Dr Chibamba further called for stronger coordination among sectors and institutions to reduce duplication of reporting and promote synergies between climate action and national development priorities.

He reaffirmed the Ministry’s commitment to providing leadership in implementing Zambia’s climate commitments in collaboration with relevant government institutions, the private sector, development partners and other stakeholders.

World.title: Rethink Youth Platform calls for free distribution of sanitary pads
World.content:
Rethink Youth Platform Executive Director Jimmy Zozi has called for free distribution of sanitary pads to girls and women to help end period poverty in Zambia.

Speaking in an exclusive with the media news, Mr Zozi said for Zambia to maintain the Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and achieve vision 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, it has to put menstrual health and hygiene first.

‎‎Mr Zozi stated that promoting menstrual health and hygiene does not end at catering for well-being but goes beyond growth as girls maintain attendance in schools and women are able to serve with poise contributing to the nation’s development.

‎He further called on government to come up with deliberate policies to support such cause, stating that it will attract agencies to come on board to drive and sustain the move

‎‎“Government is a major stakeholder in promoting this agenda, ” he said.

‎‎ “The community and other civil society organisations should also come on board to help with initiatives of sanitary pad donations.”

Meanwhile Planned Parenthood Associates of Zambia (PPAZ) member Kondwelani Kamanga bemoaned that most girls are exposed to health risks as they opt to use other means during their period cycle.

‎Mr Kamanga emphasised the importance of collaboration especially in the education sector in promoting young people who cannot afford sanitary pads to stay in school.

World.title: Two Jailed 5years for illegal ivory possession and two fined for illegal timber possession
World.content:
The Lusaka Magistrate Court has sentenced two men to five years imprisonment each for unlawful possession of elephant ivory.

Lusaka Magistrate Anna Holland sentenced Bydon Ndolo, 30, and West Ng’andu, 48, to jail after finding them guilty of unlawfully possessing a prescribed trophy under the Zambia Wildlife Act.

According to a statement issued by the Department of National Parks and Wildlife (DNPW), the two were apprehended on 1st May, 2025 along Mumbwa Road in Lusaka together with Lighton Nyirongo, 34, on suspicion of selling elephant ivory.

The three were found in possession of five cut pieces of elephant ivory reportedly intended for the Congolese market.

They were charged with unlawful possession of a prescribed trophy and denied the charges before proceeding to trial.

Delivering judgement on 23rd October, 2026, Magistrate Holland convicted Ndolo and Ng’andu and sentenced them to five years imprisonment effective from 2nd May, 2025.

The court however acquitted Nyirongo, ruling that the evidence linking him to the offence was insufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

DNPW said elephants are among the country’s most important wildlife species, playing a vital role in maintaining healthy ecosystems by dispersing seeds and shaping habitats across savannas and woodlands.

The Department noted that despite their ecological significance, elephants face growing pressure from poaching, habitat loss, human-wildlife conflict and illegal wildlife trade, with demand for ivory remaining a major driver of poaching across Africa.

The conviction, reflects government’s ongoing commitment to combating wildlife crime and reinforces the shared responsibility of safeguarding the country’s natural heritage for future generations.

Meanwhile, the Magistrate Court has also fined two men 80,000 kwacha each for unlawful possession of timber.

Lusaka Magistrate Webster Milumbe fined Chimishilo Fundolo, 53, and Gift Musole, 33, after they pleaded guilty to unlawful possession of forest produce and biological resources.

According to a statement from the Department of National Parks and Wildlife (DNPW), the case stems from a joint operation conducted on 15th June, 2026 by DNPW and the Forestry Department in Shibuyunji District, Central Province.

Five suspects were apprehended during the operation namely Charles Chisangu, 30, Gaskell Siansalama, 26, Mutunda Mihinda, 25, Chimishilo Fundolo, 53, and Gift Musole, 33.

They were found in possession of assorted timber reportedly sourced from Luampa district and destined for Buseko Market in Lusaka.

Following the arrest, four suspects – Chisangu, Mihinda, Fundolo and Musole were charged with unlawful possession of forest produce and biological resources under Zambia’s forest and environmental laws.

Appearing before Magistrate Milumbe on 23rd October, 2026, Fundolo and Musole pleaded guilty and were each fined 80,000 kwacha payable by 3rd November, 2026, failure to which they will serve nine months imprisonment.

The remaining two accused pleaded not guilty and the matter was adjourned to 13th November, 2026 for trial.

DNPW said timber is an important natural resource that supports livelihoods, local industries and healthy ecosystems, but illegal logging and timber trafficking threaten Zambia’s forests, contributing to deforestation, biodiversity loss and habitat degradation.

The Department has encouraged members of the public to report suspected illegal logging, timber trafficking and other environmental crimes to the Forestry Department, DNPW or Zambia Police Service, noting that public cooperation plays an important role in protecting the country’s natural resources.

World.title: Teachers’ Unions Welcome splitting of Ministry of Education
World.content:
The Basic Education Teachers Union of Zambia (BETUZ) and the Dynamic Teachers Union of Zambia have welcomed the splitting of the Ministry of Education into two ministries, saying the move is expected to improve efficiency and service delivery.

Speaking in an exclusive interview with the media today, BETUZ Director of Public and International Relations , Obby Chisala said the restructuring would help address long-standing administrative challenges in the education sector, including issues of teacher promotions, upgrades and salary-related concerns.

Mr Chisala said the restructuring will support the government’s Grow Zambia Agenda by creating streamlined administrative structures with specific responsibilities.

He congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema for implementing the restructuring, which was in line with recommendations previously made by BETUZ Secretary General Henry Sinkala.

“The union had earlier advocated for the splitting of the ministry to improve efficiency and enable the education sector to address its numerous administrative challenges and we are delighted that our proposal was considered,” Mr Chisala added.

Meanwhile, Dynamic Teachers Union of Zambia General Secretary, David Siamutwa added that the splitting of the ministry was a welcome development that would allow each ministry to concentrate on its specific mandate.

Mr Siamutwa explained that the former Ministry of Education had the responsibility of overseeing both basic and higher education, making it difficult to effectively implement and monitor the new curriculum.

“The separation is expected to improve the implementation, monitoring and funding of the new curriculum, provided the two ministries received adequate financial support,” he noted.

Mr Siamutwa urged Government and education stakeholders to support the two ministries to ensure they operated efficiently and delivered on their respective mandates.

He further called for increased investment in education infrastructure, with an emphasis on completing ongoing projects at colleges and universities to improve learning conditions and strengthen the sector’s contribution to national development.

World.title: Government orders councils to prioritise workers’ welfare, service delivery
World.content:
Government has ordered all local authorities with outstanding salary arrears to prioritise settling their obligations to employees, or risk restrictions on foreign travel, workshops outside their jurisdictions, and purchase of vehicles for personal use.

The directive, contained in Local Authorities Circular Number 9 of 2026, dated October 20, underscores growing concern over the accumulation of salary arrears running into several months at some local authorities.

Issued by the Ministry of Local Government and Public Works, the circular describes the situation as unacceptable, citing its negative impact on employees’ welfare and livelihoods, staff morale, productivity and the capacity of councils to deliver essential services.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Mnangagwa joins Putin, African bloc leaders as Russia courts trade ties
World.content:
RUSSIAN President Vladimir Putin has called for closer trade, banking and economic integration between Moscow and Africa’s regional organisations.

He made the remarks on Wednesday on the sidelines of the third Russia-Africa Summit, which was attended by President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who recently assumed the chairmanship of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA).

The meeting brought together leaders of countries chairing major African regional blocs and heads of their executive bodies.

World.title: Mutizwa draws on Delta success to pen corporate leadership book
World.content:
Good workmanship at Zimbabwe’s largest beverage maker Delta Corporation motivated management consultancy specialist Joe Mutizwa to pen a book aimed at helping business leaders turn strategies into tangible results.

Titled “The Trinity of Superior Execution,” the book is Mutizwa’s tenth publication and offers insights into strategy, leadership and execution, with a focus on helping organisations bridge the gap between planning and implementation.

The book was launched at the fifth edition of the Ideas Festival, currently underway at Troutbeck Resort in Nyanga, where this year’s theme, “Beyond the Idea: Execution, Capital and Scale”, aligns with its central message.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: No rush to scrap multicurrency, RBZ says, as it vows to honour all contracts and foreign currency accounts
World.content:
BULAWAYO. The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ) has ruled out a hurried move to a single local currency, saying the shift will be driven by the market and that no one’s foreign currency holdings or contracts will be forcibly converted.

RBZ deputy governor Innocent Matshe gave the assurance at the pre-budget consultations held in Bulawayo this Wednesday.

World.title: Tebekwe Mine strikes gold away from the shafts
World.content:
SHURUGWI-based gold miner Tebekwe Mine scooped a top award at a ZimCEO’s Network awards ceremony held in Bulawayo on Friday evening.

Tebekwe Mine emerged as a Gold winner in the Top Company in the Southern Region – Mining, Mining Supplies and Extraction category.
