World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 29, 2026
World.content:
One Year After Tanzania's Election Crackdown, Victims' Families Demand Justice

One year after deadly election-related violence in Tanzania that left at least 518 people dead, families of victims are demanding justice, accountability and financial assistance for medical treatment. Survivors continue to struggle with injuries and mounting hospital bills. Families of those killed or missing say they have received little support or information. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have accused authorities of failing to hold security forces accountable and intensifying repression against critics, opposition supporters and journalists. The government denies widespread human rights abuses. President Samia Suluhu Hassan was elected with 98% of the vote. The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as Hassan's two main challengers were excluded. Opposition leader Tundu Lissu remains on trial for treason amid growing concerns over political freedoms.

Rights Group Calls for Release of Missing Niger Journalist



Human Rights Watch has urged Niger's authorities to disclose the whereabouts of prominent journalist Moussa Kaka, who disappeared in August 2026. He was later confirmed by the justice minister to be in detention. The authorities have not revealed where he is being held or provided details of the alleged offence. Kaka, director-general of Radio Télévision Saraounia and a former Radio France Internationale correspondent, has previously faced arrest over his journalism. His disappearance comes amid growing concerns about political repression under Niger's military junta, which has been accused of restricting press freedom, detaining critics and weakening democratic institutions. Rights groups are calling for his safe release unless he has been lawfully charged.

Kenya Anger Grows Over Delay in Ex-British Soldier's Extradition Hearing in Murder Case



The family of Agnes Wanjiru, a Kenyan woman allegedly murdered by former British soldier Robert James Purkiss in 2012, has condemned the postponement of his extradition hearing in the United Kingdom until May 2027. Wanjiru's body was found in a septic tank near a British Army training camp in Kenya. Her family said that the latest delay prolongs their 14-year wait for justice. Purkiss, who was arrested in the UK in November 2025, denied the allegation. He is contesting extradition to Kenya. The family said it was not properly informed of the postponement and urged authorities to expedite proceedings so he can face trial. The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

Tanzania Discovers Major Natural Gas Reserves After a Decade

Tanzania has announced its first major natural gas discovery in a decade, with an estimated 223 billion cubic feet found at the Kasa-1X ST2 well in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country. Energy Minister Juma Homera described the discovery as a significant milestone expected to strengthen domestic energy supplies. Production is anticipated to begin early next month. Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet. The gas will support electricity generation, industrial activities and vehicles powered by compressed natural gas. Natural gas already accounts for nearly 80% of Tanzania's electricity generation. The discovery could help meet growing energy demand as the country expands its industrial sector.

Liberia to Lead UN Security Council for First Time in 65 Years

Liberia will assume the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December for the first time in 65 years, marking a significant milestone in its diplomatic history. President Joseph Nyuma Boakai is scheduled to chair a high-level debate on maritime security on 3 December. The government said that Liberia will draw on its experience of civil conflict, reconciliation and post-war recovery to contribute to international peace and security. Ahead of the presidency, the Foreign Affairs Ministry has announced events focused on diplomacy, women's leadership, youth participation and the country's peacebuilding legacy. Boakai also said the need for stronger international cooperation on challenges including climate change, poverty, migration and emerging technologies. He advocated for developing countries to have a greater voice in global decision-making.

Close 

WFP Chief Says Ending Conflict Is Key to Tackling Global Hunger

The new head of the World Food Programme (WFP), Executive Director Luke Lindberg, has said that reducing conflict is the most effective way to tackle global hunger, with conflict driving two-thirds of acute food insecurity affecting 266 million people worldwide. He warned that El Niño could push a further 49 million people into acute food insecurity, while supply chain disruptions are worsening the crisis. Lindberg outlined priorities including protecting humanitarian workers, strengthening donor partnerships, improving operations, investing in disaster preparedness and expanding school meal programmes. He identified Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia as areas of special concern, vowing to prevent famine and enhance food aid in the most vulnerable areas.

World.title: Kenya: Agnes Wanjiru Family Outraged as Extradition Hearing Delayed to 2027
World.content:
Fourteen years after a British soldier killed Agnes Wanjiru, her daughter is waiting for the UK to answer

The family of Agnes Wanjiru, a Kenyan woman allegedly murdered by former British soldier Robert James Purkiss in 2012, has condemned the postponement of his extradition hearing in the United Kingdom until May 2027.

The five-day hearing had been scheduled to begin in mid-November 2026 at Westminster Magistrates' Court in the UK.

Wanjiru's body was found in a septic tank near a British Army training camp in Kenya.

Her family said that the latest delay prolongs their 14-year wait for justice. The family had been fundraising to facilitate the trip and expected to travel to the UK in about three weeks to follow the proceedings.

Purkiss, who was arrested in the UK in November 2025, denied the allegation. He is contesting extradition to Kenya.

The family said it was not properly informed of the postponement and urged authorities to expedite proceedings so he can face trial.

The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

World.title: South Africa: Calls for Calm as Cape Taxi Violence Escalates - South African News Briefs - October 29, 2026
World.content:
press review

Calls for Calm as Cape Taxi Violence Escalates

Calls for calm are growing amid escalating taxi-related shootings in Cape Town, linked to route disputes between rival associations CATA and CODETA, reports EWN. The latest incident at Delft Palm taxi rank left two people injured. Several areas across the province have experienced deadly violence. Cape Town Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis has offered Metro Police support to SAPS. Western Cape Mobility MEC Isaac Sileku has warned the associations to end the violence or face decisive action. A meeting between government and taxi industry representatives is set to seek a lasting solution and protect commuters.

Pastor and Co-Accused Return to Court in Infant Murder Case

Self-proclaimed pastor Caiphus Mkhawane and his co-accused, Ntsako Makhubela and Amanda Mnguni, are set to appear in the Atteridgeville Magistrates’ Court on charges including conspiracy to commit murder and fraud, reports SABC News. Mkhawane and Makhubela also face charges of human trafficking, premeditated murder, rape, kidnapping and robbery with aggravating circumstances. The case stems from allegations that the accused lured a woman and her infant to the Hennops River under the pretext of religious rituals, where the woman was allegedly raped and the child killed. Cat Matlala Back in Court for ID and Bank Fraud Case

Alleged underworld figure Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala is set back in court in connection with an identity document and bank fraud case involving an allegedly fraudulent lease for a luxury property in Waterkloof, reports EWN. The State accused him of using an Eswatini identity document and falsified bank statements to secure the lease. Matlala abandoned his bail application after the State opposed his release, choosing instead to focus on a separate High Court matter. His wife, Tsakane, and co-accused Given Makofane and Claudette Masethe have each been granted R20,000 bail. Matlala also faces separate attempted murder charges in the Johannesburg High Court.

World.title: Africa: Shared Infrastructure Drives Africa's Push into Cotton Processing
World.content:
Shared water and power are easing factory setup costs as Africa's textile hubs expand into cotton processing.

Growing access to shared power and water treatment is shifting some of the capital burden of African textile production from manufacturers to industrial park developers.

In some of the continent's textile hubs, developers are providing common utilities that textile producers pay to use, reducing the installations each factory needs to finance.

Already, wastewater plants are operating in industrial zones in Ethiopia, Benin and Togo, alongside factory sites, grid connections and logistics services.



Such an arrangement could further ease entry into spinning, dyeing and finishing in Africa's cotton hubs, where water, energy and waste treatment traditionally added to the expense of machinery.

The model also gives developers a larger role in financing cotton processing capacity, with returns tied to attracting tenants and collecting enough revenue to maintain the shared services.

Rajeev Arora, a Kenya-based cotton, textile and apparel specialist, said shared industrial infrastructure could help connect different stages of textile production and support more sustainable manufacturing.

"Plug-and-play green parks can bring spinning and garment production together with centralised water treatment, maximising efficiency through shared infrastructure," he said at an online discussion hosted by

Africa Cotton, Textile and Apparel Centre in last week (October).

Research by the Nigerian Economic Summit Group found that shared infrastructure can reduce the cost of industrial investment and spur economies of scale.

It showed common facilities such as wastewater treatment plants, testing laboratories, logistics hubs and transport links allow firms to access services they might struggle to finance on their own.

Currently, Hawassa, Ethiopia's textile and apparel park, has a treatment plant designed to handle 11 million litres of wastewater a day, according to the state Industrial Parks Development Corporation. The city administration reports a 90% water recovery rate.

The plant uses a process known as zero liquid discharge, treating industrial wastewater for reuse within the park. For manufacturers, the service comes with the factory location, and its running costs fall partly on the public institution managing the zone.

A World Bank study found that Hawassa's system cost $3.40 per cubic metre to operate. Factories paid $0.80 per cubic metre of wastewater treated. The figures, which relate to the period examined in the study, put a price on the public support behind the service.

Such arrangements appear in proposals to expand African textile production. Countries seeking to turn cotton into yarn, fabric and clothing need mills with reliable water and energy supplies, as well as equipment to handle the waste they produce.

The demands increase with the amount of processing carried out locally since cutting and sewing imported cloth requires a different set of services from bleaching, dyeing and finishing fabric. The latter processes consume water, chemicals and heat.

"New industries should recover and reuse materials and water wherever possible," said Oluwambe Akinmoye, a Nigerian industrial designer and textile specialist.

He identified low-energy machinery, processes using less water and treatment before effluent disposal among the investments required.

The UN Environment Programme identifies wet processing, which includes bleaching, dyeing and finishing, among the textile value chain's principal sources of climate impact. The International Labour Organization also describes the same processes as energy intensive, commonly relying on coal or natural gas burned on site to generate steam.

But shared infrastructure in textile manufacturing could become a larger part of West Africa's investment offering as such efforts gain traction in Benin and Togo.

An International Finance Corporation review, updated in March 2026, records an operational common effluent treatment plant at each of two ARISE zones, Glo-Djigbé in Benin and Adétikopé in Togo.

"Textile operations within the park achieve an 85-90% internal reuse rate of water," the review says of Glo-Djigbé.

That figure concerns water reused within textile operations with the common treatment network also carrying obligations for individual factories. Firms producing more heavily polluted wastewater must undertake preliminary treatment before discharging it into the system.

The International Trade and Research Centre has proposed extending this approach through parks offering common wastewater treatment, renewable power, laboratories and waste recovery services.

In an October analysis, the ITRC argued that sharing facilities could spread investment costs across manufacturers and make environmental services accessible to smaller producers.

The centre linked the proposal to the competitiveness of African textile suppliers, citing energy reliability, resource costs and the environmental information sought by international buyers.

Dr Debanjan Das, Associate Professor in the Department of Fashion, Design and Merchandising at West Virginia University told the October 22 webinar that commercial returns had varied across the six countries whose research he examined.

Ethiopian factories faced infrastructure, technology and workforce constraints, while manufacturers in Portugal had encountered buyers unwilling to pay higher prices for greener products.

"Green practices can improve environmental performance and competitiveness, but the financial returns have not necessarily followed," he said of Ethiopia.

"Start with energy, water and waste projects that can pay back.". He urged manufacturers to make operations transparent to buyers through production records and real-time reporting.

Hawassa's experience offers a record of the expense involved after construction. The World Bank found that the treatment plant consumed substantial electricity, which the park developer paid for.

Its review also identified the transfer of technical skills to the developer's staff and the terms of service contracts as issues in operating the system.

The difference between treatment charges and operating costs left the developer financing a service that factories used at a reduced rate. The bank questioned the adequacy of tenant fees for the plant's financial viability. It cited a separate study that proposed treatment charges of $1.50 per cubic metre and sales of recovered water at $0.37 per cubic metre.

Arora proposed combining development finance and commercial loans with equipment leasing to fund new investment.

"Manufacturers can lease low-water dyeing equipment and automated looms through original equipment manufacturers and leasing firms, reducing the upfront capital required to establish a mill," he said. Grants could support feasibility studies, technical assistance and workforce training.

Power projects at other parks remain at different stages of development. IFC's review says the ARISE zones it assessed obtain electricity from national grids, with generators for emergencies. The company was considering renewable sources, including rooftop solar.

Adétikopé's developer in Togo has also published plans for a solar plant serving the industrial platform. One financing option would bring in an independent power producer under a 20-year power purchase agreement.

Close 

The project description lists feasibility work and environmental assessment among its development stages. It does not confirm that the proposed solar supply has entered operation.

The use of fuel to generate steam adds another expense to fabric production. Research reviewed by the ILO found substantial energy consumption in heating water and drying textiles, alongside the power needed by weaving machines and other equipment.

Akinmoye said solar and wind could supply some factory operations. "These may not power every energy-intensive machine, but they can support some operations," he said. "Factories should also invest in technologies that use less energy."

Environmental monitoring is also part of operating the parks. IFC's review requires checks on potential effects on community groundwater supplies around the Benin and Togo zones, where industrial water comes from deep aquifers.

Arora proposed combining development finance and commercial loans with equipment leasing to support further investment. Manufacturers could spread the cost of low-water dyeing equipment and automated looms through agreements with machinery suppliers and leasing companies, he said.

"Concessional grants can support feasibility studies, technical assistance and vocational workforce training," he told the webinar.

He also called for closer links between vocational institutions and manufacturers, with machinery suppliers helping training centres obtain modern equipment. Such partnerships could prepare local workers to operate and maintain the systems installed in new textile factories.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigeria, Other Countries Demand End to U.S. Blockade of Cuba
World.content:
The resolution passed on Wednesday with 130 countries in favour and 17 opposed, including the US and Israel.

Nigeria and the majority of other UN members have voted for an end to the US embargo on Cuba, which is crippling the country.

The resolution passed on Wednesday with 130 countries in favour. This included a majority of African countries. Morocco was the only African country that voted in support of the blockade. PREMIUM TIMES previously reported the strong historical and bilateral ties between Cuba and African states.

A total of 17 countries opposed the resolution, including the US and Israel. Also, 25 countries abstained, including Germany and Italy, which had previously voted in favour.



This resolution has been put forward and approved annually since 1992. Last year, more than 160 countries backed the proposal. Although not legally binding, the resolution reflects international opinion of the illegal US blockade of Cuba.

The resolution calls for lifting the economic, trade, and financial embargo against the island nation.

Earlier in the year, the Donald Trump administration introduced additional sanctions that cut off oil shipments to Cuba. It also imposed tariffs on countries that sold oil to the country. The move escalated Cuba's humanitarian and economic crisis.

In his response to Wednesday's vote, the Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said that through the vote, the US was "once again isolated in its attempt to continue strangling the Cuban people."

"Neither its most insane pretexts nor its pressures nor media circus will prevail over the force of facts and truth," he said.

The Cuban embassy in the US celebrated the votes for the resolution.

In a post on X, it wrote, "Victory for Cuba at the UN. Washington was isolated once again. #CubaIsNotAThreat; the blockade is."

Meanwhile, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz celebrated the votes of states that opposed the resolution or abstained.

He told reporters after the vote that he was pleased to see a shift in some countries' stance on US actions against Cuba.

He said, "I'm satisfied that so many countries now, including major economies like Korea, Germany and others, have shifted their position.

"Diplomacy takes time, but now that we've had a tripling of countries that have shifted, we expect that only to continue to grow."

World.title: Africa: Russia-Africa Summit to Test Moscow's Ambitions for Broader Influence
World.content:
A summit with more than 20 African leaders opened in Moscow on Wednesday, in a test of Russia's bid to expand its influence on the continent. The two-day Russia-Africa Summit, the third since 2019, comes as Moscow grapples with heavy sanctions over its Ukraine offensive - and as several African governments turn to it for security assistance.

A total of 48 African countries have sent delegations to the summit, including 22 heads of state, with Russian President Vladimir Putin planning to meet most of them one-on-one.

Africa plays a central role in Russia's strategy to establish itself as the leader of the Global South, said Cécile Marin, a specialist in Russian-African relations and a lecturer at Sciences Po Paris.

"Russia is putting forward a whole narrative denouncing the neocolonialism of the Western powers. Obviously, France is a major target," she told RFI.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Putin is quick to emphasise that Russia, unlike France or the United Kingdom, never colonised African countries, Marin explained. His government has also highlighted the "traditional values" it claims to share with many in Africa, she said.

Moscow has courted ties with Africa since the Soviet era, and has long looked to Africa as a counterweight to what it sees as Western domination over international affairs.

Putin said a world where power is no longer concentrated in the West was quickly becoming a reality.

"The era when the fate of entire continents was determined by a narrow bloc of states is irrevocably gone," he said as he opened an economic forum for business leaders hours before the high-level summit began.

Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger launch Tafouk TV channel to push their own narrative

Economic ambitions

The summit is expected to focus on expanding economic cooperation in particular.

Putin told delegates on Wednesday that Russia was "prepared to further expand the geographical reach of our agricultural product shipments". Attacks in the Black Sea linked to the conflict in Ukraine continue to disrupt exports of grain from both Russia and Ukraine, many of which go to Africa.

Putin also announced that Moscow planned to "localise" the production of Russian medicines and vaccines on the African continent, and stressed that Russia was "open to sharing our modern competencies and high-tech digital know-how with our African friends".

The summit is expected to end Thursday with a final declaration on deepening cooperation between Russia and African nations, alongside a separate statement on cooperation in the field of artificial intelligence.

The Kremlin said Russia will also seek to strengthen its diplomatic presence on the continent, where it aims to open a 49th embassy, in Liberia.

Leaked files reveal Russia's blueprint to expand African Sahel alliance

Security dominant

To date, economic ties remain limited. Russia-Africa relations are primarily centred on military and security issues, according to Ivan Klyszcz, a researcher at the International Centre for Defence and Security in Tallinn, Estonia, and a specialist in Russia-Africa relations.

"Most African armies were trained during the Cold War by instructors from either the Soviet Union or the Eastern Bloc," he told RFI. "This means they mainly use Soviet-style equipment, such as Kalashnikovs. These are markets in which Russia enjoys very, very privileged access."

Russian paramilitary forces are also deployed in several countries in Africa, he said, primarily to protect leaders and infrastructure. In some cases, they carry out combat missions - such as in Mali, where the government is using Russian paramilitaries to battle a jihadist offensive.

These forces are not just guns for hire, according to Klyszcz: they are managed by Russian military intelligence and also serve Russian objectives.

Madagascar marks one year since uprising as Russia's influence grows

Shadow of war in Ukraine

Yet Russia's ambitions in Africa may be limited by its war in Ukraine, which is weighing heavily on Moscow's budget.

Paul-Simon Handy, regional director for East Africa at the Institute for Security Studies think tank in Pretoria, said Russia's room for manoeuvre was reduced.

To implement the various policies it has outlined in its Africa strategy, he told RFI, "there would need to be fiscal and budgetary leeway, which does not seem to be available at the moment".

Instead, "the war in Ukraine may mean that Russia can only offer defence assistance and commercial cooperation in the supply of provisions, fertilisers and agricultural equipment".

Close 

The war has already marred Russia's relations with several African countries in another respect, after numerous reports of Africans being forcibly conscripted by Moscow to fight on the frontlines in Ukraine.

The families searching for African recruits lost in the Ukraine war

The French Institute of International Relations estimates that between 3,000 and 4,000 Africans are fighting for Russia in Ukraine, some lured under false pretences and promises of well-paid work.

Countries including Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa have publicly voiced alarm at the fate of their citizens recruited by Moscow.

In an open letter to the African heads of state and other officials attending the Moscow summit, Amnesty International voiced "deep concern regarding Russia's forced and deceptive recruitment" of African nations.

The rights group urged officials to demand that Russia "cease any ongoing and future recruitment of people from Africa and other foreign nationals into its military forces".

This story has been adapted from original reporting by RFI's French service, with additional information from AFP.

World.title: South Africa: Border? What Border? This Is What South Africa's Frontier With Zimbabwe Looks Like
World.content:
A view of the Alfred Beit Road Bridge, which crosses the Limpopo River from South Africa into Zimbabwe. On the right is South Africa, and on the left is Zimbabwe.

Trucks, elephants, donkeys and humans cross the Limpopo River freely

Whatever you want to buy, there's a good chance you'll find it in Musina, Limpopo. The town centre is abuzz from early in the morning with travellers, traders and smugglers. The myriad shops selling electronics, clothes, furniture, washing machines, fridges, toys, toiletries, cigarettes, and alcohol are doing a roaring trade.

Much of it is going across the Beitbridge border, 10km away on a good road, the last stretch of the N1. The bakkies going north are overloaded with goods, marked with the names of the people in Zimbabwe who've ordered them.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

At the border some vehicles will cross through the official border checkpoint. But many won't. Instead they'll take a little detour and drive along the dirt road, either west in the direction of Mapungubwe, or east towards where the Sand and Limpopo rivers meet.

We drove west. A few hundred metres along the road, two soldiers, next to their tent, had made a tiny roadblock out of stones. They stopped us. We had a long friendly conversation. The woman was from Potchefstroom and the man from Soweto. Their shift started in April and finishes in November. They told us they frequently turn around Zimbabweans crossing the border. The soldiers used to detain them, but they were just released to cross the border again the same day. So now the soldiers just turn them around and send them back.

We drove on, fully laden trucks passing us in one direction, empty trucks in the other. Not far from the soldiers' roadblock, we found a large hole in the barbed wire fence that runs along the border, with a makeshift road leading down a few hundred metres, to the Limpopo River.

Here goods will be offloaded onto a raft or a boat, or even a human or a donkey if the water level is low enough, and taken across the Limpopo River to Zimbabwe. Our drone showed us a raft and a line going across the river, and activity on the other side.

A man was sitting at another break in the fence. While we were there a few people walked past him across the fence towards the river. He told us he was employed by the game farm he was sitting next to, to prevent poaching. He didn't mind people going past him to cross the border so long as they didn't poach. He told us people pass here carrying all sorts of things, from groceries to blankets, beds and refrigerators, to be sold in Zimbabwe. As we were chatting, one man passed us carrying three 10kg bags of potatoes.

Many of the breaks in the fence are made by humans but some have been made by elephants wandering between the two countries.

One evening as we were driving from Beitbridge to Musina, there was a commotion at a bridge over dense bush just at the entrance to the town. Elephants had been spotted. One person said three. Another six. Several young men energetically tried to find the animals in the thick bush.

We asked one of them what they would do if they found an elephant. Kill it for the meat, was the excited reply.

The next day a traffic official, Ernest Makatu, showed us a video of people chopping up a dead elephant several months ago for its meat. It tastes good, he said.

Makatu wants to end corruption in Musina and South Africa. He is with the Build a Better South Africa political party and in 2029 he intends to stand for president of the country.

Zander Coetzer, who handles security for game farms in the area owned by Hermanus Schoeman, drove us east along the border showing us which breaks in the fence are made by elephants and which by humans, though they are probably used by both species. There are also many donkeys crossing the river, apparently without owners, grazing on both sides. Coetzer told us donkeys are useful for helping to pull stolen cars that sometimes get stuck in the river.

Every day thousands of people cross the border - legally and illegally. Some cross the breaks in the border into South Africa in the morning to work in Musina or on a farm, and return in the evening. This has been going on for decades.

A Zimbabwean man told us he used to often cross the border illegally before getting a work permit.

He said in 2003 he had seen six women drown in the flooded Limpopo at Chivara. "I have crossed that river countless times, got arrested, released, got stripped naked by criminals, but I kept coming to South Africa," he told us. "Crossing a flooded Limpopo River is no joke because the bed shifts when walking on it. Don't worry about crocodiles because they're not found everywhere."

But employment is probably not the main reason people come and go across the border: trade is. There's a huge network of people involved in moving goods from South Africa to Zimbabwe: carriers, people managing the rafts and boats, drivers - all getting a cut of the goods bought in Musina.

Why don't the buyers go through the official border? Because import duties are exorbitant on the Zimbabwean side. Determining what the duties are is hard. This webpage gives an example in which the tax on $610 worth of goods comes to $203. The percentages are laid out in a 1,162-page tariff handbook published by the Zimbabwean government. (Did you know if you import a live whale into Zimbabwe, there's a 10% duty? See page 20.)

In practice the duties appear to be negotiable. "I bought a solar pump for R8,000 in South Africa and was supposed to pay R2,500 at the border officially but negotiated it to R500 which I gave the customs officer. No receipt," one man told us.

So it's often cheaper to pay the various people involved in smuggling goods across the border, including bribing soldiers, than to go through customs.

A woman in Musina connected to cross-border trade explained to us that some shops in the town open as early as 5am. One truck delivering goods to cross the border can make five, or even more, trips a day. "Each load can earn them more than R1,000. There is a good market for chicken, usually braai packs, because it is expensive in Zimbabwe," she said. "All the trucks you see here are headed to the trading point. At the river they use small boats to ferry the loads across. If the water level is low they walk across or use donkeys."

"There are many entrances through the bushes. The one you visited is called Maroyi," she said. "When you leave here you pay a driver's fee for transport, and you also pay the boys you find hiding in the bushes R50 to look out for soldiers."

A smuggler near the border told us: "I carry the goods on my head across the river." He said he generally charges R150 per package. Crossing to the other side takes him 30 minutes. He said he carries all kinds of goods, legal and illegal. He has a Zimbabwean passport. He said he and others do this because they are unemployed and need to make a living.

In Musina we spoke to shopkeepers selling clothes and shoes. Business is not as good as it once was because there are lots of soldier roadblocks on the road to Harare where people have to pay "fees", one told us. So people have switched to other borders, including Zambia. Goods are still cheaper in South Africa, he said, but the cost of paying off soldiers along the way is pushing the cost of importing across Beitbridge too high.

Before meeting him, we were told Hennie Erwee is the lawyer you want if you're ever in trouble. He's a big guy with a big personality. We met him at his office in Musina. He has successfully litigated for Schoeman against the government for infringing his property rights. Now he's running a case, with Schoeman as his client, to get the national government to fix the border.

Close 

Schoeman has had to close his game farm along the border in part because of the uncontrolled animal traffic. "As soon as it's dry, donkeys and cows cross into the farm. If I put out lucerne for my game, the next day there's a hundred donkeys there," he said.

He pointed out that people taking goods to Zimbabwe through the breaks in the border are not breaking South African law; we don't need to worry about that. But the animal traffic is a problem, he explained. "Cattle moving freely across the border, on a daily basis, cross into my farm, mix with local cattle. A big percentage have foot-and-mouth disease."

He is sceptical that South Africa can get the foot-and-mouth disease epidemic under control while this carries on.

The state spends billions of rands protecting the border in a system that is far too bureaucratic. Three years ago the Border Management Authority (BMA) came into existence to co-ordinate the response. But it has already had a troubling audit and serious problems with corruption. And it is clearly failing to control the Beitbridge corridor.

There's a long history of the fence along the Zimbabwean border being built and rebuilt, at large expense and to no avail. Schoeman told us that his security protected the current barbed wire fence while it was put up. But as soon as the fence was built and handed over to the government, his services were no longer used, and holes immediately started appearing.

But if the government did get its act together and managed the Beitbridge border, there would be a different problem. The thriving Musina economy has developed over decades in response to the porous border. Tens of thousands of people probably depend on things being just the way they are to make a living. If every small town in South Africa was as bustling as Musina, our economy would be doing well.

Suddenly fixing the border might just destroy the town's economy.

World.title: Ethiopia: Dangote Hires Spanish Firm for Ethiopia's $4 Billion Fertiliser Project
World.content:
Addis Abeba — Dangote Group, owned by Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, has contracted Spanish engineering company Técnicas Reunidas to supply two hydrogen reformers for its fertiliser plant under construction in Gode, Somali region, as the project's estimated cost rises to more than $4 billion.

Técnicas Reunidas announced on Wednesday that it would design, procure materials for, manufacture and deliver the two units within 18 months. The reformers are expected to produce a combined output of more than 200,000 normal cubic metres of hydrogen per hour. The company did not disclose the contract's value.

The equipment will be supplied through TR-Technical, the Spanish company's heat-transfer equipment division, using process technology licensed by Danish firm Topsoe.

The Gode complex is designed to produce three million tonnes of urea annually. Dangote and Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed launched construction in October 2025, following a shareholders' agreement between Dangote Group and Ethiopian Investment Holdings, the state-owned investment fund. Dangote Group holds a 60% stake in the venture, while the Ethiopian entity owns the remaining 40%.



Initially valued at $2.5 billion, the project's investment estimate increased to more than $4 billion in May as plans expanded to include a 110-kilometre gas pipeline, a 120-megawatt power plant, a packaging facility and a blending plant with an annual capacity of two million tonnes of NPK fertiliser, Billionaires.Africa reported.

The plant will use natural gas from the Calub field in the Ogaden basin. Chinese firm GCL Group signed a 25-year supply agreement in March, according to the report.

Ethiopia currently imports nearly all its fertiliser, and the government expects domestic production to reduce foreign currency expenditure and support agricultural output.

Earlier this month, Dangote said he planned to offer at least 10% of the Ethiopian venture to local investors through the Ethiopian Securities Exchange once production stabilises. No date or pricing has been announced for the proposed share sale.

Addis Standard reported in August 2025 that Ethiopian Investment Holdings (EIH), the government's strategic investment arm, and Dangote Group had signed a shareholders' agreement to develop a $2.5 billion urea fertiliser complex in Gode, Somali Region. Under the agreement, Dangote Group holds a 60% stake in the joint venture, while EIH owns the remaining 40%.

In May 2026, Addis Standard reported that the planned investment had increased to more than $4 billion following a visit to the construction site by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote. The expanded project includes a gas pipeline from the Calub field in the Ogaden Basin, a 120-megawatt power plant, a polypropylene packaging facility and a blending plant designed to produce two million tonnes of NPK fertiliser annually.

Following the visit, Abiy described the initiative as a strategic investment in Ethiopia's agricultural transformation, food security and economic self-reliance. He said the facility would strengthen domestic production, reduce import dependence, support farmers and create employment opportunities. The government has also sought to accelerate construction beyond the original 40-month timeline.

In March 2026, Addis Standard reported on a $4.2 billion, 25-year natural gas supply agreement between Dangote Industries Limited and China's GCL Group. The agreement provides for gas from the Calub field to supply the complex, linking domestic gas extraction with fertiliser production.

Close 

The facility is designed to produce three million tonnes of urea annually, while the separate NPK blending plant will have an annual capacity of two million tonnes. The complex is expected to begin operations in 2029 and could also supply markets across East Africa.

The project comes as Ethiopia continues to rely heavily on imported fertiliser to meet domestic agricultural demand. Russian Ambassador to Ethiopia Yevgeny Terekhin told Russia's state news agency TASS that Ethiopia had become the world's third-largest importer of Russian fertiliser, driven largely by demand for diammonium phosphate (DAP). He said the state-owned procurement company requires approximately 1.2 million tonnes of DAP annually, while Russia is exploring opportunities to expand its presence in Ethiopia's agrochemical market.

World.title: Milwaukee Brewers broke baseball on their way to remarkably dominant World Series run
World.content:
The Milwaukee Brewers are 2026 World Series champions, bringing home the organization's first ever title. For the franchise and their fans, it was the culmination of years of quality scouting, drafting, international signings, player development, and remarkably successful trades.

It was also a near-perfect example of what it takes to win a championship in baseball.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

While William Contreras won World Series MVP, voters had plenty of options to choose from on the Milwaukee roster. Jackson Chourio became the first player since Babe Ruth, yes, literally Babe Ruth, to have 10 hits in the first four games of a World Series. Cooper Pratt, a light-hitting, defense-first shortstop, set a rookie record with hits in six straight at bats from game four to game five.

BREWERS RIDE RIDICULOUS, RECORD-SETTING EIGHT-RUN INNING TO DOMINANT 3-0 WORLD SERIES LEAD OVER RAYS

Brice Turang hit .316, below average hitter David Hamilton crushed what looked like a huge home run in game four. Aaron Ashby went 5.2 innings with no runs, just one hit allowed and nine strikeouts. Abner Uribe allowed just two hits in 5 innings. Jacob Misiorowski allowed only one run in 10.2 innings, winning game one and the clinching game five. Robert Gasser was equally unhittable, with just one run allowed in his game three start. A start so incredible that it was the first of its type by a left-handed pitcher since legendary Hall of Famer Sandy Koufax.

The whole team was World Series MVP. The whole team was NLCS MVP, and NLDS MVP too. Milwaukee went 11-2 in the postseason against the San Diego Padres, the hottest team in baseball in the second half, the star-studded 100-win Los Angeles Dodgers, and the 98-win Tampa Bay Rays, who tore through the American League. They won eight straight games in the playoffs. Their two losses came by a combined two runs, and their one World Series loss was on a walk-off in the 12th inning after they blew a 3-2 lead.

It's not a stretch to say it's one of the most dominant stretches of playoff baseball in the history of the sport. And it's why we can make the argument that the Milwaukee Brewers broke Major League Baseball. It's not supposed to be this easy, and it rarely is, even for some of the most expensive, talented rosters we've ever seen.

The 2024 Dodgers, with Shohei Ohtani coming off the first 50-50 season in history and a long list of other stars, were down 2-1 in the NLDS to the Padres before coming back to win. It took them six games to beat the Mets in the NLCS. They very nearly lost the clinching game five of the World Series, falling behind 5-0 to the Yankees before the New York defense went on a comical run of errors and mental mistakes. In 2025, they were down to their final two outs in game seven of the series against Toronto, until Miguel Rojas hit a miraculous game-tying homer.

Milwaukee? They never trailed in a series, or even came close. In fact, it was the exact opposite. They had a 2-0 lead in the NLDS, a 4-0 lead in the NLCS, and a 3-0 lead in the NLCS. It's remarkable.

Which raises the question, how did they do it? What was their philosophy and approach in October? The real answer, boring as it might be, they didn't do anything. Baseball happened.

That's not to say that the Brewers don't have good players or didn't have good results. Misiorowski is going to win the Cy Young Award at 24-years-old, and looks set to dominate the league for years to come. Christian Yelich is a former MVP, multiple-time Silver Slugger Award winner and borderline candidate for the Hall of Fame. William Contreras has been a top-three catcher in baseball for several years. Garrett Mitchell is a former first round pick and top prospect, as is Brice Turang. Jackson Chourio is already a star at 22.

The big secret the Brewers discovered? Have your players get hot at the right time, have a few bounces go your way, rely on some of your less talented players to hit perfectly timed home runs, and sit back and watch as your bullpen goes from very good to almost literally untouchable.

Every year, the greater baseball world looks to find some sort of meaning or blueprint from the team that wins the World Series. In 2024 and 2025, the Dodgers "proved" that you can just guarantee a title by spending money, even though the Mets and Yankees haven't won in decades. In 2023, the Rangers showed you need a veteran manager like Bruce Bochy, and that home runs, Texas hit eight in five games, are how you win in October. Very smart analysts have pointed to quality bullpens, big midseason trades, drafting and development, free agency, dominant starting rotations, home runs, or making contact and putting the ball in play. The reality? You need all of those, and you can't predict which ones you'll actually get when it matters.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Not once in these discussions does anyone acknowledge that the different paths taken by different teams demonstrate that there is no one way to win a championship. And that the disparate approaches to roster construction show that what actually matters is a combination of timing, randomness, luck, and talent. Because there has to be meaning and lessons and broad conclusions to draw from every outcome, the baseball world picks a reason and explanation, then quietly discards it when next year's team does the opposite.

Here are a few examples of why looking for meaning in playoff baseball is pointless. "Clutch" hitting is frequently praised as meaningful and predictive. Some players just have the "clutch" gene, the received baseball wisdom goes. So let's look at superstar shorstop Corey Seager as an example. Seager had an astonishing run in the 2020 playoffs, hitting. 328 with eight home runs and 20 runs batted in, winning NLCS and World Series MVP. One of the best postseasons ever. Clutch hitter, right?

In 2016 and 2017, he went a combined 18 for 82. Then in the 2019 postseason went 3-20 with two singles and no homers. In 2021, Seager was 9-48, a .188 batting average. In 2023, he was once again a force of nature for Texas, hitting .318 with six homers. So is Seager the clutch playoff force from 2020 and 2023, or the hopeless, unclutch, "moment is too big" failure from 2016, 2017, 2019, and 2021?

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Therein lies the problem. Corey Seager is an elite hitter, but even the best hitters go through hot and cold streaks. Pitchers go through hot and cold streaks. They can't pick and choose when those streaks happen, because if they could, they'd all pick to be hot in October. Derek Jeter hit .235 in the 1998 playoffs, .226 in the 2001 playoffs, .245 in 2004, .176 in 2007, and .250 in 2010 and 2011. He also had plenty of very good results in other years. That's baseball.

Aaron Ashby quite literally had the greatest October by a relief pitcher in baseball history. Next year, he could be the worst pitcher on the team in the NLDS. That's baseball. Robert Gasser could be horrible next season after his dominance in this year's playoffs. That's baseball. Look at last year's Toronto Blue Jays.

Ernie Clement, literally Ernie Clement, set the record for most hits in a single postseason with an incredible 30 in 73 at bats. In 2026, he was 20% worse than league average offensively, cost his team 14 runs compared to an average hitter, and had a .285 on base percentage. In the 2025 playoffs, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. had a .356 batting average on balls in play. Addison Barger was .422, Ernie Clement was .420, and George Springer .319. Predictably, the Blue Jays scored a lot of runs in October.



In 2026, Guerrero had a .288 BABIP, Springer was .282, Clement .272, and Barger was .063 in his few games before he got hurt. Toronto finished in last place and missed the playoffs. That is also baseball. There's no predictive value from the tournament, because players do not magically become different in October. There's just a typical distribution of outcomes, particularly among good teams, that sometimes goes your way and sometimes doesn't.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

None of this means the Brewers didn't deserve to win, or weren't a good team. They absolutely did, and they absolutely are. They deserve an immense amount of credit for identifying players in the draft or international markets, as well as in trades and free agency, that they thought they could improve or would fit specific needs. But looking for some sort of explanation or path for your favorite team to follow is insane. Because while you need good players to win, you can't predict how they'll perform over a few weeks of small sample sizes. It's just...baseball. Enjoy it when your team wins, celebrate it, and understand that the inherent variability of it ensures it can't ever be broken.

World.title: Chiefs coordinator backs Harrison Butker as starter despite Justin Tucker's 'off the charts' workout
World.content:
The Kansas City Chiefs brought in Justin Tucker amid Harrison Butker’s struggles, but special teams coordinator Dave Toub made it clear who the starting kicker is.

Butker has struggled this season, making just 11 of 16 field-goal attempts, with four of his misses coming over his last four games. Amid those woes, the team brought in Tucker to provide competition, but Toub remained steadfast in his support of Butker.

"Butker is our kicker," Toub told reporters on Thursday. "We’re trying to improve, we’re trying to get Butker right. That’s what this whole thing is about."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Toub said Butker has performed well in practice this week despite windy conditions and Tucker’s presence.

"He went 10-for-10 yesterday with Tucker standing right there," Toub said. "And he went 10-for-10. On a windy day, it was 28-mile-an-hour gusts yesterday, and he went 10-for-10. And I thought right before out to practice, I was going, ‘This poor bastard,’ I mean, it’s 28-mile-an-hour gusts and he’s got to go out there and try to — and he did it. He went 10-for-10, so that’s a good thing. So we’re going to keep working it."

The Chiefs worked out Ben Sauls, Harrison Mevis and Tucker, and Toub was asked why the team chose the former Baltimore Ravens kicker.

"Because (Justin Tucker) he is a good kicker. And I've heard he's been out making the rounds, and we talk. All the special teams coaches talk. He had four workouts before we brought—we were his fifth workout, tryout. And the word was that he was hitting the ball great, and I wanted to see it. I always thought he was a great kicker, and those two guys right now, Harrison and him, they idolized each other in the league when they were kicking together. He was out there, he did his 10-game suspension, so he was available, we brought him in," Toub said.

BOBBY BURACK: JUSTIN TUCKER SIGNING EXPOSES SPORTS MEDIA’S SELECTIVE OUTRAGE OVER NFL MISCONDUCT

Toub said he put the kickers through a "grueling workout" that included a "30 kick," extra points, seven attempts from beyond 50 yards and one from 60 yards. Tucker made every kick with exceptional accuracy.

"Not only did he make them, he was accurate. 60 percent of his kicks were inside of a six-foot cylinder in the middle of the uprights. Somebody that's struggling as a kicker is not able to put the ball with that kind of accuracy," Toub said. "So, he was off the charts good. That's the reason why we signed him to the practice squad."

Tucker served a 10-game suspension for violating the NFL’s personal conduct policy after 16 female massage therapists accused him of sexual misconduct and inappropriate behavior during sessions between 2012 and 2016, according to reporting by The Baltimore Banner in January 2025.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

On Feb. 16 of last year, the same outlet reported that seven more women had come forward with allegations of sexual misconduct against Tucker. The longtime Ravens kicker denied the allegations in a statement to OutKick.

"I maintain I did not act inappropriately at any point before, during, or after a professional bodywork treatment session, nor have I ever been told I am unwelcome at any massage therapy provider," he said. "These claims are simply not true."

"I can assure whoever is reading this that I have never intended to disrespect anyone, cross any boundary, or make anyone feel uncomfortable in any way whatsoever."

The decision to sign Tucker to the practice squad has drawn fierce criticism.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

While Toub said Butker is still the team’s kicker, that could change if his struggles continue. Toub described Butker’s missed 45-yard field goal in the team’s loss to the Seattle Seahawks as a "bad miss."

"You’ve got to make the kicks," Toub said. "The short kicks — that’s considered a short kick — you’ve got to make those in situations where it’s a tight game like that. It was an issue in that game, for sure."

The Chiefs next game is against the Denver Broncos at 4:25 p.m. ET on Sunday.

World.title: Judge grills AG’s office in Cornell sex assault case as ex-frat bro’s lawyer demands ouster over alleged bias
World.content:

A Sullivan County judge heard oral arguments Thursday to determine whether New York Attorney General Letitia James should be removed as special prosecutor in the reopened criminal investigation into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University.

The proceeding ended without an immediate ruling from Judge James Farrell.

The hearing stems from a challenge filed by defense attorney Andrew Miltenberg, who represents Gillio Lopes, one of the men accused in the case.

Lopes is one of seven former Chi Phi fraternity brothers who are accused in a lawsuit of drugging and raping a female Cornell student at their fraternity house in October 2024.

LETITIA JAMES FACES NEW PUSH TO BOOT HER FROM CORNELL RAPE PROBE OVER ALLEGED BIAS: COURT DOCUMENTS

Defense counsel argued that social media comments posted by James prior to her official appointment as "special prosecutor" demonstrate a pre-existing bias and a presumption of guilt that undermines the prosecution's neutrality.

"What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable," James had posted on social media. "I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you."

TISH JAMES CONFRONTED ON CAMERA OVER TRUMP'S ACCUSATION OF BIAS IN CORNELL RAPE CASE

Arguing before the court, Miltenberg pointed to those public declarations of support as proof of a pre-determined bias.

"Whether it affects all or just one, either the court determines the statements made by AG James take her out of contention to be neutral party reviewing case or not," Miltenberg argued, calling the initial public statements an "original sin" for the case.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

In a statement sent to Fox News on Thursday, a spokesperson for James' office said, "As indicated in our motion before the court, these claims are without merit. The Office of the Attorney General remains committed to conducting an investigation guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Representing the state, Assistant Attorney General Kaitlin Vigars defended Gov. Kathy Hochul's appointment of James and pushed back against the disqualification effort, emphasizing that public statements alone do not meet the legal threshold for removal.

CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS PROMPT NY ATTORNEY GENERAL LETITIA JAMES TO OPEN ‘ACTIVE CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION’

Vigars argued that to warrant disqualification, there needs to be a showing of actual prejudice rather than speculative claims of bias.

SEND US A TIP

CORNELL SEXUAL ASSAULT CASE REVIVES SCRUTINY OF A LITTLE-KNOWN NEW YORK LAW ON INTOXICATED VICTIMS

Farrell peppered Vigars with questions about the circumstances leading up to James’ appointment, including if Hochul was aware of James’ social media comment, if James and Hochul were standing together when the governor made remarks about the "brave young woman," if that runs afoul of professional conduct, and if the purpose of appointing the AG was to avoid bias.

Farrell also raised broader procedural concerns during the arguments, noting the potential for conflicting legal rulings if challenges proceed piecemeal across jurisdictions.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"If multiple judges come down with decisions that’s chaos," Farrell said from the bench, "and the court should not fashion chaos."

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor on Oct. 1 after stepping in to bypass the local Tompkins County district attorney, who had previously declined to bring charges.

CORNELL RAPE ACCUSER CAN REMAIN 'JANE DOE'; JUDGE WARNS THREATS COULD LEAD TO FEDERAL CHARGES

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

With no decision rendered at the conclusion of Thursday's arguments, the judge is expected to issue a formal written ruling in the coming days on whether James will remain as special prosecutor or if the investigation must be reassigned.

Hochul later said on Thursday that all sexual offense complaints at Cornell University are now being referred to New York State Police, rather than Cornell University Police, unless otherwise requested by that individual.

"Every student deserves to feel safe on their campus," she said in a statement, in part. "And when someone reports sexual assault, they deserve to be heard, treated with compassion, and know their allegations will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated by law enforcement trained to support survivors.

"What Jane Doe described is horrifying. Survivors should be able to trust the institutions responsible for protecting them. We cannot afford to let them down."

World.title: LA residents near famous Hollywood sign fed up with over-saturation of tourists and illegal vendors
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

LOS ANGELES — Los Angeles residents living near the iconic Hollywood sign have filed a public nuisance complaint over what they describe as out-of-control tourist activity that has turned the area adjacent to the landmark into a "public toilet."

Multiple residents of Hollywood Hills neighborhoods filed a complaint Monday in Los Angeles Superior Court against the city of Los Angeles, Mayor Karen Bass and City Councilwoman Nithya Raman, alleging that officials have allowed the area near the sign to become a public nuisance.

State law defines a public nuisance as "anything which is injurious to health, … or is indecent or offensive to the senses, or an obstruction to the free use of property, so as to interfere with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property, or unlawfully obstructs the free passage or use, in the customary manner, of … any public park, square, street, or highway."

POPULAR BEACH TOWN REJECTS NOISE, TRASH AND TRAFFIC AS IT WEIGHS STRICTER VACATION RENTAL RULES

According to the complaint, residents have cited illegal street vending and dumping, along with "public urination and defecation that occur regularly on the City’s property." They also point to increased traffic on surrounding streets and what they describe as an unacceptable risk of devastating fires and gridlock that severely limits their ability to leave their homes.

Visitors, they say, routinely smoke cigarettes and throw their cigarette butts into the grass, despite prohibitions against smoking and the significant fire hazard it poses. Likewise, if a fire were to break out — as has happened in the past — increased traffic could prevent fire trucks from reaching their destinations.

POPULAR VACATION HOT SPOTS SLAP LIMITS ON TOURIST RENTALS, DRIVING AND MORE TO PROTECT 'STUNNING' SPACES

Residents allege that the city is liable because it controls the land where the nuisance conditions exist. They claim the city has actively promoted the area to tourists for years while failing to take reasonable steps to control the impact of increasing numbers of visitors and vendors, as well as the numerous nuisance conditions and safety risks.

They also cite increasing obstructions on the narrow neighborhood streets and other blights that they say are "indecent and offensive to the senses."

ONCE-HIDDEN COASTAL TOWN FACING DISRUPTION AS SOCIAL MEDIA INFLUENCERS TRANSFORM LOCAL LIFE

Fox News Digital reached out to Bass and Raman for comment. Raman represents City Council District 4, which includes the Hollywood Hills.

The impact of a glut of tourists visiting the Hollywood Hills has long plagued the area, creating safety and quality-of-life concerns for residents.

STUNNING VACATION HOT SPOT TURNS INTO OVERCROWDED NIGHTMARE AS TOURISTS FLOOD STREETS

"This was a problem 20 years ago—tourists driving into the Hollywood Hills to take pictures of the Hollywood sign or hiking up to it after driving as close to the sign as possible," former Hollywood United Neighborhood Council board member Chuck Suhayda told Fox News Digital. "It caused massive traffic jams and parking problems."

Suhayda served on the board for more than a decade.

Access to what is known as the Hollywood Hills Neighborhoods — which includes Hollywoodland, Lake Hollywood Estates and Hollywood Knolls — is restricted by the area’s geography. The roads are winding, lack sidewalks and average only about 18 feet in width.

The over-saturation of tourists and the corresponding hazards were exacerbated in September 2011, when a "viewing site" of the sign at the intersection of Canyon Lake Drive and Mulholland Highway was cleared of brush on both sides of the street by Council District 4 staff. The goal was to promote tourism by creating a site now known as "Hollywood Sign Lookout."

POPULAR DESTINATION CRACKS DOWN HARD ON TOURISTS AS NEW LIMITS THREATEN SUMMER GETAWAYS

The area is zoned as open space and separates two residential zones designated for single-family homes. Residents say it has since become inundated with tourists, illegal street vendors and crippling traffic, leading to increased congestion on surrounding streets.

FURIOUS CROWDS PROTEST SKY-HIGH HOUSING COSTS AND MASS TOURISM IN MAJOR CITY

In its own documents, the city has admitted that the current situation is "unsustainable." However, residents say officials have ignored the city’s role in promoting Lake Hollywood Park, the viewing site and even the Hollywood Hills Neighborhoods, which they describe as landmarks in their own right—not only because they offer views of the Hollywood sign, but also because of their iconic architecture, steep landscapes and vistas of the Los Angeles basin.

World.title: FOX News Media teams up with Breast Cancer Research Foundation
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FOX News Media teamed up with the Breast Cancer Research Foundation (BCRF) Thursday for a special panel highlighting advances in breast cancer research and treatment while urging women to take an active role in their healthcare.

The event, held at Fox News headquarters in New York City during Breast Cancer Awareness Month, featured Kat Timpf, the "Gutfeld!" co-host and breast cancer survivor, alongside Dr. Priya Malhotra, director of research impact at BCRF.

Speaking with Fox News Digital after the panel, Timpf emphasized that while breast cancer awareness is widespread, misconceptions about the disease persist and may discourage people from asking important questions about their health.

LARRY FITZGERALD Q&A: NFL ICON TALKS BREAST CANCER AWARENESS FOR HIS LATE MOTHER, FRIENDSHIP WITH JOHN MCCAIN

"There is also so much that people don’t know. It can happen at any age, without genetic markers. I would know that," Timpf told Fox News Digital. "Talking about it is always helpful because it removes a lot of the stigma, and it makes you feel like you can ask these questions to your doctor."

Timpf was diagnosed with Stage 0 ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) in February 2025, just 15 hours before giving birth to her first child. She announced the news on social media days later, writing what she called an "unconventional birth announcement."

"Last week, I welcomed my first child into the world. About fifteen hours before I went into labor, I was diagnosed with breast cancer," Timpf wrote on X at the time.

"Now, before you worry, my doctor says it’s stage 0 and is confident that it almost certainly hasn’t spread. Or, as I’ve explained to the few people I’ve managed to tell about it so far: Don’t freak out. It’s just, like, a LITTLE bit of cancer."

VANESSA TRUMP REVEALS BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS IN EMOTIONAL STATEMENT: 'I AM STAYING FOCUSED AND HOPEFUL'

Throughout her breast cancer experience, Timpf leaned on her signature humor, a coping mechanism she said helped her through some of the most difficult moments of her diagnosis and recovery.

"Humor is how I've gotten through every hard thing that's ever happened to me," Timpf said. "I was making jokes the day I was diagnosed about getting huge replacement [implants] and stuff like that. That's just how I do things because I feel like when you say that you can't joke about a subject, you're giving it even more power over you than it already has.

"For me, making jokes about a subject is a way to instead feel power over the things that are threatening to take you down."

TRUMP'S CHIEF OF STAFF ALMOST SKIPPED SCREENING THAT DETECTED AGGRESSIVE CANCER

Timpf's central message to women was to take an active role in their healthcare, stay on top of recommended screenings and speak up when something doesn't feel right.

"Your own health is up to you. So, you have to make sure you pay attention and ask your doctor questions," Timpf said. "Don't think it can't happen to you because I thought that, and I was wrong."

Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the U.S. and worldwide, with approximately one in eight U.S. women expected to develop invasive breast cancer during their lifetime, according to the Breast Cancer Research Foundation.

LINDA PERRY SAYS SHE WAS FEELING HEALTHY WHEN DOCTORS DISCOVERED ‘ANGRY’ CANCER BY CHANCE

While breast cancer has historically been more commonly diagnosed in older women, rates are rising among younger women, including those under 40, before routine mammograms are generally recommended for women at average risk.

Dr. Malhotra emphasized that while breast cancer diagnoses in younger women account for a relatively small share of cases, the impact is profound.

"Incidence of breast cancer is rising in younger women," Dr. Malhotra told Fox News Digital.

"Maybe 10% of breast cancers are in younger women," she added. "But still, if you're one of the 10%, it's crushing."

‘X-MEN’ STAR TYLER MANE SAYS WIFE ‘SAVED MY LIFE’ AFTER SEEMINGLY HARMLESS LUMP LED TO BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS

Dr. Malhotra, who previously served on the faculty at Georgetown University, now works at BCRF to help advance breast cancer research. She highlighted the growing number of targeted treatments developed in recent decades.

"In 1977, we had one targeted treatment for breast cancer. Twenty years later, we had two," Dr. Malhotra explained. "Fast forward to today, we have over 30 targeted treatments, 19 in the last decade alone. So, it’s moving very quickly, and we're proud to say that our investigators are involved in all of those, getting them across the finish line."

She also stressed the importance of recognizing changes in one's body and speaking up during medical appointments.

"My biggest thing is to know your body because if you feel that something is out of whack — even if you think it's minor — it’s worth it to talk to your doctor about," Dr. Malhotra said.
