World.title: Alaska governor orders probe into Peltola camp after report on second Dan Sullivan in Senate race
World.content:
The Justice Department has issued at least three dozen new subpoenas and document preservation requests as part of its probe into the Alaska Senate race, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News on Thursday.

The subpoenas were sent to Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign offices and those of former schoolteacher Dan J. Sullivan, who is also running for Senate.

The move comes the same day Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced that he is ordering an investigation into Peltola’s campaign following a report that it worked with allies to recruit a candidate with the same name as incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan in an effort to siphon his votes.

The Department of Public Safety will seek to determine “whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted,” Dunleavy said in an overnight post to X. “The evidence will determine what happens next.”

Dunleavy, a Republican, referred to Wednesday’s revelations from a bombshell New York Times report as “disturbing new evidence” and said that “anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.”

Alaska’s Department of Public Safety Deputy Commissioner Austin McDaniel said Thursday that the Alaska Bureau of Investigation had initiated an investigation into the “alleged conduct in a recent New York Times article,” at Dunleavy’s request.

“The Alaska State Troopers are committed to the fair and impartial enforcement of Alaska’s criminal laws, including those that protect the integrity of our elections. We will work closely with our partners at the Alaska Department of Law to ensure that the facts are thoroughly examined and that anyone found to have violated state law is held accountable,” McDaniel said in a statement.

NBC News has reached out to the Peltola campaign on Dunleavy’s announcement.

Reached for comment on the governor’s post, a Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spokesperson provided a statement given to other news outlets.

“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan,” the spokesperson said, adding that Republicans “have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns.”

The Times’ revelations have rocked the critical battleground race. Republicans have widely condemned Democrats for allegedly trying to manipulate the ballot in an attempt to confuse voters — an accusation the GOP has been making since the second Sullivan entered the race.

President Donald Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Republicans would seat Peltola if she wins her race.

Asked by a reporter whether he thought Republicans should refuse to seat Peltola if she wins, Trump said, “you’re going to have to see what happens.” He added it was “hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”

The Times published an explosive report detailing the campaign and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s alleged efforts to recruit a Senate candidate with the same name as incumbent, citing interviews with 12 people who were involved with or were told about the plan, or were contacted as potential recruits. The report also cited dozens of text messages among participants.

The Times’ report included information from Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager, who was fired in August. Rios later contacted the Times and “retracted all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race,” the outlet said. It also reported the she had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit against the campaign but has not done so.

NBC News previously reported that the second Sullivan’s candidacy was under investigation by state and federal prosecutors in Alaska, and a grand jury issued subpoenas for information from witnesses linked to his campaign in August.

The Justice Department also filed a lawsuit last week seeking to block the certification of the election if the incumbent Sullivan loses.

Incumbent Dan S. Sullivan denounced the reported efforts to recruit the other Dan Sullivan in a phone interview with Fox News Thursday, calling it “a secret operation” to “trick Alaskans.”

“We’ll see if it’s illegal or not,” Sullivan told Fox anchor Martha MacCallum.

Reached for comment Wednesday on the Times report, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign said the campaign “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” The campaign also pointed to instances of Republicans allegedly propping up “spoiler” candidates.

NBC News has previously reported that people who worked to recruit challenger Sullivan did not necessarily violate the law.

Stephen Richer, an election analyst for NBC News, said those involved in the recruitment could be in the clear legally if there was “no inducement, like money or threats” and the candidate ran “of his or her own volition, even if we don’t agree with the reasons that the person is choosing to run.”

The Times did not report any evidence that Sullivan was coerced, and he has said he entered the race of his own accord.

Following the report, Trump called for Peltola and the challenger Sullivan to be “removed from the ballot and prosecuted.”

Asked by a reporter whether he agreed that Peltola should be prosecuted, Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday that “we should certainly look into whether she committed election fraud.”

“She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful,” he said later. “So whether it’s criminal or not, she certainly has committed, I think, a great moral failing, and hopefully the voters of Alaska punish her.”

House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer, R-Ky., said Thursday that his committee was requesting transcribed interviews with Rios and a Democratic operative, Jerid Kurtz, who reportedly was involved in recruiting the challenger Dan Sullivan.

“If you do not voluntarily appear for the interview, we will be forced to evaluate the use of compulsory process,” Comer wrote in letters to the two.

The Times reported that Kurtz did not respond to repeated requests for comment and made his social media accounts private.

Both Democrats and Republicans have a history of trying to prop up candidates who could draw votes from their main opponents.

But Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., called the reported Peltola campaign effort “unprecedented” in an interview Thursday on Fox News, saying he believed the Sullivan saga “was a concerted effort to manipulate and to deceive the voters of Alaska.”

“The voters of Alaska are going to see through that,” he said.

World.title: Patrick Stewart, actor known for iconic roles in ‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men,’ dies at 86
World.content:
Beloved actor Patrick Stewart has died following a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, his representative confirmed. He was 86.

“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” Kelly Bush Novak, his longtime spokesperson, said in a statement Thursday.

00:26 Actor Patrick Stewart dies at age 86 00:00 00:00

Stewart — whose storied career included the iconic roles of Professor X in the “X-Men” film series and Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in the “Star Trek” franchise — had spent quality time with loved ones before his death, according to the statement.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” the statement said. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection of his invincible grace.”

Stewart, an indelible part of the “Star Trek” legacy, played Jean-Luc Picard for seven seasons on “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” from 1987 to 1994, and in multiple films, and he reprised the role in the Paramount+ show “Star Trek: Picard,” from 2020 to 2023.

He stepped into the role of Professor Charles Xavier with the 2000 film “X-Men” and continued to depict the genius mutant telepath in multiple sequels.

He was featured in a trailer for the highly anticipated “Avengers: Doomsday” film scheduled to be released in December, reprising the role for the eighth time in the mega Marvel crossover.

He had most recently done voice-over work in the film “The Sheep Detectives” and appeared in the Prime Video series “Bait,” both in 2026, according to his IMDb profile.

Born in the town of Mirfield in West Yorkshire, England, he joined the acclaimed Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. He went on to make his Broadway debut in 1971 in “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” and forged a career on the silver screen.

Stewart in "A Christmas Carol" in 1999. Hallmark Entertainment / Courtesy Everett

In his theater career, he graced numerous Broadway and West End stages — including as the title character in “Macbeth” on Broadway, for which he was nominated for a Tony in 2008.

Across the pond, he won two Laurence Olivier Awards focused on London theater: the first in 1979 for best actor in a supporting role for his role in “Antony and Cleopatra” and the second in 2009 for best performance in a supporting role as King Claudius in “Hamlet.”

As a voice actor, Stewart lent his commanding baritone to the character Avery Bullock, the eccentric CIA director on the animated comedy “American Dad,” from its 2005 debut through this year. He also voiced several characters, including his own Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, on the animated comedy “Family Guy” from 2005 to 2018.

“His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,” the statement said. “He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise.”

Off the stage, he was dedicated to philanthropy and activism, including advocating for human rights, domestic violence survivors, refugees, veteran mental health services and animal welfare.

A revered figure in Hollywood — with myriad accolades spanning nominations for Emmy Awards, Golden Globes and Screen Actors Guild Awards — he was also knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his services to drama.

Stewart after he was knighted by Britain's Queen Elizabeth II at Buckingham Palace in 2010. WPA Pool / Getty

The statement closed with a quote from his 2023 book, “Making It So: A Memoir”: “Like me, Jean-Luc has lived an unusual life that has taken him far beyond the bounds of normal human experience. But he is also someone who has remained true to his earthbound roots, for they are what gave him his identity. In the end, he feels the call of home, as do I.”

Marvel Studios said in a statement that it is “deeply saddened” by Stewart’s passing.

“Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from ‘X-Men’ to ‘Logan’ to ‘Avengers: Doomsday,’” the statement said. “He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art.”

Stewart in 2017. Jamie McCarthy / Getty

Kevin Feige, president of Marvel Studios, recalled first seeing Stewart in action.

“I’ll never forget the first time I saw Sir Patrick Stewart on the set of the first X-Men. After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe — and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas,” Feige said in a statement.

“Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor. It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed,” he added.

Tributes poured in for Stewart from devoted fans and co-stars.

Hugh Jackman, who played Wolverine to Stewart’s Professor X in the “X-Men” films, shared photos of the pair on Instagram, writing: “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”

William Shatner, a fellow “Star Trek” captain, remembered Stewart as “a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor.”

“From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work,” he said on social media.

Jonathan Frakes, who played Cmdr. William Riker in “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and in “Star Trek: Picard,” wrote on his Instagram Story: “Rest in peace my friend.”

“Star Trek: Picard” executive producer Akiva Goldsman remembered Stewart as “not only a true lion of the profession, he was the rarest of alchemists, one who could literally turn the written word into flesh and blood.”

“Patrick was kind, strong, fiercely intelligent, collaborative, vulnerable and wise. His Captain Jean-Luc Picard permanently expanded the universe of Star Trek without measure. He will be deeply missed by this one fan and by so many more,” Goldsman said in a statement.

World.title: Alphabet shares record their worst day ever, shedding $500 billion in value
World.content:
Shares of Google parent company Alphabet sank Thursday by 12.6%, marking the stock’s worst one-day drop ever and wiping out $500 billion in market value.

Alphabet is America’s fourth-largest company, worth $3.47 trillion.

The market value it shed in Thursday’s trading session ranks as the second-worst one-day wipeout in U.S. market history, trailing only Nvidia’s $589 billion drop in late January 2025.

It was also the latest sign of broader anxiety across Wall Street over how long it will take big artificial intelligence companies to see consistent returns on investments worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

Late Thursday afternoon, Amazon’s stock appeared to be on track to meet a similar fate. The company reported third-quarter revenue after the bell that fell short of Wall Street’s expectations. Its shares quickly slid by 10% in after-hours trading.

Alphabet had reported its latest quarterly financial results Wednesday, revealing that revenues were less than had been anticipated and surprising investors.

It also reported lackluster advertising sales.

The “magnitude” of the slowdown in Google’s search business was “steeper than expected,” JPMorgan Chase analysts wrote in a note Thursday morning.

A senior Alphabet executive told investors Wednesday that part of the reason ad revenues from search were underperforming was Google’s own “AI Mode” search feature, which was resulting in fewer ads.

The company is working on addressing that, Senior Vice President Philipp Schindler said on the investor call, adding that “ad experiments” in the feature have “shown promising results.”

Company executives tried to soften the blow for investors by touting more than 1 billion users of its Gemini AI app.

But all that AI is coming at a massive cost to Alphabet, which disclosed that it has committed to more than $1 trillion worth of multiyear spending agreements to fund the infrastructure, energy and leases required to run AI systems.

The company said in its July earnings report that it planned to spend more than $200 billion this year, double what it spent in 2025. It also raised almost $80 billion in capital in June, also to spend on the ever-expanding AI build-out.

Alphabet’s disappointing results also came against the backdrop of better results from its peer Microsoft, whose shares initially rose in after-hours trading Wednesday before they reversed course to end the day Thursday effectively flat.

The big drop in Alphabet shares dragged down the Nasdaq Composite index, which closed down 1.38%. The S&P 500 fell slightly less, by about 0.3%.

Shares of chip companies that supply equipment for AI data centers followed Alphabet shares lower, with the Philadelphia semiconductor index dropping 1.4%.

The bleeding even spread beyond the tech sector, as shares of the construction equipment giant Caterpillar — a key supplier of the machines required to build data centers — plunged 9.2% on Thursday.

Caterpillar’s recent earnings report revealed that its revenue beat Wall Street expectations but by less than many traders had hoped.

The sharp drop in its share price that followed made the industrial giant the day’s second-worst-performing stock in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, behind only Alphabet. The Dow declined slightly more than 130 points for the day.

As investors clamor for ever-higher returns from companies linked to the costly AI build-out, stock in firms that only narrowly top earnings targets, as Caterpillar did, has been getting punished in dramatic sell-offs.

World.title: Polymarket briefly halts trading after third-party compromise and reports of stolen user funds
World.content:
Prediction markets platform Polymarket was forced to halt trading on its international platform Thursday for nearly an hour because of what it said was a compromise of third-party software.

There were also unconfirmed reports from users on Polymarket’s Discord channel who said their wallets had been drained.

While Polymarket did not confirm that users had lost money, it said in an X post that “anyone who has been impacted will be made whole.”

“We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company said in a subsequent post on X.

Polymarket said the attack appeared to emanate from the United Kingdom and that it had referred the matter to British law enforcement authorities.

The hackers gained access to the funds via software from DebugBear, a web analytics and website performance tool, according to a person familiar with the details who was granted anonymity to address an evolving security situation.

DebugBear said on X that it was experiencing an “ongoing security incident” at around 2 p.m. ET Thursday.

Crypto news website The Block reported that some $2.65 million in cryptocurrencies had been siphoned from Polymarket users’ wallets, citing data from blockchain analysis group Arkham.

A Polymarket representative declined to comment on that figure or on the precise nature of the attack.

Polymarket said in its X post that it had identified and fixed an issue affecting its international platform, Polymarket.com.

“One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement,” Polymarket said.

“Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading & are working to bring the platform back online,” it added.

Trading began again at 3 p.m. ET after nearly an hour offline.

Polymarket’s U.S.-based platform did not appear to be affected by the breach.

Compromising third-party vendors has become a common way malicious actors gain access to large platforms and websites.

These hackers’ success in stealing money from Polymarket users, however, makes this a significant breach.

Polymarket was valued at $21 billion in September after a group of investors led by Donald Trump Jr. invested $1 billion in the platform.

The company currently processes approximately $200 million worth of trading activity daily.

Polymarket, along with rival Kalshi, has become the subject of an intense, multimillion-dollar battle between U.S. states and the Trump administration over who gets to regulate the prediction-market betting that occurs on the sites.

The platforms also continue to fight off potential insider trading activity. Earlier Thursday, Bloomberg News reported Polymarket was investigating reports of suspicious bets made amid Israel’s closely watched elections.

It is also investigating “dozens” of bets related to the U.S. midterms, according to the company’s head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista.

Earlier this month, Kalshi said it was looking into suspicious bets involving Trump’s choice for press secretary.

World.title: Lawyers fighting N.Y. AG’s role in Cornell assault investigation say she is not ‘viable’ as prosecutor
World.content:
MONTICELLO, N.Y. — Lawyers for one of seven former Cornell University fraternity members accused in a high-profile sexual assault lawsuit argued in court Thursday that New York Attorney General Letitia James should be removed as special prosecutor, alleging she is biased against the defendants.

Gillio Lopes filed a petition earlier this month seeking to block James’ appointment to oversee the case. The petition argues that James has “unequivocally demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt against the defendants.” Lopes has denied sexually assaulting the plaintiff, who has been identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe.

Sullivan County Supreme Court Judge James R. Farrell did not immediately rule on Lopes’ lawyers’ request.

Lopes’ attorneys have cited a social media post James published three days before she was appointed special prosecutor. “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable,” James wrote on X on Sept. 28. “I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”

Stuart Bernstein, one of Lopes’ attorneys, told Farrell that James had “failed” in her obligation to “represent all of the citizens of New York state.”

Andrew Miltenberg, right, and Stuart Bernstein arrive to the Sullivan County courthouse in Monticello, N.Y., on Oct. 29. Seth Wenig / AP

Bernstein added that James’ appointment was no longer “viable” because her X post showed she had “publicly aligned herself” with the complainant. “She has shown that she has picked sides,” Bernstein added.

James filed a formal opposition to Lopes’ efforts last week, arguing that his petition relies on claims that are “not justiciable.” She also argued that Lopes’ attorneys lack standing to challenge her appointment, which is within the governor’s discretion.

In a statement after the hearing, a spokesperson for James’ office said Lopes’ lawyers’ “claims are without merit.” The spokesperson added that James’ office “remains committed to conducting an investigation guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law.”

Farrell during the hearing questioned whether James’s remarks in support of Jane Doe were improper, suggesting that “an ethical rule” might apply.

“You would agree with me it’s probably not a good idea for a prosecutor to engage in that type of conduct?” Farrell asked Assistant Attorney General Kaitlin Vigars, who briefly hesitated before responding.

“I’m hearing your honor’s sentiment,” Vigars said. “Ultimately, I don’t think public statements by a prosecutor are an impediment to a prosecution. … There’s nothing that prevents prosecutors from making public statements.”

Farrell also pushed Lopes’s lawyers on why their client was not joined by the other six defendants in challenging James’ role, calling it “a real issue” for him.

“It’s not a one-defendant potential case,” Farrell said. “It’s a potential for seven, so you can’t have seven different proceedings.”

Lopes’s attorney Andrew Miltenberg told reporters after the arguments that he was “confident that the other six will join, whether they want to or not” because he believes Farrell could “force them to join” if they were not all on board.

Lopes’ filing is known as an Article 78 petition, a proceeding that allows parties to challenge actions by state or local government officers or agencies.

Winston Lee, another defendant in Jane Doe’s lawsuit, separately asked a Tompkins County court to bar James from participating in any grand jury proceedings. A decision is expected Nov. 13 in the sealed matter.

Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James this month to independently investigate allegations in Jane Doe’s civil lawsuit. Doe alleges she was plied with alcohol, sexually assaulted and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca in October 2024. None of the seven men named in the lawsuit has been criminally charged.

Hochul has defended her decision to appoint James, saying in part, “I have every confidence in our Attorney General to do what she has always done: look at the facts, examine the record and draw the proper conclusions. That’s exactly what’s going to happen in this case.”

James and Hochul are both Democrats running for re-election.

World.title: Midterm elections put Social Security funding gaps on the ballot
World.content:
Next week's midterm elections could prove momentous for Social Security, with time running out to put the program on solid financial ground. Social Security trustees' most recent report projects that the program's main trust fund is on course to be depleted by late 2032, after which Social Security recipients would face a more than 20% cut in benefits.

In effect, that means the burden of repairing Social Security will fall on both sitting and newly elected lawmakers. If Congress wants to avert what would amount to a devastating financial blow for millions of Americans, it will need to solve an issue that previous generations of legislators have punted on for decades.

"The pressure on Congress is going to just be tremendous going forward," said Martha Shedden, president of the National Association of Registered Social Security Analysts, an organization that trains Social Security advisers. "Every time that the annual trustees report comes out, there's more and more consternation about what lawmakers are doing."

Social Security's funding is running low largely due to demographic factors, as the U.S. population ages. More baby boomers are claiming benefits while comparatively fewer workers are paying into the program, forcing the agency to draw down its trust funds.

Concerns over the future of Social Security — a key issue for older Americans, a powerful political constituency — have surfaced in multiple electoral races across the country, including in key battleground states.

In the Michigan Senate race, for example, Republican candidate Mike Rogers highlighted the importance of eliminating fraud when asked to outline possible fixes to the program during an Oct. 25 debate. Rogers' opponent, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, expressed support for removing the cap on income subject to employee payroll taxes "so that the rich pay their fair share."

The current payroll tax income limit is $184,500, with any earnings above that amount exempt from payroll taxes. The tax is 12.4%, with employers and workers each contributing 6.2%.

Other candidates around the country have also endorsed scrapping the cap, which would require high-income workers to pay the Social Security tax on a greater share of their income. In a recent analysis of 20 Senate races by economist Jon Schwabish, around half of the candidates said they would support raising or eliminating the cap.

Others have been more vague about their plans to shore up Social Security, simply committing to ensuring that Americans collect their full benefits rather than offering detailed policy proposals. Previous proposals have floated gradually raising the retirement age or means-testing benefits, according to Boston College's Center for Retirement Research.

Battleground battle

Social Security reform is also a hot-button issue in the battleground state of Maine, which data shows has the oldest population of any U.S. state. Around 390,000 Maine residents were collecting Social Security as of December 2025, according to the Social Security Administration, more than a quarter of the state's total population.

In a September AARP poll of nearly 1,000 likely Maine voters aged 50-plus, 81% said Social Security is one of the issues that will factor into their vote. Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, and her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, have each proposed possible ways to stabilize Social Security.

Jackson, a logger who previously served in Maine's state senate, has committed to eliminating the payroll tax income cap.

"People who work hard their entire lives should be able to retire with dignity," Jackson said in a statement to CBS News. "While Susan Collins has repeatedly voted to weaken Social Security, I'll work to scrap the cap because billionaires should pay into Social Security at the same rate teachers and loggers do. Social Security is a promise, and I intend to keep it."

Collins has painted herself as a champion for reform, having co-sponsored the Social Security Fairness Act with Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio. The bill, which passed in 2025 under former President Joe Biden, eliminated federal policies that barred employees with a public pension from collecting their full Social Security benefits and that reduced benefits for those workers' surviving spouses and family members.

In a television interview last week with News Center Maine, a local media outlet, Collins suggested creating a bipartisan commission to develop solutions to the projected Social Security shortfall, "such as potentially raising the earnings cap for Social Security taxes." She also vowed not to cut benefits, a proposal that has gained traction among some Republicans.

"As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, the author of the Social Security Fairness Act, and a longtime advocate for Maine's seniors, I remain committed to keeping the Social Security program strong for current and future generations," she said in the interview.

Shedden said Maine's Senate race could signal where the national debate over Social Security is heading after the midterms.

"The question is increasingly shifting from whether higher-income Americans should contribute more to how much more, and whether Congress can turn that emerging agreement into bipartisan legislation before the trust fund deadline forces the issue," she told CBS News.

World.title: Patrick Stewart, best known for "Star Trek" and "X-Men," dies at 86
World.content:
Legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart, best known for his work in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises and his prolific award-winning stage career, has died at 86 years old, his spokesperson confirmed.

Stewart died at home on Wednesday, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said in a statement. His death followed "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," Novak said.

"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Novak said.

Patrick Stewart attends the premiere of "Star Trek: Picard" on Jan. 13, 2020, in Hollywood, California. Rich Fury/Getty Images

Stewart began his acting career doing stage plays in the United Kingdom, joining the Royal Shakespeare Company in the 1960s.

Stewart's most recognizable role began in 1987, when he started playing Enterprise Captain Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." The show ran for seven seasons and also spawned four "Star Trek" films featuring Stewart as Picard and the rest of the "Next Generation" cast. Stewart later reprised the role for Paramount+ series "Star Trek: Picard," which ran for three seasons.

Fellow "Star Trek" legend William Shatner posted: "Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work."

George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original "Star Trek" series, said on Threads that "Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain."

Stewart also played "X-Men" leader Charles Xavier in over half a dozen films in the "X-Men" franchise. He reprised the role for the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday," which will be released in December 2026. Marvel Studios said on social media that it was "deeply saddened" by Stewart's passing, calling him a "singular talent" who defined the character "for generations of fans."

"X-Men" co-star Hugh Jackman said in a social media post "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."

Stewart appeared in dozens of other film and television roles, including voice work on Seth MacFarlane's animated shows "Family Guy" and "American Dad."

"Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us," MacFarlane wrote on social media Thursday. "... He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come ... We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet."

The bulk of Stewart's work was on the stage: He was a frequent presence on Broadway and in London's West End, where he played characters from Shakespearean villains to Charles Dickens' Ebenezer Scrooge. He appeared with "X-Men" co-star Ian McKellen in "Waiting for Godot" in London in 2010, then again in New York City in 2013. He also performed his one-man version of "A Christmas Carol" frequently over the decades.

Stewart appeared in over 60 Royal Shakespeare Company productions. The company named him an "Honorary Associate Artist" to celebrate his contributions to their work. He has also been awarded three Olivier Awards for his London stage performances and received one Tony nomination for his work on Broadway.

Stewart was nominated for multiple Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG awards for his on-screen roles. He won a Grammy Award in 1995 for "Best Spoken Word Album for Children."

In 2001, Queen Elizabeth II appointed Stewart an Officer of the Order of the British Empire. In 2010, Stewart received a knighthood, again from Elizabeth II, for his services to drama.

In 2023, Stewart published the memoir "Making It So." The book landed him on the New York Times' best-sellers list. He also recorded a companion audiobook.

Stewart was actively working until 2026. In addition to his role in "Avengers: Doomsday," he recorded an audiobook where he narrated and commented on all 154 of William Shakespeare's sonnets. He also had a voice role in the animated comedy "The Sheep Detectives."

Stewart was married three times. He wed Sheila Falconer in 1966. The pair had two children — Daniel and Sophia — before divorcing in 1990. From 2000 to 2003, he was married to producer Wendy Neuss. In 2008, he began dating singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell. The two married in 2013 and were wed until his death. Novak said Ozell was at Stewart's side when he died.

Stewart was also "a fierce advocate for causes he strongly believed in," his spokesperson said. Those causes included social justice, women's rights, domestic abuse advocacy, veterans' rights, the refugee crisis, animal rights and political reform.

"We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," Novak said. "His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre. … He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life."

World.title: Millions of French press coffee makers recalled due to burn risk
World.content:
Coffee appliance company Bodum USA is recalling 5.9 million French press makers, warning that the glass carafe can break and cause burn injuries.

Bodum USA is the American subsidiary of a Danish-Swiss company that specializes in coffee hardware. So far, the company has received 70 reports of glass carafes breaking, 48 of which resulted in burns, according to a notice posted by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.

The French press coffee makers were sold on Amazon.com, in retailers including Target and Walmart, and other stores between 1974 and October 2026.

The agency said the glass carafes can unexpectedly break if they are damaged or cracked, which can happen when customers use metal spoons to stir coffee.

The recall involves a variety of Bodum USA models, including 8-cup French presses and 12-cup Bistro, Brazil, Caffettiera, Chambord, Crema, Java, Jesper and Kenya models, according to CPSA. The recall number is 27-055.

Safety regulators said customers who purchased one of the recalled French press makers should not use metal utensils to stir the coffee and should avoid using the carafes if they are cracked or damaged. Customers can contact Bodum to receive a plastic stirring spoon.

A Bodum USA customer service representative told CBS News that the company is not offering refunds to customers.

For more information, consumers can contact the company toll-free at 888-879-8213 Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET; email at Bodum3302@sedgwick.com; or online at www.bodumfrenchpressrecall.expertinquiry.com or www.bodum.com (click on "Recall Information").

World.title: What to know about Alaska's Senate race as ballot fight heats up
World.content:
Washington — A candidate bearing nearly the same name as sitting Sen. Dan Sullivan has drawn scrutiny in Alaska's Senate race, as Republicans and the Trump administration raise the alarm bells over the possibility of confusing voters.

And although the Democrat in the race, Mary Peltola, has denied any involvement, new reporting from The New York Times details an alleged secret effort by people aligned with her campaign to help recruit the second Dan Sullivan.

The race between Sullivan and Peltola has appeared closer than initially expected in a state that President Trump won by double digits in 2024. But the second Sullivan has added a wrinkle.

Here's what to know about the Alaska Senate race:

How did two Dan Sullivans end up on the ballot?

Alaska voted to change its election system in 2020, introducing a nonpartisan primary and a ranked-choice general election. The unique system, which was first implemented in 2022, aimed to move the state away from party primaries in an attempt to stymie polarization.

Now, as Alaska voters head to the polls, they face four options for Senate, after the state held a top-four primary in August. The incumbent Sullivan — identified on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan — is facing off against a candidate by nearly the same name, Daniel J. Sullivan, another Republican, Gerald Heikes, and his main competitor, Democrat Peltola.

Under Alaska's system, voters can rank as many or as few candidates as they'd like, rather than just selecting a single candidate. If any candidate is the top choice for more than 50% of voters, they win. If nobody wins an outright majority, the count goes to a second round and the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, with their supporters' votes redistributed to their second choice. The process continues until one candidate wins a majority.

Daniel J. Sullivan came in third place in the primary, winning just 2.5% of the vote. Peltola came in first, with 49.5%, followed by Sen. Sullivan, with 41.4%.

Who is the second Dan Sullivan?

Daniel J. Sullivan is a retired teacher from rural Alaska. He announced in June that he was entering the race, prompting a push by the incumbent senator to remove him from the ballot, calling him a "sham candidate" attempting to trick voters. But Daniel J. Sullivan has denied those allegations, insisting that he is genuinely interested in running for Senate.

After the second Sullivan announced his bid, an Alaska election official determined in June that he was not eligible to appear on the ballot, citing a "determined effort and a deliberate attempt" to confuse Alaska voters. Elections Director Carol Beecher said at the time that Sullivan's entry into the race was not done to "declare an actual good-faith candidacy for the office of United States Senator, but was instead filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality."

Daniel J. Sullivan and sitting Sen. Dan Sullivan. Karen Dillman via AP / Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images

Beecher noted that at one point, Daniel J. Sullivan tried to file as just "Dan Sullivan," despite never using that iteration of his name to vote, that he tried to list "S" as his middle initial — the same initial as the incumbent senator — and that the two campaign websites looked similar, suggesting a "deliberate" appropriation of Sen. Sullivan's campaign. Beecher also said he initially asked to be listed as a Republican, but the state had no record of affiliation with the GOP.

But the challenger appealed the decision, and a judge overturned Beecher's move to keep him off the ballot later that month, finding the state didn't have the power to decide whether a candidate is running in "good faith." The state Supreme Court upheld the decision days later, paving the way for both Sullivans' names to appear.

A sample ballot shows how the two Sullivans are listed, with Daniel J. Sullivan appearing first, as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.," with no party affiliation, and Sen. Sullivan appearing next, as "Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent."

For Republicans, the ballot differentiation is the best-case scenario — although they would prefer the second Dan Sullivan not to appear on the ballot. But as Election Day has approached, the GOP has been efforting to make that distinction clear and prevent any confusion, reaching out to voters throughout the state, including with a radio jingle that says, "Dan S., Daniel, Gerry – just don't rank Mary!"

Alaska Senate candidates, as shown on sample ballot from Justice Department court filing

Reported campaign ties spur questions

Republicans have claimed for months that Daniel J. Sullivan has ties to the Democratic Party. But after The New York Times reported that a Democratic operative who worked with Peltola's campaign and national Democrats helped encourage him to run, citing text messages and interviews, Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into the Peltola campaign.

"Today's New York Times reporting reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska's elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes," Dunleavy wrote in a post on X.

Dunleavy said the Alaska Division of Elections investigated "these very concerns" earlier this year, adding that the new reporting "substantially supports the Division's findings." He said he was directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate "whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted."

A spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan's campaign said in response to the Times' reporting that "Alaskans deserve the truth."

"Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along," Nate Adams said.

The Times reported that the operative's work to encourage Daniel J. Sullivan to run appeared to be part of a wider effort to draw more candidates into the race. But Peltola's campaign has denied any involvement in getting Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot, and a spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee said it "is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan."

Peltola called the reporting "just another distraction" at a campaign stop Wednesday.

"This is all stuff to sell newspapers," she added.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has also argued that in the Senate primary and in prior elections, Republicans engaged in their own efforts to stack the Alaska ballot in order to help their preferred candidates.

Trump administration intervenes

The Times' report came after the Justice Department filed a lawsuit last week to preemptively challenge the certification of Alaska's Senate race if Sen. Sullivan loses.

If Sen. Sullivan were to lose because of votes unintentionally cast for Daniel J. Sullivan, the Justice Department argued that the election should not be considered valid. It alleged that he deliberately sought to confuse voters by running with the same ballot name — and, initially, party affiliation — as the incumbent senator.

Attorney General Todd Blanche emphasized on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" Sunday that the DOJ's lawsuit is "not saying, 'don't certify.'" But if a court determined that the race was decided "because of confusion, and not the will of the voters," then the Justice Department does not think the state should certify the election. He added that the Justice Department was looking to "put guardrails in place" with the move.

Blanche said it may "be obvious from the results and from the ballots that voters were confused," adding, "That could be obvious from the way that they rank the Dan Sullivans, or not including a Dan Sullivan on the ballot."

On Wednesday, Mr. Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, "I don't think Mary Peltola, after perpetrating such a terrible scheme, should be allowed to run, because this is ELECTION FRAUD."

The administration has faced criticism for filing the lawsuit less than two weeks ahead of Election Day, a move that Mr. Trump said came at his direction. The Peltola campaign called the DOJ's move "a despicable political threat to overturn an election."

GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, the state's other senator who's not up for reelection this cycle, opposed the lawsuit, saying, "Alaskans don't need any help voting for their preferred candidates and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year's ballot."

But after The New York Times' reporting, Murkowski was critical of the Peltola campaign, saying, "Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign," calling the revelations a "pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials."

The pushback isn't expected to change much ahead of Election Day. Under the Constitution, states have the primary authority when it comes to the "times, places, and manner of holding elections."

"The Alaska courts have already considered whether or not this might be shenanigans, and they've ruled on this under Alaska state law," election law expert and CBS News contributor David Becker said. "The DOJ's lawsuit doesn't have any legal basis, it's not going to stop certification. The voters of Alaska are still going to decide this race."

Becker said there is "almost certainly no crime committed here or nothing illegal about what's happened."

"These kind of shenanigans unfortunately happen quite a bit. This has happened on both sides of the aisle," Becker said. "This isn't unusual — it's unfortunate."

World.title: How debates became high-risk and low-reward in the viral era
World.content:
A short interruption in the Maine Senate debate from Oct. 15 is still relevant a week before Election Day. Democratic nominee Troy Jackson told five-term incumbent Sen. Susan Collins to "shut up," after she said a protester was "obviously one of Troy's supporters." Jackson has since been asked to apologize, which he declined to do, and the clip made its way into GOP attack ads.

Maine is among the close races that will determine which party controls the Senate. Jackson's comment, unprompted by a question from the moderator or an answer from Collins, speaks to the high risk of debating. Small moments can cause catastrophes, according to Democratic strategist and CBS News contributor Chuck Rocha.

"You may not win a race during a debate, but you can certainly lose one," Rocha said. "People are super cautious these days."

In this midterm cycle, 18 of 35 Senate races and 12 of the 36 gubernatorial races did not feature a debate between the major party candidates, and in those that did occur, many were defined by mudslinging and character assaults that wound up viral online.

"Debates are defined by big moments," Republican strategist and CBS News contributor Terry Sullivan said. "Ninety-five percent of what happens in debates does not matter. You're banking on not making the 5% mistake and trying to force the other guy to make the 5% mistake."

Candidates backing away from debates

Over half of the 2026 Senate races will not feature debates between the major party candidates. That number includes Ohio and Texas, two of the five races rated as toss-ups by CBS News.

In an analysis of past toss-up races from Cook Political Report, only one of the four races in 2024 and 2022 did not have debates. The seven toss-ups in 2020, nine in 2018 and seven in 2016 all had debates.

Rocha said going on stage "without any control of the messaging" can do more harm than good in these closely contested races. In Texas, which is on track to be the most expensive Senate in history, Democratic candidate James Talarico has repeatedly called on his Republican opponent Ken Paxton to debate and even suggested he would go "into the lion's den" and let Fox News host it. Talarico eventually hosted a solo CNN town hall. Rocha noted that a debate could draw new attention to Paxton's past scandals and controversies. "He don't want to be asked about all the negative [stuff] in his life," Rocha said of Paxton.

A third of gubernatorial races will not have debates, a significant jump from years past. When the same set of 36 gubernatorial seats were up in 2022, candidates in seven opted not to debate. In 2018, all but two races included debates, and in 2014, all but four did.

Candidates on both sides of the aisle have also argued there is no benefit to debating. Ohio Democratic candidate Amy Acton said she would not debate GOP nominee for governor Vivek Ramaswamy because it cannot be "a civil dialogue about facts when you're with somebody who's a chronic liar."

In Alabama, Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who is running for governor, argued there is nothing to debate with his opponent, former Sen. Doug Jones, because "we know where the Democrats stand, and we know where conservative Republicans stand." Jones held his own "debate" on Oct. 21, where he played clips of Tuberville.

Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs declined to debate her Republican opponent, Rep. Andy Biggs, because "face-to-face interactions with Arizonans are more effective than a stage that is designed for nothing but political soundbites and theater." Biggs participated in a debate alongside "No Labels" candidate Teri Hourihan and has criticized Hobbs. He wrote on X, "Your record is so disastrous you won't even get on a debate stage to defend it."

Pushing the 5% mistake

The cornering of opponents and the effect of the digital age were on display in the debates that did occur. Debates in Michigan and Alaska, which are among the crucial Senate toss-up races, also had viral moments like in Maine. Nominees appeared closer to enemies than as candidates from opposing parties, with their attacks garnering significant attention online.

In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Mike Rogers was a "sock puppet" for the president, and Rogers accused El-Sayed of being an extremist connected to the Muslim Brotherhood. Asked if there should be guardrails for flock cameras, Rogers suggested El-Sayed would want them because of a relative "that might be on the watch list." El-Sayed challenged his opponent "to go ahead and say it," leading Rogers to allege El-Sayed's mother worked for a company "that was indicted for funneling money to al Qaeda."

Alaska's Senate debate also produced viral moments for both candidates. Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan took a few notable swipes at Democratic nominee Mary Peltola. He accused her of "character fraud" over a New York Times' report on Peltola's treatment of staff that led the moderator to call for "some decorum." But in another swipe, he accused Peltola of having pre-written answers, and when moderators assured no one did, Peltola replied, "I'm prepared," leading to a viral moment for Democrats.

Debates used to be an opportunity for "people to get out of their echo chambers and their partisan media and listen to the other candidate in a way that is not filtered for them," said Kathryn Cramer Brownell, a history professor at Purdue University who focuses on the relationship between media and politics. The current media climate, however, has "undermined the potential" for debates to actually broaden a candidate's appeal.

"How do you generate more of that broad viewing experience in the age of social media?" Brownell asks. "Frequently, debates just become boiled down to very short clips that are circulated through social media, and, then, again, filtered through a more partisan lens."

World.title: Patrick Stewart, a perceptive patriarch in 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men,' dies at 86
World.content:
Patrick Stewart, a perceptive patriarch in 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men,' dies at 86

Enlarge this image toggle caption i Jack Taylor/Getty Images Jack Taylor/Getty Images

Sir Patrick Stewart's most famous characters tackled concepts such as honor, morality and courage. He played Professor X in the X-Men franchise and Jean-Luc Picard, captain of the starship USS Enterprise, on the show Star Trek: The Next Generation and its later spinoff, Picard.

Stewart died Wednesday at 86. A post on his Facebook and Instagram pages said he died at home in Los Angeles after a "brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia."

Although he was beloved for playing compassionate father figures who united families of misfits, Stewart's own upbringing in Yorkshire, England, was harsh. He remembered his father as alcoholic and abusive. He found solace in school and, eventually, in Shakespeare. He joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966 and debuted on Broadway in 1970 in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

Sponsor Message

"To stand in the middle of an empty stage in an empty theater and feel that I was at home was everything," he told NPR in 2023. "But it took a while for me to get there."

toggle caption i Evening Standard/Hulton Archive/Getty Images

Stewart played alongside some of the best Shakespeareans of his time, including Judi Dench and Ian McKellen. He was lecturing on Shakespeare at UCLA when his name came up for the lead in a new series of Star Trek.

"Don't do this, Patrick," he remembered McKellen advising him. "You're a very good stage actor. That's where you ought to be. Don't do it."

But Stewart's agent had reassured him that the show was unlikely to make it past the first season. As the actor recalled to NPR, he was encouraged to take what he believed to be a quick and easy job. "'Do six months' work. Make some money for the first time in your life and get well known. Get a suntan, and go home.' And I thought, 'Yeah, that doesn't sound too bad. I could live with that.'"

But Star Trek: The Next Generation was a tremendous hit. It aired for seven seasons, from 1987 to 1994. Stewart was embraced by fans, who adored the character's penchant for Earl Grey tea and cool-headed leadership, with such signature phrases as "Engage!" and "Make it so!"

toggle caption i Getty Images

But success on the starship Enterprise came at a cost. Throughout his career, Stewart portrayed only a handful of Shakespeare's leading men. He put some of that character energy into an award-winning, one-man version of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol, in which Stewart played more than 40 roles.

Sponsor Message

By the beginning of the 21st century, Stewart had reestablished himself on stage while also lending his voice to numerous big-budget animated films. He went on to dominate another blockbuster franchise, the X-Men, beginning in 2000. He'll appear for the last time in his role as Professor Charles Xavier in the upcoming movie Avengers: Doomsday.

As for his signature role, Stewart thought he was done playing Picard. But a team of producers — including writer Michael Chabon — had different ideas. They pitched him a new show, Star Trek: Picard, that began streaming on the CBS service now called Paramount+ in 2020.

"I would've been happy just shaking Patrick Stewart's hand and telling him how much I loved him on Star Trek," Chabon told NPR. "But to be able to actually write words that he will speak and act is — it's incredible."

In the show, Picard is struggling with the psychological damage that led to leaving Starfleet. The performance is vintage Stewart. His character is keen-eyed, haunted, weary, yet joyful. While this Picard was trapped in the past, Patrick Stewart spent his career charting the future.

World.title: What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery
World.content:
What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery

toggle caption i Ralph Vanstreels

Sailing toward the Danger Islands, Dr. Ralph Vanstreels had a good idea of what he might find: A lot of dead Adélie penguins.

It was March 2024 and a virus had been sweeping through the area, leaving deceased birds in its wake.

Vanstreels got the crime right but the culprit wrong. There were dead penguins but a virus was not to blame.

As his vessel pulled up to a landing ramp on one of the islands — located just off the Antarctic Peninsula — Vanstreels and his fellow researchers immediately noticed bumps in the snow.

"Was each bump a rock or was it a carcass? We had to do quite a bit of intensive searching [through the snow]," says Vanstreels, who is based in Argentina and is a wildlife veterinarian with the University of California, Davis.

Sponsor Message

The team ultimately found more than 537 penguin carcasses on just the ramp, which he estimates was about the size of an airport runway.

There were many more carcasses elsewhere on the Danger Islands, which are home to two mega colonies for penguins. The researchers estimate there were thousands of dead Adélie penguins and other species of birds. But they had to work quickly and couldn't do a complete count, Vanstreels says.

toggle caption i Ralph Vanstreels

"You cannot stay there very long because you might be locked down with an iceberg blocking your way out," he says.

As the team has pieced together this tragic penguin mystery, Vanstreels says, the case holds broader lessons for tracking the spread of diseases globally.

The only continent to dodge the virus — until now

Now let's time jump to Australia a few months ago for another bird disease conundrum.

In June, H5N1 — high pathogenicity avian influenza also known as bird flu — arrived in mainland Australia. Up until that point, Australia had been the only continent to dodge the virus which has traversed the globe, leaving a trail of carcasses in its path.

Since late 2021, the virus has led to the death of nearly 300 million poultry birds. Either the virus killed them or they were culled as a preventive measure to stop the spread of the disease, according to the World Animal Health Information System. Further, bird flu is estimated to have killed millions of wild animals and marine mammals, although it's hard to get an exact figure.

Sponsor Message

Researchers were amazed that Australia could stay bird-flu-free for six years. And the virus didn't take the path that scientists expected.

"We have a lot of migration of birds between Australia and Southeast Asia, so for the first few years, we're like: That's where the virus is coming from," says Dr. Amandine Gamble , an assistant professor at Cornell University in the Department of Public and Ecosystem Health.

The way bird flu eventually got there was from the other direction. It came from Antarctica likely via migrating birds.

"This is a virus that's not assisted by airplanes," Michelle Wille , senior research fellow at the Center for Pathogen Genomics at the University of Melbourne, told NPR in 2025. "This is a virus that's traveling by mass mortality after mass mortality after mass mortality after mass mortality."

"The virus loads are low"

So when Vanstreels set sail to check on the penguins, he assumed bird flu would be the culprit.

Bird flu arrived in Antarctica in late 2023 and early 2024. Vanstreels and his colleagues rapidly arranged for a trip to try to figure out exactly what was happening.

"The expedition was initially fully set up to look for bird flu because that was the panic," he explains, adding that ongoing fear of a continuing global panzootic — or pandemic among animals — is justified.

In several layers of warm clothes covered by protective gear — double gloves, coveralls, glasses and masks — Vanstreels and the team started taking samples of the penguin corpses they found.

"We looked a little bit stiff when walking — like a penguin walking almost — because of all the gear," he says. "We had very strict biosafety standards."

They brought samples from the deceased penguins back to a mini-lab on their boat. By evening, they had early results. But not the results they expected.

"There is bird flu here, but the virus loads are low," he recalls. "That was a little bit puzzling."

toggle caption i Ralph Vanstreels

The carcasses were not very old, so Vanstreels would have expected to find far more bird flu virus if that had killed the birds. Perhaps something else was the main driver? "We were unsure what was happening," he recalls.

Sponsor Message

What the microscope revealed

So what killed the 500-plus penguins on the landing ramp and the many others on the island?

Back on land several months after the voyage, in the Netherlands, Vanstreels' colleagues did more investigation. "Under the microscope, you can see that there's bacteria in the tissues," he says — not virus.

They discovered a different disease, a bacterial disease that causes avian cholera (which is distinct from human cholera).

Vanstreels and his team's findings were published in October in the journal the Proceedings of the Royal Society B .

So how worried are they about avian cholera?

The disease is not considered a major threat to humans since the strain that is specialized to birds is distinct from the strain specialized to mammals. "The risk for human infection is not really that high when you see an outbreak on birds," Vanstreels says. But, it does kill birds worldwide — especially in cold environments where the bacteria thrives.

While there's not enough research to know exactly how common avian cholera is, the disease has been on the radar of scientists for decades. However, it's not exactly top of mind. The last time researchers looked for it in the Antarctic Peninsula was 25 years ago.

"One could be misled to think that: Well, that was a unique thing that happened back in 2001, and nothing's happened ever since," says Vanstreels. Instead, it is possible that avian cholera die-offs could be occurring regularly, only scientists haven't been checking.

One of his big takeaways from this bird-flu-that-turned-out-to-be-avian-cholera event?

"Yes, there is a big thing with bird flu. But we still want to keep checking for the other diseases because they might be mixing up in the middle," Vanstreels says.

Antarctica isn't as remote as it seems

Like any good mystery, the case of the cholera-stricken penguins has got scientists wondering: Whodunit?

Sponsor Message

There's a theory that avian cholera might have been introduced to Antarctica decades ago from researchers who brought poultry from the U.S., Vanstreels says.

toggle caption i

Gamble, of Cornell University, adds that the strain of avian cholera found in penguins in Antarctica is "very close" to the strain found 5,000 miles away on Île Amsterdam in the Southern Indian Ocean.

"Antarctica is way more connected to the rest of the world than we think it is," she says.

It's hard to track diseases in Antarctica but, she says, it's turning out to be an important piece in the global pathogen puzzle.

The work of keeping tabs on what's happening has fallen to a number of different countries since Antarctica is not governed by any one government. It was designated as a continent of peace and science by the mid 20th-century Antarctic Treaty , which now has 58 parties — among them are the U.S., France, Japan and Russia. Many nations have research stations and team up on scientific undertakings, including tracking pathogens — be it bird flu or avian cholera — that travel great distances and don't respect borders.

"So this Avian cholera outbreak is just showing this is not a unique event," says Gamble. "We really need international collaboration."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: Lost your spark? The "silent sister" of depression, and a quiz to spot her
World.content:
Lost your spark? The "silent sister" of depression, and a quiz to spot her

toggle caption i Getty Images

Some people with clinical depression can't get out of bed. But what about those who exhibit other signs of depression who never stop moving, and may double down on their work?

Psychiatrist Dr. Judith Joseph says the second group often goes unnoticed, even by the people living it. She calls it "high-functioning depression": people who keep meeting their obligations at work and at home while quietly losing the ability to feel pleasure.

"When you are joyful, you have better physical health, you have better relationships, you have better productivity at work," Joseph said in an interview for the Your Turn podcast . "So why don't we prioritize it?"

Sponsor Message

At the center of Joseph's work is anhedonia: a reduced ability to feel joy, pleasure or interest in things that once brought those feelings. Joseph describes it as "the silent sister" of depression.

"One sister is depressed, and crying, and not getting out of bed, and getting all the attention," she says. "The other one is quiet and numb." Anhedonia may not seem like a crisis in the classic sense, Joseph says. "But it is an existential crisis, and it's not something to ignore."

What the research shows

In a peer-reviewed study published in the journal Cureus, Joseph and colleagues interviewed adults using a set of questionnaires designed to assess high-functioning depression, trauma and anhedonia.

The results supported the researchers' hypothesis that people with high-functioning depression have increased levels of anhedonia and trauma. Participants with higher anhedonia scores also had higher high-functioning depression scores.

Parents and caregivers had the highest anhedonia and high-functioning depression scores in the study.

The authors note that high-functioning depression is not an official diagnosis in the DSM-5, the manual clinicians use to diagnose mental health conditions. They say that is part of the problem: people who keep functioning may not recognize their symptoms or seek treatment until they reach burnout.

Sponsor Message

'Something's gonna give'

Joseph says she often sees the pattern in women who are the steady presence for everyone around them. They are so focused on their responsibilities at work and at home that they don't realize they are burned out, or close to it.

"But eventually something's gonna give," she said. "Either they do break down and they have a clinical depression and they lose their functioning, they go into distress or crisis, or they physically break down."

She said she has seen patients end up in the emergency room without understanding why, only to learn they had been carrying unresolved emotional pain.

Joseph said the pattern is common in professions that discourage vulnerability, including her own. In medicine, she said, crying after a patient died was seen as weakness.

"In medicine, we focus on the crisis," Joseph said. "You're [taught] to look for the mania, for the psychosis." She believes there should be more focus on anhedonia, the loss of sense of joy.

A self-assessment

Joseph developed an anhedonia quiz based on the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale, a measure of the capacity to feel pleasure that was published in the British Journal of Psychiatry.

The questionnaire asks about everyday experiences, such as whether you have trouble enjoying praise, whether you savor your meals or other small pleasures, and whether you struggle to enjoy your work or accomplishments because they never feel good enough.

The quiz is not a diagnostic tool. It's an invitation to take stock of what might be standing in the way of a fuller, more joyful life. If you'd like to take the quiz, you'll be asked to share your email to see the results.

Five V's

In her book, "High Functioning: Overcome Your Hidden Depression and Reclaim Your Joy," Joseph also outlines a framework she calls the Five V's:

Sponsor Message

Validation: naming and accepting what you feel.

naming and accepting what you feel. Venting: expressing emotions, through talking, writing, creative expression or maybe a good cry.

expressing emotions, through talking, writing, creative expression or maybe a good cry. Values: making time for what matters most.

making time for what matters most. Vision: having something to look forward to.

having something to look forward to. Vitals: caring for your whole self (mind + body) through sleep, nutrition and movement.

Joseph says anhedonia appears across many conditions, in many people in midlife and other times, too. "It's something that we need to learn how to detect," she said, because it can be a silent problem.

If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988, to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

World.title: Even birds get jet lagged, study shows
World.content:
Even birds get jet lagged, study shows

toggle caption i birdsonline/Getty images

New research shows that humans are not the only species to get jet lag: Some birds appear to experience it too.

A study published in the journal Science found that a type of seabird known as the Manx shearwater appears to become slightly disoriented during long flights across the Atlantic Ocean. That disorientation, the authors say, is due to the bird's internal clock falling out of sync with the sun's position in the sky.

Manx shearwaters are a common bird in the British Isles. They look a little like seagulls, but "they're actually very closely related to an albatross," said Patrick Lewin, a behavioral ecologist at the University of Oxford.

Sponsor Message

Shearwaters mate for life, and when they breed, a couple lays just one egg.

Then they take turns incubating it: "One partner will sit on the egg nonstop while the other one goes out to sea," Lewin said.

For up to two weeks the hunting partners scour the North Atlantic for fish and squid, often travelling hundreds of miles from their nests.

Once these birds' bellies are full "they absolutely bomb it back to their colony," Lewin said. Often they make the long journey home in just a day or so.

Which raised an interesting question: Do Manx shearwaters feel jet lag (or perhaps more aptly, flap lag)?

To see if these little birds really did feel the effects of flying through time zones like humans do, Lewin used a remarkable tool – for 20 years, his colleagues had been tagging birds with GPS trackers and collecting data on their flights out to the Atlantic and back.

He figured he could see the jet lag in their flights. That's because the Manx shearwaters are believed to use the sun to navigate.

"To use the sun as a compass you have to know what time of day it is," Lewin said.

In the morning, the sun is in the east, at midday it's slightly to the south (if you're in the northern hemisphere) and then in the evening it's in the west. If the shearwaters had the wrong time of day, they would fly the wrong way.

That's exactly what Lewin and his colleagues saw. As the birds rushed back to their partners and eggs, they veered ever-so-slightly off course. It wasn't much: A seven-degree error, the maximum deviation observed, only took a bird out of its way by about three miles on a 600-mile journey. "It's a really small addition," he said.

Sponsor Message

"This paper is so cool," said Alice Boyle, a biologist at the Centre for Animals on the Move at Western University in Ontario, Canada who was not part of the study.

Boyle said pretty much every creature on the planet, from corals to chipmunks, has to navigate its environment, yet it's rare to see a study showing navigation decisions in action. That's what makes this type of GPS work so valuable.

"It's using these wild birds that travel to completely remote places and we're able to learn so much about how they do that," she said.

World.title: Fishing is a key issue in Alaska's tight U.S. Senate race
World.content:
Fishing is a key issue in Alaska's tight U.S. Senate race

Alaska's U.S. Senate race is embroiled in an emotional fight over fish. Many in the state rely upon salmon to feed their families but those fish and others are increasingly hard to find.

Transcript

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

President Trump is trying to preemptively block election results in Alaska if the Republican incumbent loses. But in that state, the big issue in the Senate race has been an emotional fight over fish. And that's because the salmon that have long sustained Indigenous people are not returning to some Western Alaska rivers. While people living in remote villages feel the loss of salmon most acutely, the issue could ultimately affect the balance of power thousands of miles away in Washington, D.C. Alaska public media's Liz Ruskin reports.

(SOUNDBITE OF DOG BARKING)

LIZ RUSKIN, BYLINE: Evon Waska lives at the water's edge, where he says his parents settled when they gave up their nomadic life.

EVON WASKA: Well, this is my smokehouse, and this is where we make smoke, right?

RUSKIN: Waska's drying racks should be filled with salmon, but they're empty. Most years now, too few salmon return from the Bering Sea to his river, the Kuskokwim. To conserve fish, government agencies often close the river to fishing, even to those like Waska who fish to feed their families. Waska blames trawlers, industrial fishing boats miles offshore.

WASKA: They don't close the trawlers. They close me and my people first.

RUSKIN: Waska is up against a $1 billion industry, much of it based in Seattle. Picture a sock-shaped net that's a quarter mile long with an opening as wide as a football field. That's what trawlers tow to catch pollock. The white fish is served to you as imitation crab in McDonald's Filet-O-Fish. But also scooped up in those nets are prized king salmon and other fish. They're caught by accident and wasted, a problem known as bycatch. Alaskans are increasingly angry about it. Now, in a year where Alaska could decide the balance of power in the U.S. Senate, fish are all over political ads here.

(SOUNDBITE OF MONTAGE)

UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #1: Senator Sullivan is championing legislation to reduce bycatch and strengthen Alaska's fisheries. Call Senator Dan Sullivan. Thank him and tell him to keep fighting for Alaska fishermen.

UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #2: Dan Sullivan is taking big money from out-of-state corporate trawlers.

UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #3: Mary Peltola tells a lot of fish tales to get votes.

RUSKIN: Republican Senator Dan Sullivan has been an ally of the pollock industry. But this year, he's touting a new bill.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

DAN SULLIVAN: It's the most comprehensive bycatch legislation ever to reduce bycatch, protect seafloor habitat.

RUSKIN: Democratic Senate challenger Mary Peltola is Indigenous, from the Kuskokwim. She says she'd ban factory trawlers, the largest of the pollock fleet. She calls Sullivan's bill an election year ploy.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MARY PELTOLA: Dan Sullivan reeled in over $300,000 from trawlers and waited until the 11th hour for a half-hearted and half-baked solution.

RUSKIN: Heather Mann (ph) leads a trawlers association. She says scapegoating the pollock fishery won't help western Alaska.

HEATHER MANN: Even if you were to eliminate pollock, the chances of salmon runs being restored, what the science shows us is it would have a minimal impact.

RUSKIN: So far this year, pollock trawlers say they've caught 40,000 Alaska salmon. The waste is a tiny percentage of the massive pollock harvest.

(SOUNDBITE OF MACHINE WHIRRING)

RUSKIN: But in the Kuskokwim River village of Kwethluk, it's galling.

(SOUNDBITE OF MACHINE RUMBLING)

RUSKIN: Subsistence fishing is the main occupation here and the backbone of the culture. Tribal president Mary Nikolai steps into a neighbor's cold smokehouse. It pains her to see it was unused all summer.

MARY NICOLAI: Most of the smokehouses are like this. And it's like a slow trend of closing our workforce out.

RUSKIN: Regardless of who wins, she hopes this close Senate race tells the world of the threat they face.

For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Kwethluk, Alaska.
