World.title: Carney says Canada is working to become an 'associate member' as he hosts EU leaders in Montreal
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is working to become an "associate member" as he hosts European Union leaders in Montreal, although it remains unclear what that would look like and how viable the pitch really is.

"We share a common mission. We're in the process of forging a new alliance — alliance for the future — with Canada as an associate member," Carney said ahead of a roundtable with Canadian and European business leaders on Thursday afternoon, wading into an ongoing back and forth about how to describe the new partnership both sides are seeking.

Carney has, until Thursday, largely stayed away from using the associate member title, instead arguing the nomenclature doesn't matter.

CBC News has requested clarity from his office about his associate member comment.

Making Canada the first associate member of the EU is something European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen first championed last month, but the move faces some objection within the 27-member bloc. The status currently does not exist.

WATCH | EU chief floats 'association without accession': EU chief floats 'association without accession' for Canada | Duration closed caption 0:58 After Canada's 'associate membership' of the EU was reportedly removed from a proposed joint statement on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen mentioned the idea again on Thursday, suggesting a partnership 'that comes closer to membership than anything we've done before.'

Von der Leyen renewed her calls to carve out a special place for Canada within the union during a keynote speech hours earlier in Montreal, where she told a crowd she wants a partnership with Canada "that comes closer to membership than anything we've done before."

Von der Leyen and other European Union delegates are in Montreal for a two-day summit aimed at forging a new phase in the Canada-EU relationship, as they both seek to lessen dependence on the United States under an unpredictable and protectionist President Donald Trump.

"In a world of growing rivalries, sovereignty and independence are no longer just the freedom to act alone — it is the capacity to act together. And this is why we will build an alliance for the future," she said.

"And we start with Canada."

What to call that alliance has overshadowed the gathering and caused confusion.

The day before von der Leyen's speech, it was revealed the words "associate membership" were removed from the draft of a joint statement expected to be published on Friday and replaced with a commitment to an "ever closer association," as objections within the bloc persist.

However, von der Leyen marched on with her vision in her Thursday speech.

"It is an association without accession," she said.

The leader said becoming an associate member would see a close alignment on policies, including AI, climate, energy, security and governance.

"It means more work shared by the European Commission and the Canadian government," von der Leyen said, suggesting that could mean "parliament to parliament" and "court to court" co-operation.

As European Commission president, von der Leyen can advocate for policies but it's up to the bloc to decide what happens next.

Sources speaking to CBC News said Germany in particular opposes the "associate member" term, calling it a red line.

WATCH | Carney mentions 'associate membership' alongside European Commission president: Canada forging 'alliance for the future' with EU as an 'associate member,' Carney says | Duration closed caption 0:48 On the margins of the Canada-EU summit on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney told a roundtable meeting that Canada and the European Union are in the process of forging a new 'alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member.' Carney earlier told reporters the proposed partnership's 'name doesn't matter.'

Earlier in the day, Carney said the name of the alliance "doesn't matter."

"This new alliance is not a marketing exercise," he told reporters during a news conference.

"What matters to Canadians ultimately from this new alliance is going to be affordability, it's going to be opportunity. Opportunity for young Canadians, to live, travel, study. Opportunities for our researchers to plug into one of the most advanced research networks across a wide range of domains."

Former ambo calls debate a 'distraction'

David Plunkett, the former Canadian ambassador to the European Union, said the title is a tricky issue for the Europeans — pointing to their relations with other countries who also want to join.

"Since this thing first came up, I have thought it was an unnecessary distraction to spend a lot of time on this empty label," Plunkett said.

WATCH | EU agreement 'names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney: EU agreement 'names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney | Duration closed caption 0:42 Prime Minister Mark Carney says what 'matters' at the EU summit set to take place later this week in Montreal is 'Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation so we can live our lives as we choose.'

"I think it's far more important that the two sides continue to work on developing the broadest and deepest package of substance that they can get and at the end, once they've got everything put together, they figure out what they want to call it."

Trump has threatened retaliation

Talk of making Canada an associate member has irked Trump, who previously said if he interpreted the move as a "hostile act," he might stop trading with Europe "on many things."

It raises the question of whether the president will look unkindly at this week's gathering in Montreal.

Asked Wednesday about the possibility of retaliation from Trump, a senior Canadian government official, speaking on background, told reporters the summit isn't directed against anyone but reflected deep interests between Canada and the EU.

Carney government invests $1.6B in AI company

Over the course of the summit, the two sides are expected to continue talks on deepening trade, investment and security partnerships.

In their Thursday speeches both von der Leyen and Carney stressed the importance of collaborating on artificial intelligence. On the sidelines of the summit, the prime minister announced plans to invest up to $1.6 billion in Cohere, the Toronto-based company specializing in generative AI.

"We're not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don't know or by whom we don't trust," said Carney.

The version of the EU-Canada statement seen by CBC News also commits to reinforcing "a predictable trade environment," deepening collaboration in the Arctic, countering foreign information manipulation and interference and continued support for Ukraine.

LISTEN | More from the summit: The Current 15:11 Inside the New Canada-EU alliance Delegates from the EU are in Montreal for a summit to launch negotiations to deepen trade and other partnerships between Canada and the European Union. We hear from former leader of the federal Liberals and former Special Envoy to Europe, Stéphane Dion, and from Teresa Ribera, Executive Vice President for the European Commission, on what this new alliance means for Canada and the EU.

Both sides are also promising to launch negotiations toward deeper participation in Erasmus, the European Union's student and youth exchange program.

A source speaking to CBC News on the condition they not be named says this statement is now finalized by EU member countries, but Canada could still ask for changes before the summit wraps on Friday.

Canada's Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre called the summit a "grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words."

"No one's mortgage or grocery bill will come down," he posted on social media.

"Get EU countries to let our beef into the continent and cancel their planned carbon tariff on Canada. Otherwise stop wasting your time and our money. Both are running out."

World.title: Star Trek actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Patrick Stewart, British stage actor who found fame as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, has died. He was 86 years old.

His death was announced in a statement on his official social media account, which said he died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia."

Stewart's career spanned six decades, from the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon to Broadway to film and television.

He was best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the Star Trek: The Next Generation series and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film franchise.

Marvel Studios is remembering Stewart as an actor who brought his X-Men character to life with "extraordinary grace, intelligence and humanity." It calls him a "singular talent, generous collaborator and true gentleman."

Hugh Jackman, who starred as Wolverine in the X-Men films, also paid tribute to Stewart on Instagram, calling him "a tremendous friend and man."

Star Trek actor Jonathan Frakes, who played Picard's No. 1, Commander William Riker, was among the first of Stewart's colleagues to post a tribute to him online, simply saying, "Rest in peace my friend," on his Instagram stories.

William Shatner, who played Picard's predecessor aboard the USS Enterprise, Captain Kirk, called this a heartbreaking week, making reference to the death of his co-star Walter Koenig on Monday. Shatner said he was filled with admiration for Stewart.

"From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him," said Shatner on social media.

George Takei, who portrayed physicist Hikaru Sulu in the original Star Trek series, said his heart was heavy.

"Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity," Takei wrote on Threads.

Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.

Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of A Christmas Carol and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter's No Man's Land and Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot in repertoire with long-time friend and X-Men co-star Ian McKellen.

Early years and advocacy

Stewart was raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working class corner of northern England, and grew up without a bathroom in his house.

At age 12, he joined an amateur drama group and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor.

He was bald since he was 19 — alopecia runs in his family.

WATCH | Patrick Stewart dead at 86: Star Trek, X-Men actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86 | Duration closed caption 4:10 Patrick Stewart, the British stage actor who famously played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men, has died. The 86-year-old died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after 'a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,' according to a statement on his social media page.

His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of "repeated violence against my mother," as Stewart wrote in the Guardian.

"Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it."

Stewart would later became a patron for Refuge, an organization that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims.

Sonnets to lift spirits

In 2013, Stewart married Brooklyn songwriter and singer Sunny Ozell, with McKellen officiating.

He said it was his wife's idea to start sharing his love of Shakespeare with the public during the COVID-19 pandemic.

When people were locked down at home, he posted one sonnet a day on his social media accounts, to help lift spirits.

Sonnet 154. The final one. Here's to everyone who has been so kindly watching and listening to these sonnets. We never expected anything like this and we appreciate it enormously. Thank you! #ASonnetADay https://t.co/K2l1UAa3a0 —SirPatStew

Stewart is also survived by two children, a daughter, Sophia, and a son, Daniel.

The statement on Stewart's social media said "he has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all.

"We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace."

In lieu of flowers, the statement requests donations be made to Johns Hopkins Alzheimer's Disease Research Center Fund or Alzheimer's Foundation of America Caregiver Resources.

Fans mourn

The death of Stewart is being felt keenly by X-Men fans and Trekkies alike.

"I believe generations to come, they will look back at this absolutely remarkable, this treasure of a person, this knight of the realm, this genius of acting that was Patrick Stewart," editor-in-chief of thatshelf.com Jason Gorber told CBC News.

"Patrick Stewart's voice was one of those that was so exquisite, so luscious, so captivating, that it simply brought us in whatever he was saying."

Family Guy creator Seth MacFarlane was one of those who benefitted from his work as a voice actor.

"He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful," MacFarlane wrote on X, saying Stewart will be deeply missed "by the entire planet."

World.title: Tumbler Ridge shooting survivor Maya Gebala being released from hospital, father says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 13-year-old girl who was severely injured in the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting is being released from hospital after nearly nine months of uncertain recovery, her father says.

David Gebala shared a Facebook video Thursday of his daughter Maya Gebala in a wheelchair reacting with excitement as he tells her she'll be going home.

"It's been 262 days since you were airlifted to B.C. Children's Hospital," he wrote in the post. "262 days since we were told, 'We did everything we could, but we don’t think she’s going to make it through the night.'

"Since then, I’ve watched you fight for every single one of those days."

While the family has not been speaking to media, they have been sharing updates through social media posts and videos intended for the public.

In previous posts, Gebala's mother has indicated the family will likely have to permanently relocate to Vancouver in order for Gebala to continue receiving care, though it's not clear whether that is still the case.

Details of her injuries have been shared online and in lawsuits filed in California against tech firm OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman over their alleged roles in the deadly February mass shooting.

WATCH | Maya Gebala pumps her fist after hearing she's leaving hospital: Tumbler Ridge shooting survivor being released from hospital | Duration 0:10

Documents filed by her family in court in April 2026 say Gebala was shot three times and that a bullet struck her skull and "shattered bone fragments through her brain."

OpenAI has asked for the case to be dismissed.

In May, Gebala's family said she had undergone surgery for a cranioplasty, which involved installing a prosthetic barrier to quell swelling and deflation in Gebala's head that was a symptom of her damaged skull.

It was the fifth surgery Gebala had gone through since the shooting, and in the time since, the family has shared video of her on various outings throughout Vancouver, as she is no longer confined to B.C. Children's Hospital where she has been receiving her treatment.

Those include celebrations from her 13th birthday in September when she attended a Foo Fighters concert at B.C. Place, and enjoyed cake and games.

World.title: You can see You Can See Everything everywhere
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some movies leave you with a memorable line. You Can See Everything leaves you with a face inches from yours and plenty of parodies.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's movie about Elizabeth Holmes, Theranos founder and convicted fraudster , has become a meme machine, powered by the film's most unnerving visual signature: close talking. Online, the answer has been to turn the pauses, the proximity, the dead-serious eye contact and that discomfort into a format.

The latest take came on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon, where Jamie Lee Curtis played Holmes and Fallon took on Fielder. They delivered a shot-for-shot remake of of one of the film's most intense exchanges.

With tense music underneath, Fallon mirrored Fielder's measured questions and subtle expressions while Curtis held Holmes's wide-eyed stare and repeated her lines, including, "I'm engaging with you as a human being." The pair stayed in character until Fallon walked away and Curtis broke the tension.

The spoof quickly won over viewers online, with fans calling it Emmy-worthy and some saying Fallon looked so much like Fielder they briefly thought it was him.

WATCH | The Tonight Show parody:

This Hour Has 22 Minutes borrows the film's close-talking tension for a parody negotiation between U.S. President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney.

As Trump insists he isn't lying, Carney asks, "So you won't try to make Canada the 51st state?"

Trump promises he won't, then admits, "I lied."

Their face-to-face exchange spirals into an absurd argument about truth and trust, with Carney struggling to follow Trump's shifting story.

WATCH | This Hour has 22 Minutes parody:

The joke made its way to Washington Square Park in New York City, where dozens gathered for a Holmes and Fielder lookalike contest. Organized by comedian Maddy West and a friend, the event drew more than 200 registration responses.

The winners were Nicole Travolta, an actor and comedian who has been impersonating Holmes since 2022, and Joe Sivick, whose resemblance to Fielder was convincing enough to briefly fool one of the organizers.

Fans react online

On platforms including X, Instagram, TikTok and Reddit, users have also been reacting to Holmes and Fielder's real-life exchanges, even making parodies of their own. One Reddit user reimagined the film as You Can Eat Anything.

Other memes transplant the film's dead-serious dialogue into everyday situations. One X user posted, "It's finally fall, we're going apple picking with my college friends next Sunday at 1 pm."

A user on Reddit re-shared this one, which said, "My cat telling me she hasn't been fed yet. Why would I deceive you? There's no reason for me to do that."

A reddit user re-shared this meme that says, 'My cat telling me she hasn't been fed yet. Why would I deceive you? There's no reason for me to do that.' (jhovudi1/Reddit)

Box office success

The film's reach extends beyond social media. It took in more than $15 million US during its opening weekend, the second-largest opening weekend for a non-musical documentary in domestic box office history, behind only 2004's Fahrenheit 9/11.

It's also currently the highest-rated movie in Rotten Tomatoes history, currently sitting at 97 per cent fresh. The audience response has also prompted A24 to mount an ambitious Oscars campaign, seeking consideration for You Can See Everything in categories including best picture and best director — an unprecedented push for a feature documentary.

World.title: B.C. NDP caucus taps Jennifer Whiteside to be new interim leader
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The B.C. NDP caucus has announced Jennifer Whiteside as its choice for the party's new interim leader.

The caucus recommended Whiteside after David Eby resigned as party leader when his snap election call resulted in a resounding defeat of the NDP at the polls.

Eby's majority government fell from 47 seats in the legislature to 28, according to the initial count.

At a caucus meeting Thursday, Mike Farnworth was named house leader and Niki Sharma was named caucus chair.

Whiteside said it was a unanimous recommendation.

Eby wasn't at the in-person caucus meeting, nor was he present virtually, Whiteside said.

Whiteside said she was humbled by the caucus's recommendation.

"It is not an outcome I was necessarily expecting," she said.

She said she's looking forward to using her advocacy skills in the role.

Whiteside, MLA-elect for New Westminster-Coquitlam, previously worked as chief spokesperson and lead negotiator for the Hospital Employees' Union.

She said the caucus meeting included discussions on what the community needs.

"We are very focused on making sure that British Columbians understand that we are standing for them, that we have their backs, and we will continue to do that work in the opposition caucus."

The B.C. NDP will serve as Official Opposition to Lorne Doerkson's B.C. Conservative Party, which won 63 seats.

More to come.

World.title: Ottawa's sluggish bureaucracy leaves critical gaps in Canadian military ammo supply: AG
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A new report by the auditor general takes shots at both the Department of National Defence and Public Services and Procurement Canada over their handling of the Canadian military's strategic stockpile of ammunition.

Karen Hogan's latest report, tabled on Thursday, concluded that the Defence Department does not manage its ammunition to meet its regular use and strategic stockpile needs and the federal procurement agency was slow in efforts to restock ammunition.

Her analysis found that the strategic stockpile, which the military needs in case of war, did not contain "all the types and quantities of ammunition required" and there were significant gaps.

More importantly, perhaps, Hogan noted that the problem is affecting Canada's international commitments.

WATCH | AG on munitions shortfall: Auditor general says Canada's military stockpile has 'critical gaps' | Duration closed caption 1:40 Auditor General Karen Hogan says when it comes to managing its ammunition inventory, Canada's military has 'lots of weaknesses.'

"As at March 2026, National Defence determined that the Canadian Armed Forces' readiness level to meet North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) commitments was well below target, and ammunition was one of the contributing capability shortfalls, especially for the strategic stockpile," said the audit.

The scathing assessment was released on the same day federal officials released the country's new national security strategy, which warned Canada needed to "prepare for all contingencies up to and including war."

The auditor's report noted that in 2024, the federal government dedicated $9.2 billion over 13 years to support strategic stockpile replenishment, and some contracts have been awarded. But at the current pace, it will take several years to close the gaps.

When it comes to buying ammunition, the auditor looked at 15 regular‑use ammunition contracts and found it took an average of almost 19 months from contract signature to final delivery.

In addition, Public Services and Procurement Canada "did not consistently track and document why contracts were changed to extend delivery dates."

The audit also pointed out how the military — when it had ammunition — only used about half of what was allocated.

Hogan suggested that "limited or cancelled" training activities were likely to blame, but the Defence Department did not track or explain the reasons.

"For example, National Defence's analysis as at March 2026 noted that equipment, such as tanks and ships, was often out of service, which limited their availability for use in training and military exercises," said the audit.

"Other factors, such as a lack of personnel or poor environmental conditions, might have also prevented these activities."

Defence minister embraces recommendations

Defence Minister David McGuinty said increasing the military's supply of ammunition is among the government's top defence priorities.

"The entire auditor general report on ammunition tells us that we have progress to make, and we're making it," McGuinty told reporters after the report was tabled.

"We accept and embrace all of those recommendations. In fact, we're acting on most of them already."

Canada's former top military commander sounded the alarm three years ago about the critical state of the military's ammunition supply.

The report says the munitions shortfall will take years to resolve. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Retired general Wayne Eyre, the former chief of the defence staff, also criticized lack of industrial capacity for military ammunition.

Appearing before a House of Commons committee, he warned that if the Canadian military consumed ammunition at the same rate as seen in the war in Ukraine, Canada would exhaust much of its ammunition stock within days.

Eyre also pointed out that — at the time — no new production lines had been opened to address the shortage.

He said that when Canada started providing military aid to Ukraine, it did so from "pretty empty" shelves, noting that domestic industrial capacity to regenerate artillery pieces, rockets and ammunition was largely non-existent.

The Conservative Opposition said the situation is critical and cannot be allowed to continue.

"The Liberals must act immediately to rectify the unacceptable state of Canada's ammunition stockpiles: both inventory and accounting," said defence critic James Bezan. "This is not an insurmountable problem. It is a question of political will."

In addition to the money committed in 2024, the federal government in March of this year released a $1.4-billion framework to rapidly scale up domestic munitions production.

The plan includes a $305-million investment IMT Precision, in Ingersoll, Ont., and nearly $1 billion to General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems in Quebec for artillery round production.

Among other things, there are also plans to construct a domestic nitrocellulose production facility, which critically supports the supply of ammunition.

World.title: What's the deal with question period? Poilievre, MacKinnon trade Seinfeld-related barbs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kicking off Thursday's question period, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and Government House leader Steven MacKinnon exchanged Seinfeld references in the House of Commons.

Regular question period viewers got a little more than the usual "yada, yada, yada" on Thursday as Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and Government House leader Steven MacKinnon traded Seinfeld-related jabs.

Poilievre kicked off the reference contest with a question about the Canada-EU summit taking place in Montreal this week.

"Is this just another Seinfeld summit? A meeting about nothing?" Poilievre asked, referencing the '90s sitcom that was billed as a show "about nothing."

MacKinnon shot back at Poilievre by riffing on a line from the hit show, saying that the opposition leader "lives the same recurring nightmare every single day."

The cast of Seinfeld poses at the Screen Actors Guild Awards in 1995. (Reuters)

The Conservative leader kept the references going by arguing that Prime Minister Mark Carney acts like Jason Alexander's character George Costanza, "running around the office trying to look busy while achieving nothing at all in the real world."

MacKinnon then tried to cast Poilievre as another character, Cosmo Kramer, suggesting that the Conservative leader "just walks into the room every time and says something weird."

Ironically, Seinfeld had its own reference to question period in its final season when Kramer says he is "taping Canadian Parliament." The sitcom went off the air in 1998.

The back-and-forth comes as Carney is meeting with representatives of the European Union in an effort to strengthen ties with the 27-member bloc.

WATCH | Names for EU partnership don't matter, Carney says: EU agreement 'names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney | Duration closed caption 0:42 Prime Minister Mark Carney says what 'matters' at the EU summit set to take place later this week in Montreal is 'Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation so we can live our lives as we choose.'

While the prime minister has insisted that the substance of a new agreement with the EU is what matters, questions have swirled around what the label of the new alliance will be.

CBC News reported on Wednesday that words "associate membership" were removed from a joint statement expected to be released at the summit, but that hasn't stopped European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen from using that branding.

Conservatives have continuously raised questions about what a closer relationship with the EU would mean. Poilievre says Carney should focus on getting nine laggard countries to ratify the Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement.

World.title: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski found guilty of fraud at his jury trial in Toronto
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Aiden Pleterski, the self-described "Crypto King," was found guilty of fraud over $5,000 by the jury at his Toronto trial Thursday morning.

Pleterski, who represented himself at trial, appeared emotional after the verdict was read in Ontario Superior Court.

The jury began deliberations around 10:30 a.m. and came back with their verdict 10 minutes before noon.

Pleterski will be under house arrest as he awaits sentencing. His parents, who were in court for the verdict, will act as his sureties. Pleterski has also hired Marco Sciarra, the lawyer who represented him in his earlier effort to delay his trial, to handle his sentencing proceedings.

Both Pleterski and Crown prosecutor Scott Patterson denied requests for comment after the verdict.

Patterson's co-counsel described Pleterski as "a thief" in the prosecution’s closing statement Wednesday.

"Mr. Pleterski was no 'Crypto King.' Far from it. As it turns out he was no king at all. He was a thief. A thief who stole investor money and used it as he pleased. A thief who stole investor money using calculated lies," Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora told the jury.

"As you've seen, he burned through that money.… He lived his best life, all while his investors pleaded for updates on their money, only to be ignored."

Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora delivered a roughly 90-minute closing statement at Pleterski's fraud trial on Wednesday. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Pleterski took more than $36 million from investors for trading, but never put a cent of it into the trading platform FXChoice on their contracts. Instead, the Crown provided financial records at trial showing Pleterski spent $16.3 million of it on himself and gave another $16.1 million back to investors as returns.

At the end of the Crown's case, they dropped a second charge of money laundering against him.

A CBC News investigation was first to report on Pleterski more than four years ago when some of his investors forced him into bankruptcy in the summer of 2022. At the time, they were looking to unravel where at least $35 million they provided him ended up.

Between then and his arrest in May 2024, Pleterski was kidnapped in connection to his scheme, he continued jet-setting despite his bankruptcy, and a Canadian NBA star successfully sued to get out of his $8.4 million purchase of lakefront mansion where Pleterski used to live.

Earlier this week, Pleterski was denied a mistrial. He argued that he didn’t have a fair trial without a lawyer. Pleterski only cross-examined the first of 14 witnesses the Crown called at his trial and decided not to call any evidence in his defence or testify himself.

He did make a brief closing statement to the jury Wednesday.

Pleterski addressed the jury for the first time at his fraud trial yesterday in Toronto, giving a brief closing statement on Oct. 28, 2026. (Pam Davies/CBC)

"I am the least qualified person here to give a closing statement," said Pleterski, addressing the jury for the first time.

"However, that being said, I am innocent of these charges. That is why I pled not guilty. Had I not been forced to represent myself, that would have been proven. That's all I have to say."

Justice Shaun Nakatsuru gave his full decision denying Pleterski’s request for a mistrial Thursday morning after the jury began deliberations.

"I'm still confident if Mr. Pleterski had chosen to do so he would have been able to make full defence," Nakatsuru said in his ruling.

"Nothing I have seen at this trial has changed my view on that.... He has not brought a computer or a tablet, he has not brought any Crown disclosure…. He has not made a single note that I have seen.... I'm not even sure he was paying attention to the witnesses."

Pleterski will be back in court on Nov. 13 to schedule dates for his sentencing.
