World.title: Left-wing Berlin mayor candidate’s private Hamas remarks complicate coalition talks
World.content:
Der Spiegel asked Eralp about antisemitism within her party. Eralp acknowledged that boundaries had been crossed at some campaign events. The journalists then asked whether she was referring to Ibrahim Ibrahim, a pro-Palestinian agitator who attended the Left Party’s election-night celebration. Eralp answered “yes,” according to Der Spiegel, but later sought to remove the exchange from the interview transcript.



In private comments apparently to her assistants, inadvertently included in the returned transcript, Eralp referred to advice she said she had previously received from Berlin’s State Criminal Police Office (LKA) about publicly naming individuals linked to organized crime: “The LKA said at the time that they recommend never naming specific individuals. Back then, it was about organized crime. Now it’s about people with connections to Hamas.”

She added: “I cannot put myself and my family in danger for SPIEGEL. What do we do now? Cancel the entire interview?”

In a statement through his lawyers earlier this month, Ibrahim said he was not a member of the Left Party and said he rejected antisemitism. “I categorically reject the accusation of supporting terrorism,” his statement said.

In another private comment on the Ibrahim Ibrahim question, Eralp referred to an unidentified man by his first name, saying he “does not want to name specific individuals, neither does my husband, nor do I. He is afraid of these people, and so am I.” Der Spiegel did not identify the unknown man or explain his relationship to Eralp.

The CDU’s mayoral candidate, Stefan Evers, who placed second in the vote, said the remarks exposed a contradiction between Eralp’s concerns and her party’s position. The Left Party has called for reducing police numbers, while Evers alleged that members were working with the people Eralp feared.

“If the woman who is supposed to govern Berlin in the future is so afraid for herself and her family that she hesitates to publicly name terrorist sympathizers, while parts of her own party are working hand in hand with those very circles, then reasonable voices within the Greens and [Social Democrats] must finally pull the emergency brake,” Evers told POLITICO.

Former Berlin Mayor Michael Müller, a Social Democrat, warned that Eralp could be vulnerable to blackmail.

Eralp said Thursday she still wants to become Berlin’s mayor. Asked about the report, she told journalists: “I will not comment because private, internal information has been published. But what I can say very clearly is that, as governing mayor, I will ensure the safety of all Berliners.”

World.title: EU governments helpless as energy prices soar to four-year highs
World.content:
But at the Thursday summit, EU energy ministers broadly acknowledged that both Brussels and national capitals had run out of ideas to contain price pressures.

“We’ve exhausted most of our short-term options,” said one senior European energy official, granted anonymity to offer a candid perspective. “What’s left is really crisis management.”

For the past year, government attempts to cushion price rises with renewables schemes, windfall taxes and costly fuel subsidies have ultimately failed to contain anxieties that have since boiled over into widespread protests across the continent.

“The EU and member states don't have a magic wand to make the price increases go away,” Irish Energy Minister Darragh O’Brien, whose government holds the EU's six-month rotating presidency, told reporters. “There's a lot of measures that have been taken already in the short term. What today is about is actually seeing how we can move to more sustainable measures.”

But even crisis management is proving politically difficult. Despite calls by EU energy chief Dan Jørgensen earlier this year to encourage consumers and businesses to cut energy use, European ministers are reluctant to make such a move official policy.

“I don't want to see that we will limit people,” said Mika Nykänen, the state secretary to Finland's energy ministry. Instead, he called for policy designed to “change behavior” and reduce energy consumption less painfully. “Industry does it naturally. Normal households, normal families — they sometimes need encouragement,” he said. “For instance, subsidies to invest in the energy efficiency of houses, windows.”

World.title: Carney frames C$1.6B AI investment as national security imperative
World.content:
“Sovereignty now requires secure access to semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean energy technology, vaccines, space-based communications and artificial intelligence,” Carney said. “Canada is taking a major step forward in artificial intelligence.”

In a pre-summit speech earlier Thursday in Montreal, von der Leyen cited April’s multi-billion dollar merger between Cohere and German counterpart Aleph Alpha as a key piece of the deepening Canada-EU cooperation that is set to unfold at Friday’s talks on AI.

“Both Canada and Europe believe this technology should serve people. So we will work together to tackle head-on the safety and security issues of runaway AI. We will develop together rules and standards and strong global governance,” she said.

Carney said Canada was making a commercial investment alongside private investors including Nvidia, Bell and Germany’s Schwarz Group.

Cohere co-founder and CEO Aidan Gomez announced the initial close of its Series E funding round on Thursday, which is targeting up to C$7 billion at a C$35.7 billion valuation.

Gomez joined Carney at Mila, the Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute, for the Canadian portion of the funding announcement.

World.title: Meet the front-runners to replace Lagarde
World.content:
The choices will also be influenced by horse trading over what will likely be a package deal with the opportunity to fill the two executive board seats that will be vacant in January and May.

Softly spoken de Cos

An economist with a Ph.D. from the University of Madrid, de Cos joined the Bank of Spain in 1997, moved to Frankfurt in 2004 to be an adviser to the ECB’s executive board, before returning to the Spanish central bank. He rose through the ranks to become governor, serving from 2018 to 2024. In this role he restored the Bank of Spain’s reputation after a series of missteps before and during the financial crisis.

His achievement was implicitly acknowledged by his appointment to two terms as chair of the Basel Committee for Banking Supervision, the global standard-setter for bank regulation. He now runs the Bank for International Settlements, the institution often described as the central bankers’ central bank.

His style is low-key: a modest dove, meaning that he is more attentive than hawks to growth and employment alongside inflation. Still, when inflation surged in 2022, de Cos backed the ECB’s shift toward higher rates. Equally, he has little time for governments that put off essential pension system reforms, having published a sharp critique of the Pedro Sanchez government while at the Bank of Spain.

His case

De Cos has long been groomed by Lagarde’s predecessor Mario Draghi, whose voice continues to carry a heavy weight in European economic debates and may influence the preference of some countries as they mull who to place at the top of the Frankfurt institution.

As France faces mounting debt pressures, de Cos’ experience as a senior Bank of Spain economist during the eurozone crisis could convince EU governments that he is the best fit. Galo Nuño, vice dean and professor of economics at IE University and a former alternate member of the ECB governing council, called it “a huge advantage.”

World.title: Britain’s spy agency doesn’t know where thousands of its memory sticks are
World.content:
He noted that the devices “may contain IPA-related data” — which has a high level of sensitivity.

IPA-related data refers to information collected or held under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. That could include intercepted communications such as emails, texts and telephone calls, as well as information extracted from people’s computers or phones.

The report added that GCHQ currently estimates the number of devices “to be in the thousands” and is currently undergoing work so it can report how many of the devices have been confirmed as lost.

“We remain very concerned about this issue and are disappointed with the time it has taken GCHQ to investigate,” the report notes.

Last year IPCO disclosed that GCHQ and fellow intelligence agency MI5 had been unable to locate considerable numbers of storage devices, some of which potentially containing information classified as "TOP SECRET."

A GCHQ spokesperson said: “As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations.

"We recognise the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken."

World.title: Von der Leyen touts ‘associate member’ status for Canada over objections of EU capitals
World.content:
The Commission president said in her speech that talks about associate membership would focus on deeper cooperation across AI, climate and energy policy, as well as bolstering shared work between the European Commission and the Canadian government as well as “Parliament to Parliament” and “Court to Court,” a reference to the European Court of Justice and Canada’s Supreme Court.

Such a status, she said, would be open “only to our closest partners outside of Europe, who are ready to open a new frontier together — and to chart the course together, to think beyond the terms of our partnership today, toward the most ambitious vision we can build.”

Von der Leyen’s use of the term associate membership — which she first mentioned in September — is likely to rub some EU capitals the wrong way after a group of countries led by Germany objected to including a reference to the term in a joint EU-Canada statement that was seen by POLITICO and is due to be published on Friday.

After days of talks, EU countries opted for softer language to describe the two sides’ future relations, including the “Alliance for the Future” — the term used by the Canadian side — as well as an “even closer association ... short of full membership.”

EU diplomats have told POLITICO that while capitals support the broader aim of closer ties with Canada, they are wary of offering a status that has never been proposed before and whose legal contours remain undefined. Berlin had previously floated associate member status for Ukraine, including specific privileges such as observer status in the European Commission, but that effort was rejected.

Reacting to reports that EU countries would drop the “associate member” term, Carney said on Tuesday: “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature. What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians … and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose.”

World.title: Canada to join EU network of supercomputers
World.content:
The EU's supercomputing network is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, an EU public-private vehicle with an €8.2 billion budget. The network consists of 14 supercomputers (some ranked in the global top 10), 19 AI-focused AI factories and 10 quantum computers.

The vehicle will also run seven massive AI data center hubs, known as AI gigafactories, set to be built next year with a total investment cost of €30 billion.

Experts praised a possible EU-Canadian compute power team-up, but warned it's only the start.

“Compute cooperation is one of the most obvious short-term ‘middle power’ cooperation plays in AI,” said Anton Leicht, technology and international affairs fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

But he added that for now “it doesn’t put a dent into the actual dependence" on the U.S.

“As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn’t result in massive buildouts will help,” he said.

World.title: Former Spanish employment minister died in train crash
World.content:
Báñez served in center-right Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy’s government from 2011 to 2018 and played a central role in Spain’s response to the eurozone crisis. During that period, she developed a warm personal relationship with Ursula von der Leyen, now European Commission president, who was then her counterpart in Germany’s labor ministry.

As employment minister, Báñez oversaw the conservative government’s controversial 2012 labor-market reform, which made it easier for companies to dismiss workers and drew fierce opposition from trade unions. The administration argued the changes would make hiring more flexible and accelerate the country’s economic recovery.

Speaking from the crash site Wednesday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared three days of national mourning. “All of Spain is mourning,” he said.

“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” Sánchez added. “We are going to get to the bottom of this, and if there has been negligence, it will be revealed, and if there have been failures in the system, we will act decisively.”

Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the initial investigation suggested the collision was caused by an official at the national railway control center in Madrid who “inexplicably” instructed one high-speed train to proceed along a track where another had stalled.

Puente insisted Spain has “a safe transport system,” but acknowledged that “human action plays a role” and that, despite extensive safety regulations and protocols, “failures can occur.”

World.title: The World Judo Tour returns to Abu Dhabi with Day 1 wins
World.content:
Fresh off the World Championships, the World Judo Tour returned to the Mubadala Arena for the prestigious Abu Dhabi Grand Slam.

 

In the -48kg final Turkiye’s Merve AZAK took on Azerbaijan’s Konul ALIYEVA.

ALIYEVA got the historic win, achieving the first ever women’s Grand Slam gold medal for Azerbaijan.

Mr Marius Vizer, President of the International Judo Federation, awarded the medals.

At -60kg top seed Azerbaijan's Balabay AGHAYEV. took on 18 year old Loiq KUDBUDINOV.

Showcasing why he was the favourite Aghayev showed speed and skill to score a dynamic ippon!

International Judo Federation Vice President Dr Laszlo TOTH awarded the medals.

It’s a wonderful place. I’ve been here before. I took a bronze medal here in the past, but no i’m happy to replace that bronze medal with gold! Balabay AGHAYEV (AZE)

In the -52kg final Olympic medalist Amandine BUCHARD took on Tihea TOPOLOVEC of Croatia.

TOPOLOVEC scored a clever waza ari to win her first ever Grand Slam gold medal!

IOC Member Mr Balazs FÜRJES awarded the medals.

I’ve been a few times in Abu Dhabi, this is my first time leaving with a medal, so now it will be one of my favourite cities. Tihea TOPOLOVEC (CRO)

At -66kg Bahrain’s Sukhrob BOQIEV’s first world tour final was against Iago ABULADZE.

Boqiev defied his world ranking of 277 to take a shock gold!

The medals were awarded by International Judo Federation Vice President Mr Obaid AL ANZI.

At -57kg Brazil’s Shirlen NASCIMENTO took on France’s Martha FAWAZ.

Two waza ari scores, the first an opportune o soto after a weak attack from Nascimento.

And the second, a driving o uchi gari that travelled across the mat, gave Fawaz a second grand slam title.

International Judo Federation Vice President Mr Siteny RANDRIANASOLONIAIKO awarded her the gold medal.

The home team also didn’t disappoint, with some top action from the UAE’s Narmandakh BAYANMUNKH.

Join us for day two of the Abu Dhabi Grand Slam tomorrow.

World.title: Patrick Stewart, star of 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men', dies aged 86
World.content:
Actor Patrick Stewart has died at the age of 86.

 

Stewart died at his home in Los Angeles on Wednesday following "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to his longtime spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak.

Best known for portraying Professor Charles Xavier in the "X-Men" films and Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the sci-fi series "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and subsequent films, Stewart spent much of his career on stage.

A post on the actor's official Instagram and X accounts said: "We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia."

"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all."

Stewart is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, and his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.

A statement announcing the actor's death, on the official X account of the late Sir Patrick Stewart

A career spanning seven decades

Stewart's career on stage and screen spanned nearly seven decades. It began in Mirfield, northern England, before he trained as an actor and later joined the Royal Shakespeare Company.

His theatrical roles ranged from Claudius to Macbeth. He also frequently performed a one-man adaptation of "A Christmas Carol" and appeared alongside his longtime friend Ian McKellen in West End and Broadway productions of Harold Pinter's "No Man's Land" and Samuel Beckett's "Waiting for Godot".

Stewart received numerous honours throughout his career, including a Grammy and two Laurence Olivier Awards, as well as Emmy, Golden Globe and Tony nominations. He was also honoured with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Stewart appeared throughout the seven-season run of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" between 1987 and 1994. He also starred in four Star Trek films before returning to the role in "Star Trek: Picard" from 2020 to 2023.

Patrick Stewart arrives at the premiere of the third and final season of "Star Trek: Picard". 9 Feb 2023 Richard Shotwell/Invision/AP, File

Tributes have been paid to the internationally acclaimed actor

In a post on Instagram, actor George Takei, who also starred in the Star Trek franchise, wrote: "As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity."

"Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain."

Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside Stewart in the X-Men films, described him as a "tremendous friend and man". In a post on Instagram, he wrote: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."

"I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."

Marvel Studios also paid tribute to Stewart, saying he brought Charles Xavier to life with "extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from X-Men to Logan to Avengers: Doomsday."

Marvel Studios, which makes the 'Avengers' film franchise, paid tribute to Stewart in a post on X

The post continued: "He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art."

William Shatner, who starred alongside Stewart in "Star Trek Generations", also paid tribute to him on X. He wrote "Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work."

A tribute from Sir Patrick's Star Trek co-star, William Shatner, on X

The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also honoured Stewart. In a post on X, he wrote: "He never forgot his roots, nor did he shy away from using his voice to stand up for others, particularly those affected by domestic violence."

Stewart was also a prominent campaigner against domestic violence, speaking publicly about his childhood experiences of witnessing his father abuse his mother and supporting organisations working with survivors.

World.title: Germany and Ukraine test armed ground robot for frontline deployment
World.content:
A German and a Ukrainian defence company have tested an armed ground robot for use by Ukrainian forces, with the first systems due to be integrated and delivered by the end of 2026.

 

The cooperation agreement was signed in early October during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's state visit to Kyiv, in the presence of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Before the end of 2026, the first robotic vehicles fitted with the new weapons modules are expected to be ready for deployment and delivered in line with the needs of Ukraine's armed forces.

How the new system works

It's known as GEREON. Built by ARX Robotics, the unmanned vehicle provides mobility and power and can carry out reconnaissance using cameras and sensors.

It can be fitted with the SABER weapons module, built by Ukrainian company ROBONEERS, which is mounted on top and provides remotely operated fire support for attack and defence capabilities. The companies say this allows soldiers to operate the system from a safer distance.

ARX ROBOTICS GEREON UGV with ROBONEERS SABER ARX Robotics

Unarmed versions of GEREON are already being used for a range of tasks in Ukraine. They can transport supplies, evacuate wounded personnel, support electronic warfare, carry out reconnaissance and counter drones. The platform can also be adapted for combat missions.

The companies say the aim is to create one flexible robotic system that can be quickly adapted for different frontline missions.

The SABER weapons module is also customisable, allowing soldiers to fit different weapons depending on the mission, from rifles to grenade launchers.

ARX says GEREON is the largest fleet of Western-built unmanned ground vehicles currently being used in Ukraine.

Maximilian Wied, CFO and co-founder of ARX Robotics, said: "Modern land forces need combat platforms that can be quickly adapted to different missions, integrate new technologies and work seamlessly with existing systems."

ROBONEERS says its robotic systems have already been used in more than 15,000 frontline missions since 2014.

The two companies are already cooperating in other areas. They have set up a joint venture to expand production of another unmanned ground vehicle, the Rys Pro, in Germany and Ukraine. The companies are targeting production of more than 1,000 units in its first year.

German defence minister to visit tech company Helsing

Artificial intelligence is also a focus for German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, who is visiting defence technology company Helsing at its headquarters in Munich.

The visit will focus on the company's latest products and AI capabilities, alongside meetings with management, employees and the works council.

Helsing was founded in 2021 and has grown rapidly into one of Europe's most prominent defence technology companies.

It develops artificial intelligence and software for military systems, including technology designed to add AI capabilities to existing platforms such as tanks, submarines and fighter jets.

World.title: Kazakhstan's Tokayev calls for faster construction of nuclear power plants
World.content:
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for a long-term national uranium reserve and faster progress on building two nuclear power plants (NPPs) in his annual state-of-the-nation address on Wednesday.

 

“I believe it is possible, and perhaps even necessary, to begin construction of the Balkhash NPP as early as next year, and to sign a comprehensive cooperation agreement with the goal of launching construction of the Moyynkum NPP as soon as possible,” he said.

Tokayev highlighted that nuclear energy is one way to achieve an electricity surplus, which he described as essential for digitalising the economy and integrating artificial intelligence into all areas of public life.

He also criticised the government over inefficient energy management and corruption schemes in the sector. During winter shortages, Kazakhstan buys electricity from neighbouring countries at high prices, only to sell it back at much lower rates in summer.

“It’s a rather simple sort of ‘business’, and one that has persisted for decades. I’m assured that this is standard practice in the energy sector,” Tokayev said.

He added that such practices had also led to the deliberate obstruction of power plant construction and commissioning in several regions.

Logistics hub 'historic opportunity'

Tokayev opened his address by pointing to an increasingly unpredictable geopolitical environment, which he said “did not exist even during the Cold War."

Growing vulnerabilities along maritime routes, he argued, were increasing the importance of overland transport corridors.

“Kazakhstan must seize this historic opportunity to truly become a leading logistics hub for Eurasia,” he said.

The address came two months later than usual and was delivered at the parliament session. Press service of Kazakhstan President

He pointed to the construction of the Aral-Caspian Highway, which began in August. The project is expected to shorten the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route by 1,000 kilometres and reduce cargo delivery times to three days.

The Bakty–Ayagoz railway line is scheduled to launch next year. It will establish a third railway crossing with China and increase freight capacity by 20 million tonnes.

Tokayev said Kazakhstan needed to move beyond its role as a transit country and become an organiser of international freight flows.

He called for developing domestic logistics operators, creating distribution centres, and digitising the transport sector, while also instructing the government to focus on air transit and road infrastructure.

Address in numbers

According to the IMF's forecast, Kazakhstan's GDP will exceed €350 billion this year, making it the world's 47th-largest economy. GDP per capita is expected to surpass €17,000.

The industrial sector now accounts for more than 14% of GDP. Tokayev attributed the growth to efforts to diversify the economy.

Small and medium-sized businesses contribute 40% of GDP, while their share of fixed capital investment has approached 70%.

Infographics of Kazakhstan's GDP Galiya Khassenkhanova

Kazakhstan's gold and foreign exchange reserves, combined with the National Fund's assets, have exceeded €110 billion. Tokayev said the country should use these resources to modernise infrastructure and improve living conditions across its regions.

Domestic bank assets have surpassed €130 billion, while savings accounts have reached a record €94 billion. Around 78% of these savings are held in the national currency, which Tokayev cited as a sign of the tenge's growing value.

The president designated next year as the Year of Nationwide Construction, calling on parliament to prioritise building and modernising public infrastructure, including roads, airports, hospitals and cultural centres.

The regions plan to build around 70 medical facilities and 50 educational, sports and cultural facilities. The National Fund is expected to allocate approximately €12.8 billion for these and other infrastructure projects by the end of 2029. Nearly €3 billion of that amount is earmarked for social projects over the next four months.

Tokayev also highlighted the country's demographic profile, noting that Kazakhstan has around seven million children, accounting for 34% of the population. More than 237,000 children have special educational needs.

Tokayev said the sector grew nearly 6% last year, with total output reaching almost €30 billion.

The address followed Kazakhstan's Day of the Republic and came as the country prepares to mark the 35th anniversary of its independence.

World.title: Paris shooting suspect admits targeting Muslims and people of African origin
World.content:
The suspect in the shooting in Trappes and La Verrière, on the outskirts of Paris, has admitted specifically targeting people he perceived to be Muslim or of African or North African origin, anti-terrorism public prosecutor Olivier Christen announced on Thursday.

 

Known only as Kévin T., the 39-year-old is accused of killing one man and injuring seven other people during the attack, which was carried out both from a car and on foot on 23 October.

"He admitted having specifically targeted people who are of a Muslim or African, North African type," the prosecutor said at a press conference. The suspect is also said to have explained that he chose Trappes because he regarded it as "a hideout for Islamists".

An attack prepared over a long period

The prosecutor stressed what he described as the "very extensive preparation" of the attack.

During questioning, Kévin T. acknowledged premeditation and said he had fired "in bursts". Investigators established that from September he had bought several items intended to improve the effectiveness of his weapon, a Sten-type submachine gun dating from the Second World War. He had also bought a police armband and handcuffs.

On the day of the attack, the suspect drove between Trappes and La Verrière, shooting at several people. The man killed, Pengo Bossio Wangi, was 26 and originally from the Democratic Republic of Congo. Among the seven injured was an 11-year-old girl whose life is no longer in danger. As of Thursday, three victims remained in hospital, one of them in a life-threatening condition.

A search of the suspect's home in Plaisir, also on the outskirts of Paris, uncovered an arsenal that included magazines, two brass knuckles, a steel bayonet and a silencer. Investigators also found a Quran, a Bible and a copy of Adolf Hitler's "Mein Kampf".

Stickers bearing nationalist slogans were also discovered. Many bore the words "Long live France, RN, proud to be French", referring to the far-right National Rally party, while others carried phrases including "100% French, long live France" and "Support for the security forces". The suspect admitted having designed and ordered them online, while insisting that he was neither a member nor a supporter of any political party.

Despite these admissions, he denied intending to commit a terrorist act and considered his actions "legitimate", according to the prosecutor.

He also denied having intended to kill children, saying he may have misjudged the height of the 11-year-old victim. He nevertheless said he felt "no regret".

The suspect had reported psychological and psychiatric problems. However, according to the prosecutor, a medical examination found no acute psychiatric decompensation or signs of hallucinations or delusions that would justify compulsory hospitalisation.

The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office has opened a judicial investigation into murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist act, with an aggravating circumstance linked to the presumed origin or religion of the victims. Prosecutors have requested that the suspect be placed in pre-trial detention.

Emmanuel Macron meets residents at Trappes town hall on 23 October 2026 AP Photo

Emmanuel Macron points the finger at the far right

Appearing on the YouTube channel HugoDécrypte on Wednesday, President Emmanuel Macron denounced what he called "a racism of atmosphere" and "a disinhibition of violence".

Macron blamed far-right political movements for helping create that climate, citing National Rally and groups close to it.

The RN reacted sharply on Thursday on television channel TF1. Party MP Jean-Philippe Tanguy described the president's comments as "very problematic", accusing him of having allowed "hateful ideologies" to flourish during his time in office.

A national tribute to the victims

A national tribute will be paid to the victims of the attack. The announcement was made on Wednesday 28 October by the government, the day after a request at the National Assembly by the leader of the Green MPs, Cyrielle Chatelain.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will preside over the ceremony, minister responsible for combating discrimination Aurore Bergé told the Senate.

A date and location have not yet been announced.

World.title: EU peacekeeping helicopter crash in Bosnia kills at least four
World.content:
An Italian helicopter taking part in an EU peacekeeping operation has crashed near the town of Brčko in northern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

 

The European Union's EUFOR military mission confirmed the CH-47 Chinook helicopter had crashed on Thursday afternoon. A spokesman said four crew members had been killed and 11 were injured.

A spokesman for Brčko hospital, said three of the 15 crew members on board the helicopter were killed in the crash and a fourth died in hospital.

"Twelve people were brought to our hospital. Unfortunately, a fourth person died from his injuries in hospital," said the spokesman, Salih Ibrahimbegovic.

EUFOR also said no civilians had been injured and no civilian infrastructure, property or vehicles were damaged in the crash.

Reaction from Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and Vice-President of the European Commission

The crash happened in Gorice, about 180 kilometres (110 miles) northeast of Sarajevo.

"As a result of this crash, a number of EUFOR personnel tragically lost their lives, and others were seriously injured," EUFOR said in a later statement.

Bosnia's Defence Ministry said "it is not possible to issue further statements, while awaiting more precise information, above all about the state of health of the personnel".

EUFOR has urged people not to spread unverified information or disinformation and to rely on official channels for updates on the incident.

Brčko district mayor Siniša Milić said three people had died and 12 had been injured, with one of those injured in a critical condition.

"All have been treated in a hospital in Brčko. Medical staff are on alert," he said.

Further details about those on board and the cause of the crash are expected to be released once the authorities have completed their investigation.

EUFOR’s roughly 1,200-strong mission has operated in Bosnia since 2004, when it took over from NATO. It works under a UN Security Council mandate to help maintain security and oversee the military provisions of the peace agreement that ended the 1992–95 war.

World.title: Death toll from Spain train crash revised to 69 as royals visit victims
World.content:
Spain's Railway Accident Investigation Commission has revised the death toll from Wednesday's train crash near Urda to 69, down from the 74 fatalities previously reported by the country's transport ministry.

 

The update came as Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited a hospital in Toledo on Thursday afternoon to meet survivors and relatives of the victims.

The royal couple were welcomed by emergency workers, whom they thanked for their efforts, before speaking with injured passengers and victims' families. The hospital is currently treating 15 patients in intensive care and another eight on general wards.

Visibly moved, Felipe VI and Letizia cancelled their official engagements to travel to Toledo and hear firsthand about the condition of those receiving treatment.

Following the crash, the king expressed his sorrow over the "terrible accident", offered his condolences to the victims' families and friends during "such a difficult time", and praised the work of emergency services.

As a mark of respect, the Royal Household has suspended its official engagements for the coming days. The decision coincides with the start of three days of national mourning on Thursday and affects events scheduled in both Madrid and the Canary Islands.

World.title: US judge narrows Macrons' defamation lawsuit against American podcaster
World.content:
A judge in the United States has ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte ​could continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of the American podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.

Advertising Read more

The Macrons had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 against Owens and two companies, accusing her of helping fan online rumours about whether Brigitte is a transgender woman.

Owens, 37, an influencer with a large following on social media platforms, has claimed that Brigitte was a man.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie said in a ruling on Tuesday that Owens could not be held personally liable in the case.

But Rennie allowed the suit against two companies associated with her – Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc – to continue.

Question of jurisdiction

Rennie said the Delaware court did not hold jurisdiction over Owens because her residence was in another state, Tennessee.

The ruling means that if the French first couple were to eventually win the case, Owens' personal assets would be shielded.

In their lawsuit, the Macrons said Owens ⁠touted ​false claims and conspiracy theories ​against them "to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Rennie deferred judgment on Owens' motion to dismiss ‌the ⁠Macrons' litigation until he was briefed on how French defamation law and statutes of limitation intersect with US law.

"I am in the absolute best mood over this Macron dismissal," Owens said on X on Wednesday.

'Centuries of patriarchal history': why trans rumours are wielded against women

Damages to Brigitte Macron

Brigitte Macron, 73, has taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two French YouTubers, Natacha Rey and Amandine Roy, were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

Rey and Roy were ordered to pay €8,000 in damages to Brigitte Macron and €5,000 to Jean-Michel Trogneux.

The defendants were also given a suspended fine of €500.

Did French media silence enable Brigitte Macron fake news story to go viral?

Brigitte Macron had filed a libel complaint against the two women after their claim went viral, triggering conspiracy theories notably among the far right.

Roy, an online fortune-teller, interviewed Rey, a self-described independent journalist, for four hours on her YouTube channel in December 2021.

The women discussed the unsubstantiated rumour that Brigitte Macron had undergone gender reassignment, with Rey claiming to have uncovered a “state lie” and “scam”.

The claim went viral just weeks before France's 2022 presidential election, spreading even to the US where Owen derided the first lady in a now deleted YouTube video.

World.title: Egypt's mahrganat music: from the streets to five-star hotels
World.content:
Born in Egypt’s working-class neighbourhoods, mahraganat music is loud and raw, and these days it is practically impossible to escape. But for the artists behind it, mahraganat is more than just party music: they see it as the latest chapter in Egypt’s rich musical history.

Advertising

In this third episode of the season, we travel to the Egyptian capital, Cairo, to discover the origins of a genre that has become the soundtrack to urban life, despite receiving no official airtime.

Mahraganat evolved from shaabi: music by the people, for the people. Although it rose to prominence during the revolution of 2011–12, it has since become less overtly political.

It remains the music of happiness, partying, joy, and celebration.

Its fast rhythms and loud beats may be a far cry from the golden age of Egyptian music, but mahraganat has been on the scene since the early 2000s and it isn’t going anywhere, any time soon.

We trace its origins and evolution as we speak to one of the godfathers of the movement, his musical partner and a specialist in the genre.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora. Special thanks to Elisa Schouten for her contribution.

World.title: 'Star Trek' star Patrick Stewart dies age 86
World.content:
For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!"

In addition to Star Trek, Stewart also had a leading role in the X-Men franchise Image: dpa-Film Fox/dpa/picture alliance

In love with Shakespeare

Stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York.

'Star Trek' offer from Hollywood

In the same year, Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a big deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway."

Engage Image: Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection/picture alliance

Adventures in the universe

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time.



At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center.

In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

Stewart was a vocal and engaged civil rights activist Image: epa PA West/dpa/picture alliance

A short-lived retirement

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

Stewart returned to Star Trek for the series "Star Trek: Picard" Image: Matt Kennedy/CBS/Amazon/dpa/picture alliance

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

Translated from German by Sarah Hucal.

World.title: Justice for Maya women in Guatemala, girls back in school in India, restored land in Mali: The UN has named its 2026 SDG Action Award winners
World.content:
Champions of indigenous women's rights in Guatemala, girls' education in India, and restored farmland in Mali all featured among the winners of UN's SDG Action Awards.

A legal aid group for Indigenous women in Guatemala, a movement of village mothers in rural India, and a Malian entrepreneur who restores farmland have won this year's UN SDG Action Awards.

The winners were announced at the ninth Heroes of Tomorrow awards ceremony in Rome, Italy, run by the UN SDG Action Campaign. They were chosen from more than 7,000 entries from 190 countries.

Nine finalists were shortlisted for three categories: resilience, creativity and changemaker.

Justice for Maya women

The Resilience Award went to the Women's Justice Initiative. Many indigenous women in Guatemala face high rates of violence, poverty and discrimination, made worse by language barriers and a lack of access to information. The initiative helps women and girls get access to justice and lead change in their communities. According to the organization, more than 16,000 women and girls have participated.

"I accept the UN SDG Action Award in the honour of the Maya Kaqchikel women and girls in Guatemala who are building a more just future for their communities. Ending violence against women requires all of us. Only together, we can build a future where every woman and girl lives with dignity and realizes her full potential," said Viviana Patal, the initiative's legal director.

Jannat Al Ghezi (second from left) paid an emotional tribute to campaigner Yanar Mohammed Image: UN SDG Action Campaign/Sabrina Marchionne

Keeping girls in school in India

The Creativity Award was given to Mothers of Courage, a grassroots campaign that aims to keep girls in education in rural India. Its organizers say more than 1.2 million people have joined and pledged to keep their daughters in education and to prevent early marriage.

"This award today belongs to all the mothers in those villages, all the women leaders, who are working hard to change the destinies of their daughters and their daughters-in-law," said Khushboo Awasthi, Mothers of Courage's chief curator.

"Together, let's create a world where no girl ever has to negotiate for her right to dream and to aspire and to thrive."

Trees and livelihoods in Mali

The Changemaker Award when to Malian entrepreneur Rokiatou Traore. Her organization, Herou Alliance, helps women and small farmers bring worn-out land back to life by planting trees alongside their crops. The trees also help farmers generate extra revenue, allowing them to sell products from moringa and other valuable trees.

"Receiving this award means a lot to me. It is a reminder of why I started this journey," said Traore. "I invite you all to join us, to plant more trees, to empower more women, and above all, to create a future full of opportunities for communities for today and for future generations."

The UN Trust Fund to End Violence against Women and Girls received an honorable mention. Speaking about the award, President of the Organization of Women's Freedom in Iraq Jannat Al Ghezi paid a tearful tribute to its founder Yanar Mohammed, who was assassinated outside her home in Baghdad in March.

'Be that change'

UN Assistant Secretary-General Michelle Muschett said the finalists "remind us that the future is something we create together and that each of us has the power to help shape it and open doors for the next generations."

"When they tell you that one person cannot make a difference, prove them wrong," UN SDG Action Campaign Director Marina Ponti told the audience. "Change has always begun with people who refused to accept that the world could not be different. So be courageous. Be persistent. Be that change."

Italian singer-songwriter Roshelle performed at the ceremony Image: UN SDG Action Campaign/Sabrina Marchionne

How are the awards organized?

A panel of 20 judges from UN leadership, government, civil society, the arts, business and youth activism chose the winners. They included UN Development Programme Administrator Alexander De Croo, Oxfam International Executive Director Amitabh Behar, and Otto Group Vice President Tobias Wollermann.

The awards are run by the UN SDG Action Campaign, a special initiative of the UN Secretary-General. The campaign supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals, 17 targets adopted by member states that cover areas including poverty, hunger, education, gender equality and climate protection.

The awards are supported by Italy's Foreign Ministry and Germany's Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Editor's Note: DW Director General Barbara Massing was a member of the 20-person jury panel.

World.title: Berlin's Elif Eralp under fire over Der Spiegel interview
World.content:
Left candidate Elif Eralp has sparked controversy after Der Speigel reported she was advised against mentioning a pro-Palestinian activist for fear of reprisals against her family.

Elif Eralp, the candidate on course to become the next mayor of Berlin, sparked controversy on Thursday after having unintentionally aired personal security fears that appeared to be linked to pro-Palestinian activists in the city.

The controversy came about based on internal remarks that were part of her interview with the German news magazine Der Spiegel.

Eralp, whose Left Party (Die Linke) came out on top in local elections in Berlin last month, appeared to suggest in remarks made during an internal authorization process for an interview that she gave to Der Spiegel that she couldn't make references to a particular pro-Palestinian activist out of fear for her own safety.

"I can't put myself and my family in danger for Der Spiegel," the magazine cites her as having written in a Word Document edit, which was inadvertently sent back to the reporters.

"What do we do now? Cancel the whole interview?" she is cited as having asked her press officer and other party colleagues, while stating in another remark, "I should never have agreed to this interview."

Elif Eralp under pressure to clearly label out threats she sees

In the Der Spiegel interview, which was conducted on Monday in Eralp's office in Berlin's House of Representatives, the 45-year-old was asked about allegations of antisemitism that have been leveled at members of her socialist party.

Those accusations came about after at least two instances where people with questionable backgrounds showed up to celebrate after Eralp's party won elections in the city state last month.

For instance, the Left Party election celebration in the Berlin district of Neukölln was attended by a controversial pro-Palestinian activist associated with the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which is classified as a terrorist organization by the European Union.

In the past, Ibrahim Ibrahim has described Yahya Sinwar, the former head of Hamas in Gaza, widely regarded as the mastermind behind the deadly terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, as a "martyr" and a "hero." He has since rejected accusations of antisemitism and of supporting terrorism or Hamas.

Asked by Der Spiegel whether she was referring to the Ibrahim incident, Eralp initially responded with a "yes." But she later returned the interview transcript to the magazine with the question crossed out and the comment regarding her and her family's safety.

In Germany, it is standard practice for an interviewee to review and approve direct quotations with media outlets before the interview is published.

In notes included in the approved version of the transcript, which Der Spiegel believes were left in by accident, Eralp wrote that Berlin police had previously advised her not to comment on specific individuals.

Der Spiegel on why it published the notes

That Eralp chose to conceal her concerns publicly led some politicians to ask whether she was the right person to be the mayor of Berlin.

Der Spiegel wrote in its story:

"There were reasons not to publish – Eralp's security concerns first and foremost," the magazine wrote. "But the political importance of her notes outweighed them. Der Spiegel believes that the public should know."

It added that the story begs the question: "Can a woman who is too scared to name a terrorist sympathizer in an interview be responsible for the security of all Berliners?"

SPD, Greens also weigh in

Rival politicians weighed in, including from the Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens, with whom the Left Party is due to conduct coalition talks in Berlin next month.

"I would advise my party to distance itself from an alliance with the Left Party," said the SPD's Karl Lauterbach, who rose to prominence as Germany's health minister during the Covid-19 pandemic.

"Further talks about a coalition with this party should be out of the question for any social democrat," added SPD internal affairs spokesman Sebastian Fiedler.

Katharina Dröge, the leader of the Green Party's parliamentary grouping, asked in the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, "Will [Eralp] continue to let herself be influenced by those in her own ranks who are close to criminal groups and who tolerate threats and intimidation towards their own lead candidate? Or will she manage to give a clear and tough response?"

The chairman of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, warned: "The SPD and the Greens have a duty not to hand governmental responsibility for Berlin and for the security of the Jewish community to the Left Party" and claimed the story showed that "the Left Party is incapable of distancing itself from terrorist sympathizers and antisemites."

Eralp issues tough response, hits out at critics

Eralp hit back later on Thursday, slamming a "truly toxic debate," vowing not to be intimidated and promising a tough stance "against organized crime, against organizations that glorify violence, against violence, against terror."

She said she wouldn't comment on the specifics of the Der Spiegel story but insisted that she would "ensure the security of all Berliners."

Eralp also received backing from the vice-president of the German parliament and veteran Left Party colleague Bodo Ramelow, who criticized the Der Spiegel story as "more than questionable."

He said the reporting "targeted a person who feels vulnerable and made them even more vulnerable." He said internal communications had been used to depict the "anachronistic cliché" of a "weak woman."

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: Iraq: Life sentences for 3 French 'Islamic State' suspects
World.content:
The three were among 47 French "Islamic State" suspects transferred from Syrian detention. So far, ten French nationals have received prison terms after being convicted of belonging to the group.

Three French nationals on Thursday received sentences of life imprisonment in Iraq after being convicted of joining the so-called "Islamic State" terror group.

The criminal court in Baghdad sentence Charly S., Kamal M, and Amir A. to life terms in prison which amounts to 20 years of imprisonment in Iraq.

What more do we know?

The trio were found guilty of "the crime of joining the terrorist Islamic State organisation and of having contributed, together with members of the group, to spreading terror," an AFP correspondent said.

Tuesday saw another six French nationals from the same group sentenced to life in prison and a seventh to 15 years for belonging ​to the Islamist militant group.

All of the French nationals sentenced thus far belong to a group of 47 French nationals who were transferred from detention in Syria last year.

The 'Islamic State's' years of terror in Syria and Iraq

The militant group carried out a campaign of terror as it sought to establish a self-proclaimed caliphate in Iraq and Syria from 2014 under its leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi.

Thousands of foreign nationals from across the world joined the group, which carried out mass executions and other atrocities, many of them filmed and shared on social media platforms.

Among its most heinous crimes was the capture and killing of thousands of Yazidis in Iraq’s northern Sinjar region. Many Yazidi women and children were forced into sexual slavery and other forms of enslavement.

In 2014, IS also captured and killed hundreds of Iraqi military cadets at Camp Speicher in Iraq's Tikrit in 2014, much of the massacre filmed and shared on social media.

The terror group also carried out a series of executions of Western journalists and aid workers in highly choreographed videos as part of its media campaign.

Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over IS in 2017, and along with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces would go on to ultimately defeat the group territorially in Syria two years later.

The remaining fighters were eventually cornered and defeated in Baghouz in Syria's eastern Deir Ezzor, near the Iraqi border in March, 2019.

World.title: EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said EU seeks "association without accession" for Canada, after EU members snub "associate member" designation.

European Union and Canadian leaders are set to meet at a special Canada-EU summit to discuss critical policies like artificial inteligence (AI), climate, energy and ⁠security.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday, ahead of the summit, which begins on Friday, that the EU will continue to explore Canada's prospects for becoming the bloc's first "associate member."

But despite her comments, the summit's declaration is expected to exclude the term "associate member," a move pushed by Germany and other members.

"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession," Von der Leyen clarified. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."

"We both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible," von der Leyen added.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had said this week he wasn't concerned about the "associate member" status, or "specific names" to be given to the new alliance with the EU.

"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians," Carney added.

Canada's EU ties are part of a broader strategy, expert tells DW

Ottawa's quest for deeper ties to Europe is seen as a move to reduce its reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Frederic Merand, political expert on EU-Canada relations at the University of Montreal, spoke to DW about how the summit serves as "political impetus" to improve the bilateral trade relationship and to free Canada of its reliance on the US.

"It's not going to happen, over time, overnight. And every time we move closer to the Europeans, we realize how dependent we are on the US and how also vulnerable we are to, for example, us retaliation," Merand said.

But he added that courting the EU is also part of a broader strategy "to reinvent the Canadian economy, to create a single market, to attract more investment," as well as to diversify our partnerships with China, India and also other parts of the world.

The EU is "a natural partner" to work with, Merand said, given its existing free trade agreement with Canada, in addition to the close historical and cultural ties between the two partners.

Are the EU and Canada moving closer? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What's on the agenda for the summit?

An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Canada and the EU sought to align policies in areas such as climate, energy and artificial intelligence, allowing Ottawa to participate in some EU programs.

Canada has critical minerals needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines, something for which Europe normally relies on China.

But Canada is in need of major infrastructure investment to develop its mining industry.

There are hopes that the summit can result in a plan for the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.

EU and Canadian leaders are also looking into a digital trade deal that can allow for faster and cheaper online transactions.

Additionally, Canada could be allowed to participate in the EU's Erasmus youth program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad.

World.title: Israel election: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims
World.content:
Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud claims large-scale foreign involvement in the elections led by Qatar and Turkey, with Israel’s authorities so far refuting the claims.

Israel woke up on Thursday to allegations by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party that foreign actors may have sought to influence voter mobilization efforts in Arab communities during this week's legislative election.

No'am Sohlberg, the Supreme Court judge who heads Israel's Central Election Committee, sent a letter to Israel's internal security agency Shin Bet to look into the Likud's claims.

According to Likud's statement, Arab parties Ra'am and the Joint List — which received a record share of the vote, mostly due to unprecedented turnout in communities of Arab and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship — allegedly used "severe criminal offenses" to spur voters to go to the polls, including bribery, threats and other forms of election fraud.

"Severe suspicions were brought to my attention about improper intervention in the elections by foreign funding by outside actors that act against the Israeli interest," Sohlberg wrote in the letter, adding that he was "unable to testify" as to whether the allegations are true.

The Likud party has complained about alleged voter fraud in Arab communities Image: Katrine Dige Houmoller/MEI/SIPA/picture alliance

"The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party claimed in a statement. His own coalition lost seats, leaving both the prime minister and his opponents short of a majority — unless they were to work with one or both of the Arab parties.

Likud and other right-wing figures pointed to the unusually high turnout in Arab communities, reports of organized transportation to polling stations and concerns over foreign-funded voter mobilization campaigns as grounds for requesting an investigation. They argue that a formal review is necessary to maintain public confidence in the electoral process, regardless of whether wrongdoing is ultimately found.

Authorities refute allegations

Israel's elections are administered by the Central Election Committee, a body comprising representatives of parliamentary parties and chaired by a Supreme Court justice. Large-scale election fraud has historically been rare, although disputes over campaign conduct and voting procedures regularly arise.

Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative” nor "informative.”

Left-wing demonstrators demanded that the Arab parties be allowed to take part in Israel's new government Image: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP

"Election day went with a minority of irregular incidents in the area of election integrity, also compared to other elections," it said in a statement.

A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.

"We don't have any basis for claims of 'stolen elections,'" Dean Livne, the Committee's acting director general, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan 11, adding that the committee received "claims rather than evidence" from Likud and other parties.

Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor and the head of the Yashar party, blamed the Israeli leader for leading an "improper influence operation" to cast doubt on the elections and create what he called "a fictive delegitimization" for the next parliament.

However, Eisenkot, also called for Likud's allegation of electoral fraud to be investigated.

The religious Muslim Ra'am party denied any involvement and said it would cooperate with any investigation.

Qatar released a statement denying any involvement in the Israeli elections, calling them "false propaganda aimed at dragging Qatar's name into Israel's political conflicts."

The controversy comes against the backdrop of growing polarization in Israeli politics and increasing public distrust between rival political camps.

Likud's motivation could be to decrease the Arab influence on Israeli politics, according to Amira Halperin, a senior fellow at the Palm Beach Center for Democracy and Policy Research. "The Arab votes were very, very important in this election," she said.

The Arab parties celebrated their historic success in Israel's election Image: Jamal Awad/dpa/picture alliance

Such allegations could also hurt the public's trust in the election process Halperin argued: "We need to be cautious about predicting a failure of the democratic system."

Shin Bet head in focus

Israeli media reports have suggested that some of the concerns cited by Likud were based on intelligence assessments examined by the Shin Bet, though the agency has not publicly confirmed the details of any such findings.

Public broadcaster Kan reported the suspicions' extent as "relatively small," citing sources familiar with the Shin Bet investigation. Israeli daily Ha'aretz, too, quoted sources familiar with the allegations as saying the reports are "being blown out of proportion.”

David Zini, the head of the agency, said on election day that the elections in Israel are "safe, sound and supervised," adding that the Elections Committee and Israeli police are "successfully" preventing anyone from hurting it.

Zini's appointment earlier this year was criticized by opposition figures, who questioned both his qualifications for the role and Netanyahu's motives in selecting him. Supporters of the appointment rejected those criticisms, arguing that Zini's military experience and security background made him suitable for the position.

Separately, the Shin Bet, has been involved in investigating several of Netanyahu's closest aides on allegations of undisclosed ties to Qatar. Those investigations are unrelated to the current election allegations.

Pre-planned tactics?

Israeli outlet N12 has reported that in the weekend before the elections that Likud officials were discussing potential election-integrity complaints ahead of voting, although no evidence of actual irregularities had been presented at that stage, with a focus on Arab and Palestinian communities .

"They sat and brainstormed to find creative ideas of how to complain about this issue," said Daphna Liel, the reporter who broke the story.



Voter turnout reached historic levels during Israel's election Image: Jalaa Marey/AFP

Historic turnout

Arab and Palestinian participation in this week's election was unprecedented, with turnout jumping from around 50% in 2022 to about 80% in 2026, according to reports in Israel.

Arab voter participation has fluctuated significantly in recent decades. Turnout has often been influenced by debates within Arab society over whether participation in national elections can effectively advance the interests of Arab citizens, who comprise roughly 20% of Israel's population. The exceptionally high turnout in this election was widely seen as a sign of renewed political mobilization.

Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party campaigned with the slogan "right wing or Palestine" Image: Jewel Samad/AFP

This resulted in huge success forthe Joint List and Ra'am, with 11 and eight parliament seats, respectively, in comparison to six and four in the 2022 election. Both parties have already voiced their willingness to cooperate with Israel's Zionist opposition to replace Netanyahu.

Most parties in Israel's Zionist opposition promised not to join a coalition with Arab parties ahead of the elections, with the exception of left-wing Zionist party "The Democrats” (HaDemocratim).

On election day, there were also allegations over "systematic delays" in voting in Arab and Palestinian polling stations, according to Adalah, an Israeli-Palestinian NGO for the legal rights of the Arab minority in Israel.

World.title: India increases growth forecast for fiscal year
World.content:
India's Ministry of Finance has increased its growth forecasts for the current fiscal year. But it also warned about inflation, particularly for fuel and energy, amid continued instability in the Middle East.

India's Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it said in its October economic review .

The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.

India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.

The report contrasted these figures with global growth predictions of nearer 3%, saying "India's growth momentum, by comparison, has held firm."

The ministry said growth in various key indicators like energy consumption, port traffic, goods and services tax (GST) collections, and car sales had accelerated in the previous quarter.

Inflation, fueled by El Nino and geopolitics, poses a threat

However, the ministry also warned of continued inflationary pressure and pressure on the rupee currency, as well as downside risks from the El Nino weather phonemenon that could threaten soil moisture ahead of the winter sowing season.

It said that external factors like oil prices and "global uncertainties" — seemingly a reference at least in part to the instablity in the Middle East — continued to pressure the rupee's value and pose inflationary risks.

Consumer price inflation (CPI), the wholesale price index (WPI), food cost prices and fuel and power prices were all rising month for month, albeit at very different rates.

The CPI was up 5.54% year-on-year in September, but the WPI had risen more sharply at 11.39%. Food index inflation was up by 8% in rural areas, and a slightly more modest 7.18% in urban centers.

But, as in many other countries, fuel and power costs increases were in an entirely different league, at 25.85% inflation in September 2026 comapred to the same month a year earlier, prior to the outbreak of fighting in the Middle East.

Ministry says FX reserves ample, rupee's decline appears manageable

Although it has been a comparatively slow decline, the rupee has been consistently losing value against the US dollar over the past five years, threatening the country's relative purchasing power internationally. This slide has picked up pace in the last 15 months or so.

But the ministry pointed to foreign exchange reserves worth some $721 billion and said that India was "well-positioned" to weather such risks and sustain its expansionary trajectory..

World.title: China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
World.content:
The CCP session emphasized internal discipline — as expected, but left the question of Xi Jinping's successor unanswered. The party seems anxious of any instability as geopolitics heats up and China's economy cools down.

The top echelon of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) held a four-day session behind closed doors in Beijing this week, with the talks focusing on strict leadership and discipline inside the ruling party.

Xi Jinping, who is both the CCP's general secretary and the head of state in China, signaled he would not only deepen the existing anti-corruption effort, but also ensure that party officials demonstrate more loyalty and more initiative at all levels.

According to the press release published on Thursday, the committee published a resolution praising the leadership and Xi Jinping for "enormous political courage and strong sense of responsibility" in tackling the issues of corruption and the weakening of the Party's governance.

The statement emphasized the need to "consistently advance comprehensive and strict Party leadership."

China's leadership fears instability

Kerry Brown, head of the Lau China Institute at King's College London, says Xi wants to minimize potential sources of instability.

Amid the current international tensions and the internal problems in China, including economic difficulties, Xi is pursuing his anti-corruption campaign and by demanding loyalty. "This is just going to intensify because if [the CCP] isn't disciplined and united, the party believes that it will go the same way as everywhere else in the world at the moment and become disunited and unstable," Brown told DW.

Trump, Putin or Xi: Who really runs the world? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'Two-faced' party members targeted by Xi

Xi also recently spoke of the necessity to identify and remove "two-faced functionaries" from the political system.

In his speech, which was published in mid-October by the party's Qiushi Magazine, Xi referred to people professing loyalty to the central leadership while working against its instructions and following their own "individualistic" goals. The Chinese president described them as "political opportunists." He also criticized party officials pretending to be "nice guys," as in, those who use harmony as an excuse to stand aside when problems arise.

Brown points out that China's political system is now facing a crucial dilemma: If officials at all levels are now indeed expected to show innovation and courage in solving problems, the party's control could grow weak. This could, in turn, boost corruption.

However, if CCP leaders lean more on the "strict Party leadership" aspect and ramp up the pressure on the rank-and-file, there is also the danger of suppressing initiative. This could go beyond the party itself and could even affect the military.

The party is "very, very risk averse," Brown points out.

China 'kind of works' in a messy world

Chong Ja Ian, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore, notes that party functionaries under Xi only have a limited space to make their own decisions.

Taking this into account, the party's push for individuals to show initiative is not necessarily a major issue.

"I believe Xi would like for the officials to act proactively and decisively by conducting specific tasks; but he still doesn't want them thinking for themselves so much that they can question the agenda he prescribed. The 'proactivity' demanded by Xi is limited to the implementation, not decision-making," he told DW.

Brown adds that Xi seems to be ready to sacrifice a certain amount of operational flexibility to gain more control and stability.

"As long as you have unity, you live for another day, right? But if you have disunity, you probably die the same day," he told DW.

This approach "kind of works," at least at the moment, he added.

"It's not like the Chinese economy is disastrous. It's not great, but it's not disastrous. In any case, look at the outside world. It's a mess."

New World Dis-Order: Is the age of peace and stability over? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who will succeed Xi Jinping?

Outside observers are also focusing on Xi's future and possible successors for the 73-year-old leader.

For now, Xi seems to be firmly in control. It is highly likely that he would be confirmed as the party's general secretary next fall, and could stay in that position until 2032.

This is due to the changes pushed by Xi in 2018, which removed term limits for state and party leaders.

Both analysts told DW that the issue of succession plays a major role in Xi's push towards internal stability.

"There's always a danger of differences in the party fragmenting it, especially when the question of succession comes up," says Brown. "And even though we don't expect to see a successor anytime soon, you know, there's going to be speculation about who might succeed Xi."

"He can't go on forever," he added.

How Xi Jinping's authoritarianism is killing China's economy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Political scientist Chong Ja Ian says that Xi currently holds all the power. Therefore, the CCP leader could be afraid of his authority being undermined if he named a successor ahead of time.

"On the other hand, a failure to make preparations on time could create a power vacuum that can cause major instability," he told DW.
