World.title: Hong Kong leader apologizes for deadly Tai Po fire, pledges reform
World.content:
APOLOGY. Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee and other officials bow in apology during a press conference to announce the findings of an investigation into the 2025 fatal fire in Tai Po, Hong Kong, on October 29, 2026.

John Lee also announces the resignation of Hong Kong's Housing Secretary Winnie Ho — the first official to resign over the inferno

HONG KONG – Hong Kong leader John Lee apologized on Thursday, October 29, for the deadly blaze that killed 168 people in the city last November, as he released an independent report that held four government departments partially responsible for a fire that erupted after more than a year of safety complaints.

Lee promised swift but extensive reforms to the city’s building industry and regulatory system. The more than 1,000-page report by the judge-led panel detailed governance and supervisory failings, including widespread bid rigging.

“The fire has been put out, but the reform has only just begun,” the report stated.

“The Committee finds that no Government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum.”

The blaze ripped through seven 31-story tower blocks at the Wang Fuk Court residential complex, which was undergoing renovation work in the northern Tai Po district and shrouded in dust netting and scaffolding.

Residents had repeatedly raised safety concerns over the work for more than a year before the fire, which the report said was most likely started by a “glowing source…likely a cigarette.”

It was the deadliest in the city since 1948. Thousands of residents were displaced after their homes became uninhabitable.

“As chief executive and head of the government, I am deeply saddened,” Lee said before bowing with seven other officials in a rare show of official contrition.

“On behalf of the SAR government, I offer my apologies to the victims and the public at large.”

Lee also announced the resignation of Hong Kong’s Housing Secretary Winnie Ho — the first official to resign over the inferno.

Disciplinary action

Wang Fuk residents and other critics have in recent months expressed anger at a perceived lack of government accountability.

The Hong Kong government has set up an independent team to investigate which officials should be held accountable and to outline disciplinary actions.

Lee, whose five-year term ends next June, did not directly respond to press questions over whether he would seek another term, saying “implementing the reforms is the goal” rather than personal matters.

Lee said Hong Kong’s Chief Secretary Eric Chan will now head a steering committee to oversee reforms advocated in the report, which will include laws to criminalise bid rigging across the construction industry with fines of up to HK$10 million and 10 years’ imprisonment.

The committee report said contractor Prestige Construction & Engineering Co Ltd and project consultant Will Power Architects Co Ltd should bear primary responsibility.

At least 25 criminal charges related to the Wang Fuk Court fire have been made against Prestige, Will Power and seven individuals, including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, money laundering and tax evasion.

But the report also went further, outlining widespread unlawful and dubious construction practices as a “corrupt eco-system.”

The rigging of bids in the industry involved many different parties, some linked to triad organized crime gangs, it said.

The committee held 30 hearings this year with 80 witnesses, including residents, property management and renovation personnel, engineering and fire experts, government officials and regulators. It evaluated more than one million files and submissions as it investigated the cause of the fire and reviewed oversight of building renovations.

Before the report’s release, critics had said the committee lacked the statutory powers of a full public inquiry, which could potentially limit its ability to establish the full facts and accountability.

Some groups in the Asian business hub have called for more transparency and accountability, amid warnings from authorities that any attempts to politicise the disaster would be severely punished. – Rappler.com

World.title: ECB President Lagarde resigns at time of mounting challenges for Europe
World.content:
FILE PHOTO: European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde gestures as she addresses the press following the ECB's Governing Council meeting, at the ECB headquarters in Frankfurt, Germany, on February 5, 2026.

A source with direct knowledge of the matter says Christine Lagarde resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in her native France and globally

FRANKFURT, Germany – European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde announced her resignation on Thursday, October 29, ending months of speculation about her future just as Europe enters a period of rising economic volatility and divisive electoral politics.

Lagarde will step down on February 7, giving current European Union leaders time to pick a successor well before a French presidential election that polls show far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favored to win.

The move comes as the ECB battles inflation risks from an Iran-driven oil shock while a sharp rise in bond yields, especially in France, threatens to dampen growth.

“I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future,” Lagarde said in a short video shared on social media.

A source with direct knowledge of the matter said Lagarde had resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in her native France and globally. As ECB president, she was expected to remain neutral to safeguard the institution’s independence.

European Council President Antonio Costa said in a statement the process to find a successor for Lagarde would begin immediately. The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are widely seen as frontrunners.

“The rumored successors are both very competent, well-established central bankers, so for markets, it won’t matter too much,” Piet Haines Christiansen, an economist at Danske Bank, said.

Financial markets did not move much after the announcement, with some analysts noting the ECB had by now built a reputation that outlived any of its leaders.

“The ECB is now quite well-established, the market is familiar with the way it operates,” Goldman Sachs’ head of Fixed Income Macro Investing Simon Dangoor said. “Our view is that institutional behavior is likely to outlast Lagarde, and be quite similar, whoever takes over.”

Lagarde’s term was scheduled to run until the end of October 2027, but speculation about an early departure had been mounting for months, with the World Economic Forum seen as a likely destination.

Rate hikes and bond turmoil

The ECB is in the middle of a rate-hiking cycle aimed at preventing an oil-price shock linked to the Iran war from feeding into other prices and wages.

But it must also contend with a surge in government bond yields — especially in debt-laden France — that has pushed up borrowing costs for households and businesses and which Lagarde has said will curb growth and inflation.

Caught between persistent inflation fueled by a renewed surge in energy costs and deteriorating financing conditions, the ECB is widely expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday while signaling that another increase, potentially as soon as December, remains likely.

“There is likely a low bar to another hike in December, given the likelihood of another upward revision of the ECB’s inflation forecast due to higher energy prices,” Oliver Rakau at Oxford Economics said.

The ECB is due to announce its interest rate decision at 1315 GMT on Thursday, followed by Lagarde’s regular press conference at 1345 GMT.

Money markets are currently pricing another three rate increases from the ECB by the end of next year, which would take the deposit rate to 3.25%, a level that is widely seen as restricting economic growth.

French turmoil in focus but no action

The more immediate challenge for policymakers may be turmoil in bond markets.

A global rise in yields, fueled by stronger growth expectations, higher debt issuance and massive investment linked to artificial intelligence, is pushing up borrowing costs for governments, households and businesses alike.

In France, investors have become increasingly uneasy about the country’s growing debt burden and uncertain fiscal outlook following this year’s elections. Concerns have been amplified by suggestions from parts of the political left that debt held by the ECB could be written off.

The result has been a sharp increase in French borrowing costs. France is now paying some of the highest yields in a quarter-century to raise money on bond markets, while the premium investors demand to hold French debt over benchmark German bonds is larger than for any other euro zone country.

That has fueled speculation that the ECB might be forced to respond, if only verbally for now.

“They’ve typically come up with a new tool that’s customised for that specific set of circumstances,” said Dangoor at Goldman Sachs.

The ECB’s first line of defence would probably be flexible reinvestment of proceeds from bonds acquired during its vast asset-purchase programs of the previous decade.

Beyond that, it could activate its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument, a scheme designed to counter what policymakers deem unjustified market pressure. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No report of Indonesian President confronting, scolding Marcos
World.content:
The video contains no footage, audio, or documentation of the alleged confrontation. Instead, the content features an unidentified male commentator reacting to a third-party social media post unrelated to the claim.

Claim: Indonesia’s president publicly confronted and scolded President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., telling him to “fix yourself and your country.”

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The YouTube channel “PINAS BALITA TV” with 175,000 subscribers published a video bearing the title: “GRABE NA! NAKAKAH1YA TO! IND0NESIAN PRESIDENT HARAPANG SINUP4L-P4L at NA-REALTALK si BEBE EM?” (This is too much! How embarrassing! Indonesian President confronted and engaged BBM in real talk?)

The video’s thumbnail, posted on October 17, 2026, shows an enraged Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto pointing directly at the President’s face before press microphones and cameras.

In the video’s original thumbnail, the uploader claimed that the Indonesian leader told Marcos to “fix your country and yourself,” though this line has since been edited out as of writing.



As of writing, the video has garnered 3,100 views and 234 likes.

The facts: No credible news reports or official footage confirm that Indonesia’s Subianto confronted or publicly engaged Marcos in real talk before the press.



AI image detectors IsThisAI reveal that the thumbnail of the video is 99% likely to be AI-generated. Meanwhile, SightEngine flagged it as 87% likely to have used generative AI, and TruthScan estimated an 85% edit probability with high confidence.



“The background crowd appears to be cloned or manipulated, showing unnatural repetition patterns. Shadows on the subjects’ faces and clothing are inconsistent, further suggesting digital editing,” the TruthScan findings said.

Lack of evidence: The video contains no footage, audio, or documentation of any confrontation. Instead, the content features an unidentified male commentator reacting to a third-party social media post.

The commentator compares how both governments address climate challenges — particularly El Niño — contrasting Indonesia’s reported distribution of water pumps with the Philippine government’s recommendation to collect rainwater using buckets. The commentator heavily criticized the administration’s suggested solution.



Existing ties: Diplomatic ties between the Philippines and Indonesia remain stable as of writing. Both countries held bilateral meetings in 2024, and Marcos, along with First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, formally welcomed President Subianto during the opening ceremony of the 48th ASEAN Summit held in Cebu in May 2026.

Marcos also traveled to Jakarta to attend Subianto’s presidential inauguration in 2024.

Debunked: Marcos has been a frequent subject of false claims, particularly controversies:

– Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com

Lyndee Buenagua is a Metro Manila-based journalist who primarily covers Bicol and Baguio. She is also an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: LIST: Evidence submitted by prosecution to impeach court vs Sara Duterte
World.content:
PROSEC. Members of the prosecution listen to a ruling during Day 22 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 7, 2026.

Rappler obtained a copy of the prosecution's formal offer of evidence. Here are key documents that are part of the submission.

After the prosecution wrapped up the presentation of its case in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, it submitted its formal offer of evidence to the court.

It’s a mandatory submission that allows the prosecution to state the specific purpose of each piece of evidence, although the defense may still contest it.

Rappler obtained a copy of the formal offer of evidence. Below are key documents that are part of the submission.

1. Her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs) from 2007 to 2025, from the Office of the Ombudsman

Her SALNs show her or her husband’s continued stake with Gencorp, Metro City Chow Foods Corporation, and Cale88 Foods Corporation, while she is already a sitting vice president, apparently in violation of Article VII, Section 13 of the Constitution.

Her SALNs supposedly prove she did not declare her 51 firearms, her properties in Matina and Kembali, her cash on hand and in bank from 2019 to 2025, and various insurance policies and investments.

Prosecutors say her ending bank balances from 2022 to 2025 do not match her declared total personal assets for those years.

2. Corporate records of companies tied to her and her husband Mans Carpio

The prosecutors submitted SEC records of the following entities to prove that she and/or her husband are either an incorporator, shareholder, or member of the board of directors. City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation Metro City Chow Foods Corporation Gencorp Industries Cale88 Foods Corporation Mati City Ice Plant and Cold Storage Geometry Security and Investigation Agency Great Jolly Times Food Corp Timesquare Bee Foods Corp Davao New Royal Taipan Foods Corporation Davao Emerging Taipans Corporation 3Kids Trucking Services CYK&T Davao Corporation SGT Fortune Horse Corporation Davao Bounty Times Foods Corporation Madayaw Fisheries Amianan Shores Cabletow 88 Shipping and Marine Services Carpio Lawyers Pikimong Pikimong Philippines Corporation JTC Group of Companies Philippines

The general information sheets and/or audited financial statements of many of these companies supposedly prove Duterte and/or her husband did not receive dividend income from the firms.

The SEC records of some of these companies also show that Duterte and/or her husband subscribed a paid-up capital to the firms, yet the shareholdings were not declared in the SALN.

3. Philippine Statistics Authority records

Their marriage certificate establishes that there is no prenuptial agreement between them.

4. Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilgGEPS) records of contracts won by their supposed companies

The procurement records between Gencorp and either Davao City LGU, PhilHealth Region 10, and the Overseas Workers Welfre Administration Region 11 supposedly prove she violated the constitutional prohibition on government officials being financially interested in government contracts. Most notably, Gencorp bagged 19 contracts worth at least P34 million with the Davao City LGU led by her brother Mayor Sebastian Duterte from 2022 to 2026.



Play Video

5. Records of her firearms with the Philippine National Police

The certifications issued by the PNP Firearms and Explosives Office (FEO) to Duterte and her husband document their combined total of 51 guns worth P7.2 million, assets not declared in her SALN.

6. Land Registration Authority (LRA) records of relevant properties

The transfer certificates of title, among other LRA documents, detail Duterte and her husband’s properties in Kembali and Matina, which are absent from her SALNs.

7. Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) reports

AMLC records detail covered transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious transaction reports (STRs) involving Duterte and her husband worth P4.4 billion from 2007 to 2025. The amount includes P424 million during her stint as vice president.

.The AMLC reports cover large US dollar cash withdrawals, time deposit renewals, single-day multi-million peso transfers, and significant over-the-counter cash withdrawals/check encashments.

One of their companies, Cale88, supposedly received P368.8 million in foreign remittances, including P319.3 million from senders in China.

8. Bank records

Prosecutors submitted records from the following banks: BDO Unibank (seven accounts) BPI (six accounts) Landbank (one account) Metrobank (three accounts) Philippine Savings Bank (two accounts) Security Bank (one account) PNB (four accounts) Unionbank (one account) Asia United Bank (two accounts)

Prosecutors say the 27 bank accounts show total year-end balances of P207.6 million from 2022 to 2025, which were not declared in her SALNs for those years.

9. Insurance and investment company records

Duterte and her husband have active insurance policies across seven companies from 2022 to 2025, none of which were declared in her SALN.

These companies are: BDO Life (two insurance investments) BDO Securities (seven securities/ other investments) BPI AIA (one insurance investment) FWD Life (one insurance investment) Manulife (six insurance investments) Allianz (two insurance investments) Prulife (five insurance investments)



10. Tax records with the Bureau and Internal Revenue (BIR)

The BIR records of the couple show their combined income of P85.3 million from 2027 to 2025, which prosecutors assert is vastly disproportionate to their declared net worth and calculated unexplained wealth.

Some of the documents also show that Duterte earned income from practicing law and received funds from Davao City Hall while she is vice president.

11. Forensic examination report

The forensic report of veteran Certified Public Accountant or CPA lawyer Alexander Cabrera found that Duterte and her husband have an unexplained wealth of at least P817.8 million from 2022 to 2025.

Play Video

– Rappler.com

World.title: Cartoon Campaign Boosts Myanmar Regime’s Hydropower Dreams
World.content:
The military regime has launched a campaign of cheesy cartoons across the propaganda media to push its bid to revive the shelved Myitsone Dam hydropower project.

Regime newspapers started featuring cartoons since Oct. 20, with uplifting messages suggesting the project will deliver 24/7 cheap electricity to households in Kachin State and beyond while boosting domestic industry.

They also lash out at opponents of the harebrained scheme. On Oct. 25, the Kyemon Daily carried a cartoon portraying critics as obstinate and unwilling to assess the project’s pros and cons objectively. The cartoon insisted the dam would cause no suffering, dismissing public concerns as baseless.

Cartoons have long been a propaganda tool for successive juntas, their simplified, condescending messages used to smear civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, ethnic leaders, and Western governments, while glorifying the regimes’ various leaps forward into the past. The habitual public response is to laugh at them.

The project to dam two tributaries to the Irrawaddy River, the N’Mai and Mali, was conceived under dictator Than Shwe. It was suspended in 2011 under President Thein Sein after unprecedented opposition over potential environmental destruction, mass displacement, the sites’ cultural significance for the Kachin people, and lack of transparency.

But now, the regime of Min Aung Hlaing is making relentless efforts to revive the project. Naypyitaw is touting it as a solution to its chronic electricity shortages—even though, under the original contract, most of the power generated by the dams was to have been exported to China.

As part of the new campaign, the regime has been marshalling local populations into a publicity blitz. Regime-appointed Kachin State Chief Minister Khet Htein Nam and the Myitsone Support Committee have staged more than 50 public meetings across the state, often strong-arming locals into attending. Yet executives from the mooted Chinese dam developer have been conspicuously absent.

With the cartoon strips across national newspapers, the campaign is going nationwide.

Officials insist the dam will bring many benefits, particularly to foreign investors setting up factories in Myanmar, and any seismic and environmental risks have been ironed out since the project was first proposed.

Experts warn otherwise. They point out that blocking river flow could allow seawater intrusion into the Irrawaddy delta, damaging agriculture and drinking water supplies. Sudden releases during monsoon season could also cause flash floods downstream.

Amid the revival campaign, resistance remains strong. Civil society groups, ethnic organizations, and ordinary citizens continue to oppose the project.

And a China analyst notes that the supposed Chinese financiers and builders are nowhere to be seen, no feasibility studies are being conducted, and Beijing has anyway long graduated from the need for extra power from the Myitsone project over the last 25 years.

“It’s really just the regime one-sidedly making efforts to revive the project because it sees Myitsone as leverage for political gain,” she said. She also pointed out that Myanmar would likely have to repay heavy costs incurred by the project’s suspension, which the cash-strapped regime can ill afford.

Indeed, during Min Aung Hlaing’s latest Beijing trip, Chinese officials made no mention of the dam, emphasizing instead the China–Myanmar Economic Corridor projects (CMEC) under its sweeping Belt and Road Initiative.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Begins Releasing Rakhine Deportees After Malaysia Pressure
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime has begun releasing hundreds of ethnic Rakhine deported from Malaysia last month after Kuala Lumpur sought clarification on their detention.

The first Rakhine deportees were released on Wednesday, just 48 hours after Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan faced questions about their fate in parliament.

Malaysia deported nearly 1,500 Myanmar refugees and migrants in late September, including over 400 from Rakhine, where the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) has seized 14 of the state’s 17 townships and is now pushing to claim the capital Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, home to a China-backed seaport and economic zone.

While other deportees were allowed to return home on arrival, the ethnic Rakhine were held for interrogation at two military detention centers in Yangon’s Thanlyin and Hlaingthayar. Those with identification cards were allowed to return home starting Wednesday, according to the Khamee Youth Unity Association, citing testimony from a released individual.

The association, which represents an ethnic subgroup of Rakhine, stated that 26 Khamee individuals were among the detainees.

Previous efforts by their families to secure the deportees’ release had fallen on deaf ears, with the regime offering no explanation for their prolonged detention.

“My younger brother was only set free yesterday,” a Khamee man, who requested anonymity due to security concerns, told The Irrawaddy. “I didn’t even know he was among those released.”

He had been seeking his brother’s release since October 21 after being informed of his detention by a regime administrator. He was told the delay was due to incomplete paperwork for a national registration card and smart card.

“Once we sent the complete documentation over, he was released within a week.”

The regime barred ethnic Rakhine from returning to their home state in late 2023 and early 2024 as AA forces made sweeping gains on the western front.

Malaysia sent back 1,479 Myanmar nationals on September 29, in the first phase of a repatriation plan that has drawn heavy criticism from the United Nations refugee agency and international rights groups. Kuala Lumpur claims all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation under the plan to deport 5,000 Myanmar nationals in stages from Malaysia, where over 10,300 others remain in detention.

The United Nations warns that civil war triggered by the 2021 coup makes safe repatriation impossible under international law. Concerns are rising over reports that the regime is forcibly conscripting returnees into the military.

Malaysia has repatriated around 8,000 citizens by air and 1,500 by sea so far this year, according to regime data cited by AFP.

World.title: Myanmar Navy Loses 3 More Ships as Arakan Army Tightens Sittwe Noose
World.content:
The Arakan Army (AA) said it destroyed three military vessels at the mouth of the Kaladan River in Rakhine State on Monday, bringing the total number of Myanmar Navy ships eliminated in the past month to six.

AA spokesman Khaing Thukha said two of the vessels were sunk and the other wrecked. “We commend our officers and technicians for this successful operation,” he posted on Telegram.

A frontline source confirmed that three Navy vessels had been obliterated on Monday, dealing a further blow to the regime’s Rakhine counteroffensive. Dubbed Operation 4926, the counteroffensive has dragged on for nearly two months without progress as the AA tightens its siege on the state capital, Sittwe. Despite repeated assaults, regime troops have failed to secure AA‑held Nga Pyi Island, which guards the river mouth.

Both sides have suffered casualties, but the AA claims regime losses are heavier with around 50 soldiers killed on the first day of fighting at Nga Pyi Island alone.

The island is a key AA stronghold, blocking regime access upriver to AA-controlled Pauktaw and Ponnagyun townships.

The assault on Nga Pyi began on Oct. 7, spearheaded by gunboats and landing craft and backed by air and artillery strikes from encircled Sittwe.

The move aims to break the AA’s blockade of the Kaladan River corridor while shielding the Navy’s Shwe Mingan base in Sittwe, which sits on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides.

Regime troops are waging defensive battles around Sittwe on three fronts: the Shwe Mingan naval base, along the Sittwe–Ponnagyun border, and near Mayu River in Rathedaung Township. Sources say the AA has seized several regime outposts near Shwe Mingan and along the Sittwe–Ponnagyun road.

With its frontline bases collapsing, the military has resorted to air and artillery strikes against villages in Pauktaw and Ponnagyun townships.

Clashes have also intensified down the coast in Kyaukphyu Township, where AA forces are attacking regime positions near Taung Maw Oo naval base. A frontline source said the military has already lost two outposts in the area.

The AA controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships along with Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State, with the regime maintaining a foothold in Sittwe, Kyaukphyu, and the sparsely populated Manaung island.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seizes Historic Nawnghio Mosque Over Rebel Links
World.content:
The central military regime has seized the only mosque in northern Shan State’s Nawnghkio after jailing two trustees for allegedly supporting the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) during its brief rule of the town. Locals say the charges are baseless and amount to suppression of religious freedom.

The regime alleges that mosque trustees Hla Htwe and Soe Thein provided money, food and supplies to TNLA when it captured Nawnghkio in July 2024.

Once the regime recaptured the town a year later, both men were arrested, and earlier this month they were sentenced to 11 years each under the Counter‑Terrorism Law.

Residents recall that the mosque was first raided by soldiers, police and civilian officials on July 17, 2025. It was then temporarily closed without explanation on July 31.

A court ruled that the mosque should be seized as public property pending an appeal, according to a local resident.

“The court said an appeal can be filed within the given deadline, otherwise the mosque will be closed,” the resident said, “It has now been sealed for over a year and community leaders are working to submit the appeal.”

Locals insist the mosque never sheltered TNLA or allied People’s Defense Force (PDF) fighters, and that food donations were given only to displaced civilians. “The military searched every corner of the mosque, even smashing floors, but found nothing,” one resident said.

Muslims believe the campaign is motivated by sectarian spite. Requests to establish a temporary prayer site while the mosque is sealed were denied, and the regime has responded to home prayer gatherings with arrests and fines.

“There is only one mosque here,” a worshiper explained. “Without it, we can’t have funerals, festivals and Friday prayers, and children can’t attend Quran lessons.”

Built during the colonial era in 1899, the same time as the famous Goteik Viaduct, the Nawnghkio mosque has stood for 127 years near the Mandalay–Lashio highway.

A lawyer said, “Under existing laws about public property, religious sites can’t be seized. For example, if drugs are found on a bus, you don’t seize the bus itself. The accused individuals and the building are separate matters. The mosque is a communal religious building.”

Since recapturing Nawnghkio, the junta has conducted a vicious vendetta against anyone suspected of links to the TNLA, the PDF and the Danu People’s Liberation Army (DPLA), sealing or seizing more than 80 homes.

World.title: China’s Risky Plan to Restrict Hi-Tech Exports
World.content:
Beijing’s latest export-control proposals mark a significant shift in how it intends to manage its technological rise. China’s ministries of commerce and of science and technology proposed adding 40 technologies across AI, advanced gene and cell technology, and solar power to a catalogue of prohibited or restricted exports. Fourteen would be subject to complete export bans and another 26 to restrictions. A public consultation will run until Nov. 15, but registration requirements for certain technology transfers have already taken effect.

China has spent years expanding its manufacturing base, attracting foreign investment and building expertise in technologies that other economies are now trying to develop domestically. Having established a strong position in several of these, China is growing more and more chary of them.

The shift is particularly visible in solar manufacturing. China dominates the global supply chain for solar panels and the equipment to produce them. Restricting access could preserve that advantage as the U.S., India and European countries attempt to build competing production capacity.

Beijing portrays the proposed measures as necessary for national security and the responsible management of sensitive technologies, and these concerns cannot simply be dismissed, but the breadth of the measures raises larger questions.

From manufacturing dominance to control

Solar power provides the clearest example. China accounts for more than 80 percent of global solar-panel component production and is home to the world’s leading suppliers of solar manufacturing equipment. Its dominance extends across much of the supply chain, from polysilicon and wafers to cells and finished modules. This concentration has helped drive down the cost of solar power worldwide, but it has also made other countries dependent on Chinese production and expertise.

This April, Chinese officials were already considering restrictions on exports of advanced solar manufacturing equipment to the United States. following reports that Tesla was seeking to buy approximately US$2.9 billion worth of equipment from Chinese suppliers as part of its plans to establish large-scale solar manufacturing in America. The proposed restrictions could have affected equipment used to manufacture so-called high-efficiency heterojunction solar cells.

The concern in Beijing was not simply that the technology might be transferred to a strategic rival: a successful American manufacturing expansion could also create a formidable competitor for Chinese producers at a time when their domestic industry was already struggling with overcapacity and financial pressure.

The October proposals now give this concern a broader institutional form. Rather than relying only on tariffs or restricting access to imported foreign technology, China is considering tighter control over the export of its own technological capabilities.

The lesson from rare earths and critical minerals

In 2023, Beijing introduced licensing requirements for exports of gallium and germanium, two materials used in semiconductors, defense electronics, fiberoptics and other advanced technologies. It subsequently tightened controls on graphite, a key material for battery anodes. In December 2024, it prohibited exports of certain dual-use items to U.S. military users or for military end uses and tightened restrictions on several critical materials destined for the U.S.

The effects were not confined to diplomatic statements. Chinese gallium exports fell sharply after the introduction of controls, while restrictions on germanium disrupted established supply relationships. By May 2025, gallium prices in Rotterdam had reportedly reached US$687 per kilogram, more than 150 percent above pre-control levels.

The controls did not permanently deprive foreign industries of these materials: buyers adjusted procurement, accumulated inventories and explored alternative suppliers. But substitution takes time, particularly where production depends on specialized refining processes and limited alternative capacity.

The episode demonstrated that China does not need to ban every export to influence another country’s industrial calculations. Licensing requirements, uncertainty over approvals, and the possibility of delayed shipments can themselves affect investment decisions. The new technology proposals extend this logic beyond raw materials toward the knowledge and equipment required to manufacture advanced products.

The new controls on AI are particularly significant because they go beyond physical equipment. China wants to restrict 23 technologies including certain models, AI agents and computing-cluster technologies. The measures would regulate their overseas transfer or deployment, while access through application programming interfaces, websites, applications and software-as-a-service platforms would remain exempt. Publicly available technologies, like those found in academic papers or open-source projects, would also fall outside the proposed controls.

That would suggest Beijing is not seeking to prevent all international use of Chinese AI. What it wants is greater control over the underlying technology that companies might otherwise transfer to foreign partners. For firms such as DeepSeek and Alibaba, the rules could allow continued international expansion while placing tighter limits on the transfer of proprietary capabilities. Yet they also introduce uncertainty over which technologies can be licensed, transferred or incorporated into overseas operations.

Restricting technology transfers may help China retain commercially valuable intellectual property. But it could also complicate collaborations, licensing agreements and the movement of research capabilities between countries. The eventual effects will depend on how the rules are defined and enforced, but the direction is clear: Beijing wants greater authority over the international movement of technologies it considers strategically important.

Contradictions

There are ironies here. China has long benefited from foreign investment, international research collaboration and access to overseas markets. Its industrial development was supported not only by domestic policy but also by the movement of capital, equipment, expertise and intellectual property across borders. Now that Chinese companies have established competitive advantages of their own, Beijing is suddenly becoming more selective about which technologies can travel across borders and which cannot.

China is of course also taking the risk that tighter controls will encourage other countries to accelerate efforts to reduce their dependence on Chinese technology. U.S. investment in domestic solar manufacturing, India’s production-linked incentives for solar equipment and Europe’s bid to strengthen clean-technology supply chains all reflect that desire. In other words, measures intended to preserve China’s technological lead could make foreign governments less willing to depend on it in the long term.

The restrictions are not yet a settled policy. The consultation process could change the scope of the controls, and the distinction between prohibited exports, licensed transfers and permitted commercial access will determine their practical impact.

Nevertheless, they reveal an important change in Beijing’s priorities. Technological success is no longer only about producing goods more cheaply or capturing larger shares of global markets but increasingly about controlling the capabilities that allow other countries to produce those goods themselves.

In many ways thatt is a logical response to American technology restrictions and intensifying strategic competition. But the approach also carries costs. The central question is whether China intends to remain the world’s leading supplier of advanced technologies or to use its position to determine how far others can advance. The two objectives are not necessarily incompatible, but the more Beijing relies on export controls to preserve its lead, the more likely it is that other economies will treat dependence on Chinese technology as a liability.

Chandu Doddi is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Chinese Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi.

World.title: China’s Monroe Doctrine and Its Strategic Blunder in Myanmar
World.content:
The United States has its Monroe Doctrine, which asserts American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere, placing Latin America within its sphere of influence. Over the past three decades, China’s rapid economic growth and military expansion have transformed it from a regional power into a global superpower. It is therefore unsurprising that Beijing would seek to establish a similar sphere of influence over neighboring Southeast Asian countries.

Myanmar holds particular strategic importance for China. Through Rakhine State, Beijing can access the Indian Ocean, bypassing the strategically vulnerable Strait of Malacca during a crisis. Myanmar also possesses substantial deposits of rare earth elements essential to modern technologies. Furthermore, the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) is one of the six major economic corridors under China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

Yet in pursuing these geopolitical objectives, China appears to be missing the forest for the trees. Its decision to prop up Myanmar’s military junta at the expense of democratic forces represents a serious strategic miscalculation—a bet on the wrong horse. Following a widely discredited sham election, the junta has attempted to rebrand itself as a civilian government under former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing, with a ruling party dominated by military officers and loyalists. Such a regime is ill-equipped to deliver what China needs: a stable, secure and predictable neighbor capable of supporting its long-term economic ambitions through the BRI and its broader maritime strategy.

The culprit behind an unstable neighbor

Since the 2021 military coup, Myanmar has become increasingly unstable, while ethnic resistance organizations (EROs) have expanded their territorial control. Ironically, many resources and infrastructure projects China hopes to develop now lie in territories controlled by EROs and People’s Defense Forces (PDFs). Rare earth deposits are concentrated in Kachin State, where the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO) exercises substantial control. The Chinese-backed Kyaukphyu deep-sea port, a strategic gateway to the Indian Ocean, lies in Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army (AA) has established extensive territorial control. Significant stretches of the China-Myanmar gas pipeline also pass through areas where resistance forces operate in Magway and Mandalay regions.

So far, PDFs and EROs have shown considerable restraint in refraining from attacking these strategic assets. This reflects, in part, their desire to earn Beijing’s goodwill and demonstrate their ability to safeguard Chinese investments.

An unreliable partner turning to criminality

Myanmar’s economy has deteriorated sharply under the weight of military expenditure, corruption, nepotism and mismanagement. The junta is in no position to fulfill its commitments under numerous bilateral economic agreements with China, particularly because it cannot guarantee security in project areas. Worse, the regime has allowed scam centers to proliferate, with some military officers reportedly maintaining close ties to the warlords operating them. Many centers, particularly in northern Shan State, have targeted Chinese citizens. Despite repeated requests from Beijing, the military failed to take effective action.

Operation 1027, launched by an alliance of ethnic armed organizations, proceeded with Beijing’s tacit approval after the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) framed it partly as a campaign against scam operations. Among those subsequently handed over to China was Bai Suocheng, a former lawmaker from the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party.

Beyond its inability to provide stability and security, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime is hardly a trustworthy ally. He has repeatedly sought to balance competing powers against one another and could readily turn against China if doing so served his interests. His efforts to court Western goodwill were evident in a recent TIME magazine interview, a low-profile U.S. delegation visit to Naypyitaw in September and the expensive hiring of Washington-based lobbying firms to advocate on its behalf.

Previously, Min Aung Hlaing courted Russia to counterbalance China’s influence, only to turn back toward Beijing when Moscow could not meet his needs. Beijing should think twice before entrusting its long-term strategic interests to a regime whose loyalty is conditional and whose survival is increasingly uncertain.

Why the opposition is a more reliable partner

Many EROs have concluded that genuine autonomy, security, and prosperity are unattainable under military-dominated rule. They increasingly see their future in a federal democratic union. For decades, these organizations understood that none could defeat the military alone. They also recognize that their battlefield successes since 2021 would have been far more difficult without the nationwide Spring Revolution, which fundamentally transformed the country’s political landscape.

This convergence of ethnic resistance and the broader pro-democracy movement has created an unprecedented opportunity. In March 2026, the movement took a significant step forward with the formation of the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF). It brings together influential resistance actors, including the KIO, KNU, CNF, Karenni National Progressive Party (KNPP), Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), and National Unity Government (NUG). A few months later, the federal units of Sagaing, Mandalay, and Magway joined the initiative.

The SCEF combines political leadership and military coordination within a common framework. It seeks not merely to defeat the junta but also to lay the institutional foundations for a future federal state. For China, this emerging coalition offers an alternative to continued dependence on a weakening military regime.

The assumption that China cannot tolerate a flourishing democracy in its neighborhood oversimplifies Beijing’s strategic interests and Southeast Asia’s political realities. China already maintains important economic and diplomatic relationships with democracies such as Japan, South Korea and India. Myanmar is comparatively small, and any government emerging from the current conflict will have compelling geographic and economic reasons to maintain constructive relations with its powerful neighbor. A federal democratic Myanmar has no inherent reason to be antagonistic toward Beijing.

Myanmar’s democratic forces are also learning that the West is unlikely to sustain its strategic attention. The Trump administration included Myanmar among the countries subject to a full travel ban, while its dismantling of USAID disrupted American assistance. Washington’s reported attempts to reengage clandestinely with the junta have further frustrated the democratic movement.

In contrast, the NUG has adopted a pragmatic approach toward Beijing. Its 10-point Position on China, released on January 1, 2024, explicitly commits to safeguarding Chinese investments and cooperating with China against online scams and human trafficking. Democratic forces thus recognize the importance of maintaining a workable relationship with their powerful neighbor.

A strategic opening for Beijing

China’s ambition to achieve national rejuvenation and modernization by the centenary of the People’s Republic of China in 2049 requires long-term strategic thinking rather than short-term political expediency.

By recalibrating its Myanmar policy, Beijing has a rare opportunity to earn the goodwill of the Myanmar people at a pivotal moment. Supporting a political settlement that recognizes the aspirations of ethnic nationalities and democratic forces would not undermine China’s interests. On the contrary, it could help establish the stability, security, and predictability Beijing has long sought.

China should therefore engage constructively with the SCEF and other credible democratic stakeholders rather than continue to prop up a failing junta. Such engagement could protect Chinese investments, improve regional stability and strengthen Beijing’s international standing.

The underlying principle of a Chinese Monroe Doctrine—a regional sphere of influence shaped by strategic interests—is understandable as a geopolitical ambition. But achieving that ambition requires choosing partners wisely. If China wants to secure its long-term interests in Myanmar, supporting the forces capable of building a stable federal democratic union would be a far more prudent investment than backing a military regime marked by declining territorial control, economic mismanagement and uncertain loyalty.

Than N. Oo is a co-founder of advocacy group Free Myanmar and writes frequently about Myanmar’s political developments.

World.title: Nationalist Regime Supporters Turn Against China Over Northern Shan
World.content:
Staunchly nationalist supporters of the Myanmar military are growing wary of the regime’s increasing dependency on China on all fronts, voicing rare criticism of the way Chinese money and influence are being allowed to shape their country.

It was the question of northern Shan State that finally galvanized this resentment among the pro-military crowd.

Many nationalists believe that China enabled Operation 1027, the offensive by an alliance of three ethnic armed groups that dealt a serious blow to the Myanmar military in 2023-24. They staged protests at the time accusing Beijing of interference, and the sentiment has recently resurfaced over what they see as the “Sinicization” of borderlands that the regime has lost in northern Shan.

“We accept them making investment in our country. But supplying arms and funds to ethnic armed groups to capture towns and interfering in our government is unacceptable,” a nationalist told The Irrawaddy. “Public opinion must be voiced openly.”

The renewed criticism comes after the Shan State Joint Action Committee (SSJAC)—an ethnic coalition comprising the Shan State Progress Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), the Shan Nationalities League for Democracy (SNLD), and a Shan militia group—issued a statement on Oct. 23 accusing Kokang’s Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) of imposing Chinese language in schools, granting land rights to foreigners, and erasing local traditions in territories it seized during Operation 1027. The MNDAA swiftly rejected the allegations as unfounded.

Earlier this month, Shan civil society organizations released an open letter warning that the MNDAA’s cultural and administrative practices threaten ethnic coexistence and the stability of the China–Myanmar border.

Ta’ang civil society groups similarly condemned the MNDAA in April after it seized Kutkai Township, where ethnic Ta’ang communities form the majority.

At the peak of Operation 1027, China pressured armed groups to agree ceasefires with the regime in northern Shan, but since then has allowed them to consolidate their quasi-autonomous administrations there rather than handing back all the territory they had gained to the regime.

No other armed group has been able to consolidate administrative control as rapidly as the MNDAA, which analysts say would be impossible without Beijing’s backing.

Regime supporters were initially silent about this perceived Sinicization, but started to voice concerns when exiled independent media widely covered Chinese border encroachment in northern Shan areas controlled by the MNDAA. The regime warned domestic outlets not to publish stories that could damage bilateral ties, but the concerns persisted.

The pot seems to have boiled over when Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun in mid-October recommended “high-level autonomy” for ethnic monitories. His remark was interpreted in different ways across Myanmar’s political circles, stirring debate over China’s intentions.

Along Myanmar’s eastern frontier, three armed groups are widely regarded as being under heavy Chinese influence, the others being the United Wa State Army (UWSA) and the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA). The latter two have upheld ceasefires with the Myanmar military for nearly four decades, and in return they exercise de-facto autonomy in their fiefdoms, serving as effective buffers that insulate China from Myanmar’s instability.

Under the 2008 Constitution, the MNDAA’s Kokang—with a population of fewer than 200,000—is a self‑administered zone, but that covers only Laukkai and Kongyan townships east of the Salween River. But after Operation 1027, the MNDAA reorganized both that original enclave and newly captured areas into four districts: Laukkai, Kutkai, Hsenwi, and Monekoe. Governance in these territories increasingly mirrors administrative practices seen in Beijing, raising alarm not only among staunch nationalists but also among some lawmakers.

“We don’t like it when a powerful neighbor interferes in our sovereignty,” one MP remarked. But he admitted, “The Myanmar government is not in a position to shut out China. We don’t have that strength, and we are deteriorating in every aspect.”

Democracy activists, for their part, accuse Beijing of propping up the military since the coup, reaping political and economic benefits. The exiled leader of the Democratic Party for a New Society, Hnin Hnin Hmwe, said the regime itself is starting to worry about its over-reliance on China.

“China has pushed its interests so far that even the regime is beginning to feel constrained,” she said. “At the same time, China maintains ties with revolutionary forces. China is shrewd to keep the balance.”

World.title: Resistance Forces Inflict Heavy Losses on Regime Troops in Indaw
World.content:
A Myanmar junta offensive to reclaim territory in Sagaing Region’s Indaw Township near the Kachin State border has suffered heavy losses in resistance ambushes, resistance sources said.

Dozens of junta troops were killed and many, including a tactical commander, were reportedly captured by pro-democracy forces.

Troops from two regime Tactical Commands advancing south from Indaw town toward Wuntho and Tigyaing were ambushed by resistance forces on October 4. According to reports, the regime units buried the bodies of dead soldiers in local villages, and one Tactical Command lost contact with its base.

The regime retook control of Indaw town and the Mandalay-Myitkyina road from resistance forces at the end of April. However, it is still conducting clearance operations in the area.

On October 4, roughly 700 troops from Indaw, led by Colonel Kyaw Win Tun, deputy commander of the 33rd Light Infantry Division (LID), advanced south and split into two Tactical Commands: Tactical Command 331, led by Col. Myo Thein, and Tactical Command 332, led by Col. Kyaw San Win.

Both were ambushed by resistance forces, sparking fierce clashes and prompting the regime to bomb the area from the air, Indaw Revolution (IR), a local news information page, reported on Monday.

IR reported that locals found the bodies of 50 regime soldiers near Nanthe Village and cremated them on October 23. Other soldiers’ bodies were spotted near villages on the Indaw-Tigyaing road, it said.

“Eyewitnesses reported over 50 dead bodies. More than 20 [regime soldiers] surrendered, and it is initially understood that a tactical commander was among them,” a source close to the resistance forces told The Irrawaddy.

Intense clashes were reported between regime troops and resistance groups—including the civilian National Unity Government’s People’s Defense Force (PDF), the Kachin Independence Army, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front and allied groups—on October 25 and 26.

Zin Yaw, a military defector and military analyst, told The Irrawaddy that both Tactical Commands had suffered heavy losses.

“Tactical Command 332 led by Col. Kyaw San Win lost communication with the base for 48 hours,” Zin Yaw said.

The troops led by Col. Kyaw San Win advanced along the Indaw-Tigyaing road and ended up near Ma Au Kone Village, which is 23 km south of Indaw town.

According to the reports, some regime soldiers were captured by or voluntarily surrendered to resistance forces.

However, The Irrawaddy couldn’t independently verify the situation, and there has been no official statement from resistance forces or the regime yet.

Madaya Myohman force, which is under the command of the Mandalay PDF and is believed to have taken part in the ambushes, stated that the regime’s 33rd LID faced heavy losses on Monday.

The clashes and bombing in the area forced residents of at least 35 villages in Indaw and Wuntho townships to flee their homes, according to a source close to the resistance.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s GDP Is Growing, but Is Its Economy Transforming?
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan should think like a small, open economy and look to California’s transformation beyond oil, rather than relying on higher commodity prices and government spending to sustain economic growth, former World Bank chief economist Indermit Gill told The Astana Times on Oct. 29.

Gill, who, alongside economist Homi Kharas, coined the widely used term “middle-income trap” in a landmark 2007 World Bank report, pointed to California’s evolution from an oil-producing economy into a major center of technology, entertainment and agriculture as an example of the transformation Kazakhstan could pursue.

The comparison offers a different way to view Kazakhstan’s resource wealth. Oil and gas revenues have helped finance the country’s development, but the more consequential question is whether that wealth can generate industries that can sustain prosperity independently of commodity prices.

“I think Kazakhstan has done a good job in terms of converting resources that are underground into converting, into resources that are above ground. Astana, for example, it’s a great achievement. But you have to reinvent yourself,” Gill told The Astana Times.

“The most successful case of a resource-rich economy becoming diversified is California. California used to depend a lot on oil. But now you hear about services like entertainment services. You hear about Silicon Valley. You hear about agriculture. That’s the kind of thing that I’m thinking about for Kazakhstan,” he said.

His comments came on the sidelines of an international economic conference organized by the Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development (EFSD) in Astana, where economists and policymakers discussed the foundations of sustainable growth and structural transformation.

The productivity gap

According to Gill, the distinction between temporary economic expansion and lasting transformation comes down to productivity: how effectively an economy converts capital, labor and energy into goods and services.

He pointed to Kazakhstan’s experience of rising per capita income followed by periods of decline, illustrating how growth supported by favorable external conditions can prove difficult to sustain without changes in the underlying economy.

“It has grown, then it’s come down again. And the reason why it’s come down is because that structural transformation didn’t take place, so you didn’t have a new structure which could sustain a high income. That comes from having a more productive economy,” said Gill.

During the plenary session, Gill presented data showing that middle-income economies produce roughly one-fifth as much output per worker as the United States, despite possessing capital equivalent to approximately 70% of that in high-income economies. The disparity suggests considerable potential to increase output by improving how existing resources are used.

Gill said Kazakhstan has become more efficient, but much of its income growth has been driven by higher commodity prices, including oil, gas and agricultural products.

“I think Kazakhstan has become more efficient, but I think that more of the gain has actually come from a higher price of the output. (…) I would worry that a big part of this is actually coming from an external shock, and I would worry that it is coming from an expansion of government spending, rather than greater productivity among enterprises,” said Gill.

EFSD Chief Economist Sergei Ulatov echoed this concern, emphasizing that investment alone does not guarantee sustainable growth. He said projects that fail to improve productivity could leave future generations with financial obligations rather than stronger economic capacity.

“As Indermit Gill emphasized, investment alone is not the answer to sustainable growth. If investments are inefficient and unproductive, they are likely to become a burden on future generations. That is why, when we implement projects, the quality of investment and the quality of individual projects are extremely important,” Ulatov told journalists.

He noted that public investment can stimulate economic activity immediately, while its contribution to long-term growth may only become clear years later. The key question is whether projects expand productive capacity or merely increase spending and demand.

From connectivity to innovation

Gill also emphasized that Kazakhstan should regard itself as a small economy despite its relative size within Central Asia. Compared with the world’s largest markets, most economies depend on international integration to access technologies, capital and expertise unavailable domestically.

Openness becomes more important as economies develop. Gill explained that low-income countries can make substantial progress through investment, while middle-income economies must use resources more efficiently and adopt existing technologies. Upper-middle-income economies such as Kazakhstan must eventually develop their own innovation capabilities.

This progression is particularly relevant to Central Asia’s expanding transport corridors. As Kazakhstan strengthens connections between major markets, infrastructure development must be accompanied by greater openness to foreign investment, technologies and skilled workers.

Gill linked this to “technology infusion,” the process of importing and spreading existing technologies throughout an economy. He cited China’s experience of incorporating foreign technologies, products and business practices into domestic production.

“The success of countries like China has been that they have actually been very open to external influence in terms of new ideas, new forms of entrepreneurial organization, new products. If you go to China, for example, you find trains that look Japanese, you have cars that look like Tesla. So, basically, they just infuse these technologies into the economy and as a result, they become better and better,” said Gill.

When growth becomes the goal

For Ulatov, one obstacle to structural transformation is governments’ emphasis on headline GDP growth, which can encourage short-term investment decisions over productivity improvements.

“If economic growth becomes the only political KPI, that is a very bad idea. If you target it, you are most likely to take the easy route. And the easy route, if you have the resources, is simply to increase domestic demand through investment,” he said.

Ulatov said Central Asian economies still require substantial investment in roads, electricity systems and water infrastructure. However, he distinguished such public needs from financing large state-owned enterprises whose commercial viability and long-term economic contribution remain uncertain. The concern extends to competition, particularly when governments select enterprises for continued financial support rather than allowing more productive businesses to expand.

“We discussed today the concept of ‘too big to fail.’ Very often, governments choose their own winners – what economists call ‘picking winners’ – and then continue supporting those companies. The question is whether this distorts competition and pushes small and medium-sized enterprises out of the market. These are the companies that should be growing. They could become the source of your future economic growth. Governments need to think carefully about this.” he said.

The foundations of sustainable growth

Brian Pinto, a former World Bank senior adviser specializing in sovereign debt and economic policy, expanded on the relationship between competition, fiscal discipline and long-term economic performance.

“If the private sector or the bond markets are concerned about the sustainability of debt, real interest rates and risk premia are going to rise, and this is going to affect the investment climate for the private sector,” said Pinto.

“At the same time, if you don’t have strong microeconomic foundations for growth, you’re eventually going to have problems raising enough tax revenue, creating concerns about budget risks, higher inflation, uncertainty and potentially higher taxes down the road. And this, in turn, is going to stifle private investment,” he said.

He outlined three measures he called the “microeconomic policy trio”: hard budget constraints, competition and pragmatic management of exchange rates and interest rates.

Hard budget constraints require governments, banks and enterprises to operate within financial limits rather than repeatedly supporting loss-making businesses. Effective bankruptcy procedures let capital and labor shift to more productive activities, while competition pushes companies to improve efficiency.

Pinto said the relatively favorable macroeconomic conditions in EFSD member economies provide an opportunity to implement reforms before economic pressures intensify.

“So the big lesson, of course, for the EFSD countries, they have a very good situation right now. The macroeconomic situation is relatively good. But in order to enhance structural transformation, now is the time for them to think from a position of strength of implementing the micro-policy trio,” said Pinto.

World.title: Tokayev’s Wage, Digital Economy Reforms Must Protect Workers’ Rights, Expert Says
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s plans to raise the minimum wage and expand digital employment should be accompanied by stronger labor protections, safeguards against algorithmic decision-making and fairer access to social assistance, said Dr. Muslim Khassenov, associate professor at Astana-based Maqsut Narikbayev University, in response to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s Oct. 28 state-of-the-nation address.

In the comment to The Astana Times, Khassenov said the proposed economic and technological reforms must be assessed by their impact on people’s purchasing power, working conditions and access to legal protection.

The expert highlighted five areas in the address requiring particular attention: minimum wages, digital employment, social assistance, scientific research and the planned overhaul of Kazakhstan’s Civil Code.

Higher wages and purchasing power

One of the address’s most immediate measures is the planned increase in the monthly minimum wage from 85,000 tenge ($187) to 110,000 tenge ($242) starting Jan. 1, 2027. According to Tokayev, the increase will affect nearly 1.8 million people, including more than 370,000 public-sector employees.

Khassenov said the nearly 29% increase carries broader implications for wage policy, particularly as inflation continues to erode household purchasing power.

“Of course, an increase in the minimum wage does not automatically oblige employers to raise all salaries proportionally. However, it is a compelling reason to review compensation systems, promote collective bargaining, and improve wage indexation mechanisms,” he explained.

Even when nominal salaries remain unchanged, inflation effectively reduces their value, he said, making real purchasing power a more meaningful measure of workers’ economic well-being.

Digital employment

Tokayev also instructed the government to establish a simplified legal framework for digital employment by the end of 2026, as part of efforts to transform Kazakhstan from a consumer of digital services into a more productive digital economy.

Khassenov sees this proposal as a way to expand economic opportunities for young people, rural residents and people with disabilities by allowing them to earn income regardless of their location.

“Simplifying the legal framework for digital employment should mean, first and foremost, reducing administrative barriers and streamlining registration, taxation, and the formalization of working relationships, but not lowering the level of social protection for citizens,” said Khassenov.

A central concern is the distinction between genuinely independent contractors and workers who depend economically and organizationally on digital platforms.

Although platform workers may formally operate as independent service providers, companies can determine their compensation, allocate assignments, monitor performance and unilaterally restrict their access to work.

According to Khassenov, regulation should address these power imbalances by ensuring access to social insurance, protection against occupational risks, transparent payment systems and effective dispute resolution mechanisms.

The growing use of artificial intelligence in employment decisions creates additional challenges.

“Algorithms are already being used to evaluate employee performance, assign tasks, and make personnel decisions. Employees must understand the data and criteria on which decisions affecting their rights are based and have the opportunity to challenge those decisions,” he said.

“The more digital monitoring tools employers and platforms acquire, the more effective digital mechanisms for protecting workers’ rights must become,” he added.

The professor also suggested that digital technologies could strengthen labor protections through automated working-time records, smart contracts and systems designed to ensure timely wage payments.

Social assistance should remain accessible

Another major theme of Tokayev’s address was the need to make state assistance more targeted, ensuring support reaches those who genuinely need it.

While acknowledging the importance of improving the efficiency of social spending, Khassenov warned against relying too heavily on formal income indicators or automated eligibility assessments.

“Targeting must not become a mechanism for reducing the number of social assistance recipients at any cost,” he said.

He explained that a household’s actual financial situation may depend on factors beyond reported income, including the number of dependents, medical expenses, disability and debt obligations.

The effectiveness of social policy, Khassenov noted, should be measured by whether assistance reaches vulnerable households in a timely manner, rather than primarily by the amount of public money saved.

Scientific development requires better working conditions

Khassenov also emphasized the importance of improving employment conditions for researchers as Kazakhstan pursues technological modernization.

He emphasized that investment in scientific infrastructure and equipment alone is insufficient without addressing the administrative and legal barriers that limit researchers’ productivity.

“The primary resource of science is the scientist, his or her intellectual freedom, time, and the opportunity to conduct research,” said the professor.

“Today, there are certain legal and administrative restrictions that make it difficult to balance teaching and research, for scientists to participate in multiple research projects, and to receive fair compensation for the work actually performed,” he said.

Khassenov called for more flexible employment arrangements, fairer remuneration and reduced reporting requirements.

He also noted that digitalization itself can sometimes increase bureaucracy by introducing additional electronic reporting systems rather than eliminating administrative tasks.

A new Civil Code

Tokayev’s proposal to adopt a new Civil Code by the end of 2027 also presents an opportunity to modernize Kazakhstan’s legal framework.

The current code, developed in the 1990s, predates many of the technologies now reshaping business and employment, including digital assets, electronic transactions and smart contracts.

“However, it is important that the modernization of civil law not be limited solely to technological innovations,” said Khassenov.

One priority, he noted, is preserving a clear distinction between civil law contracts and employment relationships. Without such safeguards, new contractual arrangements could be used to circumvent labor obligations and deny workers access to social protections.

In his address, Tokayev also announced plans to allocate 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.2 billion) from the National Fund through 2029 for a nationwide infrastructure modernization program. The initiative will cover social, transport and utility infrastructure, with 1.5 trillion tenge (US$3.3 billion) earmarked for social projects in 2026 and the first two months of 2027. The President also proposed declaring 2027 the year of nationwide construction.

Khassenov stressed that the success of any reforms should be measured by their tangible impact on citizens.

“A strong state is one where people can work with dignity, receive fair compensation, benefit from modern technologies, develop their abilities and count on effective protection of their rights,” he said. “People, their dignity, work and well-being must remain the central purpose of all reforms.”

World.title: Central Asian Lawmakers Discuss Regional Integration at Dushanbe Forum
World.content:
ASTANA – Parliamentarians from five Central Asian countries discussed regional security, economic integration and digital cooperation at the fourth Inter-Parliamentary Forum of Central Asian States in Dushanbe on Oct. 29, Kazinform reported. The forum brought together lawmakers from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

Kazakhstan’s delegation was led by Kurultai Chairman Aibek Dadebay. Participants discussed Kazakhstan’s political reforms and recent presidential initiatives, which the delegation said could create new development opportunities across the region.

The Kazakh lawmakers also emphasized parliament’s role in maintaining regional peace and security through timely legislation. Discussions addressed the continued importance of Central Asia’s nuclear-weapon-free zone and the proposed establishment of an International Agency for Biological Security.

Economic and digital cooperation

The Kazakh delegation proposed exchanging legislative practices in e-commerce, digital customs administration, investment, transport and industrial cooperation to remove regulatory barriers and create a more integrated regional business environment. The initiative was linked to Kazakhstan’s goal of increasing intra-regional trade to $20 billion.

Participants also discussed strengthening water and climate security, with the Kazakh delegation stressing the importance of adopting a framework convention on water use.

Digital cooperation featured prominently, including proposals to strengthen educational ties and provide legislative support for Kazakhstan’s initiative to develop a Central Asian partnership program on artificial intelligence.

The delegation also proposed parliamentary support for volunteer initiatives and suggested establishing an annual Central Asian Week of Environmental Responsibility. The discussions underscored the role of regional cooperation in addressing shared challenges, including security, water management, environmental protection and the development of emerging technologies.

The forum concluded with the adoption of the Dushanbe Declaration.

World.title: Kazakhstan Ranks 41st Worldwide for Public Order and Security, Global Index Shows
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 41st out of 143 countries and jurisdictions in the Order and Security factor of the 2026 World Justice Project (WJP) Rule of Law Index, improving one position from last year, according to the organization’s latest report.

The ranking measures one of eight areas the index assesses, evaluating how the rule of law functions worldwide. The Order and Security factor covers the absence of crime, civil conflict and violent methods of resolving disputes.

Kazakhstan ranked 42nd in this category in the previous edition of the index. However, the improvement in the security-related measure contrasts with Kazakhstan’s overall performance. The country ranked 67th out of 143 jurisdictions in the 2026 index, down from 66th in 2025. Its overall score declined 1.4% to 0.53.

The index assesses eight areas: constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice.

In the 2026 edition, Kazakhstan ranked 102nd in constraints on government powers, 67th in absence of corruption, 80th in open government, 98th in fundamental rights, 58th in regulatory enforcement, 40th in civil justice and 69th in criminal justice. Denmark topped the overall ranking, followed by Norway, Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg.

The WJP Rule of Law Index draws on household surveys and surveys of legal practitioners and experts. The 2026 edition covers 143 countries and jurisdictions, representing approximately 95% of the world’s population.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Georgia Work to Expand Cross-Border Access to Financial Markets
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Georgia are working to make it easier for financial institutions to access each other’s capital markets, with regulators exploring mutual market recognition mechanisms to support cross-border investment and financial services. The initiative was a key focus of AIFC Connect: Tbilisi 2026, an event hosted by the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), the National Bank of Georgia, GFTN and ITS on Oct. 28 as part of the Tbilisi Finance Summit 2026.

The initiative builds on a memorandum of understanding signed on Sept. 9 by the Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA), the AIFC’s financial regulator, and the National Bank of Georgia. The agreement provides a framework for regulatory cooperation, information exchange and developing mechanisms to facilitate access to the two markets, particularly in capital markets and asset management. Under the memorandum, the regulators will develop practical arrangements that account for the legal and regulatory requirements of both jurisdictions.

“Our shared priority now is to translate these commitments into practical measures,” said Evgeniya Bogdanova, AFSA chief executive officer.

She said the goal was to expand opportunities for financial institutions, facilitate entry into new markets and support cross-border services while maintaining investor protection standards.

The Tbilisi event brought together regulators, banks, investment firms, stock exchanges and financial and technology companies from both countries to discuss economic trends, capital markets and opportunities for closer cooperation.

Bakhtiyar Tleubekov, chairman of the AIFC Authority’s management board, said the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route added another dimension to Kazakhstan-Georgia cooperation by improving connectivity between Asia and Europe and creating opportunities for trade and infrastructure investment.

“The AIFC is well positioned to contribute to these efforts through its internationally recognized legal and regulatory framework and capital market infrastructure,” he said.

The event also featured an overview of Georgia’s economic outlook and capital markets by Irakli Gabriadze, head of the Economic Development Corporation of Georgia, and a presentation on Kazakhstan’s capital market by Birzhan Astayev, chief markets and products officer of the Astana International Exchange.

A panel discussion brought together representatives of financial and investment institutions to examine opportunities for cross-border transactions, investment and business cooperation. Participants included representatives of Kazakhstan’s National Investment Holding Baiterek, Halyk Bank Georgia, ITS, TBC Capital and Galt & Taggart.

Trade and investment ties

Economic ties between Kazakhstan and Georgia provide a foundation for deeper financial cooperation. Bilateral trade reached $184.5 million in 2025, while trade turnover totaled $53 million in January-April 2026, according to the AIFC. Kazakhstan has invested more than $500 million in Georgia’s economy, while more than 600 companies with Georgian participation operate in Kazakhstan.

The AIFC also serves as a platform for Georgian businesses seeking access to Kazakhstan’s market and international financial services. Twenty companies from Georgia are registered in the center, representing sectors including finance and insurance, information and communications, manufacturing and agriculture. The center offers a legal and regulatory framework based on English common law principles.
