World.title: Political analyst: ‘If Aliyev has to choose between Russia and Turkey, he will choose Russia’
World.content:
Tensions between Azerbaijan and Turkey

Political analyst Arastun Orujlu has discussed the reasons for the recent tensions between Azerbaijan and Turkey, as well as their possible consequences, in an interview with Meydan TV.

In his view, one of the main reasons for the disagreement between Baku and Ankara is Azerbaijan’s growing closeness to Israel.

– Mr Orujlu, what do you think is the main reason for the tensions that have emerged between Turkey and Azerbaijan in recent days?

– The tensions between Turkey and Azerbaijan have nothing to do with Islam or religious values. These factors serve merely as a pretext, primarily for official Baku, which uses them to provoke conflict. However, I do not rule out personal motives either. Experience shows that personal considerations often lie behind the Azerbaijani authorities’ strong reactions to the actions of other countries.

Ilham Aliyev views every issue through the prism of his personal interests. Nevertheless, I believe the current tensions are primarily political. They reflect Azerbaijan’s desire to distance itself from neighbouring countries and pursue a foreign policy oriented towards Tel Aviv and Washington. This trend is now clearly visible.

– You link these tensions to Azerbaijan’s foreign policy. In Turkey, however, people have criticised the Azerbaijani authorities both over their policies on the hijab and over their relations with Israel. To what extent does this criticism reflect political considerations? Are there genuine disagreements between Ankara and Baku on these issues?

– These are separate issues, so let me address them one by one. The hijab has always been a matter of principle for Turkey’s Justice and Development Party (AKP). For a long time, it sparked heated political debates in Turkey. The country experienced serious upheaval and a painful period over this issue. Therefore, if the current Turkish government, led by the AKP, had failed to respond to what was happening, it would undoubtedly have damaged its standing among its own voters.

In fact, the first reaction did not come from the AKP leadership. It began on Turkish social media, where journalists and individual users started protesting. Only later did the AKP leadership respond, and not at government level. The response came from Oktay Saral, an adviser to Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on party affairs.

As for Israel, the problems here are genuinely serious and entirely political. Turkey and Israel are engaged in an intense struggle for influence in the South Caucasus, the Middle East and the eastern Mediterranean. Israel is effectively seeking regional dominance. Turkey, meanwhile, believes it should take the leading role because it has stronger moral and historical claims to it, as well as greater military capabilities than Israel. Turkey’s strong reaction to the genocide unfolding in Gaza also plays an important role.

We know these problems have existed for quite some time. There is no doubt that Israel is trying to expand its influence in Central Asia through Azerbaijan and the South Caucasus. Central Asia is one of Turkey’s key foreign policy priorities, and Israel has already begun strengthening its position there. The two sides have very sharp disagreements over this issue.

It is also well known that the Azerbaijani authorities maintain exceptionally close relations with Israel. After the United States, Azerbaijan may well be Israel’s closest partner.

– In this context, how do you assess Azerbaijan’s decision to declare 31 Turkish citizens persona non grata? How might this decision affect relations between the two countries?

– As far as I can tell, Ilham Aliyev is trying to weaken Turkey’s influence in Azerbaijan. I do not mean its influence over the government, but rather Turkey’s role in Azerbaijani society. Although no opinion polls have been conducted, the situation clearly suggests that Turkey became the most popular country among Azerbaijanis after the 44-day war. Deep historical, cultural and ethnic ties explain this. Perhaps this is precisely what worries Ilham Aliyev.

He effectively signalled that a conflict was brewing at the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) congress. For some reason, many observers overlooked his remarks. In his speech, Ilham Aliyev addressed not only economic and social problems but also put forward three political arguments with an underlying message.

First, he stated directly that nobody had provided Azerbaijan with free support, and that even weapons and ammunition had been sold at global market prices. Azerbaijanis immediately thought of Turkey when they heard these words. Yet Ilham Aliyev himself has repeatedly said that Azerbaijan would have found itself in a difficult position without Turkish support. At the Victory Parade following the 44-day war, he stood alongside Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on the main podium. Now, suddenly, he has made this statement. It is quite clear that he directed it specifically at Turkey.

Second, in the same speech, he stressed the need to improve the quality of education. But if Ilham Aliyev genuinely wants to improve education, he should appoint professionals to senior positions in the sector. Today, Azerbaijan’s education system is run entirely by brokers, shopkeepers and traders who have nothing to do with education.

The third point concerned strengthening patriotic sentiment. Aliyev was effectively saying: “I will fight against Turkey, and your first homeland is Azerbaijan.” That was the message behind his words.

Look at who took part in all the disputes and conflicts that followed. They included media outlets linked to the Azerbaijani authorities, individuals, influencers, media platforms, experts and even people who call themselves opposition party leaders. They all joined the campaign. It was carefully planned.

Let me repeat: it appears that Ilham Aliyev has set himself the task of weakening Turkey’s standing and influence in Azerbaijani society. Alternatively, someone may have assigned him that task.

– We have previously seen the Azerbaijani authorities use similar rhetoric and pressure tactics when relations with other countries deteriorated. For example, when relations with Europe worsened, independent NGOs and media representatives became targets. When tensions with Russia escalated, authorities targeted the Sputnik news agency and several politicians. During tensions with Iran, they put pressure on religious believers. Now we see a similar approach towards Turkey. Which specific issue, in your view, lies at the heart of the disagreement between Azerbaijan and Turkey?

– I believe the issue concerns foreign policy alone. As I have already said, Azerbaijan is moving closer to Israel, and this process is advancing very rapidly. Moreover, Azerbaijani media have featured not merely people who support Israel, but individuals with direct links to Israeli organisations. They have accused Turkey of wrongdoing while defending the Azerbaijani authorities’ position.

For example, the English-language Azerbaijani website News.Az published an article by a certain Roman Gurevich. After reading it, I noticed that subsequent events in Azerbaijan unfolded according to the scenario described in that article. This shows that Israel has considerable influence over Azerbaijani media.

All the websites and media outlets that belong to Global Media Group also have links to Israel. People in Turkey can see this and understand that Azerbaijan is moving away from them. Relations between Israel and Turkey have deteriorated to such an extent that Azerbaijan has effectively found itself having to choose a side. Ankara can clearly see that Azerbaijan — or, more precisely, Ilham Aliyev and his family — are choosing Israel. I believe this is the main reason for the current conflict.

But what measures can they take against Turkey? Turkey has no levers of influence within Azerbaijan. Western countries, for example, once had some influence over certain NGOs and media outlets. The authorities arrested their representatives on fabricated charges. When relations with Iran deteriorated, they arrested religious believers. During tensions with Russia, they detained IT specialists whom the Azerbaijani authorities themselves had invited into the country.

Turkey has no comparable resources in Azerbaijan. Taking such steps against Turkey would also carry serious risks. Azerbaijan itself has considerable leverage in Turkey, including a network of lobbyists it funds and media resources. In addition, Azerbaijani investments in Turkey amount to around $20 billion.

Nevertheless, I do not think relations will deteriorate to the point of a complete break. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s phone call was more than an invitation. It was also a warning with a clear message: “Stop this process.” The Azerbaijani authorities had been orchestrating an extremely dirty campaign against Turkey, including at the military leadership level. Perhaps even Russia and Iran have not faced attacks this harsh.

– How might the current tensions affect the future of relations between the two countries?

– These tensions have already affected relations. The relationship between Azerbaijan and Turkey rests on several distinct foundations, unlike Azerbaijan’s ties with other countries.

The first is the relationship between the two states. The second is the personal relationship between Ilham Aliyev and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, which brings together various interests. For example, companies close to the AKP operate in Azerbaijan. The third foundation is the connection between the two societies. This is the most reliable pillar of their relationship.

The concept of “One nation, two states” is more than a slogan. The relationship between the two peoples has deep historical roots stretching back at least 120 to 130 years. This third pillar has suffered the damage.

Various groups hostile to Turkey have become more active in Azerbaijan and taken advantage of the situation. They have effectively received a signal that they can now criticise, insult and accuse Turkey. As a result, they have dealt a significant blow to the most important foundation of relations between the two countries.

– At what level will the two countries maintain their political and strategic alliance after this?

– That will depend on many external factors. The results of elections in Israel and the political situation in the United States will play an important role, for example. Recently, an American researcher published a book alleging that large sums of money had been transferred to Donald Trump’s son-in-law through Azerbaijan. This should not surprise us, because Azerbaijan conducts much of its foreign policy through lobbying and financial mechanisms.

Future developments will depend on these factors. For example, if the Republican Party loses the US midterm elections and Trump’s influence weakens, Ilham Aliyev will have to realign himself with either Russia or Turkey.

I say this with full responsibility: if Aliyev has to choose between Russia and Turkey, he will choose Russia. Around 70% of people in Azerbaijan’s current leadership have ties to Russia, while 30% have ties to Israel. There are virtually no people in the Azerbaijani leadership who look to Turkey.

Tensions between Azerbaijan and Turkey

World.title: Georgia’s new gambling tournament law raises ombudsman concerns, draws Patriarchate response
World.content:
International gambling tournaments in Georgia

Georgia‘s parliament has passed a bill in its second reading that would allow casinos to organise international gambling tournaments. The initiative provides for permits to hold such tournaments, the introduction of relevant fees and fines for violating permit conditions.

Under the bill, an “international gambling tournament” is defined as a competition organised by a casino in which the prize fund is guaranteed in advance by the organiser and at least 80% of participants are foreign nationals.

Georgian government representatives have justified the move by citing its potential to boost tourism and economic activity. However, the country’s ombudsman has criticised the fast-tracked legislative process and the lack of a proper assessment of potential social harm.

Metropolitan Anton of Vani and Baghdati said the Georgian Patriarchate would discuss the issue on 30 October and present its unified position to the public following the meeting.

What will change?

Under the bill, organisers will be exempt from paying fees for the use of gaming tables used exclusively for international gambling tournaments if the prize fund exceeds 3 million lari. Organisers will also be allowed to generate revenue from holding such tournaments.

International gambling tournaments may be held both at licensed casino premises and at other venues.

The annual permit fee for organising such tournaments will be 100,000 lari (approximately $39,000). Violating permit conditions will carry a fine of 50,000 lari, while organising or holding an international gambling tournament without the required permit will result in a fine of 150,000 lari.

According to the bill’s authors, the amendments aim to improve the legal framework governing gambling and establish clear regulations for organising international gambling tournaments.

The bill’s sponsors note that existing legislation neither defines the term “international tournament” nor contains provisions regulating such events. They argue that this creates uncertainty for businesses and regulatory authorities.

What does the ombudsman say?

Following the bill’s first reading, Georgia’s ombudsman called on parliament to halt its further consideration and adoption.

According to the ombudsman, the fast-tracked consideration of an issue affecting the public interest is particularly problematic, especially without a proper expert assessment or comprehensive analysis of potential human rights risks.

The ombudsman argues that the bill lacks an assessment of its impact on public health and a proper analysis of potential social harm and the costs of preventing it. Furthermore, relevant experts and organisations were not involved in drafting the legislation, while international experience was not taken into account.

The ombudsman also notes that the bill’s explanatory memorandum claims the proposed changes will not affect children’s rights but provides no justification for this conclusion.

“When considering bills of this kind, it is crucial to conduct a comprehensive and thorough examination of the issue, including by ensuring broad participation of experts in the relevant field,” the ombudsman stressed.

The ombudsman emphasises that discussions of the proposed amendments should not focus solely on potential economic benefits. Instead, their impact on public health and social well-being, as well as the associated risks, must be given due consideration.

What does the Patriarchate say?

According to Archpriest Andria Jaghmaidze, head of the Georgian Patriarchate’s public relations department, no prior discussions were held on the issue, and the Patriarchate itself has not yet examined the bill in detail.

Jaghmaidze noted that the Patriarchate has been actively involved in developing regulations governing gambling since 2017. He also said that the Patriarchate had reviewed the ombudsman’s position and largely shared the arguments presented.

“The Patriarchate cannot remain on the sidelines of such a process. We hope that dialogue with the bill’s sponsors will lead to a positive outcome,” Jaghmaidze said.

Metropolitan Anton of Vani and Baghdati said the Georgian Patriarchate was examining the legislative initiative concerning international gambling tournaments and preparing its official position on the matter.

According to the metropolitan, the Patriarchate will hold a discussion on 30 October to examine potential risks associated with the bill, after which it will formulate and publicly announce its unified position.

“Judging by what is apparent so far, I see certain risks. We have not yet fully examined the details — I have only heard some discussions about the issue on television. Of course, we will study the details and express our opinion. Frankly, much remains unclear, although we may still receive further explanations,” Metropolitan Anton said in an interview with InterPressNews.

He added that the Patriarchate intended to discuss the issue with government representatives and formulate its position on the bill in consultation with other senior clergy.

“Of course, we cannot remain indifferent,” the metropolitan said.

How has government policy on gambling changed?

In recent years, the Georgian Dream party’s gambling policy has primarily focused on tightening restrictions and limiting the number of people allowed to gamble.

During the early years of Georgian Dream’s rule, parliament twice rejected legislative initiatives aimed at banning gambling s and tightening regulations, in 2013 and 2019. In 2013, one of the arguments against such measures was the potential damage to the advertising industry, while Bidzina Ivanishvili warned of the risk of creating an unfavourable investment climate.

The situation changed significantly in late 2021, when parliament adopted a comprehensive package of gambling regulations. According to the government, the measures were intended to restrict access to gambling and limit its advertising.

Major restrictions came into force in March 2022:

The minimum gambling age for Georgian citizens was raised to 25.

Socially vulnerable individuals, public officials and people included in a designated register were banned from gambling.

Gambling s were banned on television, outdoors and on Georgian websites, with limited exceptions for certain forms of sponsorship.

Taxation and regulatory oversight were tightened.

The minimum gambling age for foreign nationals remained 18.

Subsequent changes revealed a distinct approach: maintaining strict restrictions for the local population while encouraging the development of the gambling industry targeting foreign customers.

According to an industry review published in June 2026, the government introduced a bill to establish preferential licensing and tax arrangements for online gambling companies targeting overseas customers.

The initiative proposed incentives for operators serving foreign markets, while maintaining a higher tax burden on the segment of the industry catering to Georgian citizens.

World.title: Armenian parliament ratifies framework agreement on Trump Route (TRIPP) project
World.content:
Armenia ratifies agreement on TRIPP project

The parliament of Armenia has ratified a framework agreement on strategic co-operation under the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project. The parties initialled the document during Marco Rubio’s visit to Yerevan on 26 May 2026 and signed the final version remotely just a few days later.

TRIPP (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) is a road that will connect Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory. The project also aims to reopen regional transport links. As a result, Armenia will gain access to third countries via Azerbaijan. For several years, Yerevan and Baku could not agree on this issue. Azerbaijan demanded a road that it called the “Zangezur corridor”. Armenia’s authorities said they were ready to reopen all transport routes but rejected the term “corridor”, arguing that it implied a loss of Armenian control and sovereign rights over the territory. The two sides reached an agreement only on 8 August in Washington. Under the deal, the road will remain under Armenia’s sovereign control, while the US will join the project as a business partner. The initiative took the name “Trump Route” after the US president, who mediated the agreement.

Parliament ratified the agreement with 63 votes in favour and 32 against. Only MPs from the ruling faction supported it.

The parliamentary opposition had announced in advance that it would vote against ratification of the framework agreement. Opposition MPs argued that the document took US and Azerbaijani interests into account but failed to protect Armenia’s interests.

MPs from the ruling faction, by contrast, believe the project will reopen regional transport links on the basis of reciprocity. In their view, this would benefit Armenia economically. The opposition disagrees, pointing to the lack of any financial assessments.

Debates on ratifying the TRIPP project began in parliament the previous day. MPs had only two hours for the discussion. However, opposition lawmakers managed to raise all their concerns and put forward several proposals.

Opposition MP on the interests of the US, Armenia and Azerbaijan

Anna Grigoryan, head of the opposition Armenia faction, noted that Armenia and the United States had signed a bilateral document concerning the implementation of TRIPP. However, she said, the document also refers to a third party — Azerbaijan.

“Azerbaijan’s interests are actually reflected in this document more directly and clearly than the interests of the Republic of Armenia.”

Grigoryan also outlined what she believes each side stands to gain from the project.

“The US gains a direct presence in the region, particularly along the border with Iran, in a strategically crucial area. Azerbaijan secures a link between Nakhchivan and the rest of the country — a goal that both Azerbaijan and Turkey have long pursued.”

When asked what Armenia stands to gain, she said the question was harder to answer.

“When the political majority tries to answer this question, the first word they use is ‘unblocking’. But on the ground, no transport links are being reopened and no borders are opening. So that part of the answer does not reflect reality.”

Should the launch of TRIPP be linked to the signing of a peace treaty?

Narek Karapetyan, leader of the opposition Strong Armenia faction, is concerned that Azerbaijan may lose its incentive to sign a peace treaty once the Trump Route begins operating.

“Azerbaijan gets what it set out to achieve, while what we are supposed to get — peace — could be postponed for five to ten years. Why would they sign a peace treaty with Armenia if they are already getting a link to Nakhchivan?”

Official Yerevan has not ruled out the possibility that the Trump Route could begin operating before Armenia and Azerbaijan sign a peace treaty.

The MP argues that the two important issues should not be treated separately. He proposes linking the implementation of the Trump Route to the signing of a peace treaty.

Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Ruben Rubinyan disagreed. In his view, it is a positive development that TRIPP can proceed without depending on the signing of a peace treaty.

“If you argue that we should not implement this project in order to secure the signing of a peace treaty, you are saying that TRIPP is a bad initiative for Armenia. But TRIPP is by no means a bad initiative for Armenia.”

The ruling party representative welcomed the prospect of “elements of peace taking shape on the ground” independently of the peace treaty. By “elements of peace”, Rubinyan means both the launch of the Trump Route and the ongoing process of delimiting and demarcating the border between the two countries.

Background to the Trump Route project

The Trump Route offers Armenia a real opportunity to reopen regional transport links. For Azerbaijan, it provides the shortest route connecting the country with Nakhchivan.

The project envisages using the railway along a stretch of about 43km through Armenian territory. A motorway, energy infrastructure and digital communications links will also run through the area.

All infrastructure located on Armenian territory will remain under Armenia’s sovereignty and jurisdiction.

The ratified framework agreement provides for the establishment of TRIPP Development Company, which will oversee the project’s development and implementation.

Initially, the US will own 74% of the company’s shares and Armenia will hold 26%. After 49 years, if the parties extend their co-operation for a further 50 years, Armenia’s stake will rise to 49%. Armenia will grant TRIPP Development Company exclusive rights to use and develop land, along with other necessary powers within the areas allocated to the project, for 49 years.

Armenia and the US still need to agree on and adopt the company’s charter and shareholder agreement.

It also remains unclear what border-crossing arrangements will apply to Armenian citizens travelling through Nakhchivan.

Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said the two sides had yet to agree on the technical details of travel through Azerbaijani territory.

“We still need to discuss these issues with Azerbaijan. They fall within the framework of Armenia–Azerbaijan relations.” Armenia–Azerbaijan relations.”

Armenia ratifies agreement on TRIPP project

World.title: ‘Like a black cat in a dark room’: Georgia’s opposition ban case enters sixth day of hearings
World.content:
What happened at Georgia’s opposition ban hearing

On 28 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the sixth day of hearings on a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties. The court is currently hearing submissions from the parties involved. On Tuesday, it heard arguments from representatives of the Coalition for Change.

The lawsuit names the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that these parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties whose aims include overthrowing or forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments is that the parties refuse to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The United National Movement faces additional accusations of undermining Georgia’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. The lawsuit holds the party responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia over South Ossetia, when it was in power. All five opposition parties reject the accusations. Hearings are scheduled to continue through 30 October. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the claim, meaning at least four of the seven judges must vote in favour.

The Coalition for Change is represented in court by Nika Gvaramia, Tengo Tevzadze, Maia Kopaleishvili, Giga Lemonjava and Marika Arevadze. None of their motions was granted.

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia clashed twice with the coalition’s representatives, over their citation of a European Parliament resolution and their reference to the “Russian doctrine”.

The hearings will resume on 29 October at 11 a.m.

Judge Nadaraia: “European Parliament resolution is irrelevant to this case”

Giga Lemonjava presented an 8 October 2026 European Parliament resolution at the hearing. The resolution compared the Georgian ruling party’s bid to ban opposition parties with the Russian and Belarusian models, describing it as part of a strategy to eliminate political pluralism and turn Georgia into a one-party state.

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia interrupted the presentation and asked how the resolution was relevant to the proceedings. Lemonjava replied that it was not directly relevant to the case but that the public should be informed about it.

Nika Gvaramia commented: “Public hearings mean that participants are speaking not only to the court but also to the public.”

Nadarაიa responded: “Public hearings mean that everyone can follow the proceedings, not that someone can make political statements here.” He also reprimanded Gvaramia, saying: “You are interrupting me and disrupting the proceedings.”

Judge Nadaraia says comparison with Russia’s new doctrine is irrelevant to court proceedings

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia raised a similar objection for a second time during Giga Lemonjava’s address.

The opposition representative drew attention to two claims in the lawsuit against the opposition: that the previous government, when the United National Movement was in power, artificially restored the borders of the former South Ossetian Autonomous Region in 2007 and started the war with Russia in 2008.

Lemonjava argued that these claims closely matched Russia’s new foreign policy and security doctrine. If the court accepted them, he said, a Georgian state institution would be giving legal legitimacy to Russia’s version of events for the first time. “You need to be aware of this danger,” he told the judges.

Lemonjava also argued that giving legal force to these claims would contradict Article 78 of Georgia’s Constitution, which obliges state institutions to take all measures to ensure the country’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

Nadaraia did not allow Lemonjava to continue with this line of argument, describing his remarks as “demagoguery” and saying he had gone beyond the scope of the proceedings. The judge again told him not to interrupt.

Judge Gotsiridze: “Do not look for a black cat where there is none”

Maia Kopaleishvili, representing the Coalition for Change, and Constitutional Court judge Eva Gotsiridze previously served together on the court’s panel. At the hearing, they clashed over a section of the lawsuit concerning an alleged attempt to enter parliament.

Kopaleishvili questioned whether Gotsiridze had studied the ruling party’s lawsuit thoroughly enough. The judge called the remark inappropriate.

“Perhaps this issue simply needs clarification. Do not look for a black cat where there is none,” Gotsiridze replied.

Opposition representative Kopaleishvili tells ruling party lawyers: “You were my students”

Maia Kopaleishvili addressed Archil Gorduladze and Tornike Cheishvili, who are representing the ruling party in court.

“You said opposition parties should be banned to protect future generations from a threat. You were my students. What threat do my colleagues and I pose to the country’s future?” Kopaleishvili asked.

Gvaramia warns of return to Soviet-style one-party elections

Nika Gvaramia noted that 28 October marked 36 years since Georgia held its first multiparty elections in 1990, as the Soviet Union was breaking apart.

“And now we are going back to where we started,” he said.

Gvaramia also described as a “distorted reality” the attempt to remove Lelo opposition party leader Badri Japaridze from politics, despite his being one of the signatories of Georgia’s 1991 Act of Restoration of State Independence.

Opposition assesses court hearing

Tornike Artkmeladze, a member of Lelo, said after the hearing that banning opposition parties in a single move would destroy what had been painstakingly built over the past 35 years.

“This is preparation for the first stage of clearing the political field — first of parties, and then they will move on to banning any active political activity. Georgian Dream wants to be the only force on the political scene. But they fail to understand that there are at least a million people in this country who will not give up their freedom,” Artkmeladze said.

World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 30. Progress in dialogue with the United States can only be achieved after the seven conditions put forward by Iran have been agreed upon.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote this on his X page.

“Iran’s conditions have been repeatedly and clearly stated to the mediators. The carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran. Progress can only be achieved once Iran’s seven conditions have been agreed upon,” he said.

Meanwhile, tensions between Iran and the United States remain high following the months-long conflict that began with US and Israeli airstrikes on February 28. A peace memorandum was signed between the two countries on June 18 under Pakistani mediation, but talks on a final agreement have faced repeated difficulties amid mutual accusations of non-compliance and continued pressure.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 30, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 30. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 34-th day of the second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev made a post on his official Twitter account that the Azerbaijani Army liberated several villages in Jabrayil, Zangilan and Gubadli districts from the occupiers.

- President Ilham Aliyev called Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry released information on the latest situation in the frontline. The battles continued mainly in the direction of Aghdara, Khojavand and Gubadli. A list of destroyed military equipment of the Armenian Armed Forces was announced.

- A number of Azerbaijani settlements were shelled in the morning. A video of the destruction of Smerch, from which the Armenian Armed Forces shelled Barda, was released.

- Another high-ranking Armenian serviceman who committed a war crime was killed.

- Gubadli was subjected to artillery fire from the territory of Armenia.

- A video of the destruction of the missile-artillery depot of the Armenian Armed Forces was released.

- A video report from the liberated Khudafarin village of Jabrayil district was released.

- A video of the destruction of two more 'Smerch' missile systems, from which Armenian troops shelled the cities of Barda and Tartar, was released.

- Armenian armed forces launched 'Smerch' missile at Alasgarli village of Tartar.

- A video of exact strikes on the Armenian troops, as well as video of the destruction of another 'Osa' anti-aircraft missile system of Armenian troops were released.

World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 29. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and U.S. President Donald Trump held a telephone conversation.

This was stated in a press release issued by the Turkish Presidency.

According to the statement, Trump called Erdogan during a dinner attended by heads of state, organized on October 29 to mark Republic Day and the summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS).

During the conversation, Erdogan conveyed to the US president the greetings of the OTS member states’ leaders who attended the dinner. He also noted that decisions aimed at further advancing the organization would be adopted at the upcoming summit. World.title: First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva attended performance of “The Seagull” (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 29. On October 29, the Maly Drama Theatre – Theatre of Europe from St. Petersburg, Russia, presented its interpretation of Anton Chekhov’s play The Seagull at the Azerbaijan State Academic Musical Theatre as part of the Baku International Arts Festival (BIAF 2026).

First Vice-President of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva attended the performance alongside her daughter Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva.

Directed by Lev Dodin, a recipient of major Russian theatre awards, including the Golden Mask, the production is regarded as one of the most acclaimed interpretations of the classic play.

The set and costume designer is Alexander Borovsky.

The cast includes Sergey Kuryshev, People’s Artist of Russia, and Honored Artists Elizaveta Boyarskaya and Igor Chernevich, among others.

This is the second edition of the Baku International Arts Festival. Running until November 8, the festival is organized with the support of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Culture. BIAF 2026 features more than 20 events, including concerts, ballet and theatre performances, film screenings, meet-and-greet sessions with artists, and masterclasses.

The festival brings together artists and creative ensembles from Azerbaijan, the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada, Russia, the United States, France and other countries.

World.title: Australia sitting on unused goldmine of old gigantic tyres
World.content:
Among the largest tyres ever manufactured, they help extract and haul billions of dollars of Australian resources.

But recyclers say the huge amount of rubber discarded by mining companies is its own kind of buried treasure.

For decades, the mining industry has been legally allowed to bury, stockpile, or send to landfill more than 100,000 tonnes of end-of-life tyres every year.

It is in sharp contrast to the rest of the tyre market, which collects about 96 per cent of passenger and commercial tyres for recycling, according to the Australian Tyre Recyclers Association (ATRA).

A haul truck operating in Kalgoorlie-Boulder's Super Pit gold mine. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

ATRA executive officer Robert Kelmen said just two per cent of off-the-road (OTR) mining tyres were recovered.

"These are very big mining tyres. They might be four, five, six tonnes," Mr Kelmen said.

" That is a lot of rubber and a lot of rubber that's really being sought out now internationally. "

Dip in rubber production

Long argued on environmental grounds, a new report is mounting the economic case for OTC tyre recycling.

ATRA found up to $200 million of raw, natural rubber was being buried annually on mine sites.

That dollar figure is expected to climb as global rubber production lags behind demand.

"There are risks to virgin rubber production, which is essential for these mining tyres," Mr Kelman said.

"The mining industry should be a part of shoring up the production of new tyres, getting that material off site, [and] getting it into the recovery markets."

Global production of natural rubber is expected to fall short of demand. (Reuters: Nguyen Huy Kham)

The Association of Natural Rubber Producing Countries forecasts a natural rubber shortfall of 317,000 tonnes in 2026, citing erratic weather across tropical forest plantations in south-east Asia.

Miles Kenney-Lazar, a rubber expert at the University of Melbourne, said the commodity often cycled through highs and lows, but now other factors were affecting production.

"More recently, there's a lot of environmental changes that are impacting rubber plantations, like flooding and climate change," he said.

Meanwhile, the need for the material has only grown alongside electric vehicles, which tend to be heavier and wear through rubber more quickly.

"If better systems can be put in place to ensure those tyres can efficiently be recycled and put on the market, then I don't see why … mining companies or others wouldn't want to take advantage," Dr Kenney-Lazar said.

Large public investment

The West Australian and Commonwealth governments have collectively invested $20.7 million into six tyre recycling infrastructure projects under the Recycling Modernisation Fund, while a further $62 million has been kicked in by industry.

One of those facilities was built by Tyrecycle in WA's Pilbara region — home to 49 per cent of the nation's mining tyres.

But 18 months after opening for business in Port Hedland, the plant is processing a fraction of its 30,000 tonne capacity.

Tyrecycle's Port Hedland facility is operating at 10 per cent of its capacity. (Supplied: Tyrecycle)

"It has been slow going, to be honest," company spokesperson Ashley Battilana said.

"We can do 30,000 tonnes easily and, with some more infrastructure put in there, we could easily go a bit more, but currently we're only doing 2,000 to 3,000 tonnes per annum."

Mr Battilana called on lawmakers to tighten regulations and force companies to face the up-front costs of recycling.

"The government's undermining the tyre recycling industry by allowing the burial of tyres," he said.

"The infrastructure is there to process these tyres. The offtake is there as well, both domestically and internationally.

" It's just the incoming feedstock to keep these plants busy. "

Industry says logistics challenges remain

Western Australia's Chamber of Minerals and Energy said the sector aimed to minimise waste "wherever feasible."

Policy and advocacy director Anita Logiudice pointed to existing partnerships with tyre recyclers to produce crumb for road bitumen.

"However, some barriers remain," she said.

"These include logistical challenges associated with transporting OTR tyres from remote mines to the nearest recycling plant, as well as the relatively small market for crumb rubber in WA."

The Chamber of Minerals and Energy says logisitics remain the biggest barrier to tyre recycling. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Earlier this year, a parliamentary inquiry made 12 recommendations to the federal government, including the staged, legislated reduction of onsite burial for OTR tyres over the next five years.

A spokesperson for Industry and Innovation Minister Tim Ayres said the government was still considering its response.

World.title: For the fans who became heroes, Samoa vs Tonga is bigger than a grand final
World.content:
Ahead of their sold-out Rugby League World Cup match on Sunday, the new faces of the eternal rivalry between Tonga and Samoa didn't quite go straight from the stands onto the field, but they went pretty close.

Four years ago, when the two met in the last World Cup, Francis Manuleleua was hunched over in his bedroom in South Auckland, watching the game on his phone.

He was 18, with the rugby league world at his feet, and after Samoa held on for a pulsating 20-18 victory, he snatched up a flag and marched into the street because his life had changed forever.

Loading...

"Growing up I was always picked in the Kiwi teams, Under 16s and Under 18s and that, so there was a feeling of wanting to pull on that black jersey in either league or union," Manuleleua said.

"But after that 2022 World Cup, seeing all the boys play, how much it meant to them, that's when it changed for me and I thought to myself 'this is the jersey I'd want to put on if I ever get the opportunity'."

Across the Tasman, Sua Fa'alogo was part of the same celebratory throng, wherever the four winds could take Samoans from their islands.

The parades of the Samoan and Tongan fans have become legendary. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

The 23-year-old was born and raised in Samoa, in the village of Si'umu, and lived there until he was nine, when his parents moved to Melbourne to find a better life for him and his eight siblings.

Leka Halasima's story was similar: he was born in Tofoa, Tonga, before moving to New Zealand as a boy.

In 2024, a few months after his NRL debut and well before every league fan knew his name, he watched his two nations go head-to-head in the Pacific Championship, cheering on the Mate Ma'a in a 25-24 victory.

Halasima has gone from admiring his heroes to playing alongside them. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

"Then the next year I was playing with them," Halasima said.

Now the 21-year-old Warriors tyro is doing more than just playing, he is starring alongside the heroes of his childhood and taking forward what they started.

"For a young person like me, I've been a fan since that 2017 World Cup and to go from being in the stands cheering to playing alongside people like Jase (Jason Taumalolo), who I look up to, it's an honour. It's a privilege," Halasima said.

Fa'alogo, Manuleleua and Halasima are not just three of rugby league's brightest young stars; they are part of a new generation inheriting a relationship thousands of years in the making.

Samoa creates rugby league magic The passion of the Pacific shines through in Samoa's rugby league team, and the pride the people have is evident on the island.

The history and culture of Tonga and Samoa are proudly separate and distinct but also irrevocably intertwined by centuries of love and blood and faith, first back in the islands and now within the great Pasifika diaspora.

Today, that relationship plays out in all its colour and splendour on the rugby league field, in grand occasions that prove Tonga and Samoa are a people as much as they're a place.

That place can be wherever either nation plays on their own, but it happens the most when they face one another.

Tonga and Samoa can meet anywhere in the world and their people will find them. (Getty Images: Michael Steele )

It's been this way long enough that players like Manuleleua, Fa'alogo, and Halasima grew up on occasions like this and dreamed of being part of it.

"Since the draw came out, I've been thinking of this day. I'm pretty sure every islander around the world can't wait for it," Halasima said.

"This is pretty much finals footy, this is what it's all about."

Manuleleua played in the NRL grand final for Newcastle earlier this month in what was the most important night of his young life — until Sunday.

Tonga and Samoa renew rugby league's greatest international rivalry Between them they have a population smaller than Canberra, but when they meet on Monday morning for a shot at the semi-finals, Tonga and Samoa will be the talk of the rugby league world.

"This will probably be the biggest game I've ever been a part of it. A grand final is pretty big too, but the rivalry between Samoa and Tonga runs deeper than footy," Manuleleua said.

"A few of my mates are Tongan, and we know deep down we have that hatred for each other when it comes to coming up against them.

"As soon as we cross that white line there's no friends, but after those 80 minutes we'll get together, have a beer and everything will be all sweet."

These games can happen anywhere, because while the islands are always home, the Pasifika diaspora has taken them to the world, and another home can happen wherever Samoans or Tongans come together.

Last year's Samoa-Tonga game attracted more than 45,000 people. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Four years ago it happened in Warrington, 12 months ago it happened in Brisbane in front of 45,000 people in a game that felt like the State of Origin of the new century, and on Sunday it will happen in Parramatta.

Manuleleua's parents are coming over from Auckland but his siblings, he jokes, will have to make their own way.

Halasima will have his partner and newborn son there, as well as his parents, sisters, aunts, and uncles coming from New Zealand and up from Melbourne.

For Fa'alogo it will be an even more special day because his father, Eti, has never seen him play for Melbourne or Samoa in the flesh but he will be there on Sunday to watch his youngest become a part of history.

Sunday will mark a special occasion for Fa'alogo. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

"I can't wait. He's done so much for me," Fa'alogo said.

"I just want to give back to him for everything he did, for bringing me over and trying to give me the opportunity for a better life."

The game itself is a coin flip. Tonga is bigger, stronger and more battle-hardened; Samoa is faster and has more strike as proven by their big win last year.

The former is already locked into a semifinal spot, and the latter may well be by kick-off depending on the scoreline between England and Papua New Guinea, but this is a game that is bigger than a World Cup and larger than life.

The fresh faces feel the legacy of the history between the two nations even as they write its latest chapter, and they want to pass it down just as it was passed to them.

Earlier this year, Fa'alogo went back to Si'umu as part of a trip with the Storm.

He went to his old house and his old school and caught up with family.

Wherever he went, children followed. It has been that way ever since he made his NRL debut in 2023 and his Samoan debut a few months later, but Fa'alogo might not ever get used to it.

"I was shocked," Fa'alogo said.

"Back then I was one of them."

World.title: Last drinks called as council prepares to demolish town's only pub
World.content:
More than 10 years after a fire gutted the only pub in the Victorian border town of Robinvale, the remains are to be demolished, just two years shy of the building's 100th birthday.

The Swan Hill Rural City Council in north-west Victoria voted this week to step in and demolish the building, after an independent structural engineering report found the site "critically unsafe".

The Robinvale Hotel, built in 1928, had long been an important tourist drawcard for the region, as well as a place for locals to meet and socialise.

Its demise was a loss to the town's estimated 8,000 residents, who have grown increasingly frustrated at the lack of movement at the site.

An independent heritage assessment carried out last year found it was not practical to repair the building and that it was "highly regrettable" that works to stabilise and weatherproof it were not able to be completed shortly after the fire.

The Robinvale Hotel was extensively damaged by fire and its condition has since deteriorated. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

Time for action

Swan Hill mayor, Stuart King, said council had worked with the building's owner for a very long time.

"But the time has now come for action," he said.

A safety exclusion zone was erected on Perrin Street earlier this year, forcing residents to take a detour.

Cr King said safety was the biggest priority.

"The building is unsafe, it needs to be demolished and so we will take action to have that work done," he said.

The ABC was unable to reach the owner for comment.

The building's heritage report noted its Spanish Mission influences and Canary Island palm trees. (Supplied: State Library Victoria)

Local history

Former local resident Anniemae Goldring launched a petition last year calling for the council to reject the initial demolition application. She spent her formative years at the pub with her nan, a bartender and cleaner.

She said it will be a sombre occasion when the building comes down

"Differences aside, I'm glad that there will be some change for the township," she said.

Ms Goldring remains frustrated that the old pub was not better protected after the fire, and hopes it does not become a vacant lot.

The site was reserved for a hotel when sold in 1924 by Herbert Cuttle, the founder of Robinvale. (Supplied: State Library Victoria)

New opportunities

Just over the border in Euston, NSW, bowling and recreation club chief executive Guy Fielding said he was glad to finally see something happen.

"It's been a long time (coming)," he said.

"The more facilities we have in our community, the better it is for our town and makes it more attractive for not only the locals but for tourists."

He said it would be "fantastic" to see the hotel rebuilt.

"Every town needs a pub," Mr Fielding said.

The hotel was an important focus for local social activity and recreation. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

Cr King said the demolition provided a "fresh start" for the town, which has a diverse population of more than 45 nationalities.

"No town wants a burnt-out, half fallen down, derelict building sitting in the middle of the CBD," he said.

Plans for the site are not known. Cr King said any new building would likely need to meet a number of conditions due to the site's heritage overlay.

An assessment will be done on the bottle shop next door after the demolition to decide its future.

World.title: Live: Federal government launches probe into future of Australia Post
World.content:
The CSIRO has told a Senate estimates hearing that job losses are a part of the organisation's efforts to stay "contemporary and modern".

The science agency has slashed hundreds of jobs in recent years and said it is currently consulting on changes that could affect another 86 full-time jobs in its biosecurity and technology research units.

CEO Doug Hilton said the units could potentially be merged or transferred to make room for reinvestment in other research areas.

"There are opportunities to invest in areas that we think could generate more impact for the community," he said.

The reinvestment process could create 150 new roles, but Mr Hilton said it's not always possible to transfer staff between units.

CSIRO said it generally undergoes an annual review cycle across its research portfolio, which may result in redundancies.

Mr Hilton said this process had occurred for around 20 years.

World.title: Live: ASX set to edge up despite $US500b Alphabet share slump overnight
World.content:
We've had a flurry of central bank meetings this week, with the Bank of Canada lifting its benchmark rate for the first time in three years to 2.5%, while the Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised markets by staying on hold at 2.75% and the US Fed surprised no-one by doing the same to keep rates at 3.75-4%.

Last night it was the turn of the European Central Bank, which stuck with the on-hold club.

"The ECB kept its policy rates unchanged at its October meeting and reiterated a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach to setting policy," writes ANZ's G3 economist Brian Martin. "We continue to think that the ECB will raise the deposit facility rate 25bp [basis points] to 2.75% at its next meeting in December. "The dovish signal in the post-meeting statement that tighter financial conditions, owing to the rise in government bond yields, will weigh on growth and inflation, was offset by President Lagarde retaining a hawkish bias and noting that the Governing Council had considered a rate hike at this meeting. Market expectations for further hikes were ultimately little changed on the day. "Lagarde announced she will depart the ECB in February. Pablo Hernandez de Cos and Klaas Knot are the frontrunners to replace her."

Next cab off the rank is the Bank of Japan later today, with markets pricing just a 2% chance it will hike today, but an 80% chance it will raise rates in December.

Of course, the Reserve Bank of Australia meets next Monday and Tuesday, with markets this morning pricing around a 90% chance of a rate hike being announced at 2:30pm AEDT on November 3.

I had a great chat with Carrington yesterday about the various central bank decisions to that point, of which the most interesting was the RBNZ's hold against 95% market expectations it would raise rates.

World.title: Controversial goldmine subject of new Aboriginal protection application
World.content:
A faction of the Orange Local Aboriginal Land Council (OLALC) has made a fresh bid to halt a billion-dollar New South Wales gold project weeks after the Federal Court threw out a protection order over the same area.

"Concerned members" of the council have submitted a section 9 application, seeking emergency protection for a section of the McPhillamys Gold Project near Blayney, in the state's Central West.

The application, submitted independently of the OLALC, describes the area as being under "imminent threat of desecration".

The concerns of a dozen members were raised in an email seen by the ABC that was sent to the federal Environment Minister Murray Watt this week.

"We respectfully urge you to consider this application as a matter of urgency and take all available lawful steps to protect these Sacred Waters from irreversible harm," the application said.

"The Bila Bula [Belubula] is far more than a River."

" It is a Sacred Songline of particular significance to the Wiradjuri people … [it] is sacred, the giver of life and the lifeblood of our people. "

Regis Resources argued the Commonwealth's decision rendered its goldmine unviable in its current form. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

Former minister's decision overturned

On October 14, Regis Resources successfully challenged the former federal environment minister Tanya Plibersek's decision in August 2024 to grant an Aboriginal protection order over the site in question.

The project had been put on hold and the company said the minister's declaration meant the open-cut operation was "not viable".

The original application was made by Wiradyuri elder Aunty Nyree Reynolds and supported by the Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation (WTOCWAC).

The declaration was made under Section 10 of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act to protect the headwaters and the springs of the Belubula River, where the tailings dam that holds mining waste was to be built.

But a fortnight ago the court ruled Ms Plibersek's decision was "invalid" due to procedural errors with how additional information about the area's cultural significance was assessed.

The Belubula River starts between Bathurst and Orange, stretching through farmland into the mouth of the Lachlan River. (ABC News: Xanthe Gregory)

In considering the fresh application, the environment minister must now decide if he is satisfied that the site is a significant Aboriginal area that is under serious and immediate threat of injury or desecration.

The Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) has confirmed the application is being assessed, and no decision has been made.

OLALC CEO Annette Steele said she expected the department would ask OLAC to respond to the application submitted privately by a group of its members.

"Our response will be guided by the senior Wiradjuri elders who hold cultural authority for the area in question," Ms Steele said.

She said that all Aboriginal people within the OLALC's boundaries were eligible to be members, whether or not they were traditional owners.

"For this reason, cultural heritage matters are typically decided by those people with cultural authority, not the membership as a whole," she said.

"However, LACLs are democratic organisations and members are free to raise any concerns that they may have at meetings or to the board."

Cultural significance disputed

The new application highlights disputes playing out between the region's Aboriginal groups, including disagreements over who holds positions of cultural authority and who has the right to speak for country.

In 2019, before the mine was initially approved, OLALC made a submission in response to the McPhillamys Gold Project environmental impact statement.

It objected to the State Significant Development on the basis that "the proposed project will detrimentally and irreversibly impact the Aboriginal cultural heritage significance of the study area".

The Orange Local Aboriginal Land Council holds a "neutral" position on the mine. (ABC Central West: Xanthe Gregory)

In 2023 OLALC changed its position on the mine from "object" to "neutral".

It has publicly questioned the accuracy and veracity of claims made about the area, including a Dreaming story.

The new section 9 application raises concerns that "Wiradjuri and other First Nations people with cultural connections and responsibilities to this country, were not given a meaningful opportunity to have our say".

"We were not consulted or asked for our views when the change in stance by the executive of the Orange Aboriginal Land Council was announced previously," it said.

In her statement of reasons for granting the protection order in 2024, Ms Plibersek found that development of the mine's tailings dam would cause "irreversible" and "permanent" loss to Aboriginal heritage.

She found the Belubula headwaters were sacred to the Wiradjuri people and their Blue Banded Bee Dreaming Tradition, which narrates how the springs were formed.

The site of the proposed McPhillamys goldmine near Blayney. (ABC Central West: Tim Fookes)

In his federal court judgement delivered in October, Justice James Stellios referenced a brief from DCCEEW that said the declaration was contrary to submissions and advice from OLALC.

The department concluded that "a consensus view amongst all Wiradjuri people is not necessary".

But it was the timing of the revelation about the Dreaming story that would ultimately unravel the legality of Ms Plibersek's declaration.

Justice Stellios's judgement said his decision to overturn the Commonwealth's section 10 was not "about the merits of the claim … whether it's a significant area or under threat of injury or desecration".

He found that "the decision-making process was fundamentally flawed because of the failure to treat the revelation of the Blue Banded Bee Dreaming story as a new application".

During the court case, Regis Resources argued that the Dreaming story did not exist and challenged why it was not raised in the initial protection order application.

In a statement provided to the ABC, Regis Resources said the project had been approved through both the NSW State Significant Development pathway and the federal Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, "each of which considered Aboriginal cultural heritage matters".

The company said it "supports the protection of Aboriginal cultural heritage, through a planning process that provides certainty for all parties".

The ABC understands that a second section 9 application has also been lodged by a different group.

World.title: First Guardian investors dealt another 'utterly devastating' blow
World.content:
Thousands of First Guardian investors have received the devastating news that they may not be able to recover the millions of dollars they invested in the scheme that later collapsed.

Out of nearly half a billion lost in the collapse, liquidators have been able to recover about $8 million, but some $7 million has already gone in liquidation fees.

The corporate regulator ASIC is taking legal action against several players involved in marketing and running the schemes.

The liquidators of Falcon Capital, Ross Blakeley and Paul Harlon of FTI Consulting, said they still couldn't tell 6,000 First Guardian investors how much, if anything, they'll get back from asset sales.

That's because much of the funds appear to have been channelled offshore.

They expect to give a firmer picture after a series of court hearings involving some of the major players in November and December this year.

The directors valued the fund's investments at about $512.8 million.

So far the liquidators said they had recovered $8.02 million, or just 1.56 per cent.

'Utterly devastating'

First Guardian investor Melinda Kee, who also runs the group Save our Super, felt broken after hearing the news.

In November 2023, Ms Kee was given financial advice to switch her super from a retail fund into First Guardian and she lost $400,000 of her retirement savings.

Deep flaws in Australia's $4.3 trillion system exposed The collapses of the First Guardian and Shield schemes have exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia's $4.3 trillion superannuation sector.

She is one of 11,800 investors who collectively lost more than $1 billion in retirement savings after moving their super into First Guardian and the Shield-managed investment schemes, both of which later collapsed.

"It is utterly devastating that after 18 months, just $8 million has been recovered from more than $512 million in investments, while almost $7 million has already been absorbed by liquidation costs," Ms Kee told ABC News.

"Behind these shocking figures are real Australians whose life savings, retirement dreams and financial security have been shattered," she said.

"People living with unimaginable stress and uncertainty, watching their futures slip away while they continue to wait for answers, justice and accountability."

First Guardian investors still at a loss

In December, under a deal with the corporate regulator, Netwealth reimbursed about $100 million to about 1,000 First Guardian investors who invested through its platform.

Investors consider class action over super scam Investors who lost out in a superannuation scam are considering a potential class action.

The settlement raised suggestions two other financial services groups, Diversa and Equity Trustees, through which clients invested in First Guardian, would also do a similar deal with the regulator.

But the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) is pursuing both Diversa and Equity Trustees in court, and they have said they will defend the lawsuits.

Some First Guardian investors are considering a class action to try recover their money.

Others can apply through what's known as the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, but that's capped at $150,000 and some investors lost far more than that.

Money channelled into 'speculative' investments

In their report, liquidators FTI Consulting, sort the investments into three main groups.

First Guardian investors to lose super Six thousand First Guardian investors have been told by the fund's liquidator there may be insufficient funds to pay back the superannuation funds they invested.

These include "written off" or "settled" investments worth about $117.6 million.

Of these, only $3.49 million, about 3 per cent, has come back, and the liquidators don't expect much more, since several of the companies involved are themselves in liquidation.

The second category includes "further recoveries expected" based on investments totalling $50.75 million.

So far $4.53 million (or 8.9 per cent) has come back, but the liquidators said they don't expect to recover the full value.

The third category the liquidators list falls under "uncertain" recoveries worth about $344.5 million.

In this case, nothing has been recovered so far and may never be, as they are mostly investments that the fund's operators channelled into overseas property and "speculative technology start-ups".

FTI Consulting also reports the value of the fees it is taking in the process—payments were about $6.96 million. The biggest items were their legal fees ($3.33 million) and liquidators' remuneration ($3.23 million).

Regulator 'considering all options' to disrupt InterPrac sale

On Thursday, ASIC told Senate Estimates that the corporate regulator is considering all options to disrupt the sale of InterPrac Financial Planning to Bellbird Australia.

Loading...

Of the more than 11,000 investors who pumped more than $1 billion of their retirement savings into the First Guardian and Shield schemes, more than 6,000 were clients of advisers under InterPrac, which is owned by publicly listed company Sequoia.

These 6,000 clients put $680 million into the two funds on the advice of their financial planners who were licensed under InterPrac, and worry that the sale could shrink the pool of money available to compensate them.

ASIC chair Sarah Court told Senate Estimates that the regulator was "considering all options" on whether it could stop InterPrac's attempted sale of its business to Bellbird Australia.

World.title: Empty chairs and a shock promotion as Xi warns purges will continue
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaInside China Empty chairs and a shock promotion as Xi warns purges will continue Lisa Visentin October 30, 2026 — 8:54am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Beijing: In about a year from now, if the weight of expectations holds, Xi Jinping will secure an unprecedented fourth term as China’s paramount leader. Having already abolished term limits in 2018, and purged factional friends and foes alike, Xi is preparing the ground for the loyalists he wants by his side when he extends his reign for another five years at the 21st Party Congress, due in the second half of next year. President Xi Jinping speaks at the “fifth plenum” in Beijing on Thursday. Xie Huanchi/Xinhua via AP One of those loyalists appears to be Zhang Shengmin. The top general, and Xi’s anti-corruption enforcer inside the military, was promoted to the powerful Politburo during a meeting of hundreds of party officials on Thursday. Zhang is just one of two remaining members on the party’s Central Military Commission, China’s supreme military decision-making body. The other is Xi.



Over the past two years, Xi has purged the five other generals he hand-picked to serve on the commission, in a near-total decapitation of the leadership of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). Since 2012, hundreds of other senior and lower-ranked officials throughout the party have been removed or placed under investigation as part of Xi’s campaign to root out corruption and disloyalty. Zhang’s elevation should see him survive through to next year’s party congress, but nothing is guaranteed. General Zhang Shengming during the opening session of the National People’s Congress at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing in March. AP Photo/Andy Wong “It’s hard to read a PLA general’s future these days,” says Shengyu Wang, a researcher of Chinese elite politics at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “It’s a case of now you see me, now you don’t.”



Zhang’s promotion is the first time in decades the party has restocked the Politburo during the middle of a five-year term. The decision was announced after the conclusion of the “fifth plenum” – a gathering of several hundred delegates on the party’s hollowed-out Central Committee, which meets annually to rubber-stamp Xi’s agenda. Related Article Analysis

China relations ‘Nobody is safe’: What Xi’s purges say about his control over China’s military For four days this week, these officials were holed up behind closed doors at a guarded hotel in Beijing to endorse the president’s directives on strict party governance and discipline. Dozens of faces were missing from this year’s cohort. Just 279 delegates were present, an attendance rate of 74 per cent — the lowest on record since the Mao Zedong era, and a sign of the sharpness of Xi’s scythe in his long-running anti-graft campaign.



Among the confirmed fallen were 33 officials, including former Politburo member Ma Xingrui and former senior military leader Zhang Youxia, who were expelled from the party. The message delivered at the plenum, and intended to filter down to millions of party cadres across the country, is that there will be no slowing down. Members of the Politburo standing committee, from left, Li Xi, Cai Qi, Zhao Leji, Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Wang Huning and Ding Xuexiang. Li Xiang/Xinhua via AP “We must maintain a high-pressure stance against corruption,” said a communiqué released after the meeting wrapped on Thursday. The document endorsed the strategy of “not daring to be corrupt, not being able to be corrupt, and not wanting to be corrupt” as key to strengthening party discipline – a slogan that was repeated three times.



For connoisseurs of China’s elite politics, plenums are also an empty chair watching exercise – who’s in, who’s out and who’s been promoted – with extra attention paid this year in the run-up to the big show next year. Related Article China relations Binoculars over the border: The Chinese town visited by Kim Jong-un “This is a very interesting time for China watchers to see who is actually still sitting in the meeting hall, which means they are still safe at this moment,” says Mingda Qiu, senior analyst of Eurasia Group’s China practice. “And if they disappear or if they are not attending the plenum without an explanation, then that person might be in trouble.” Analysts will now study, frame by frame, the shots of the meeting hall aired by China’s state broadcaster CCTV to gauge who was missing and who might be under investigation.



For months, Xi has been sketching out his vision for party building and governance, signalling his frustration that directives from Beijing were not filtering down and duly obeyed by provincial officials. Related Article Inside China ‘Not accepted. Not forgiven!!’ : French superstar’s ‘dictator Mao’ meme ignites fury in China In a speech published this month, he complained about “two-faced people” who loudly commit to major party decisions “while inwardly resisting, acting arbitrarily, and even disobeying order”. They must be exposed and eliminated, he warned. China expert Neil Thomas and his colleagues at the Asia Society have likened Xi to Leninist Logan Roy, the patriarch in HBO hit series Succession. “He presides over an enormous enterprise, exercises commanding authority, and remains perpetually disappointed by the people expected to carry out his wishes,” they said in a recent paper.



Xi has made a point of ensuring he has no successor, a move designed to firm his grip on power. But it’s left him with another challenge: grooming a new generation of trusted cadres, while filling vacancies in senior leadership positions from a shrinking talent pool.
