World.title: Chris Minns loses first frontbencher as David Harris announces exit before NSW election
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Chris Minns loses first frontbencher as David Harris announces exit before NSW election Jessica McSweeney October 30, 2026 — 8:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The state’s racing minister David Harris will retire at the next election in March, leaving NSW Labor with a fight to retain his Central Coast seat against a likely significant challenge from One Nation. Labor had delayed opening preselection in the seat of Wyong as Harris weighed up his options. In a statement early on Friday morning, Harris confirmed he would retire after 16 years as an MP. NSW Gaming and Racing Minister David Harris. Nikki Short Harris currently holds the gaming and racing, veterans and Aboriginal affairs and treaty portfolios. The minister said he would continue in his current ministerial roles until the March 13 poll. “Before entering the NSW parliament I spent 23 years in public education as a teacher, executive and principal, working to shape the futures of local children,” Harris said.



“I hope the next Labor candidate shares my passion for education as I have found that is the lifeblood of our community.” Related Article Exclusive

NSW Votes Labor warns MPs party could lose a dozen seats at March election Harris thanked Premier Chris Minns for his support while navigating “challenging yet essential reforms” and said they tackled “controversial issues”. The state Labor government faced a revolt from rank and file party members over pokies reforms, with Harris ultimately backing a motion to force the party into a stronger stance against the machines at this year’s state conference. The state government isn’t bound to the motions passed at the conference, and the government is yet to implement the reforms.



Harris’ retirement makes him the first of Minns’ frontbenchers to quit politics before the March state election, which NSW Labor is treating as a fight against right-wing populist party One Nation rather than the Coalition. Related Article NSW State Parliament Kellie Sloane loses second senior frontbencher in as many weeks NSW Labor officials have warned MPs of a worst-case scenario in which the party could lose more than a dozen seats, as part of closed-door briefings organised by party headquarters. MPs have been warned it is possible Labor could lose seats in the Hunter, Central Coast, south-west Sydney and southern NSW. Regional MPs have said they expect One Nation, rather than the Liberals or Nationals, to be their main competition. Liberal leader Kellie Sloane, meanwhile, has lost a slew of MPs jumping ship before March.



Senior frontbenchers James Griffin and Alister Henskens have both announced they will not recontest their seats in Manly and Wahroonga, and earlier this month the MP for Kellyville, Ray Williams, who triggered the Operation Rosny ICAC inquiry when he aired allegations about his own party in a speech to parliament, also announced his political retirement. Badgerys Creek MP Tanya Davies has also resigned. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: ASX set to rise, Alphabet’s historic plunge weighs down Wall Street; ECB chief Lagarde to exit
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Alphabet’s historic plunge weighs down Wall Street; ECB chief Lagarde to exit Stan Choe Updated October 30, 2026 — 8:44am ,first published 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A historic drop for Alphabet’s stock dragged the US market lower after the company behind Google and YouTube reported weaker growth for the summer than analysts expected. The report underscored worries about whether all its huge investments in artificial-intelligence technology will pay off. The S&P 500 fell 0.3 per cent for its first loss in four days, even though the wide majority of stocks rose within the index and across Wall Street. The Nasdaq composite tumbled 1.4 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132 points, or 0.3 per cent. Alphabet’s drop sent Wall Street’s benchmark index into the red. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.59am AEDT pointing to a gain of 32 points or 0.4 per cent at the open. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was 0.3 per cent lower at US70.34¢. Alphabet is one of the most influential stocks on Wall Street because it’s one of the largest, and the Class A shares of its stock fell 12.6 per cent for their worst day since they began trading more than 20 years ago. The tech giant had been under pressure to at least meet analysts’ expectations for growth amid concerns about how much it’s spending to invest in AI.



Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve ‘Politics played no role’: Fed hits pause button ahead of midterms Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Alphabet said that it burned through more cash during the latest quarter, according to a measure called free cash flow, after its purchases of property and equipment topped $51 billion. Worries are weighing on the entire AI industry following a frenzy to build data centres and fill them with AI chips. Not only are concerns high that the AI revolution may not produce as much profit and productivity as hoped, future spending on data centres is also under pressure because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to buy more chips. Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current fourth quarter that encompasses the critical holiday shopping period after delivering fiscal third-quarter results after the closing bell that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations. The Seattle-based tech giant, however, posted strong sales growth in its prominent cloud computing unit. Sales in its so-called Amazon Web Services rose 39.3 per cent during the latest quarter ended September 30, higher than the 37 per cent clip in the previous quarter. It marked the fastest growth rate in nearly five years, the company said.



Still, shares were down more than 5 per cent in after-market trading when the results were released as investors focused on the core business. Alphabet’s drop overshadowed what would have otherwise been a good day for the US stock market. Four out of every five stocks within the S&P 500 climbed, and the index would have been higher if not for Alphabet. Many companies rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected, including KLA Corp. The company, whose equipment helps make semiconductors, rose 5.5 per cent. Eli Lilly climbed 6.6 per cent , Mastercard rose 4.2 per cent and Merck added 3.8 per cent. DoorDash rose 5.6 per cent after saying it agreed to buy Instacart in a deal valuing it at $US17 billion. DoorDash also reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings steamed 13.4 per cent higher after likewise topping expectations for summertime profit and revenue. It benefited from cruisers spending more money once aboard ships than the company expected, among other things. ECB chief Christine Lagarde will resign in February, nine months before the end of her term. AP Expectations are high for profit growth broadly across US companies. That’s what allowed the S&P 500 to set its record earlier this month despite high interest rates and other worries weighing on the stock market. All told, the S&P 500 fell 23.59 points to 7,720.39 Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132.54 to 52,342.56, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 365.13 to 26,184.72. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased following several mixed reports on the US economy.



The overall economy’s growth may have accelerated more during the summer than economists expected, thanks to spending by US consumers and businesses investing in AI, according to a preliminary report. But Americans’ growth in incomes was weaker in September than economists expected, while a measure of inflation worsened. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, meanwhile, which could indicate few layoffs across the country. Following the jumble of reports, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94 per cent from 5.05 per cent late Wednesday. It’s been generally pulling back since it topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002. Helping to drag yields lower on Thursday was a drop in oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 0.8 per cent to $US110.80. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe after the European Central Bank held interest rates steady on the continent. The bank’s president, Christine Lagarde, also said she will resign in February, nine months before the end of her term.

World.title: The ‘Chinese spy’ who sparked panic at the White House
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence. A top executive at a Singapore-based data centre company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence chips to China. And now US officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset, funnelling information to Beijing. Jensen Huang with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, or Huang Le, at a party in Taipei in June 2024. NYT But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO. For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in AI. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Jensen Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution as well as an influential ally of President Donald Trump, set off alarms at the White House. Roughly a year ago, Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China. This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts.



Related Article AI Toilet paper, recording devices and one-way tickets: Inside the OpenAI spying case that has rattled America US officials already suspected that Alice Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced AI chips. But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities, including that Jensen Huang had insights into Trump’s thinking on an issue of vital importance to both nations, one likely to come up when the president visits China next month. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the United States has maintained in developing cutting-edge AI models. Jensen Huang has not received a defensive briefing, warnings sometimes given to Americans who are being targeted by foreign intelligence services, people briefed on the surveillance said. The surveillance of Alice Huang continues, they said, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips. Nvidia said the company that employed her, Megaspeed, was like any other regional customer and that it had previously investigated and debunked claims the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” The close relationship between the president and Jensen Huang has impeded efforts to clamp down on Nvidia’s chip sales abroad, current and former US officials said. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson



Nvidia is “confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” Rizzo said. Customers like Megaspeed, he added, “receive ordinary business information — not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.” The White House, the CIA and the National Security Agency all declined to comment. In a statement to The New York Times, Megaspeed said its “current leadership” takes the matter “extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations.” It added that “outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the US government that we are fully committed to cooperating.” Alice Huang did not respond to requests for comment. It is not clear how closely she is still connected to Megaspeed. A person familiar with Megaspeed’s operations said she had become less active in the company in the wake of the US investigations. Asked about the American conclusion that Alice Huang has been collecting intelligence on behalf of Beijing, Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said the United States was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against China. When Trump was initially briefed on the intelligence last year, US officials did not believe the Nvidia executive knew that Alice Huang was gathering information for the Chinese. It is unclear whether intelligence officials have since updated their assessment, but some senior officials inside the Trump administration doubt that Jensen Huang could have remained unaware of what they had concluded was her intelligence-gathering role for China. Questions about whether Megaspeed was providing AI chips to China became public through articles published last year by the Times and Bloomberg News. Related Article Opinion

AI ‘Bold, but sane’? The future of AI is riding on Anthropic’s float Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist



Jensen Huang has successfully lobbied the administration during Trump’s second term to loosen regulations on AI companies and roll back tighter restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China. He also negotiated a deal with Trump that allowed the US government to take a 25 per cent stake of certain Nvidia chips that the government allows to be sold to China. The close relationship between the president and Jensen Huang has impeded efforts to clamp down on Nvidia’s chip sales abroad, current and former US officials said. They described some investigations and proposed trade sanctions involving China or Nvidia as having ground to a halt within the Commerce Department, the agency in charge of regulating chip exports. Nvidia has said that it complies with the law and that there is no evidence of its chips being smuggled to China. Rizzo said China’s government has “blocked US AI chips, protecting its own industry.” Many questions about the situation remain unanswered, at least publicly. It is unclear whether concerns about protecting the surveillance played a role in the decision not to inform Jensen Huang. Telling him could have alerted Alice Huang that she was being watched, which is a common reason intelligence officials hesitate to give defensive briefings. It could not be determined which intelligence agency or agencies have been involved in monitoring Alice Huang, or what prompted them to start. It is also not clear under what circumstances she began gathering information for Beijing, what information she passed along or its value to China. A large data centre under construction by Megaspeed in Malaysia. The US government has been investigating the company since late 2024. NYT



The previous reporting about Alice Huang by the Times described her meteoric and somewhat mysterious rise. A Chinese businessperson and investor, she eventually became a top official with Megaspeed, which the Commerce Department, toward the end of the Biden administration, began to suspect was helping China evade US prohibitions and gain access to the computing power of Nvidia chips. The US government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data centre in Malaysia and found the site to be suspicious. The Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes, suggesting it was being shipped in or out rather than installed there. Singapore has conducted its own investigation into Megaspeed. In 2025, Singaporean authorities brought Alice Huang in for questioning, but subsequently released her. The Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed was handed over this year to the Justice Department, administration officials said. Megaspeed is among the firms in Southeast Asia that buy chips to build data centres and then rent their computing power to companies in China. Megaspeed is essentially a middle man. It has bought Nvidia chips from the American arm of Inspur, a Chinese server maker. The US has blacklisted Inspur’s parent company for funnelling technology to the Chinese military, though the US firm remains free of sanctions. Megaspeed has then provided that computing power to Alibaba and other Chinese companies. US officials believe the firm is one piece of a sprawling international effort by Chinese companies to access the chips needed to build and run AI. Investigators suspect that some Nvidia chips acquired by Megaspeed are also finding their way illegally into China.

World.title: ‘Rest in the heavens, Captain’: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86
World.content:
Updated CultureCelebrityVale ‘Rest in the heavens, Captain’: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86 Kayla Olaya and Nell Geraets October 30, 2026 — 7:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Patrick Stewart, the classically trained stage actor who scaled the Shakespearean canon and added gravitas to a Star Trek franchise and X-Men films, has died. He was 86. Stewart, who was knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions to drama, died at his Los Angeles home after being diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, according to a statement on his X account. Patrick Stewart, best known for his Star Trek performances and pictured in the backyard of his Los Angeles home in 2023, died on Wednesday (Thursday AEDT). “We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife, Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” it said. His death comes just days after Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, in the original Star Trek series and seven subsequent feature films, died at the age of 90.



While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the X-Men and Star Trek: The Next Generation series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career on stage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of A Christmas Carol and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land and Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot in repertoire with his good friend Sir Ian McKellen. Stewart became an actor at 18, gaining acclaim on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company beginning in the 1960s. He spent decades working on stage and performing various roles in UK TV productions. Patrick Stewart (front row, second from left) with the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation. But it wasn’t until he was cast in Star Trek: The Next Generation from 1987 to 1994 that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s.



He leaves behind his wife Sunny Ozell and two adult children – son Daniel Stewart and daughter Sophie Stewart, whom he shares with his first wife, Sheila Falconer. William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk alongside Stewart in Star Trek: Generations (1994), honoured the renowned performer on social media as “a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor”. “What a heartbreaking week it has been,” Shatner wrote on Facebook. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed.” Fellow Star Trek actor George Takei, who played Sulu in the original 1960s TV series, paid tribute on social media dedicated to fans across the world, “mourning the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend”. “As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before,” Takei wrote on Bluesky. “He inspired a whole next generation of stargazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”



Australian star Hugh Jackman also paid tribute to Stewart, noting the time they spent together filming the X-Men films. “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days,” the Wolverine star wrote on Instagram, paired with two photos of the actors arm-in-arm. Born in 1940 in the Yorkshire town of Mirfield in England’s north in coal-mining country, Stewart grew up in the era of ration ­coupons, lamplighters in the streets and once-a-week baths in a zinc tub in front of the coal stove, he told Good Weekend in 2023. Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation. MEDIANET



When his father was demobbed from the army following the end of World War II when he was five, Stewart recalls him returning hardened and abusive towards his wife after bouts of drinking. Books and then films became an escape for the young Stewart. In his teenage years, he took acting courses, threw himself into amateur theatre and, at 17, won a place at the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theatre School. The local council gave him a full scholarship. Related Article Good Weekend ‘I am just sad a lot of the time’: A former Star Trek captain on his life on earth Stewart went on to marry choreographer Sheila Falconer, have two ­children and a 20-year stage, film and TV career – until he was randomly summoned to the United States to meet Gene Roddenberry, the creator of Star Trek. A producer had spotted Stewart lecturing American students on William Shakespeare and suggested him for a role in a new series of the ­franchise, The Next Generation. According to Stewart, the meeting didn’t go well, and Roddenberry was not a fan.



So it came as a shock when he was recalled to audition for Star Trek: The Next Generation and then cast as captain of the Enterprise. “During ­filming [Roddenberry] would come down from his comfortable ­office and sit in his director’s chair, arms folded, ­frowning at me and clearly thinking, ‘But I didn’t want him; what’s he doing in my show?’” Stewart told Good Weekend. The network salary also changed things for him. “The cast were all buying cars: Mercedes and Audis. I bought a Honda Prelude, to the dismay of my fellow ­actors. [Co-star] Jonathan Frakes accused me of having a ­poverty mentality.” Actors James McAvoy, Patrick Stewart, and Hugh Jackman from X-Men: Days Of Future Past, in 2014. Getty



Head of Marvel Studios Kevin Feige reminisced on the first time he met Stewart while on the set of the first X-Men film, describing it as a moment he will never forget. “After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe – and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas. Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humour,” the studio head said in a statement shared with The Hollywood Reporter. “It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him … His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.” Seth MacFarlane, who worked with Stewart on comedy productions like Family Guy, Ted and American Dad!, said he was a rare actor who “could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful”.



“I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day one of a new film,” MacFarlane wrote on Instagram. “He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, ‘Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed’. We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet.” Stewart also acted in Star Trek: Picard, a sequel to The Next Generation, featuring Picard in his post-Starfleet retirement and drawing in characters from other Star Trek shows, notably Seven of Nine (Jeri Ryan) from Star Trek: Voyager. “I will never say goodbye to Jean-Luc Picard, to his ideals, to his struggles to create an honest world, an unprejudiced world. That will always remain inside me in the same way that other roles have,” Stewart told this masthead in 2022. With Reuters, AP

World.title: Empty chairs and a shock promotion as Xi warns purges will continue
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaInside China Empty chairs and a shock promotion as Xi warns purges will continue Lisa Visentin October 30, 2026 — 8:54am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Beijing: In about a year from now, if the weight of expectations holds, Xi Jinping will secure an unprecedented fourth term as China’s paramount leader. Having already abolished term limits in 2018, and purged factional friends and foes alike, Xi is preparing the ground for the loyalists he wants by his side when he extends his reign for another five years at the 21st Party Congress, due in the second half of next year. President Xi Jinping speaks at the “fifth plenum” in Beijing on Thursday. Xie Huanchi/Xinhua via AP One of those loyalists appears to be Zhang Shengmin. The top general, and Xi’s anti-corruption enforcer inside the military, was promoted to the powerful Politburo during a meeting of hundreds of party officials on Thursday. Zhang is just one of two remaining members on the party’s Central Military Commission, China’s supreme military decision-making body. The other is Xi.



Over the past two years, Xi has purged the five other generals he hand-picked to serve on the commission, in a near-total decapitation of the leadership of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). Since 2012, hundreds of other senior and lower-ranked officials throughout the party have been removed or placed under investigation as part of Xi’s campaign to root out corruption and disloyalty. Zhang’s elevation should see him survive through to next year’s party congress, but nothing is guaranteed. General Zhang Shengming during the opening session of the National People’s Congress at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing in March. AP Photo/Andy Wong “It’s hard to read a PLA general’s future these days,” says Shengyu Wang, a researcher of Chinese elite politics at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “It’s a case of now you see me, now you don’t.”



Zhang’s promotion is the first time in decades the party has restocked the Politburo during the middle of a five-year term. The decision was announced after the conclusion of the “fifth plenum” – a gathering of several hundred delegates on the party’s hollowed-out Central Committee, which meets annually to rubber-stamp Xi’s agenda. Related Article Analysis

China relations ‘Nobody is safe’: What Xi’s purges say about his control over China’s military For four days this week, these officials were holed up behind closed doors at a guarded hotel in Beijing to endorse the president’s directives on strict party governance and discipline. Dozens of faces were missing from this year’s cohort. Just 279 delegates were present, an attendance rate of 74 per cent — the lowest on record since the Mao Zedong era, and a sign of the sharpness of Xi’s scythe in his long-running anti-graft campaign.



Among the confirmed fallen were 33 officials, including former Politburo member Ma Xingrui and former senior military leader Zhang Youxia, who were expelled from the party. The message delivered at the plenum, and intended to filter down to millions of party cadres across the country, is that there will be no slowing down. Members of the Politburo standing committee, from left, Li Xi, Cai Qi, Zhao Leji, Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Wang Huning and Ding Xuexiang. Li Xiang/Xinhua via AP “We must maintain a high-pressure stance against corruption,” said a communiqué released after the meeting wrapped on Thursday. The document endorsed the strategy of “not daring to be corrupt, not being able to be corrupt, and not wanting to be corrupt” as key to strengthening party discipline – a slogan that was repeated three times.



For connoisseurs of China’s elite politics, plenums are also an empty chair watching exercise – who’s in, who’s out and who’s been promoted – with extra attention paid this year in the run-up to the big show next year. Related Article China relations Binoculars over the border: The Chinese town visited by Kim Jong-un “This is a very interesting time for China watchers to see who is actually still sitting in the meeting hall, which means they are still safe at this moment,” says Mingda Qiu, senior analyst of Eurasia Group’s China practice. “And if they disappear or if they are not attending the plenum without an explanation, then that person might be in trouble.” Analysts will now study, frame by frame, the shots of the meeting hall aired by China’s state broadcaster CCTV to gauge who was missing and who might be under investigation.



For months, Xi has been sketching out his vision for party building and governance, signalling his frustration that directives from Beijing were not filtering down and duly obeyed by provincial officials. Related Article Inside China ‘Not accepted. Not forgiven!!’ : French superstar’s ‘dictator Mao’ meme ignites fury in China In a speech published this month, he complained about “two-faced people” who loudly commit to major party decisions “while inwardly resisting, acting arbitrarily, and even disobeying order”. They must be exposed and eliminated, he warned. China expert Neil Thomas and his colleagues at the Asia Society have likened Xi to Leninist Logan Roy, the patriarch in HBO hit series Succession. “He presides over an enormous enterprise, exercises commanding authority, and remains perpetually disappointed by the people expected to carry out his wishes,” they said in a recent paper.



Xi has made a point of ensuring he has no successor, a move designed to firm his grip on power. But it’s left him with another challenge: grooming a new generation of trusted cadres, while filling vacancies in senior leadership positions from a shrinking talent pool. World.title: Chris Minns loses first frontbencher as David Harris announces exit before NSW election
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Chris Minns loses first frontbencher as David Harris announces exit before NSW election Jessica McSweeney October 30, 2026 — 8:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The state’s racing minister David Harris will retire at the next election in March, leaving NSW Labor with a fight to retain his Central Coast seat against a likely significant challenge from One Nation. Labor had delayed opening preselection in the seat of Wyong as Harris weighed up his options. In a statement early on Friday morning, Harris confirmed he would retire after 16 years as an MP. NSW Gaming and Racing Minister David Harris. Nikki Short Harris currently holds the gaming and racing, veterans and Aboriginal affairs and treaty portfolios. The minister said he would continue in his current ministerial roles until the March 13 poll. “Before entering the NSW parliament I spent 23 years in public education as a teacher, executive and principal, working to shape the futures of local children,” Harris said.



“I hope the next Labor candidate shares my passion for education as I have found that is the lifeblood of our community.” Related Article Exclusive

NSW Votes Labor warns MPs party could lose a dozen seats at March election Harris thanked Premier Chris Minns for his support while navigating “challenging yet essential reforms” and said they tackled “controversial issues”. The state Labor government faced a revolt from rank and file party members over pokies reforms, with Harris ultimately backing a motion to force the party into a stronger stance against the machines at this year’s state conference. The state government isn’t bound to the motions passed at the conference, and the government is yet to implement the reforms.



Harris’ retirement makes him the first of Minns’ frontbenchers to quit politics before the March state election, which NSW Labor is treating as a fight against right-wing populist party One Nation rather than the Coalition. Related Article NSW State Parliament Kellie Sloane loses second senior frontbencher in as many weeks NSW Labor officials have warned MPs of a worst-case scenario in which the party could lose more than a dozen seats, as part of closed-door briefings organised by party headquarters. MPs have been warned it is possible Labor could lose seats in the Hunter, Central Coast, south-west Sydney and southern NSW. Regional MPs have said they expect One Nation, rather than the Liberals or Nationals, to be their main competition. Liberal leader Kellie Sloane, meanwhile, has lost a slew of MPs jumping ship before March.



Senior frontbenchers James Griffin and Alister Henskens have both announced they will not recontest their seats in Manly and Wahroonga, and earlier this month the MP for Kellyville, Ray Williams, who triggered the Operation Rosny ICAC inquiry when he aired allegations about his own party in a speech to parliament, also announced his political retirement. Badgerys Creek MP Tanya Davies has also resigned. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Alphabet’s historic plunge weighs down Wall Street; ECB chief Lagarde to exit Stan Choe Updated October 30, 2026 — 8:44am ,first published 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A historic drop for Alphabet’s stock dragged the US market lower after the company behind Google and YouTube reported weaker growth for the summer than analysts expected. The report underscored worries about whether all its huge investments in artificial-intelligence technology will pay off. The S&P 500 fell 0.3 per cent for its first loss in four days, even though the wide majority of stocks rose within the index and across Wall Street. The Nasdaq composite tumbled 1.4 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132 points, or 0.3 per cent. Alphabet’s drop sent Wall Street’s benchmark index into the red. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.59am AEDT pointing to a gain of 32 points or 0.4 per cent at the open. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was 0.3 per cent lower at US70.34¢. Alphabet is one of the most influential stocks on Wall Street because it’s one of the largest, and the Class A shares of its stock fell 12.6 per cent for their worst day since they began trading more than 20 years ago. The tech giant had been under pressure to at least meet analysts’ expectations for growth amid concerns about how much it’s spending to invest in AI.



Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve ‘Politics played no role’: Fed hits pause button ahead of midterms Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Alphabet said that it burned through more cash during the latest quarter, according to a measure called free cash flow, after its purchases of property and equipment topped $51 billion. Worries are weighing on the entire AI industry following a frenzy to build data centres and fill them with AI chips. Not only are concerns high that the AI revolution may not produce as much profit and productivity as hoped, future spending on data centres is also under pressure because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to buy more chips. Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current fourth quarter that encompasses the critical holiday shopping period after delivering fiscal third-quarter results after the closing bell that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations. The Seattle-based tech giant, however, posted strong sales growth in its prominent cloud computing unit. Sales in its so-called Amazon Web Services rose 39.3 per cent during the latest quarter ended September 30, higher than the 37 per cent clip in the previous quarter. It marked the fastest growth rate in nearly five years, the company said.



Still, shares were down more than 5 per cent in after-market trading when the results were released as investors focused on the core business. Alphabet’s drop overshadowed what would have otherwise been a good day for the US stock market. Four out of every five stocks within the S&P 500 climbed, and the index would have been higher if not for Alphabet. Many companies rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected, including KLA Corp. The company, whose equipment helps make semiconductors, rose 5.5 per cent. Eli Lilly climbed 6.6 per cent , Mastercard rose 4.2 per cent and Merck added 3.8 per cent. DoorDash rose 5.6 per cent after saying it agreed to buy Instacart in a deal valuing it at $US17 billion. DoorDash also reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings steamed 13.4 per cent higher after likewise topping expectations for summertime profit and revenue. It benefited from cruisers spending more money once aboard ships than the company expected, among other things. ECB chief Christine Lagarde will resign in February, nine months before the end of her term. AP Expectations are high for profit growth broadly across US companies. That’s what allowed the S&P 500 to set its record earlier this month despite high interest rates and other worries weighing on the stock market. All told, the S&P 500 fell 23.59 points to 7,720.39 Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132.54 to 52,342.56, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 365.13 to 26,184.72. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased following several mixed reports on the US economy.



The overall economy’s growth may have accelerated more during the summer than economists expected, thanks to spending by US consumers and businesses investing in AI, according to a preliminary report. But Americans’ growth in incomes was weaker in September than economists expected, while a measure of inflation worsened. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, meanwhile, which could indicate few layoffs across the country. Following the jumble of reports, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94 per cent from 5.05 per cent late Wednesday. It’s been generally pulling back since it topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002. Helping to drag yields lower on Thursday was a drop in oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 0.8 per cent to $US110.80. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe after the European Central Bank held interest rates steady on the continent. The bank’s president, Christine Lagarde, also said she will resign in February, nine months before the end of her term.

World.title: The ‘Chinese spy’ who sparked panic at the White House
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence. A top executive at a Singapore-based data centre company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence chips to China. And now US officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset, funnelling information to Beijing. Jensen Huang with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, or Huang Le, at a party in Taipei in June 2024. NYT But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO. For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in AI. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Jensen Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution as well as an influential ally of President Donald Trump, set off alarms at the White House. Roughly a year ago, Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China. This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts.



Related Article AI Toilet paper, recording devices and one-way tickets: Inside the OpenAI spying case that has rattled America US officials already suspected that Alice Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced AI chips. But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities, including that Jensen Huang had insights into Trump’s thinking on an issue of vital importance to both nations, one likely to come up when the president visits China next month. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the United States has maintained in developing cutting-edge AI models. Jensen Huang has not received a defensive briefing, warnings sometimes given to Americans who are being targeted by foreign intelligence services, people briefed on the surveillance said. The surveillance of Alice Huang continues, they said, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips. Nvidia said the company that employed her, Megaspeed, was like any other regional customer and that it had previously investigated and debunked claims the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” The close relationship between the president and Jensen Huang has impeded efforts to clamp down on Nvidia’s chip sales abroad, current and former US officials said. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson



Nvidia is “confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” Rizzo said. Customers like Megaspeed, he added, “receive ordinary business information — not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.” The White House, the CIA and the National Security Agency all declined to comment. In a statement to The New York Times, Megaspeed said its “current leadership” takes the matter “extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations.” It added that “outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the US government that we are fully committed to cooperating.” Alice Huang did not respond to requests for comment. It is not clear how closely she is still connected to Megaspeed. A person familiar with Megaspeed’s operations said she had become less active in the company in the wake of the US investigations. Asked about the American conclusion that Alice Huang has been collecting intelligence on behalf of Beijing, Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said the United States was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against China. When Trump was initially briefed on the intelligence last year, US officials did not believe the Nvidia executive knew that Alice Huang was gathering information for the Chinese. It is unclear whether intelligence officials have since updated their assessment, but some senior officials inside the Trump administration doubt that Jensen Huang could have remained unaware of what they had concluded was her intelligence-gathering role for China. Questions about whether Megaspeed was providing AI chips to China became public through articles published last year by the Times and Bloomberg News. Related Article Opinion

AI ‘Bold, but sane’? The future of AI is riding on Anthropic’s float Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist



Jensen Huang has successfully lobbied the administration during Trump’s second term to loosen regulations on AI companies and roll back tighter restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China. He also negotiated a deal with Trump that allowed the US government to take a 25 per cent stake of certain Nvidia chips that the government allows to be sold to China. The close relationship between the president and Jensen Huang has impeded efforts to clamp down on Nvidia’s chip sales abroad, current and former US officials said. They described some investigations and proposed trade sanctions involving China or Nvidia as having ground to a halt within the Commerce Department, the agency in charge of regulating chip exports. Nvidia has said that it complies with the law and that there is no evidence of its chips being smuggled to China. Rizzo said China’s government has “blocked US AI chips, protecting its own industry.” Many questions about the situation remain unanswered, at least publicly. It is unclear whether concerns about protecting the surveillance played a role in the decision not to inform Jensen Huang. Telling him could have alerted Alice Huang that she was being watched, which is a common reason intelligence officials hesitate to give defensive briefings. It could not be determined which intelligence agency or agencies have been involved in monitoring Alice Huang, or what prompted them to start. It is also not clear under what circumstances she began gathering information for Beijing, what information she passed along or its value to China. A large data centre under construction by Megaspeed in Malaysia. The US government has been investigating the company since late 2024. NYT



The previous reporting about Alice Huang by the Times described her meteoric and somewhat mysterious rise. A Chinese businessperson and investor, she eventually became a top official with Megaspeed, which the Commerce Department, toward the end of the Biden administration, began to suspect was helping China evade US prohibitions and gain access to the computing power of Nvidia chips. The US government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data centre in Malaysia and found the site to be suspicious. The Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes, suggesting it was being shipped in or out rather than installed there. Singapore has conducted its own investigation into Megaspeed. In 2025, Singaporean authorities brought Alice Huang in for questioning, but subsequently released her. The Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed was handed over this year to the Justice Department, administration officials said. Megaspeed is among the firms in Southeast Asia that buy chips to build data centres and then rent their computing power to companies in China. Megaspeed is essentially a middle man. It has bought Nvidia chips from the American arm of Inspur, a Chinese server maker. The US has blacklisted Inspur’s parent company for funnelling technology to the Chinese military, though the US firm remains free of sanctions. Megaspeed has then provided that computing power to Alibaba and other Chinese companies. US officials believe the firm is one piece of a sprawling international effort by Chinese companies to access the chips needed to build and run AI. Investigators suspect that some Nvidia chips acquired by Megaspeed are also finding their way illegally into China.

World.title: ‘Rest in the heavens, Captain’: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86
World.content:
Updated CultureCelebrityVale ‘Rest in the heavens, Captain’: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86 Kayla Olaya and Nell Geraets October 30, 2026 — 7:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Patrick Stewart, the classically trained stage actor who scaled the Shakespearean canon and added gravitas to a Star Trek franchise and X-Men films, has died. He was 86. Stewart, who was knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions to drama, died at his Los Angeles home after being diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, according to a statement on his X account. Patrick Stewart, best known for his Star Trek performances and pictured in the backyard of his Los Angeles home in 2023, died on Wednesday (Thursday AEDT). “We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife, Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” it said. His death comes just days after Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, in the original Star Trek series and seven subsequent feature films, died at the age of 90.



While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the X-Men and Star Trek: The Next Generation series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career on stage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of A Christmas Carol and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land and Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot in repertoire with his good friend Sir Ian McKellen. Stewart became an actor at 18, gaining acclaim on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company beginning in the 1960s. He spent decades working on stage and performing various roles in UK TV productions. Patrick Stewart (front row, second from left) with the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation. But it wasn’t until he was cast in Star Trek: The Next Generation from 1987 to 1994 that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s.



He leaves behind his wife Sunny Ozell and two adult children – son Daniel Stewart and daughter Sophie Stewart, whom he shares with his first wife, Sheila Falconer. William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk alongside Stewart in Star Trek: Generations (1994), honoured the renowned performer on social media as “a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor”. “What a heartbreaking week it has been,” Shatner wrote on Facebook. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed.” Fellow Star Trek actor George Takei, who played Sulu in the original 1960s TV series, paid tribute on social media dedicated to fans across the world, “mourning the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend”. “As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before,” Takei wrote on Bluesky. “He inspired a whole next generation of stargazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”



Australian star Hugh Jackman also paid tribute to Stewart, noting the time they spent together filming the X-Men films. “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days,” the Wolverine star wrote on Instagram, paired with two photos of the actors arm-in-arm. Born in 1940 in the Yorkshire town of Mirfield in England’s north in coal-mining country, Stewart grew up in the era of ration ­coupons, lamplighters in the streets and once-a-week baths in a zinc tub in front of the coal stove, he told Good Weekend in 2023. Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation. MEDIANET



When his father was demobbed from the army following the end of World War II when he was five, Stewart recalls him returning hardened and abusive towards his wife after bouts of drinking. Books and then films became an escape for the young Stewart. In his teenage years, he took acting courses, threw himself into amateur theatre and, at 17, won a place at the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theatre School. The local council gave him a full scholarship. Related Article Good Weekend ‘I am just sad a lot of the time’: A former Star Trek captain on his life on earth Stewart went on to marry choreographer Sheila Falconer, have two ­children and a 20-year stage, film and TV career – until he was randomly summoned to the United States to meet Gene Roddenberry, the creator of Star Trek. A producer had spotted Stewart lecturing American students on William Shakespeare and suggested him for a role in a new series of the ­franchise, The Next Generation. According to Stewart, the meeting didn’t go well, and Roddenberry was not a fan.



So it came as a shock when he was recalled to audition for Star Trek: The Next Generation and then cast as captain of the Enterprise. “During ­filming [Roddenberry] would come down from his comfortable ­office and sit in his director’s chair, arms folded, ­frowning at me and clearly thinking, ‘But I didn’t want him; what’s he doing in my show?’” Stewart told Good Weekend. The network salary also changed things for him. “The cast were all buying cars: Mercedes and Audis. I bought a Honda Prelude, to the dismay of my fellow ­actors. [Co-star] Jonathan Frakes accused me of having a ­poverty mentality.” Actors James McAvoy, Patrick Stewart, and Hugh Jackman from X-Men: Days Of Future Past, in 2014. Getty



Head of Marvel Studios Kevin Feige reminisced on the first time he met Stewart while on the set of the first X-Men film, describing it as a moment he will never forget. “After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe – and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas. Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humour,” the studio head said in a statement shared with The Hollywood Reporter. “It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him … His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.” Seth MacFarlane, who worked with Stewart on comedy productions like Family Guy, Ted and American Dad!, said he was a rare actor who “could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful”.



“I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day one of a new film,” MacFarlane wrote on Instagram. “He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, ‘Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed’. We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet.” Stewart also acted in Star Trek: Picard, a sequel to The Next Generation, featuring Picard in his post-Starfleet retirement and drawing in characters from other Star Trek shows, notably Seven of Nine (Jeri Ryan) from Star Trek: Voyager. “I will never say goodbye to Jean-Luc Picard, to his ideals, to his struggles to create an honest world, an unprejudiced world. That will always remain inside me in the same way that other roles have,” Stewart told this masthead in 2022. With Reuters, AP

World.title: Precinct puts downtown development on ice
World.content:
One of Auckland's biggest proposed developments has been shelved despite strong demand for the office space, because the developer says inflation, interest rates, the weak Kiwi dollar and construction risks have made the economics no longer stack up.

Precinct Property has announced it will not proceed with its downtown development at 29 Customs Street West in Auckland's Commercial Bay.

The development, which gained fast-track approval from the government, was set to be one of Auckland's largest commercial developments, comprising a 55-storey office tower accommodating more than 7000 workers, three podium levels of retail, restaurants and hospitality, as well as public spaces, with the possibility of a future second tower.

Despite engaging an early-stage contractor and being in advanced negotiations for 50 percent of the office space, the company said changing economic conditions meant it was no longer confident its numbers would stack up for shareholders on completion.

Precinct said it had secured resource consent, appointed Built on an early contractor engagement basis and advanced pre-leasing negotiations covering around half the office space.

Precinct blamed escalating project costs due to higher financing costs, elevated long-term interest rates, a lower NZ dollar pushing up imported costs, and stubbornly high inflation producing an unacceptably high risk of a blowout in building costs.

"We are disappointed that current market conditions do not support proceeding with the Downtown development." Precinct CEO Scott Pritchard said.

Pritchard noted that while today's decision was in the best interests of shareholders, he didn't rule out returning to the project in the future if economic conditions changed. Precinct said future development of the site would remain an objective for the company.

"It is an outstanding site at the heart of Auckland's waterfront, and the strong occupier interest and rental levels commercially agreed reinforce our conviction in the quality of the opportunity."

Pritchard said Precinct remained committed to its strategy of focusing on premium, well-located assets and, despite today's announcement, it still had around $900 million of other developments underway.

The Electoral Commission says it's looking into the 'Split Your Vote' website created by entrepreneur Harry Mowbray.

It said it was investigating the "advertising" and whether it was "authorised", and it wouldn't be appropriate to comment further at this stage.

Party messaging must come with an authentication statement, for transparency reasons.

Mowbray created a website, splityourvote.co.nz - which is now no longer online - encouraging voters who want a centre-right government to give their party vote to ACT or New Zealand First.

Earlier this week he said he'd been pushing the message that a centre right government could "best be achieved" by vote splitting, "supporting the local National MP or candidate with their electorate vote but giving their Party vote to NZFirst or ACT as coalition partners".

"That gives their party vote some effect while giving the centre right coalition a better chance of winning."

World.title: Consumer confidence down for October but some optimism in tough economic conditions
World.content:
October consumer confidence is down but seen as resilient given economic conditions.

ANZ-Roy Morgan Consumer Confidence eased 2 points in October to 96.2 points.

Any reading under 100 was considered a negative, though October's level was 16 points above April's low.

"New Zealand consumers remain under the pump," ANZ Bank chief economist Sharon Zollner said.

"Fuel prices are extremely high, and broader inflation is running well ahead of income growth.

"The weak currency isn't helping, though export-focused sectors are benefiting."

Key points:

The net proportion of households thinking it's a good time to buy a major household item dropped 10 points to -17%, as cost of living pressures dented spending plans.

Inflation expectations (2 years ahead) eased from 4.5% to 4.2%, the lowest level since March 2025.

House price expectations eased from 2.4% to 2.0%, their lowest level since July 2023. After a few false starts in recent years, consumers are increasingly negative on that front.

"In the absence of a housing upswing, a more meaningful lift in the consumer mood is likely to have to wait for an improvement in the labour market," Zollner said, adding a lift in employment was expected to be reflected in new weeks labour market data.

Zollner said it was good to see some optimism amid the data.

She said the outlook on expectations about personal finances a year ahead was solidly in the black, and had risen in each of the last four months.

"Indeed, one interesting feature of the data this month was a drop in house price inflation expectations to its lowest level in three years.

World.title: Super Typhoon In-fa: Marianas braces for fifth major storm
World.content:
Super Typhoon In-fa has regained strength, packing maximum sustained winds of 150 miles per hour as it approaches the Northern Islands of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI).

The US National Weather Service (NWS) said the category 4 storm is expected to pass near or over Agrihan on Friday afternoon or evening.

Typhoon warnings remain in effect for Agrihan, Pagan, and Alamagan, where destructive winds are expected.

At 4am Friday, In-fa was located about 290 miles east-southeast of Agrihan and 295 miles east-northeast of Saipan, moving west at 18 miles per hour.

NWS meteorologist Landon Aydlett said satellite imagery showed a powerful, well-organised storm with a large, clearly defined eye.

He said In-fa appeared to have reached peak intensity and was expected to weaken gradually as it moved through the Marianas.

In-fa is the fifth super typhoon to threaten or pass near the region this year, following Sinlaku in April, Bavi in July, Choi-wan in early October, and Champi less than two weeks ago.

Choi-wan moved north of the Marianas before strengthening into a super typhoon, while Champi narrowly missed southern Guam before reaching super typhoon strength as it moved away from the islands.

The region appears fortunate that In-fa is tracking well north of the main population centres of Guam, Rota, Tinian, and Saipan, sparing them the worst of the storm.

However, the Northern Islands remain at risk, particularly Agrihan, where the storm could pass directly overhead. The remote islands are believed to have only three CNMI residents, although that figure has not been independently confirmed.

Unlike Sinlaku, which moved slowly through the Marianas in April, In-fa is travelling at 15 to 20 miles per hour and is expected to pass through the island chain relatively quickly.

Guam, Rota, Tinian, and Saipan are expected to experience generally favourable weather conditions, although dangerous marine conditions remain a major concern.

Saipan and Tinian are under a high surf warning, with waves of 12 to 18 feet expected, along with possible minor coastal flooding and seas reaching 14 feet.

Guam and Rota are under a high surf advisory, with waves of 10 to 14 feet and seas reaching 10 feet.

High rip current risks remain in effect through Saturday across all four islands.

Wellington charity offers lifeline to woman stranded in Cooks Pacific Waves Download MP3 2m

A charitable trust in Wellington has offered to escort a Sri Lankan woman currently stranded in the Cook Islands through New Zealand and back home.

Cook Islands News first reported that the 49-year-old has been stuck in Rarotonga since at least February 2024, having been repeatedly denied a transit visa by both New Zealand and Australian immigration.

Tahir Nawaz from the Deen Welfare Trust said that athough he had never met the woman stranded in the Cook Islands, he felt compelled to act.

"There's got to be somebody there to do something. It shouldn't be just the news," he told RNZ Pacific.

Nawaz said he had been in touch with Immigration New Zealand (INZ) with an offer to escort her, promising to remain with her at all times and to keep within designated airside or transit zones.

He said he had a flight booked to the Cook Islands next week and is now attempting to make contact with the woman directly.

"I've been thinking about it, that person is so desperate. They want to be handcuffed and go."

The women told the Cook Islands News: "Living by myself for three years without seeing family is torture. It is a psychological nightmare. I genuinely want to return home. I have no intention to stay in New Zealand."

INZ had doubts over whether her intentions were genuine, given she had previously claimed asylum in New Zealand.

Nawaz, who supports recent immigrants and refugees looking to base themselves in Aotearoa, said it ignores a basic right of movement that all people have.

"They should be able to freely travel, and if there's a risk that they might claim asylum, that's where they should have some mechanism."

Tahir Nawaz Gerry Keating, Image Services / VUW

He added that he would like to see New Zealand's treatment of refugees improve overall.

"When the refugee comes here, they are generally given very heavy support when they come in for first two years," he said.

"What we experience that after two years, all of a sudden everything gets stopped.

He said that changes were needed.

"When we support our people here when they come in, there should be a good [work] pathway ... straight to contributing to the country."
