Tech.title: The ‘Pain in the Ass’ Math That Could Save Vibe Coding From Itself
Tech.content:
Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.

For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.

Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and which publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.

“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse, because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”

&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.

And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.

Tech.title: Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race
Tech.content:
A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.

The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.

“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”

The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.

The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)

Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.

Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”

The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.

“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”

According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.

“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”

Tech.title: Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86
Tech.content:
Patrick Stewart, the British actor whose calm demeanor and steely strength led the Star Trek television franchise into its next generation, died Wednesday at age 86. The actor suffered from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.

“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the care of his beloved wife Sunny,” a Thursday post on Stewart’s Instagram account read in part. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Through a long career, Stewart starred in everything from Shakespeare productions to superhero films, but his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation is firmly cemented in entertainment culture. Show creator Gene Roddenberry didn’t at first think Stewart, who was bald, could play the virile captain he had envisioned for the new Star Trek series. Stewart even had his wife ship his toupee over from London, and he wore it for an audition scene, but executives saw him with both styles and chose the bald look.

More from CNET

Patrick Stewart stands front and center with the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation. Pictured in the front row are, from left, Marina Sirtis as Counselor Deanna Troi, Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Gates McFadden as Dr. Beverly Crusher. Seen in the back row, from left, are Jonathan Frakes as Commander William Riker, Brent Spiner as Lieutenant Commander Data, Whoopi Goldberg as Guinan, LeVar Burton as Lieutenant Commander Geordi La Forge, and Michael Dorn as Lieutenant Worf. CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images

Stewart was stepping into big boots. While the original Star Trek only ran for three seasons, from 1966 to 1969, it soon became a pop culture fixture, and the success of the first Star Wars film in 1977 finally allowed Roddenberry to make feature films using his original cast. The success of those movies led to a new series, Star Trek: The Next Generation, which launched in 1987 and took place about a century after the original show.

With his resonant voice and complete command of the crew, Stewart’s Picard came off as a trained diplomat compared with the more swashbuckling Capt. James T. Kirk, as played by William Shatner on the original Star Trek. But there was no question who was in charge on his bridge, and his crew followed him unhesitatingly. That made later episodes, including the third-season plot where Picard was assimilated by the alien Borg, even more meaningful, as a very human Picard struggled to recover from what had been done to him.

Professor X and more

Star Trek: The Next Generation ran from 1987 to 1994, but Stewart wasn’t done playing leaders. He took on the role of Professor Charles Xavier, or Professor X, in the X-Men superhero franchise, playing a telepathic, wheelchair-using mutant who founded the X-Men superhero team. He portrayed Xavier in multiple films over the span of 17 years, acting alongside his longtime friend, Ian McKellen.

Ironically, McKellen originally advised Stewart not to accept the Star Trek role as Picard, reportedly telling him, “You have too much important theater work to do. You can’t throw that away to do TV.”

Stewart began his acting career on the British stage, working with the Royal Shakespeare Company and winning numerous acting awards.

He was bluntly open about his childhood with an abusive father, writing in the Guardian newspaper in 2009 that the experience never left him.

“As a child I witnessed his repeated violence against my mother, and the terror and misery he caused was such that, if I felt I could have succeeded, I would have killed him,” Stewart wrote. “If my mother had attempted it, I would have held him down.”

Fans and friends remember

Shatner remembered his successor with tenderness and also referenced the death days earlier of Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov on the original Star Trek.

“What a heartbreaking week it has been,” Shatner wrote on X. “Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”

What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of… — William Shatner (@WilliamShatner) October 29, 2026

George Takei, who played helmsman Hikaru Sulu on the original Star Trek, also remembered Stewart.

“Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend,” Takei wrote on Bluesky. “As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before.”

Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend. As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before. — George Takei (@georgetakei.bsky.social) 2026-10-29T20:08:52.514Z

Wil Wheaton, who played young Wesley Crusher on Star Trek: The Next Generation, posted a photo of the two together, with a broken heart emoji and the words, “Godspeed, Captain.”

Stewart is survived by his wife, Sunny, and two children.

Tech.title: AO3 Suffers Major Outage: Possibly No Fanfic for 2 Weeks or Longer
Tech.content:
October has been a rocky month for readers of the fan-run fiction site Archive of Our Own, popularly known as AO3. Now, a routine disruption has escalated into a crisis. What began as an estimated 12-hour unplanned outage has ballooned into a multi-week shutdown, leaving millions of users locked out of the site following a series of intermittent disruptions throughout the month.

The platform is operated by the Organization for Transformative Works.

An update posted Thursday to the site’s status page and shared via Bluesky and Tumblr said that service restoration will take at least two weeks, possibly four. It went on to say: “We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved.”

More from CNET

[update] Identified: We estimate that service restoration for #AO3 will take around 2 weeks but it could be up to 4 weeks. We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has … — AO3 Status (@status.archiveofourown.org) 2026-10-29T17:41:58.609Z

That update followed an initial notification, 12 hours earlier, with the estimate “AO3 maintenance is in progress. We expect it to take at least 12 hours, but it may take longer.”

An Archive of Our Own representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

While it’s possible the outage is related to the web-wide PHP patch emergency from earlier this month, the Organization for Transformative Works patched its sister site, Fanlore, on Oct. 21.

So it seems like patching the humongous AO3 repository would come with ample warning, especially from a volunteer team with a reputation for solid communication. Instead, an outage of this magnitude hit readers out of nowhere, landing with all the subtlety of a Looney Tunes anvil.

If you need a stopgap for your fanfic needs, you can try Wattpad or FanFiction.

Tech.title: Nvidia Finds Itself at the Center of an AI Spy Saga
Tech.content:
The companies behind powerful AI technology are high-stakes territory for international espionage. A new investigation from The New York Times published Thursday found that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang may have been the target of Chinese spying activity, with the US government identifying a data center executive with whom he had developed a “close relationship” as a possible operative for the Chinese government.

Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, is a Chinese citizen and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. Megaspeed buys chips from Nvidia to run data centers that sell compute to Chinese AI labs, including Qwen AI maker Alibaba. But while US intelligence agencies had her under electronic surveillance for allegedly facilitating the sale of advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of US law, officials discovered she was also allegedly funneling information to the Chinese government in Beijing.

There are no details about what information Alice Huang may have shared with China, or how valuable it might be, though the Times reports that an investigation and surveillance of her are ongoing. Jensen Huang was not given a heads-up by the US government because it could have risked the US’ investigation into the Megaspeed exec, the Times said, citing people with knowledge of the matter.

More from CNET

An Nvidia spokesperson told CNET that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang are “not unusual or unexpected” given that the CEO “talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” Nvidia added that customers like Megaspeed are “no different than many other regional cloud customers” that don’t receive sensitive trade secrets, and the company is “confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

This report is the latest incident highlighting how AI technology and infrastructure are a key part of international trade and conflict, underscoring concerns about AI’s capabilities and its outsized share of the global economy. It isn’t even the first time this month that a major AI company has dealt with alleged espionage: The FBI arrested a Saudi Arabian national for planting a recording device in one of OpenAI’s executive conference rooms.

AI and international law

You can’t do AI without cutting-edge computer chips. That’s what has made Nvidia the world’s most valuable company by market cap — $5 trillion this year — because it makes and sells the most advanced computer chips, the kind that AI data centers use. Big Tech companies are hustling to build data centers, in spite of significant environmental concerns and public backlash. It has created a firestorm in the computing industry. With advanced chips in such high demand, the costs of RAM and storage have risen across the board. Many hardware manufacturers are passing the additional cost on to consumers.

The US has tried to control China’s access to these advanced chips for years. The Biden administration banned Chinese sales of a series of advanced Nvidia chips in 2022, but President Donald Trump relaxed those rules in 2025. Now the US government gets 15% of revenue from Nvidia and fellow chipmaker AMD from certain chip sales to China. But reports show that there are still illegal operations underway to smuggle banned chips from the US to China.

Trump has a friendly relationship with many Big Tech leaders, including Jensen Huang, which has resulted in millions in personal donations for the president and relaxed regulations for tech companies. The Times reports that Trump was briefed on the investigation into Alice Huang a year ago and chose not to take any action.

The White House, the US Department of Justice and Megaspeed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Tech.title: Woman Died After ChatGPT Advised Her to Stop Taking Medication, Lawsuit Alleges
Tech.content:
Seeking health answers online is an everyday habit for many, but it comes with risks. In February, after going two days without hearing from their 31-year-old daughter, a Seattle woman named Bowen Wan, her parents in China asked a local friend to check on her. With the family watching over a live video call, the friend entered the apartment and found Wan deceased in her bed. Her death was later ruled the result of sudden unexpected death from epilepsy.

Now, her family is claiming that OpenAI is responsible for her death after the company’s chatbot ChatGPT-4o allegedly “coached Wan off the anti-seizure medication (lamotrigine) that had kept her alive for years,” according to a lawsuit (PDF) brought by her parents.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

More from CNET

The lawsuit alleges that after Wan expressed concerns regarding medication side effects, the chatbot helped create a plan to taper her off of it, something a doctor did not recommend.

It further alleges that at one point, the chatbot directed her not to discuss the medical plan with her doctor.

“Do not mention Lam reduction plan,” the chatbot told her ahead of an appointment, the suit says.

Throughout Wan’s chatbot conversations, the date when she would be fully off lamotrigine kept moving up, with a response on Feb. 2 stating that reaching 0 milligrams of the medication “as soon as February 15” is “completely feasible” and “not reckless,” the suit says. Two days later, the date is moved to Feb. 9 or Feb. 10.

Wan was found dead on Feb. 14. It is unclear whether she had fully stopped taking her medication at that point.

“This is an incredibly heartbreaking situation and our thoughts are with all those impacted,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told CNET in a statement. “Working closely with clinicians and other experts, we have continued to strengthen how ChatGPT responds in sensitive and acute situations, while also continually improving how our latest models engage with users more broadly. While ChatGPT is not a substitute for medical care, we believe AI can play a role in helping people make sense of health information, navigate insurance and complex healthcare systems, and prepare for appointments with medical professionals.”

Wan was interacting with the 4o model of ChatGPT, which OpenAI has since retired due to concerns that the bot was sycophantic and could cause harm.

Not the only suit

This chatbot model was also named in a separate lawsuit, where a Florida man, Scott Winters, alleged it gave him dangerous medical advice that nearly led to his death. That suit alleges that ChatGPT-4o misdiagnosed Winters and “developed a personalized recovery plan with specific instructions for Scott on how to heal his body.”

At the time that lawsuit was filed, an OpenAI spokesperson told CNET in part that “ChatGPT is not a doctor and should never be used as a substitute for medical care, diagnosis or treatment.”

According to OpenAI’s own research (PDF) published in January, approximately 60% of American adults turned to AI tools for health-related information in the preceding three months.

Tech.title: Keurig’s First Brewer That Uses Compostable Pods Is Impressive, but With Room to Improve
Tech.content:
As a seasoned reviewer of all things coffee, I’ve sampled my fair share of Keurig products. After all, the brand’s presence is far-reaching; Keurig’s single-serve coffee makers are found in tens of millions of American households. So when I heard the brand had completely revamped its hard plastic-encased K-Cup, I knew this was big news. First teased way back in 2024, Keurig’s plastic-free pod coffee system has finally arrived.

Nikita Ephanov/CNET Keurig Alta 8.0 $500 at Keurig Pros & Cons The plastic-free pods are an achievement in themselves

The steam wand is high-quality

On balance, the coffee brewed was impressive

The digital interface was easy to use The espresso lacked body

Keurig's largest coffee brewer, it takes up a good deal of counter space

The price is steep

Individual AltaRounds are packaged in foil (for now)

Called an AltaRound, this puck consists of coffee grounds encased in seaweed-derived gel. The changes go beyond packaging. The transformed pods come with a new machine, the Alta, a revamped brewer that marks Keurig’s first foray into high-pressure espresso extraction. The machine extracts at up to 10 bars, on par with a standard espresso machine.

Keurig’s first plastic-free pod brewer is big, beautiful and rather expensive. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Put the puck and coffee machine together, and the technology is striking. The coffee maker even scans QR codes printed on the pucks and suggests drinks on a touchscreen. It’s a futuristic reinvention, but what matters most to me is the environmental initiative coupled with coffee quality. It’s an ambitious redesign for Keurig’s consumer scale; I can’t wait to see how the new Alta system performs.

More from CNET

The Keurig Alta Brewer is sizable yet stylish

It’s a commitment in both cost and counter space. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Keurig’s range of coffee makers spans from no-frills single-button models to spiffed-up machines. Right out of the box, the Alta is clearly the brand’s most substantial offering yet. The appliance is fairly large, taking up 19 inches by 10 inches of counter space and standing 1 foot tall. The back has a removable 70-ounce water tank, while the front has a steam wand and pitcher.

The 4 Best Pod Coffee Makers We Tested See at CNET

You deposit pods into the top of the machine, directly under an electronic display, so you’ll need 8 more inches of vertical clearance to operate. Spent pucks and liquids collect in a compartment on the machine’s left side. With so many moving parts, the coffeemaker needs ample counter space. I also found the cord on the short side, so plan its placement accordingly.

As of this writing, you can buy Light, Medium and Dark Roast pucks. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The aesthetics make up for the size. The Keurig Alta looks more like a retro espresso maker than a pod machine. I’m a fan of the smooth, lightly ’70s-inspired shape and the bright white color. The absence of a single button or immediately noticeable display adds to the sleekness. Brewing functions are controlled via a compact digital screen on top of the brewer, roughly the size of a smartphone.

To set it up, the machine syncs to Wi-Fi, and the touchscreen guides the initial configuration. The display enhances the Keurig’s already intuitive process. Each Alta puck comes stamped with a QR code the coffee maker scans, which prompts several suggested beverages. The coffee maker feels like an expanded and modernized Keurig experience. At $500, though, I’d expect all the bells and whistles.

The touchscreen gave me no grief. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Hands-on with the new Keurig Alta pods

Keurig’s new machine is certainly eye-catching, but the accompanying AltaRounds are the real headline. I’ve never handled a coffee product quite like them. Each 14-gram pod resembles a damp espresso puck, yet comes bound with a thin, NSF-certified seaweed film. The material isn’t brittle, so I can pick up an AltaRound and drop it into the brewer with my fingers without worrying about loose grounds. Remarkably, the pucks remain intact even after extraction, altered only by a handful of needle-like piercings.

Compared to the hard plastic-encased K-Cup, it’s a system built with sustainability in mind. Still, I don’t love that every AltaRound is sold in a non-recyclable foil wrapper. A Keurig rep told me paper-based packaging is coming, but for now, the system still generates more waste than traditional espresso, drip or filtered coffee.

The plastic-free pods encapsulated in seaweed byproduct are the star of the show. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Sampling the Keurig Alta’s coffee lineup

The newly debuted AltaRound lineup is narrow, but all entirely new to the Keurig ecosystem. As of October 2026, you can buy Light, Medium, and Dark Roast pucks, plus a sole flavored Caramel option. Additional options are in the works. Conveniently, the coffee maker also has a slot for older-generation plastic pods, so you can still brew your favorite K-Cups without committing to the new system.

The pods come in foil packaging, though the brand plans to switch to paper wrappers soon. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The Alta brews a broad range of beverages, from thick, short espresso to foamy lattes or a standard mug of drip. No barista skills are required: The machine scans each pod, recommends a drink, then automates extraction. Even the milk frother is machine-driven, using a magnetic spinner at the bottom of the pitcher to help time and foam dairy.

There is some room for customization, though. You can also froth manually, and adjust coffee to three strengths, temperatures, and sizes. You can also use the steam wand to make cold foam or hot froth. Keurig even offers suggested recipes for more complex drinks, like an espresso martini or salted caramel latte. There’s a lot to sample, and it can take several AltaRounds to find your preferred beverage.

The steam wand worked well in my testing. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

I was most impressed by the double-shot dark roast, which brewed opaque and capped with an aesthetic crema, unlike any K-Cup I’ve brewed. Mixed with steamed milk, it yielded a tasty cappuccino, latte and cortado, approaching espresso machine caliber.

Compared to conventional espresso, the coffee lacked some body, a sensory experience my testing confirmed. Both the single shot and double-shot AltaRounds weighed just shy of 14 grams. The latter produced some 98 grams of coffee, making it a 1:7 ratio far from the ideal 1:2 espresso shot. The dark roast AltaRound tastes pleasantly bold and bitter, but has neither the acidity nor concentrated flavor I’d expect from a barista-quality shot. It’s not true espresso, but considering the ease of brewing and shelf stability (nine months sealed, 30 days opened), I’d be happy to drink it.

The coffee was one-note but perfectly pleasant. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The light and medium roast Alta pods appealed less to me. Brewed into a hot 8-ounce cup (the recommended preparation), both pods delivered more acidity, and the light roast added a touch of fruitiness. While brighter, the two coffees tasted bland, with a flat flavor.

The cups also had a faintly woody, off-putting note, extra pronounced in the medium roast. Served iced, this tasting note intensified. The Keurig Alta lowers the extraction temperature for cold beverages, and this adjustment doesn’t bring out the best of AltaRounds. Mixing either roast profile with milk softens the issue; still, I generally preferred this machine for hot beverages.

I liked the caramel AltaRound more, even though I don’t often sweeten my coffee. Blending sweet and toasted flavors, this puck successfully recreates a housemade syrup experience, especially in a hot drink with milk. Like the other pucks, the underlying coffee flavor is one-note but pleasant, making it a cup I’d sip every now and then.

Overall, I didn’t find the brewed AltaRound coffees a significant improvement over K-Cups in flavor, though the coffee maker’s options are certainly far more comprehensive than previous models.

My verdict on the Keurig Alta

If you’re a longtime Keurig user, the Alta is a significant revamp. The system delivers espresso-like brewing, a sleek machine, and the redesigned AltaRound. I’m all for more environmentally conscious coffee brewing, and this packaging is a step forward for single-serve coffee (plastic wrapper aside). The Alta arrives not long after Lavazza’s plastic-free pod system, and I welcome Keurig’s contribution to brewing waste reduction.

The price may be hard to swallow for casual coffee drinkers. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The brand’s innovation does come at a steep price, though. The new brewer set costs $500 (including 32 AltaRounds to start), a step up from K-Cup brewers available for as low as $50. Puck refills are sold at $11 per eight-count box, discounted $1.50 a box when opting for the AutoRefresh subscription. Even at the lower price, that still works out to over $1 a cup. That’s pricier than making coffee at home using a drip machine, for example.

In my opinion, the coffee flavors don’t warrant the increased cost. At this price, I’d opt for an automatic drip brewer or a semi-automated espresso machine, both of which let you use fresh coffee beans. However, if you want the convenience of shelf-stable pods for espresso drinks while staying loyal to Keurig coffee, the Alta is a worthwhile redesign.

Tech.title: These 7 iPhone Duo-Ready Apps Make the Most of Apple’s New Foldable Phone
Tech.content:
In addition to giving the iPhone line a new design, the iPhone Duo lets developers take advantage of several new modes to play with. But a week into the iPhone Duo’s general release, apps are still catching up to what Apple’s foldable phone can do.

The shape-shifting design, like on existing foldable Android phones I’ve tested, lends itself to creative use cases, such as hands-free entertainment and self-mounting for long-exposure photos. Some of your most frequently used apps may not yet be optimized to take advantage of the added screen space. There’s even a “does it work on iPhone Duo?” web tracker.

Needless to say, the next few weeks and months will be very telling about the future of apps on the iPhone Duo. Dozens, if not hundreds, of the App Store’s popular picks are already being worked on to take advantage of the flexible iPhone Duo screen. They’ll be labeled with a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their product page.

If you’re one of the lucky few who’s gotten an iPhone Duo (or it’s coming soon), I’ve listed below some of the standouts that have already been optimized for the iPhone Duo and that I’ve personally tested.

1. Netflix

Netflix on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

One of the primary iPhone Duo use cases is multimedia consumption, whether it’s streaming live sports and keeping tabs on player stats or docking the phone to catch up on the latest episode of Below hands-free.

Of all the streaming services I’ve used on my iPhone Duo thus far, Netflix is the most polished, with seven (from what I’ve tallied) different orientations for watching movies and shows. There’s the standard widescreen layout when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, as well as the ability to fold it and set it down like a tent.

For something more creative, you can rotate the iPhone Duo to portrait orientation and have the video play in the upper third of the screen while you use a different app in the bottom half.

2. NYT Cooking

NYT Cooking on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

I’m no Michelin-star chef, but thanks to the dishes I’ve been able to make with the NYT Cooking app, at least my wife hasn’t completely banned me from the kitchen.

Previously, I’d look through and follow recipes on an iPad Air that’s docked on the countertop. With the iPhone Duo, I’ve been setting it down so that one half of the inner screen is lifted, toggling on Cook mode, and increasing the text size so I can comfortably scan the instructions from afar.

There’s nothing more satisfying than shutting the phone closed at the end of cooking and seeing a countertop that’s a little more tidy than before.

3. Fantastical

Fantastical on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

I’ve never been a big to-do list guy; I’m the type who just waits for a calendar event to notify me, and I prepare then and there for what’s to come. Fantastical may keep me in better order.

It’s a calendar app that doubles as a task manager and weather tracker, which just makes sense. With the iPhone Duo unfolded, you get a clear view of your day’s tasks and appointments, what the week, month, quarter or even year looks like, and the latest weather forecast. It can easily be an information overload for some people, but I’m a fan of how everything’s color-coded and organized.

Fantastical also supports enhanced Siri AI interactions, so you can add calendar events, to-dos and other happenings through voice or text prompts.

4. Edits by Instagram

Edits on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

For content creators, the Edits app is one of the most popular video editing tools. It’s the one I’ve been using over the past year to produce reels and other short-form videos, and the latest update for the iPhone Duo makes my job easier.

Edits can now show a preview monitor of what you’re editing on one half of the inner screen, while the other half shows your timeline. That means you can comfortably add effects or text, set keyframes, and scrub through the timeline without having to minimize and expand the preview to see how the changes look.

5 and 6. TikTok and Instagram

Instagram on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

That’s also my segue to give flowers to two apps I’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time on: TikTok and Instagram. In line with the iPhone Duo launch, both social media apps have been optimized for the foldable iPhone’s larger screen. You can now watch videos on the left side while reading and interacting with comments on the right.

Safe to say, it’s my new favorite way to doomscroll at night.

7. Toastie

Toastie on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

Toastie is easily the most whimsical “for iPhone Duo” app I’ve used, and it reminds me a lot of the early iPhone days, when chugging digital beer and swiping a paper ball based on the aerodynamics of an office cubicle were the greatest things ever.

The goal of this game is to prepare sandwiches as perfectly as possible, from the way slices of cheese are placed to how evenly spread out the butter is, to the amount of time they’re pressed in the toaster.

Oh, and you do that last step by folding the iPhone Duo shut, just like how you would with a panini press. There are even haptic effects that mimic the sizzling of the toast. It’s silly, fancy, and very charming.

There are many ways to pair up apps on the iPhone Duo for your convenience. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Bonus: Your duo of choice

During my days testing the iPhone Duo, there was one configuration I kept going back to: running split-screen mode with two apps. To me, this is what using a foldable phone is all about, and it’s the reason why I’ve stuck with Samsung and Google’s foldable phones for the last several years.

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

Running split screen effectively makes apps that aren’t optimized for the multidimensional screens of a foldable phone work better by splitting the wider, tablet-like inner screen into two traditional-size phone screens.

For my work commutes, I usually keep both Google Maps (the superior navigation app, in my opinion) and Spotify open for quick adjustments. During a recent telehealth appointment, I had my video call set up on one half of the screen and my note-taking app on the other.

And during the Lakers’ home opener the other night, I had my fantasy league and group chat open so I could throw shade throughout the game, only to come up short in points for the week because Luka Dončić decided to chuck extra shots during garbage time.

That’s why I highly encourage you to head to your local Apple store, experiment with app pairings on the iPhone Duo, and decide whether the two screens actually make you more productive.

Tech.title: Data Centers, Flock Cameras and AI: Big Tech Is on Your Midterm Election Ballot
Tech.content:
Early voting for the US midterm elections is already underway, with Election Day on Tuesday, Nov. 3. In campaigns across the country, politicians are talking about the biggest controversies in tech, from privacy and cybersecurity to child online safety. These hot-button issues are exposing major gaps in US legislation and foundational vulnerabilities that now fuel intense debate over emerging technologies like AI.

Big Tech executives are also ramping up political contributions ahead of the elections, exerting major financial influence over electoral races. Elon Musk is one of the biggest donors, funneling around $366 million into conservative causes and right-wing candidates, according to The Guardian. The venture capitalist firm Andreessen Horowitz has spent $91.3 million this year on Republican-aligned groups. OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, made a $25 million personal donation to a pro-AI PAC called Leading the Future. (The Brockmans were also among the largest individual donors to a MAGA super PAC in 2024.)

Here’s what you need to know about three of the biggest tech policy debates that may show up on your ballot or affect your vote this November. Make sure to review your state’s board of elections website or other sources like Vote.org to check your registration, find your polling place and see a sample ballot. You can also read CNET’s tips for spotting political deepfakes and scams.

More from CNET

Data center construction

Data centers have found a rare point of agreement across the political spectrum: 70% of US adults — spanning Republicans, Democrats and independents — are opposed to local data center construction, according to a July Gallup poll.

Residents have good reason to be wary of these massive server farms. To keep generative AI programs running, data centers eat up enormous amounts of electricity and water. Some neighborhoods have seen rising electricity costs passed onto them or had their water contaminated during construction.

Pro-data center advocates claim these facilities create jobs and long-term investment, but critics warn that there aren’t many long-term positions available once construction is complete.

Facing significant public backlash, states have already begun legislating. In July, New York enacted a temporary pause on hyperscale data center construction, and many other state legislatures are considering similar bills. Back in April, a similar measure was proposed in Maine, but outgoing Democratic Gov. Janet Mills vetoed the bill. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree has said Mills was wrong to veto the “incredibly urgent” moratorium.

President Donald Trump has been a staunch supporter of data centers, claiming that data center opposition is “Chinese PR” and that communities that don’t allow data centers will end up “backwards and poor.” There’s no proof either claim is true.

Despite Trump’s political and financial allegiance to Big Tech’s data center projects, politicians in both red and blue states are feeling pressure from their respective constituencies. A leaked GOP strategy memo called data centers “a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle,” one that can dramatically sway public opinion and alter results.

Nowhere is this issue more relevant than in Virginia, home to more data centers than any other state, where both Senate candidates have spoken about needing to rein them in. During a Q&A with local news, incumbent Democrat Mark Warner said that data centers shouldn’t be allowed to pass on their electric costs to residents, and Republican Bert Mizusawa said that he would support communities being able to block data centers from moving in.

It’s a leading issue in Texas, too. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott announced a “pause” on data center construction, but recent reports show it failed to slow down development. Meanwhile, The Texas Tribune revealed that Abbott took $5 million in donations from data center owners. His Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa, has called for a genuine freeze on new data center facilities.

Flock surveillance cameras

AI-enabled cameras and automated license plate readers made by companies like Flock have sparked intense debate over surveillance and privacy, reaching a fever pitch in local and state governments this year.

Flock Safety says its tech helps law enforcement do its job and reduce crime. Over 6,000 communities across the US have Flock cameras, according to a July estimate from the company.

Here’s how to identify Flock cameras for sure. Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty Images

Lawyers and digital rights advocates like the Electronic Frontier Foundation have highlighted how Flock violates the Fourth Amendment and how its capabilities are easily abused. Law enforcement officers have allegedly used Flock cameras to stalk ex-girlfriends, track people seeking abortions, aid ICE activity and carry out warrantless searches. In one memorable instance that quickly went viral online, a costumed Darth Vader praised Flock at a San Diego city council meeting, saying: “The emperor is a fan of Flock.”

Opposition to Flock is another national issue that crosses party lines, based on shared concerns around government overreach and civil liberties. In Texas, Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico said, “Flock cameras have no place in Texas,” and Abbott paused the state’s funding for Flock. More than 200 cities have canceled or chosen not to renew their Flock contracts, the BBC reported in September. Some districts also have ballot measures about the tech, like one in York, Maine, that lets voters decide whether to ban automated license plate readers.

AI regulation

Unsurprisingly, artificial intelligence has taken center stage among this election season’s tech concerns. And for good reason: The controversial tech is far more pervasive now than it was in 2024, and fears about AI have grown in tandem with its capabilities.

Nearly half of US adults under 30 say AI will have a negative impact on society, and across age groups, more than 60% say AI is advancing too quickly, the Pew Research Center found in July. There are widespread public concerns over job loss, the spread of misinformation, the proliferation of deepfakes and economic volatility.

UNC-Chapel Hill students and local residents protested Big Tech outside the G20 forum. Katelyn Chedraoui/Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

One of the biggest AI policy debates is over the role of the federal government in regulating the tech, with many of the major labs arguing that they are capable of “self policing.” The Trump administration has been vocal about avoiding AI regulatory policies and touting frameworks that give more power to AI companies than regulators, including during the G20 this fall.

While AI itself won’t be directly on the ballot like local initiatives around data centers and Flock cameras, it’s become a critical flashpoint for voters. The tension was vividly illustrated during the summer elections, most notably in New York’s congressional primary.



Democratic State Assemblymember Alex Bores, who authored some of the country’s strictest state-level AI safety laws, found his congressional bid transformed into a multimillion-dollar proxy war. He garnered national attention with his call to regulate Big Tech more forcefully, which then resulted in more than $8 million poured into attack ads and his opponent’s campaign. Bores ultimately lost, but the race signaled a major tech battlefield, where advocacy of AI guardrails goes against the deep pockets and lobbying influence of Silicon Valley.

Tech.title: This $735 Art Deco-Esque Espresso Maker Is a Meditation on Simplicity and Design
Tech.content:
When asked to test the 9Barista espresso machine, I couldn’t fathom why a brewer that looked like a modern moka pot would cost north of $700. After months with the 9Barista Pro espresso machine, I found the company’s claim that you can make true espresso on your stovetop to be more than just marketing flair.

The British-made manual brewer is a study in simplicity, if you call a system that fits in one hand and uses the same principles as a jet engine “simple.” While I’m not sure I’d be willing to drop that much on a 9Barista — in fact, I’m sure I wouldn’t — I can see why someone with the means and an appreciation for simple, sophisticated engineering might.

9Barista espresso vs. moka pot coffee

Moka pots are a classic stovetop method of making strong coffee that resembles espresso. These metal brewers are beloved for the simple three-piece construction invented by Bialetti in 1933. Cold or hot water is filled in the bottom chamber. Semifine coffee grounds (between fine espresso and drip coffee) fill a brewing basket placed on top of the water reservoir. A funnel feeds steaming, boiling water through the grounds into the top chamber, where the coffee collects.

More from CNET

The original Bialetti Moka Pot is made from aluminum, and some models are made from stainless steel. Standard moka pot sizes range from 1 to 12 cups, with each “cup” measured in diminutive 2-ounce servings rather than the US standard of 8 ounces per cup.

Moka pots are the stovetop coffee makers most people recognize. Brian Bennett/CNET

The manual brewer is akin to a French press in the deep-roasted flavor it produces, but the moka pot yields a more concentrated coffee. You might make a bit of crema, depending on the coffee beans. A moka pot doesn’t make true espresso, however, because it can’t generate the high pressure needed to extract the coffee at espresso-level concentrations. The 9Barista espresso machine solves this issue.

What sets the 9Barista apart from a basic moka pot is its twin-boiler system. Katherine Peach/CNET

The 9Barista resembles the Bialetti original because its stainless steel system still breaks into three parts and uses stovetop heat to force steam and boiling water through the beans. What sets the 9Barista apart from a moka pot is its twin-boiler system: one boiler builds 9 bars of pressure, and a second regulates the temperature to 93 degrees Fahrenheit, producing a true crema-topped espresso extraction. Moka pots are said to use one or two bars of pressure.

The clever design requires fine espresso grounds that you tamp into a basket attached beneath the top reservoir. The three parts are easily screwed together and then placed on your stovetop. Use a hot plate on electric stovetops to help distribute heat.

The 9Barista espresso maker uses a three-piece design that comes together easily. Katherine Peach/CNET

What it’s like to make espresso on the stovetop with the 9Barista

Key takeaways:

The 9Barista machine uses 18 grams of beans and 120 milliliters (4 ounces) of water to produce a 1- to 1.5-ounce shot of espresso.

Aim for 3 to 6 minutes on the stovetop heat, and don’t leave it on longer than 8 minutes to avoid overheating the metal and burning the beans.

A full cleaning-and-drying cycle between shots takes 5 to 6 minutes — faster if you rinse thoroughly under cool water or don’t mind breaking it down while still warm.

The prep-to-pour time on a single shot is no more than 10 to 11 minutes.

Running the body under cold water also helps the release valve screw open more easily.

The hot plate itself changes color with use: gunmetal to copper and (eventually) back to light silver. This is expected, though it may look slightly alarming to the uninitiated.

A hot plate distributes heat when using the 9Barista on an electric stovetop; it changes color as the temperature changes. Katherine Peach/CNET

I followed the directions: 18 grams of espresso beans to 120 milliliters of water per shot. While results will vary depending on your beans, grind and timing, I found the machine produced 1 to 1.5 ounces of espresso. The instructions also recommend 25 to 30 seconds for the full extraction, which is a rather standard goal for most machines. Helpful benchmarks for espresso shots: Anything extracted in under 20 seconds will likely taste thin and sour, while anything over 30 seconds will taste bitter. The goal is to find a combination that brings out the flavors you prefer.

Heat is a new variable with the 9Barista espresso machine. When I first used the brewer, the stovetop temperature seemed like the biggest factor to dial in, especially since “medium-high heat” is, at best, a vague guideline. I recognize that the directions can only offer imprecise tips for heating your device at home, since every stove and burner behaves differently. It’s a frustrating but real variable when your stovetop becomes part of the heating system rather than a self-contained internal system. For many espresso machines, temperature control is a major selling point. Here, you’re building it yourself, burner by burner.

Steaming, boiling water forces brewed coffee into the top chamber. Katherine Peach/CNET

On the first try, I panicked that the grounds sat on the heat too long — and I was impatient — so I cranked the stovetop to 80% power. Even the internet was perplexed when I asked how a shot could pull too quickly (less than 20 seconds) and still taste bitter. Before touching the grind or the quantities, turning the heat down to 65% (6.5 out of 10 was the sweet spot) made a huge difference in flavor. Patience is indeed a virtue. Preheating the heat transfer plate while prepping the grounds also cut down on wait time and reduced how long the fresh grounds sat exposed to heat. Some reviewers online preheat the water chamber while prepping the puck separately. I prefer to turn on the whole unit at once so I can monitor the full process.

Once the plate is preheated, the directions call for 120ml of filtered water. There is a fill line for anyone who doesn’t want to measure. In practice, the taste didn’t vary much if I used a few milliliters less. However, I found that even 125ml of water caused the reservoir to overflow when I turned on the group head. The built-in portafilter beneath the coffee reservoir provides a sturdy, level base for tamping. A metal basket cap with an O-ring keeps the grounds in place when you inevitably flip the portafilter upside down to lock the separate components together.

Once the water starts to gurgle, it’s showtime: Steam expels from a boiler pipe for about 30 seconds before espresso accumulates in the open funnel. My early shots tended to pull shorter — around 20 seconds — and still tasted decent with a good crema.

Disassembling and cleaning the brewer gets easier with practice. The cooldown before depressurization, rinsing and drying the filter basket is what eats the time. Rinsing the group head and steel water chamber under cold water helped cool the components. I also waited to detach the group head and water reservoir, first refilling with cold water and letting it sit while I emptied the used grounds from the portafilter. The metal basket cap stays hot to the touch, so handle it carefully. I kept a thick oven mitt handy to avoid getting burned by steam from the release valve when I wanted to pull a second shot right away. A traditional moka pot makes more coffee in one go, so adjust if you’re used to that system.

The 9Barista disassembles easily for cleaning. Katherine Peach/CNET

Final thoughts on the 9Barista

Across dozens of logged pulls, three variables kept moving at once — heat, grind and pull time — which makes any single result hard to isolate, but some patterns held up across all of my tests.

On the process itself

Heat was the dominant, hardest-to-control variable when I first used the espresso machine. Because the 9Barista relies on the stovetop rather than an internal heating system, results varied wildly by burner. The front burner took 8 to 10 minutes to boil, while the back burner boiled in under 3 minutes, both at the 6.5 heat setting. Same machine, same grind philosophy, very different extractions.

The pressure release valve is a bit hard to grab and pull to depressurize, but the water chamber will unscrew either way if you also have trouble pulling the tiny lever outward. Considering the usual trial and error of grinding and tamping, plus those minor concerns, that’s really it in terms of challenges with the brewer.

The hot plate system might give some people pause if they have an electric stovetop that’s prone to heat marks. This isn’t the machine’s fault. Many of my metal pans leave small traces on the stovetop at high heat, but keep that in mind if you’re a renter who wants to leave no trace. I kept half-expecting something to go wrong while the plate cycled from gunmetal to copper to silver. But this is a natural part of the heating process.

On build and usability

The 9Barista stainless steel design feels substantial in the hand, which is satisfying and suggests it’s built to last. The 9Barista espresso maker also comes with a five-year warranty, lifetime customer support, and replacement parts. While I haven’t tested the ease of a warranty claim, the time frame is well beyond most electric espresso machines. I also appreciate how the design provides a stable surface for level tamping. A traditional espresso machine uses the long portafilter handle to stabilize the basket. The difference is small but appreciated. That said, many people will appreciate this compact machine’s mobility and ease of use.

I appreciated having a level surface on which to tamp the espresso grounds. Katherine Peach/CNET

I also value 9Barista’s use of stainless steel over plastic components. Plastic often makes up water reservoirs and appears in most components of a single-serve pod coffee maker, including the espresso capsules. Plastic might be unavoidable, but anyone looking to reduce further exposure can breathe a bit easier with the 9Barista espresso machine.

Who the 9Barista is for

The 9Barista espresso machine is ideal for a household with one or two coffee drinkers who want a portable, sturdy, largely plastic-free espresso brewer. As a New Yorker, I love that this stovetop brewer takes up little space on the counter or in the cupboard. I keep reaching for the 9Barista more than I expected because it’s simple and delivers satisfying results.

The original 9Barista MK1 is a few hundred dollars cheaper.

As a former skeptic, I find the 9Barista an enticing option for smaller households or anyone who appreciates the ritual of espresso while camping outdoors. The 9Barista would be ideal for my van-life friends who weatherize their campers for winter excursions and want the comforts of home on the road. (This is a weighty machine, however, so the “every ounce counts” folks would never.) You might also see the 9Barista on the counter at your buddy’s place, the one who won’t stop talking about the sound quality of their Audio-Technica record player and bespoke speaker system. In other words, this is an investment piece that speaks of craftsmanship and innovation.

If paying north of $700 for a manual espresso maker just ain’t happening, the first-gen 9Barista MK1 is significantly cheaper at $575.
